docs.title: Volume 15: Kṛṣi and Jīva Vijñāna
docs.text:
Agriculture, Plants and Animals · Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā

Farming, water, soils and crops; the science of trees and plants; livestock, elephants, horses, birds and fishes in Indian texts and practice

docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This is Volume 15 of the series Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā: Kṛṣi and Jīva Vijñāna: Agriculture, Plants and Animals. It is about the knowledge with which the people of the subcontinent fed themselves and lived alongside plants and animals: how fields were prepared, watered and manured, how rain was forecast, which crops were grown and where they came from, how trees and gardens were tended, how plants were named and classified, how cattle, buffaloes, sheep, goats, camels, elephants and horses were bred, kept and treated, and how birds, insects and fishes were observed and used.

Two kinds of evidence run through the book. The first is textual: Vedic hymns, the Arthaśāstra, the Bṛhatsaṃhitā of Varāhamihira, the medical saṃhitās, and a small group of specialised treatises — the Kṛṣi-Parāśara, Surapāla’s Vṛkṣāyurveda, the Upavanavinoda, the Kāśyapīya Kṛṣisūkti, Pālakāpya’s Hastyāyurveda, the horse books ascribed to Śālihotra, Someśvara’s Mānasollāsa — together with Tamil poetry, Persian chronicles and inscriptions. The second is the evidence of practice: archaeobotany and zooarchaeology, surviving irrigation works, farmers’ and herders’ vocabularies, and the observations of travellers and colonial officials. The texts are precious but partial. Most were written by and for elites, many are late, and none of them records the full knowledge of the cultivators, labourers, pastoralists and fisherfolk who did the work; the book tries to keep both in view, and to be honest about caste, labour and gender in Indian agriculture.

This volume combines and corrects two earlier drafts, one centred on the Kṛṣi-Parāśara and agriculture, the other on plant and animal science. In the course of revision the editors removed a great deal: verses that could not be found in the texts they were ascribed to, invented tables and “modern validations”, statistics without a source, and claims that ancient texts anticipated modern science. Where a quotation is given, it is one the editors believe to be genuine; where a traditional claim is reported, it is reported as a claim. Dates are given as the range accepted in current scholarship, with traditional dates labelled as such. Several texts discussed here — among them the Kṛṣi-Parāśara, which is not the work of the Vedic sage, and the Mṛgapakṣiśāstra — are later or less secure than popular accounts suggest, and the book says so.

Nothing in this volume is advice on the treatment of people or animals. Medicinal plants are treated here as plants; their use in medicine is the subject of Volume 13 (Āyurveda), and readers are referred there and to qualified practitioners. References to editions, translations and studies are given in the text and collected in the select bibliography; a glossary and a chronology of the principal texts are provided at the end.

Nikhil Kumar Rajput Ramanujan College, University of Delhi Guru Pūrṇimā, 2026

Zvelebil, Kamil V. 1973. The Smile of Murugan: On Tamil Literature of South India. E. J. Brill.

docs.title: Chapter 1: Introduction: Knowledge of Fields, Plants and Animals
1.1 Scope of the Volume
docs.text:
This volume is about how people in the Indian subcontinent grew crops, tended trees and gardens, kept and treated animals, and thought and wrote about living things. Its title, Kṛṣi and Jīva Vijñāna, joins three Sanskrit words. Kṛṣi, from the root kṛṣ, “to draw (a furrow), to plough”, is the ordinary word for agriculture. Jīva, “living being”, is the widest of the three: in Jain, Buddhist and Brahmanical thought alike it covers animals and, with qualifications discussed below, plants. Vijñāna means knowledge, especially knowledge of a discriminating, systematic kind, and is used here in the broad sense of “science”. Two further words recur throughout the book. Vṛkṣāyurveda, “the science of the life of trees”, is the name of a small group of texts on arboriculture and horticulture; and paśu, “domestic animal”, names the cattle, buffaloes, sheep, goats and other animals on which farming depended.

The Arthaśāstra groups agriculture, animal husbandry and trade together under the name vārttā, “livelihood” or economics, one of the four fields of knowledge a king must master (Arthaśāstra 1.4.1; (Kangle 1965)). That grouping is a useful reminder that in South Asia, as elsewhere before the modern period, agriculture, gardening and animal-keeping were not separate sciences but parts of a single economy of field, pasture, forest and household. For that reason this volume treats them together. It brings into one book material that the series had previously divided between a volume on agriculture and a volume on plant and animal knowledge.

Two kinds of knowledge run through the book. The first is practical knowledge: the skills of cultivators, herders, gardeners, fishers, mahouts, horse-keepers, cattle-healers and many others, learned by doing and passed on by example and word of mouth. Most of it was never written down by the people who held it. The second is textual knowledge: what Sanskrit, Tamil, Kannada, Persian and other authors chose to record about fields, plants and animals, usually for patrons and readers far removed from the plough. The two overlap, but they are not the same, and much of this book is concerned with the relation between them.

The volume does not claim that this knowledge was uniquely profound, that it anticipated modern science, or that it offers ready-made solutions to present-day agricultural problems; the reasons are set out once, in Section 1.5. The Indian record is rich enough to be studied on its own terms: as the experience of farmers and herders in a monsoon environment over nine thousand years, and as a literate tradition that tried, in its own categories, to describe and regulate that experience.

Cross-Reference: Related volumes

Medicinal plants and therapeutics are treated in Volume 13 (Āyurveda); the nakṣatra calendar and astronomy in Volume 12 (Khagola Jyotiṣa); minerals in Volume 14 (Rasāyana); textiles in Volume 17 (Śilpa–Kāru); law, kingship and the Arthaśāstra in Volume 18 (Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra); trade and the monsoon in Volume 19 (Vāṇijya and Samudra); war elephants and cavalry in Volume 20 (Yuddha); and tribal knowledge, sacred groves and water harvesting in Volume 23 (Jana–Jāti).

docs.title: 1.2 The Sources
docs.text: No single source, and no single kind of source, gives an adequate picture. The chapters that follow draw on the following groups.

docs.title: 1.2.1 Vedic literature
docs.text:
The Ṛgveda and Atharvaveda contain hymns addressed to the field, the furrow, the plough, the rain and the plants, as well as charms for the growth of crops and the protection of cattle. The later Vedic prose texts (Brāhmaṇas and Śrautasūtras) describe ritual ploughing and sowing, and the early Upaniṣads use agricultural and food imagery to make philosophical points. These texts were composed by and for a priestly elite and are primarily religious, but they are our earliest written evidence for the crops, implements and animals of northern India (Chapter 2).

The Ṛgveda’s hymn to the plants (10.97), often quoted for its “hundred and seven domains” of the plants, is a healer’s praise of medicinal herbs, not a botanical survey; its opening verse is given and discussed in Chapter 6, and its medical setting in Volume 13.

docs.title: 1.2.2 Dharmaśāstra and Arthaśāstra
docs.text: The legal literature (Dharmaśāstra), above all the Mānava-Dharmaśāstra or Manusmṛti (Olivelle 2005), sets out who may farm, who may own land and cattle, the liabilities of herdsmen for lost animals, the penalties for damage to crops and trees, and rules on food. The Arthaśāstra (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013) is a treatise on statecraft with chapters on crown farms, pastures, cattle, horses, elephants, forests, slaughterhouses and irrigation dues. Both are normative texts: they tell us what their authors thought ought to happen, which is not necessarily what did happen.

docs.title: 1.2.3 Saṃhitās and Purāṇas
docs.text: The Bṛhatsaṃhitā of Varāhamihira (6th century CE) is an encyclopaedia of omens and natural knowledge. Its chapters on forecasting rain (21–28), on finding groundwater (54, dakārgala) and on the care of trees (55, vṛkṣāyurveda) are among the most important early sources for this volume (Bhat 1981). Several Purāṇas, notably the Agni Purāṇa, contain chapters on tree-planting and on the treatment of cattle, horses and elephants. These compilations borrowed freely from one another and from the specialised treatises, and the numbering of their chapters varies between editions.

docs.title: 1.2.4 Āyurveda
docs.text: The medical compendia of Caraka and Suśruta (Sharma 1981; Bhishagratna 1907) classify plants and animals for the purposes of diet and therapy, describe the qualities of grains, pulses, vegetables, fruits, milk and meat, and distinguish types of land and the animals that live on them. They are therefore indispensable for the history of food and of natural history, even though their concern is the human patient (Wujastyk 2003; Meulenbeld 1999).

docs.title: 1.2.5 The specialised treatises
docs.text: A small number of Sanskrit and regional-language works are devoted wholly or largely to agriculture, horticulture or the care of particular animals: the Kṛṣi-Parāśara and the Kāśyapīya Kṛṣisūkti on field agriculture; Surapāla’s Vṛkṣāyurveda, the Upavanavinoda and the relevant parts of the Lokopakāra and Viśvavallabha on trees and gardens; the Mānasollāsa, a royal encyclopaedia with sections on gardens, animals, hunting and fishing; the Hastyāyurveda and Mātaṅgalīlā on elephants; and the Śālihotra and related texts on horses. They are later than often supposed, mostly dating from the late first and the second millennium CE, and their dates and authorship are frequently uncertain. Table 1.2 summarises current scholarly opinion.

docs.title: 1.2.6 Tamil and other regional literatures
docs.text: Classical Tamil poetry organises its themes by landscape (tiṇai), each with its own plants, animals, occupations and seasons, and so preserves a picture of farming, herding, hunting and fishing in early south India. The Tirukkuṟaḷ devotes a chapter to ploughing (Pope 1886). Kannada, Telugu, Marathi, Bengali, Hindi and other literatures contain agricultural lore, and the Kannada Lokopakāra is itself a regional-language treatise. Chapter 2 discusses the Tamil material.

docs.title: 1.2.7 Persian sources
docs.text: From the thirteenth century, Persian chronicles, memoirs and administrative manuals add a new kind of evidence. Bābur’s memoirs describe the plants and animals of Hindustan as a newcomer saw them (Thackston 1996); Jahāngīr’s memoirs record close observations of birds and animals (Thackston 1999); and Abū’l-Faẓl’s Āʾīn-i Akbarī gives crop lists, revenue rates, prices, fruits, and the management of the imperial elephants, horses and cattle (Abū’l-Faẓl 1873). Persian translations and adaptations of Sanskrit veterinary works also circulated. These sources, and the revenue records of the Mughal state analysed by Habib (1999), are treated in Chapters 15 and 18; the Persian agricultural record as a whole is surveyed in Section 18.7.

docs.title: 1.2.8 Inscriptions
docs.text: Stone and copper-plate inscriptions are the best evidence we have for actual, datable arrangements on the ground. Aśoka’s edicts record the planting of trees and medicinal herbs and the digging of wells; Rudradāman’s inscription at Junagadh (150 CE) records the history of the Sudarśana reservoir; thousands of later land grants name fields, crops, trees, tanks, pastures and the rights and dues attached to them. South Indian temple and village inscriptions document the management of tanks and the gifts of cattle and land that supported temples. See Chapters 2, 8 and 18.

docs.title: 1.2.9 Archaeology
docs.text: Archaeobotany (the study of charred seeds, plant impressions and microscopic plant remains) and zooarchaeology (the study of animal bones) have transformed the early history of farming in South Asia since the 1970s. They show farming at Mehrgarh from about 7000 BCE, the local domestication of zebu cattle, several independent centres of plant domestication within the subcontinent, and the arrival of crops from south-west Asia, Africa and East Asia (Fuller 2006, 2011). Archaeology is the only source for the first five millennia of farming, and it remains an essential check on the texts thereafter.

docs.title: 1.2.10 Folk sayings and practice
docs.text: Much agricultural knowledge survives in proverbs and weather sayings attributed to legendary figures — Khanā in Bengal, Ghāgh and Bhaḍḍarī in the Hindi-speaking north — and in the practice of farmers, herders and craftspeople recorded by ethnographers, colonial officials and modern researchers. Two colonial scientists in particular, the agricultural chemist J. A. Voelcker and the economic botanist Albert Howard, recorded Indian practice with respect (Sections 7.5.2 and 10.7). Such sources are invaluable, but the dates of oral sayings are almost always unknown, and observers’ reports reflect their own purposes.

docs.title: 1.3 Dating the Texts
docs.text:
Few Indian texts are dated by their authors, and many survive only in late manuscripts. Popular literature often assigns very early dates to agricultural and veterinary works on the strength of their attribution to ancient sages. This volume follows current academic opinion and hedges where the evidence is weak. Tables 1.1 and 1.2 give the dates used throughout.

Table 1.1. General sources used in this volume, with approximate dates. The pattern that emerges is clear. The Vedic and early historic sources speak of agriculture and animals in passing, within religious, legal or political works. The specialised agricultural and veterinary treatises belong overwhelmingly to the period after about 900 CE. This matters, because a practice described in a twelfth-century text cannot be assumed to have existed a thousand years earlier simply because the text is ascribed to an ancient sage.

docs.title: 1.4 Reading Śāstra and Practice
docs.text:
The Sanskrit word śāstra means both a body of systematic knowledge and an authoritative text that prescribes. Śāstric writing on agriculture and animals has several features that the reader should keep in mind.

First, it is prescriptive. A text that tells the farmer to plough when the moon is in a particular nakṣatra, or a king to establish a superintendent of crown lands, records an ideal. Whether farmers or kings followed the prescription must be established from other evidence, and often cannot be.

Second, it is written from above. With few exceptions, the authors were literate men from priestly, scribal or courtly backgrounds, writing for patrons who owned land and animals rather than for those who worked them. Some authors clearly had first-hand experience; others compiled from earlier works. Verses on rain forecasting, for example, circulate between the Bṛhatsaṃhitā, the Kṛṣi-Parāśara, the Purāṇas and later almanacs, so that agreement between texts may mean borrowing rather than independent observation.

Third, it is selective. The texts say much about rice, barley and wheat, and about cattle, horses and elephants, which mattered to their patrons; they say little about the millets and pulses that fed most of the rural population in dry regions, about shifting cultivation, or about the knowledge of pastoral and forest communities. Archaeology, inscriptions, travellers’ accounts and ethnography are needed to fill these gaps.

Fourth, it mixes what we would call empirical, ritual and astrological knowledge. Instructions on manuring, seed storage or the treatment of a lame horse stand beside rules on auspicious days and omens. It is anachronistic to separate the “scientific” parts and discard the rest; it is equally misleading to present the whole as an early form of modern science. This volume therefore describes what the texts say, in their own terms, and does not claim that they “anticipated” modern discoveries. Where a practice described in a text has been tested by modern research, the research is cited by name; where it has not, nothing is claimed.

Finally, modern editions and translations differ greatly in reliability, a point taken up in the next section.

docs.title: 1.5 Popular Claims and This Volume
docs.text:
Much that is written about Indian agriculture and biology in popular books, websites and some textbooks cannot be traced to the sources it cites. Because the same claims recur from topic to topic, they are described here once, and the later chapters do not argue with them again. They fall into four kinds.

The first is the invented or misattributed text: verses with chapter-and-verse numbers that are not in any edition of the work named, and tables built from them. Examples include classifications of twelve soils, earthworm tests and pesticide recipes credited to the Kṛṣi-Parāśara; tables of grafting methods, companion plantings, water requirements and special prescriptions for medicinal trees credited to Surapāla and the other vṛkṣāyurveda texts; and tables of well depths in modern units credited to Varāhamihira. The second is the late or doubtful text presented as ancient, such as the Vṛkṣāyurveda ascribed to Parāśara (Section 4.1) or the Mṛgapakṣiśāstra (Section 17.3). The third is the “modern validation”: yield increases, efficiency percentages and trials reported without a source that can be checked. The fourth is the claim of priority or descent, that a text anticipated a modern discovery, or that a modern preparation such as jīvāmṛta or a “homa” ritual descends from a classical one (Chapter 20).

This volume does not repeat these claims or rebut them case by case. The later chapters say plainly what each text contains, on the authority of the editions named, and add a correction only where a specific misreading would otherwise mislead. A reader who meets a striking claim elsewhere should ask for the edition and verse number and check them. The practice of the present volume is to cite only verses that can be checked against an edition, and otherwise to paraphrase with the locus.

docs.title: 1.6 Conceptual Frameworks
docs.text: Several ideas recur across the sources and are worth introducing here.

docs.title: 1.6.1 The five elements
docs.text: Brahmanical, Buddhist and Jain thought all analysed the material world into elements (bhūta). The classical Sanskrit scheme has five: earth (pṛthivī), water (āp, jala), fire (tejas, agni), wind (vāyu) and space (ākāśa). The Taittirīya Upaniṣad (2.1) gives a famous cosmogony in which space, wind, fire, water and earth arise in turn, then plants from earth, food from plants, and the person from food (Olivelle 1998). Āyurveda uses the elements, and the three doṣas derived from them, to explain the qualities of foods and drugs; the vṛkṣāyurveda texts extend the same vocabulary to trees, describing some of their disorders as disturbances of vāta, pitta and kapha (Chapter 4). These frameworks organised observation; they were not measurements.

docs.title: 1.6.2 Plants as living beings
docs.text:
Whether plants are living, sentient beings was a long-standing question. The Manusmṛti (1.49) says that plants, enveloped by the darkness that results from past actions, are “inwardly conscious” (antaḥsaṃjña) and experience pleasure and pain (Olivelle 2005). Jain thought is the most explicit: plants are among the beings with a single sense, touch, along with earth-, water-, fire- and air-bodies, and harming them is a form of violence (hiṃsā) (Tatia 1994). Buddhist monastic rules forbid monks to destroy plant life, though Buddhist doctrine generally did not count plants as sentient in the full sense. These views had practical consequences: they shaped attitudes to ploughing, to the felling of trees and to the occupations Jains and some others considered acceptable.

J. C. Bose’s experiments on the electrical responses of plants, sometimes hailed as a vindication of these ideas, belong to plant physiology and neither confirm nor refute a doctrine about consciousness (Section 4.2.3).

docs.title: 1.6.3 Dry land and wet land
docs.text: Āyurvedic texts classify country (deśa) into three kinds: jāṅgala, dry, open land with sparse trees and thorny scrub; ānūpa, wet, marshy land with abundant water and vegetation; and sādhāraṇa, land of a middle character. Each has its characteristic animals, plants and diseases, and the meat of dry-land animals is generally preferred in diet. Francis Zimmermann (1987) showed how this scheme structures Āyurvedic thinking about food and health, and pointed out that the English “jungle”, borrowed from jāṅgala, has come to mean almost the opposite of the original. The Sanskrit word names dry, open savanna; the English word names dense, wet forest. The same distinction between dry and wet land appears in the Arthaśāstra’s rainfall norms (Chapter 2) and in later soil classifications (Chapter 7).

docs.title: 1.6.4 Seasons and the calendar
docs.text: The texts divide the year into six seasons (ṛtu) of two months each and time agricultural operations by the lunar months and the nakṣatras, the twenty-seven or twenty-eight lunar mansions. Farmers in practice relied as much on the onset and behaviour of the monsoon as on the almanac. The familiar terms kharīf (monsoon crop), rabī (winter crop) and zāid (the minor summer crop) are Arabic in origin and entered Indian usage through the revenue administration of the Sultanate and Mughal periods; they are not classical Sanskrit categories. The crop calendar is set out in Section 9.12 (Figure 9.1), the lunar calendar of the texts in Chapter 3, and its astronomy in Volume 12.

docs.title: 1.7 Transmission and Modern Editing
docs.text:
Agricultural and veterinary skills were transmitted mainly within households, castes and occupational communities, by apprenticeship and oral instruction. Texts were transmitted in manuscripts on palm leaf, birch bark and paper. Many of the treatises discussed in this volume survive in only a handful of manuscripts, sometimes in a single one, and copyists added, omitted and altered material. Critical editions are few.

Modern study of the agricultural texts began largely in Bengal. Girija Prasanna Majumdar published a translation of the Upavanavinoda in 1935 (Majumdar 1935) and, with Sures Chandra Banerji, an edition and translation of the Kṛṣi-Parāśara in the Bibliotheca Indica in 1960 (Majumdar and Banerji 1960). From the 1990s the Asian Agri-History Foundation in Secunderabad, associated above all with the plant pathologist Y. L. Nene, published a series of translations in its Agri-History Bulletin series, including Nalini Sadhale’s versions of Surapāla’s Vṛkṣāyurveda (Sadhale 1996) and the Kṛṣi-Parāśara (Sadhale 1999) and S. M. Ayachit’s Kāśyapīya Kṛṣisūkti (Ayachit 2002). M. S. Randhawa’s four-volume History of Agriculture in India (Randhawa 1980) remains a useful survey, though it should be used with caution on dates; the multi-author History of Agriculture in India (up to c. 1200 AD) edited by Lallanji Gopal and V. C. Srivastava (Gopal and Srivastava 2008) goes deeper into the Sanskrit and epigraphic sources. These works made the texts accessible; they should be read alongside the original Sanskrit wherever possible, since translators sometimes interpret technical terms in the light of modern agronomy.

European study of Indian plants began with the trading companies. The Hortus Malabaricus (Amsterdam, 1678–1693), compiled for the Dutch governor of Malabar, Hendrik van Rheede, rested on the knowledge of the Ezhava physician Itty Achuden and Konkani brahmin scholars and was later used by Linnaeus (Section 6.9; (Manilal 1980)). Colonial botanical gardens, surveys and gazetteers followed. George Watt’s Dictionary of the Economic Products of India (Watt 1889) and Kirtikar and Basu’s Indian Medicinal Plants (Kirtikar and Basu 1935) compiled vernacular names and uses on a vast scale. This colonial science depended heavily on Indian informants whose contributions were often unacknowledged, and it served the revenue and commercial purposes of the state (Arnold 2000). It is nevertheless the foundation of much later ethnobotany, and it is discussed in Chapters 6, 12 and 18.

docs.title: 1.8 Who Did the Work
docs.text:
Any honest account of Indian agriculture must ask who ploughed, sowed, weeded, harvested, herded and skinned, and who owned the land and the animals. The answers are uncomfortable. The Brahmanical texts assign agriculture, cattle-keeping and trade to the vaiśya and service to the śūdra, but they also discourage the higher varṇas from ploughing themselves (Manusmṛti 10.83–84; Chapter 2). In practice, from at least the first millennium CE, the actual cultivators were very often śūdra peasants, dependent tenants and labourers, while ownership and the rights to the produce lay with landholding lineages, temples, brahmin grantees and the state (Sharma 1980).

Below the cultivating castes stood communities later called untouchable and today Dalit, who in many regions supplied the agricultural labour force, often in hereditary bondage, and who also did the work of removing dead cattle, flaying and tanning on which the leather buckets of irrigation wells and the harnesses of ploughing depended (Ambedkar 1948; Prakash 1990). Pastoral communities — Ahīr, Gujar, Rabārī, Kuruba, Dhangar, Gaddi, Toda and many others — managed the herds and much of the knowledge of breeding and animal health. Fishing, the catching and training of elephants, the keeping of horses and the gathering of forest produce were each the work of particular communities. Women did much of the transplanting, weeding, harvesting, processing of grain, dairying and seed selection, while being largely excluded from ownership of land (Agarwal 1994).

The knowledge of these people is mostly absent from the texts discussed in this volume, which were written by and for those who did not do the work. The volume tries to keep them in view, and Chapter 18 discusses the history of land, caste and labour from the early centuries CE to 1950 in detail; the place of hides, leather and cattle in the caste order is discussed in Chapter 13.

docs.title: 1.9 Conventions
docs.text:
Sanskrit, Pali and Prakrit words are given in the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration (IAST). A short guide to pronunciation: a line over a vowel (ā, ī, ū) marks a long vowel, and e and o are always long; c is pronounced as in English “church”; ś and ṣ are both close to English “sh”; consonants with a dot below (ṭ, ḍ, ṇ) are retroflex, made with the tongue curled back; h after a consonant is aspirated, so that th is as in “hothouse”, not “thin”; ṛ is a vowel, now usually pronounced ri; ṃ nasalises the preceding vowel; and ḥ is a light breath after a vowel. Tamil follows the transliteration of the Tamil Lexicon of the University of Madras, which adds ḻ (a retroflex approximant, as in Uḻavu), ṟ (a trilled r) and ṉ (an alveolar n) and distinguishes short e and o from long ē and ō. Persian and Arabic words are transliterated in a simplified form of the system used by the historians cited (for example Āʾīn-i Akbarī, zamīndār), with ʿ for the Arabic letter ʿayn and ʾ for the glottal stop. Words from Hindi and the other modern languages are given in their modern form, with long vowels marked where this helps (khejrī, bājrā), and without the final a that Hindi does not pronounce. Personal names of modern people, place names and the names of communities are given in their usual English spelling (Bishnoi, Raika, Kannauj) unless a transliterated form is needed to show a Sanskrit or Tamil word. Dates follow the tables above.

Primary texts are cited by the divisions of the edition named: the Ṛgveda and Atharvaveda by book, hymn and verse; the Mahābhārata by the book, chapter and verse of the Poona critical edition; the Arthaśāstra by the book, chapter and sentence of Kangle’s edition; the Bṛhatsaṃhitā by the chapter numbers of Bhat’s translation; and the Sutta Nipāta by sutta number with the verse number of the Pali Text Society edition (so “Sn 1.4, v. 77”). Quotations from primary texts are given in the original only when both the wording and the reference can be verified; otherwise the content is paraphrased and attributed. Where chapters discuss poisons, remedies for humans or animals, or the consumption of cattle products, they include a safety note: classical prescriptions are described as historical evidence, not as advice, and no doses or usable recipes are given.

docs.title: 1.10 Plan of the Volume
docs.text:
The volume has twenty chapters. The first two are introductory and historical; Chapters 3 to 12 deal with agriculture and plants; Chapters 13 to 17 with animals; and the last three with agrarian history, the rise of agricultural science, and the present. Readers who want the social frame before the treatises may read Sections 18.2 and 18.3 of Chapter 18 after Chapter 2.

  1. Introduction (Chapter 1): scope, sources, dating and frameworks.

  2. From Mehrgarh to the early historic period (Chapter 2): archaeobotany and the domestication of plants and animals; Harappan and Neolithic farming; agriculture in Vedic, Buddhist, Jain, Mauryan and early Tamil sources.

  3. The Kṛṣi-Parāśara and rain forecasting (Chapter 3): the Kṛṣi-Parāśara, the Bṛhatsaṃhitā’s rain chapters, folk forecasting, and the other agricultural treatises.

  4. The vṛkṣāyurveda tradition (Chapter 4): the texts on arboriculture and horticulture, from the Bṛhatsaṃhitā to the Upavanavinoda and the Viśvavallabha.

  5. Gardens, flowers and aromatics (Chapter 5): the flowers of worship and poetry, garland-makers and temple gardens, perfumery and the attar distillers, and betel.

  6. Classifying plants (Chapter 6): Vedic, legal, medical, lexical, Jain and Buddhist schemes; folk taxonomies; comparison with Linnaean botany.

  7. Soil, tillage and implements (Chapter 7): concepts and classifications of soil, manuring and conservation, and the plough and other tools of field work.

  8. Water and irrigation (Chapter 8): tanks, anicuts, canals, wells and stepwells, lifting devices, and the social management of water.

  9. Crops and seeds (Chapter 9): the major crops, introduced crops, seasons, rotation and mixed cropping, seed saving and landraces.

  10. Agroecology (Chapter 10): pest management, crop–livestock integration, agroforestry, home gardens, shifting cultivation and the farming systems of the Himalaya and the North-East, and the limits of “sustainability” claims.

  11. Forests and sacred groves (Chapter 11): forests in texts and inscriptions, sacred groves and trees, the Bishnoi and Chipko, and colonial forestry.

  12. Medicinal and useful plants (Chapter 12): identification, cultivation, trade and conservation of plants used in medicine.

  13. Livestock and veterinary knowledge (Chapter 13): domestication, cattle and other livestock, pastoralists, breeds, ethnoveterinary knowledge, the history of cow veneration, and hides and caste.

  14. Dairy and food processing (Chapter 14): milk products, fermentation, grain processing, oil pressing, sugar and preservation.

  15. Elephants and horses (Chapter 15): the Hastyāyurveda, the Mātaṅgalīlā, the capture and keeping of elephants, the Śālihotra tradition and the horse trade.

  16. Wild animals (Chapter 16): wild mammals in texts and art, hunting and its critics, royal and colonial hunting, the history of wildlife protection, and conflict between wildlife and farming.

  17. Birds, insects and aquatic life (Chapter 17): birds in literature and practice, silk, lac and bees, fish and fisheries, pearls and fishing communities.

  18. Agrarian society and change, from the early centuries CE to 1950 (Chapter 18): land grants, Indo-Islamic agriculture and gardens, the Mughal agrarian system and the Persian agricultural record, caste and labour, and colonial agrarian change.

  19. Agricultural science and the state, 1870–1970 (Chapter 19): famine commissions and agricultural departments, Pusa and the research institutes, crop breeding, crop surveys, the Royal Commission on Agriculture, and the coming of the high-yielding varieties.

  20. The modern period (Chapter 20): the Green Revolution and its critics, natural-farming movements, genetically modified crops, the documentation and protection of traditional knowledge, biodiversity law and conservation.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This volume treats agriculture, plants and animals together because they formed a single economy in which field, pasture, forest and household depended on one another. Its sources are diverse: Vedic hymns, legal and political treatises, medical compendia, the Bṛhatsaṃhitā, a small number of specialised agricultural, horticultural and veterinary treatises that mostly date from after 900 CE, Tamil poetry, Persian memoirs and records, inscriptions, archaeology, and the sayings and practices of farmers and herders. The texts are prescriptive, written from above and selective, and they should be read as evidence of what their authors thought and recommended, not as proof of early modern science. The people who did most of the work — śūdra and Dalit cultivators and labourers, pastoralists, fishers and women — are largely absent from them, and the chapters that follow try to keep both the texts and the workers in view.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Fuller (2006) is the best synthesis of the archaeological evidence for early agriculture. Gopal and Srivastava (2008) is the fullest critical survey of the Sanskrit, Pali and epigraphic evidence for agriculture up to about 1200 CE, and Randhawa (1980) offers a broad, well-illustrated survey of agricultural history. Zimmermann (1987) is a classic study of ecological ideas in Āyurveda. Sadhale (1996) gives an accessible translation of a major horticultural text. Trautmann (2015) shows how a single animal can illuminate Indian political and environmental history, and Ludden (1999) provides the long-term agrarian context.

docs.title: Chapter 2: From Mehrgarh to the Early Historic Period: Agriculture in Early India
docs.text: Farming in South Asia is some nine thousand years old. For more than five thousand of those years our only evidence is archaeological: seeds, bones, buildings and tools. Texts begin with the Ṛgveda in the second millennium BCE, and for many centuries afterwards they speak of agriculture only in passing, in hymns, ritual manuals, philosophical dialogues, legal rules and poetry. This chapter follows both kinds of evidence from the first farming villages to the early centuries CE, when land grants, the Arthaśāstra and the Tamil anthologies give a fuller picture. The later agrarian history of the subcontinent is taken up in Chapter 18.

docs.title: 2.1 The Evidence of Archaeology
docs.text:
Two specialised fields supply most of what we know about early farming. Archaeobotany studies plant remains recovered from excavations: seeds and grains preserved by charring, impressions of grain and chaff in pottery and mud-brick, and microscopic remains such as phytoliths and starch grains. Since the 1970s the systematic recovery of charred remains by flotation (washing soil samples in water so that light plant material floats free) has greatly increased the quantity and reliability of the data. Zooarchaeology studies animal bones, identifying species, estimating the age and sex of slaughtered animals, and measuring changes in size and shape that may indicate domestication.

Both fields depend on careful identification and on secure dating, usually by radiocarbon. Many older reports, including some still widely quoted, rest on identifications that have since been questioned or on dates obtained from material not directly associated with the plants concerned. The syntheses by Dorian Fuller (Fuller 2006, 2011) sift this evidence critically, and this chapter relies on them for the overall picture. For the Indus civilisation the standard accounts are those of Allchin and Allchin (1982), Kenoyer (1998) and Possehl (2002).

docs.title: 2.2 Mehrgarh and the First Farmers of the North-West
docs.text:
Mehrgarh lies on the Kachi plain at the foot of the Bolan Pass in Balochistan, Pakistan, where the hills of the Iranian plateau meet the Indus plain. Excavated by a French mission under Jean-François Jarrige from 1974, it is the best-documented early farming site in South Asia. Its earliest levels, without pottery, begin around 7000 BCE (Allchin and Allchin 1982; Possehl 2002).

The people of early Mehrgarh lived in houses of mud brick, some of them divided into small compartments that the excavators interpreted as storerooms. Their plant remains are dominated by barley, with smaller amounts of wheat. Whether these crops were brought from south-west Asia, where wheat and barley were first domesticated, or whether barley at least was domesticated locally from the wild barley that grows in the region, is still debated; current opinion favours the introduction of most of the cereal crops from the west, adapted to local conditions (Fuller 2006).

The animal bones tell a clearer story. Richard Meadow’s analysis showed that in the earliest levels hunted animals — gazelle, deer, wild cattle, wild sheep and goats, wild pig, the onager — are well represented alongside goats, which may already have been domestic. Over the following millennia the proportion of cattle, sheep and goats rises until they dominate the assemblage, and the cattle, sheep and goats all become smaller in size, a change Meadow interpreted as evidence for local domestication (Meadow 1996). In the case of cattle, the animals concerned are the humped zebu (Bos indicus), which was domesticated in this region independently of the humpless taurine cattle of south-west Asia. Zebu cattle were to become the foundation of South Asian agriculture, as draught animals, as sources of milk and dung, and as a measure of wealth (Chapter 13).

Mehrgarh has also yielded some of the earliest evidence for cotton anywhere. Moulherat et al. (2002) identified mineralised cotton fibres preserved inside a copper bead from a burial dated to around the sixth to fifth millennium BCE. Whether the plant was cultivated or gathered from the wild cannot be determined from fibres alone, but the find shows that cotton was being processed into thread at a very early date. The later history of cotton textiles is treated in Volume 17.

docs.title: 2.3 Many Centres of Domestication
docs.text:
Older accounts, following the botanist N. I. Vavilov, treated India as one of a small number of “centres of origin” of cultivated plants (Vavilov 1951). Archaeobotany has replaced this with a more complex picture. Fuller has argued that the subcontinent contained several distinct regions in which local wild plants were independently taken into cultivation, in addition to receiving crops from south-west Asia, Africa and East Asia (Fuller 2006, 2011). Among the regions he identifies are:

  • the southern Deccan, where mung bean (Vigna radiata), horse gram (Macrotyloma uniflorum) and small millets such as browntop millet (Urochloa ramosa, syn. Brachiaria ramosa) and bristly foxtail (Setaria verticillata) were cultivated by Neolithic communities;

  • Gujarat and Saurashtra, where native small millets, probably including little millet (Panicum sumatrense), formed the basis of early farming;

  • the Ganga plain, where a form of rice was cultivated and eventually domesticated (Section 2.5);

  • the greater Indus region, which contributed sesame (Sesamum indicum), domesticated from a wild relative native to India, and probably the tree cotton Gossypium arboreum, as well as zebu cattle and, probably, the water buffalo.

The evidence is uneven and some identifications and dates remain disputed, but the general conclusion — that South Asian agriculture was built from several local beginnings combined with crops that arrived from outside — is now widely accepted. Table 2.1 summarises the main groups of early crops, and Figure 2.1 shows the sites named in this chapter.

Figure 2.1. Some early farming sites named in this chapter: Mehrgarh; the Harappan sites of Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Kalibangan, Banawali, Rakhigarhi, Dholavira and Rojdi; the Ganga-plain rice sites of Lahuradewa, Senuwar and Chirand; the Deccan villages of Inamgaon and Daimabad; and the ash-mound site of Kupgal in the southern Deccan. Positions are plotted by latitude and longitude, and open circles mark approximate positions; the coastline is simplified, islands other than Sri Lanka are omitted, and no rivers or political boundaries are shown. The regions of domestication discussed in the text are not drawn, because their limits are not precisely known. docs.title: 2.4 Harappan Agriculture
docs.text: The Indus or Harappan civilisation developed out of the farming cultures of the north-west. Its Early Harappan phase begins around 3300 BCE and its Mature, urban phase lasts from about 2600 to 1900 BCE. At its height it extended from Balochistan and the Indus valley to Gujarat, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, with cities such as Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Ganweriwala, Rakhigarhi and Dholavira and hundreds of smaller settlements (Kenoyer 1998; Possehl 2002). The cities depended on the surplus of a large farming and herding population.

docs.title: 2.4.1 Crops and seasons
docs.text:
The Harappan crop repertoire combined winter crops of south-west Asian origin — wheat, barley, lentil, pea, chickpea, grass pea and linseed — with summer crops sown with the monsoon: small millets, native pulses such as mung and urd, sesame, cotton and, in some areas, rice. Fruits such as the jujube (ber) were collected or grown. The combination of a winter and a summer crop season, which remains characteristic of much of South Asian agriculture, is thus visible in the Harappan period, though its importance varied from region to region.

Steven Weber’s study of the plant remains from Rojdi in Saurashtra showed an agriculture based mainly on summer-grown small millets rather than on wheat and barley, and a crop mix that changed over the life of the settlement (Weber 1991). In a later synthesis he argued that Harappan farming was regionally diverse: winter cereals predominated in the Punjab and the Indus valley, summer millets in Gujarat, and the combination of the two seasons allowed some communities to spread risk and to increase production (Weber 1999). There was no single “Harappan agriculture”, but a set of regional systems adapted to differences in rainfall, river regime and soil.

docs.title: 2.4.2 Fields, ploughs and water
docs.text:
At Kalibangan in northern Rajasthan, excavators found beneath later deposits a field surface of the Early Harappan period (first half of the third millennium BCE) bearing criss-cross plough furrows. The furrows ran in two directions, closely spaced one way and widely spaced the other, and the excavator B. B. Lal compared this pattern with the local practice, still observed in the twentieth century, of sowing two different crops in the same field in rows at right angles (Allchin and Allchin 1982). It remains one of the earliest excavated ploughed fields anywhere. A terracotta model of a plough from Banawali in Haryana confirms the use of the ard, a simple plough that scratches rather than turns the soil. Bullock carts are known from numerous terracotta models, and zebu oxen were evidently the draught animals.

There is no clear evidence for large-scale canal irrigation in the Mature Harappan heartland. Agriculture seems to have relied on rainfall, on the annual floods of the Indus and its tributaries, which deposited moisture and silt on the fields for winter sowing, and on wells: Mohenjo-daro alone had a very large number of brick-lined wells. At Dholavira, in the arid Rann of Kachchh, large rock-cut reservoirs stored water for the city. The history of water management is followed in Chapter 8.

docs.title: 2.4.3 Storage
docs.text: Large buildings at Mohenjo-daro and Harappa were identified by Mortimer Wheeler as state “granaries”. Later excavators have questioned this: no grain was found in them, and they may have been halls or warehouses of other kinds (Kenoyer 1998). Storage jars, bins and sealings show that goods, including grain, were stored and controlled, but the scale and organisation of grain storage remain uncertain.

docs.title: 2.4.4 Animals
docs.text:
Animal bones from Harappan sites are dominated by cattle, most of them zebu, followed by sheep and goats; water buffalo and pigs are also present, together with wild animals and large quantities of fish (Meadow 1996; Possehl 2002). The elephant, rhinoceros, tiger and buffalo appear on seals; their depiction does not imply domestication. No securely identified domestic horse has been found in a Mature Harappan context; horses and spoked-wheel chariots become prominent only with the Ṛgveda (Chapter 15).

Harappan craftspeople also used animal products in sophisticated ways. Analysis of fibres from Harappa and Chanhu-daro has shown that silk from wild silk moths was being used in the third millennium BCE (Good et al. 2009); silk and other insect products are discussed in Chapter 17.

docs.title: 2.4.5 African millets and the late Harappan period
docs.text: From about 2000 BCE, crops of African origin — sorghum, pearl millet and finger millet among the cereals, hyacinth bean and cowpea among the pulses — appear in Gujarat, the Indus region and peninsular India, probably having crossed the Arabian Sea through contacts with Arabia and East Africa (Fuller 2006). Some early identifications, especially of finger millet, have been questioned, and the routes and dates are still being refined. These drought-tolerant summer crops became important in the late and post-urban phases of the Harappan tradition, when settlement shifted eastwards and southwards and, in several regions, summer cropping increased. Sorghum (jowar), pearl millet (bajra) and finger millet (ragi) were to become staples of the drier parts of India (Chapter 9).

docs.title: 2.5 Rice and the Ganga Plain
docs.text:
Rice has a complicated history in South Asia. Wild rices grow widely in the subcontinent, and their grains were gathered long before domestication. Rice remains reported from the middle Ganga plain, at sites such as Lahuradewa in Uttar Pradesh, have been dated by their excavators as early as the seventh millennium BCE. These claims are debated: the rice may have been wild or gathered from wild stands, and the association between the dated material and the rice is not always secure. More generally accepted evidence for domesticated rice in the Ganga plain, at sites such as Senuwar and Chirand in Bihar, belongs to the third and second millennia BCE (Fuller 2006, 2011).

One influential model, developed by Fuller, holds that people in the Ganga plain cultivated a local wild rice for a long period without its becoming fully domesticated, and that domesticated japonica rice, arriving from East Asia in the late third or early second millennium BCE, hybridised with it to produce the domesticated indica rices of South Asia (Fuller 2011). Other scholars favour a more independent domestication in India. Rice also appears at a number of Harappan sites, particularly in the eastern Harappan region, but how much of it was cultivated or domesticated is debated. Whatever the details, by the first millennium BCE rice was the principal crop of the middle and lower Ganga plain and of the eastern and southern river deltas, and it is the crop around which the Kṛṣi-Parāśara and the Kāśyapīya Kṛṣisūkti were later written (Chapter 3).

docs.title: 2.6 Neolithic South India and the Deccan
docs.text:
In the southern Deccan — northern Karnataka and western Andhra Pradesh — a Neolithic culture flourished from about 3000 BCE. Its most striking monuments are the ash-mounds found at sites such as Utnur, Kupgal and Budihal: great accumulations of burnt cattle dung, sometimes vitrified, which mark places where cattle were penned and the dung periodically burnt. F. R. Allchin interpreted them as the cattle stations of a pastoral society, and the large proportion of cattle bones at southern Neolithic sites confirms the central place of herding (Allchin and Allchin 1982). The burning of dung heaps may have had ritual as well as practical purposes; their exact function is still discussed.

These cattle-keepers were also cultivators. Archaeobotanical work at southern Neolithic sites has shown that their staples were native crops: the pulses mung bean and horse gram, and small millets such as browntop millet and bristly foxtail. Wheat and barley from the north and, later, African millets and pulses were added to this base (Fuller 2006). The pairing of millets and pulses on rain-fed land, with cattle supplying traction and dung, is a pattern that persisted in the peninsula for millennia.

Further north in the Deccan, Chalcolithic farming villages of the second millennium BCE, such as Inamgaon and Daimabad in Maharashtra, grew barley, wheat, lentils, other pulses and millets, and kept cattle, sheep, goats and pigs. At Inamgaon the excavators reported an embankment and channel that they interpreted as a work for diverting flood water to fields. Such villages show that farming had spread across most of the subcontinent long before the earliest written references to it.

docs.title: 2.7.1 The Ṛgveda
docs.text:
The Ṛgveda (core c. 1500–1200 BCE) was composed in the north-west, in the land of the Indus and its tributaries, by communities for whom cattle were the chief form of wealth. Cows are prayed for, fought over and praised; a word for battle, gaviṣṭi, means literally “desire for cows”. But the hymns also know agriculture. They speak of the field (kṣetra) and the fertile field (urvarā), of grain (yava, usually understood as barley but sometimes grain in general), of the plough (lāṅgala, sīra), the ploughshare (phāla), the furrow (sītā), the ploughman (kīnāśa) and the sickle (sṛṇi), and of oxen yoked to the plough (Jamison and Brereton 2014).

The fullest agricultural hymn is Ṛgveda 4.57, addressed to the Lord of the Field (kṣetrasya pati), to the pair Śuna and Sīra, and to the Furrow (Sītā). It asks for the success of ploughing: that the ploughshares cut the earth auspiciously (śunam), that the ploughmen go with their draught animals, that the furrow be turned towards the worshippers and give them good fortune, and that Parjanya, the rain god, water it. The furrow personified as a goddess is the background to the later story, told in the Rāmāyaṇa, that Sītā was found by King Janaka in a furrow as he ploughed ground for a sacrifice. A late hymn (Ṛgveda 10.101) uses the images of yoking the ploughs, sowing seed in the prepared furrow and drawing water from a well to describe the work of the priests.

A well-known verse comes from an unexpected source, the lament of a ruined gambler:

Ṛgveda 10.34.13

akṣair mā dīvyaḥ kṛṣim it kṛṣasva Do not play with dice: plough your field.

The verse goes on to bid the gambler take pleasure in the wealth that farming brings, for there are his cows and there his wife (Jamison and Brereton 2014). Agriculture here stands for a settled, respectable livelihood.

docs.title: 2.7.2 The Atharvaveda
docs.text:
The Atharvaveda contains many charms concerned with everyday life, including the success of ploughing (3.17 is a ploughing hymn), the growth of grain, protection against pests that damage crops, rain, and the health and increase of cattle (Whitney 1905). Its twelfth book opens with the long hymn to the Earth (Pṛthivīsūkta, 12.1), which praises the earth as the ground on which food and the ploughed fields came into being, on which plants and trees grow, and which supports all creatures. One verse asks that whatever is dug from her may quickly grow again, and that the digger may not wound her vital parts. The best-known line declares:

Atharvaveda 12.1.12

mātā bhūmiḥ putro ahaṃ pṛthivyāḥ The Earth is my mother; I am the son of the Earth.

The same verse names Parjanya, the rain-cloud, as father. The hymn is a religious and poetic text, not an agricultural manual; but it shows that the dependence of human life on soil and rain was a theme of reflection at an early date. Modern readings of it as an environmental ethic are a later interpretation, and should be presented as such.

docs.title: 2.7.3 The later Vedic period
docs.text:
Between about 1200 and 500 BCE the centre of Vedic culture moved east into the Ganga–Yamuna doab and the middle Ganga plain, and agriculture became much more prominent in the texts. Rice (vrīhi) now appears alongside barley, together with wheat (godhūma), pulses, sesame, millets and sugarcane (ikṣu), while wild grains such as nīvāra (wild rice) retained a place in ritual. A passage of the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (5.1.7) observes that the crop ripens twice a year (Macdonell and Keith 1912), reflecting the two cropping seasons already seen in the archaeological record. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (6.3.13) lists ten “village” (grāmya) grains used in a ritual preparation — rice, barley, sesame, beans, two small millets, wheat, lentils and two pulses of uncertain identity — in contrast to the wild (āraṇya) plants, a distinction that runs through Vedic ritual classifications of both plants and animals; the verse is quoted in Chapter 9 (Olivelle 1998).

The Brāhmaṇas describe ritual ploughing as part of the construction of the great fire altar: the site is ploughed with a team of oxen and sown with seeds of many kinds. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa summarises agricultural work as ploughing, sowing, reaping and threshing. Some texts speak of ritual plough teams of six, eight, twelve or even twenty-four oxen; whether such large teams were ever used in ordinary farming is doubtful.

The spread of agriculture in the Ganga plain coincided with the spread of iron, which appears in northern India from around the end of the second millennium BCE. D. D. Kosambi argued that iron axes and ploughshares made possible the clearing of the plain’s forests and the expansion of plough agriculture that underlay the growth of states and cities in the mid-first millennium BCE (Kosambi 1956). Later scholars have qualified this view: iron tools are scarce in early levels, forests could be cleared with fire, and iron ploughshares become common only later. The relation between iron, agriculture and social change remains a subject of debate (Singh 2008).

docs.title: 2.8 Food in the Upaniṣads
docs.text:
The early Upaniṣads (c. 7th–5th century BCE) often use food (anna) as a philosophical theme. In the third section of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, Bhṛgu, son of Varuṇa, asks his father to teach him brahman. Told to practise austerity and discover it himself, he first concludes:

Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.2

annaṃ brahmeti vyajānāt He perceived that brahman is food.

The text continues that from food beings are born, by food they live, and into food they pass at death. It is important to read this in context. Food is the first and lowest stage of Bhṛgu’s inquiry: he returns to his father and is sent back to practise austerity again, and successively identifies brahman with breath, mind, perception and finally bliss (ānanda) (Olivelle 1998). The passage is a teaching about levels of reality, not a doctrine about agriculture. Later in the same section, however, the text lays down as vows that one should not despise food, should not reject it, and should make food plentiful — injunctions that connect the philosophy of food with the duty of hospitality and the reality of scarcity.

That reality appears elsewhere. The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (1.10) opens a story with the country of the Kurus devastated — by hail or, as some translate, by locusts — and the learned Uṣasti Cākrāyaṇa reduced to begging leftover beans from an elephant-keeper. Crop failure and famine were familiar experiences.

docs.title: 2.9 Varṇa, Vārttā and Labour
docs.text:
The Brahmanical texts assign occupations to the four varṇas. Agriculture, cattle-keeping and trade together form vārttā, the livelihood proper to the vaiśya. The Bhagavad Gītā states the scheme concisely:

Bhagavad Gītā 18.44

kṛṣigorakṣyavāṇijyaṃ vaiśyakarma svabhāvajam | paricaryātmakaṃ karma śūdrasyāpi svabhāvajam || Agriculture, cattle-herding and trade are the vaiśya’s work, born of his nature; work consisting of service is likewise the śūdra’s, born of his nature.

The Manusmṛti (1.90) likewise lists protecting animals, agriculture and trade among the vaiśya’s duties (Olivelle 2005). Yet the same text is ambivalent about ploughing. It advises a brahmin or kṣatriya forced to live by a vaiśya’s occupation to avoid agriculture, which involves violence and depends on others; some, it says, consider agriculture good, but it is condemned by the virtuous, because the wooden implement with its iron tip injures the earth and the creatures that live in it (Manusmṛti 10.83–84). This concern with the killing of small creatures in the soil was shared with Jain and Buddhist thought (Section 2.10), and it contributed to the low status of the actual work of ploughing.

The scheme of four varṇas was an ideal, not a description. In practice, the people who worked the land were often not vaiśyas. Pali texts speak of dāsa-kammakara, slaves and hired workers, labouring in the fields of wealthy householders (gahapati) (Chakravarti 1987). The Arthaśāstra has crown lands worked by slaves, hired labourers and people working off fines. R. S. Sharma showed how, over the first millennium CE, the śūdra came increasingly to be identified with the peasant cultivator; the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang in the seventh century described the śūdras as agriculturists (Sharma 1980). Below them, groups regarded as untouchable were increasingly confined to the most degraded forms of labour. The history of caste, land and agricultural labour is treated more fully in Chapter 18, and that of hides and leather in Chapter 13.

docs.title: 2.10 Buddhist and Jain Perspectives
docs.text:
The Buddha (c. 480–400 BCE) taught in the agrarian kingdoms of the middle Ganga plain, and Pali texts are full of agricultural images. In the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta (Sutta Nipāta 1.4, vv. 76–82), the Buddha comes for alms to a brahmin farmer at sowing time, when five hundred ploughs are being yoked. The brahmin rebukes him: he himself ploughs and sows and then eats, and the Buddha too should plough and sow before he eats. The Buddha replies that he also ploughs and sows, and explains in a sustained metaphor: faith is his seed, austerity the rain, wisdom his yoke and plough, mindfulness his ploughshare and goad, and effort his draught ox; and his ploughing yields the deathless. The dialogue shows both the dignity of the landowning farmer and the challenge that the renouncer’s life posed to it.

Buddhist tradition also connects the Buddha’s first experience of meditation with agriculture. In the Majjhima Nikāya he recalls sitting in the shade of a rose-apple tree as a boy while his father was at work; later tradition places the scene at a royal ploughing festival. Royal ploughing ceremonies to open the agricultural season are still held in Thailand and Cambodia, and ritual ploughing by kings is mentioned in several Indian texts.

Buddhist monastic rules forbid monks to dig the ground or destroy plant life, and Jain ethics go further. Because Jain doctrine holds that earth, water and plants are themselves inhabited by living beings (Tatia 1994), ploughing and digging necessarily involve violence. Jain lay codes discouraged occupations involving much harm, and some lists of forbidden trades include digging and ploughing the earth. This is often cited as one reason why many Jain lay communities came to be concentrated in trade rather than agriculture, though economic and historical factors were also at work.

docs.title: 2.11 The Mauryan State and the Arthaśāstra
docs.text: The Mauryan empire (c. 321–185 BCE) was the first state to rule most of the subcontinent. The Greek envoy Megasthenes, whose account survives only in quotations by later Greek writers, reported that India had two harvests a year, because rain fell in both summer and winter, and that farmers formed a large class who were left unmolested even when armies fought nearby. These reports are idealised and filtered through Greek expectations, but they confirm the double cropping already attested in Indian sources.

docs.title: 2.11.1 The Superintendent of Agriculture
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra, traditionally attributed to Kauṭilya, minister of Candragupta Maurya, is in its present form a composite text compiled between about 50 BCE and 300 CE (Olivelle 2013). It cannot therefore be read as a direct description of Mauryan administration, but it reflects long experience of governing agrarian kingdoms. Its chapter on the Superintendent of Agriculture (sītādhyakṣa, 2.24) concerns the management of crown land (sītā). Because this chapter is drawn on in several later chapters of this volume, its contents are summarised here once. Its opening sentence (2.24.1) requires the superintendent to be conversant with the science of agriculture (kṛṣitantra) and the science of the life of plants (vṛkṣāyurveda), or to be assisted by those who are (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013). A third term in the same compound is transmitted in two forms: gulma, “shrubs”, in the text translated by Shamasastry (1915), and śulba, literally “cord”, in the text adopted by Kangle. Since the cord was the surveyor’s measuring line, śulba may refer to the measurement of land, though it has also been taken to mean knowledge of water; its sense here is uncertain, and this volume renders the qualification simply as agriculture and the science of plant life. The superintendent is to collect in good time the seeds of all grains, flowers, fruits, vegetables, bulbous roots, creepers, flax and cotton, and have them sown, on land ploughed many times, by serfs (dāsa), hired labourers and those working off fines. Work is not to be held up for want of ploughs and other implements, bullocks, or the smiths, carpenters, rope-makers, snake-catchers and other workers who serve the farm.

The rest of the chapter covers the matters taken up later in this volume. It states the normal annual rainfall of dry (jāṅgala) and wet (ānūpa) country and of named regions, measured in droṇas with a rain gauge kept at the royal storehouse, and links the expected rain to planetary signs (Section 3.5); the jāṅgala/ānūpa distinction is the same one found in the medical texts (Section 1.6). It classes crops by sowing time (Section 9.12), prescribes the treatment of seeds and cuttings before sowing (Section 9.14), and matches particular crops to particular ground, from river banks to the ridges between beds (Section 7.1). It ranks crops by their returns, placing rice and similar grains highest and sugarcane lowest because it is exposed to many dangers and costly to grow. And it fixes a water rate (udakabhāga) for those who irrigate from the king’s water-works, graded by the method by which the water reaches the field: by hand, carried on the shoulder, by a water-lifting device, or drawn from rivers, lakes, tanks and wells (Kangle 1965). How far such rules were ever applied is unknown. They show at least that the authors treated seed, the relative risks of crops and the cost of irrigation as matters of state concern.

Other superintendents described in the Arthaśāstra were responsible for cattle (go’dhyakṣa, 2.29), pastures, horses, elephants, forest produce, and the slaughter of animals and the protection of certain species. These are discussed in Chapters 13, 15 and 11, and the text as a whole in Volume 18.

docs.title: 2.11.2 The Sudarśana reservoir
docs.text: The best documented water project of the period is the Sudarśana lake near Junagadh in Gujarat, built under Candragupta Maurya, given conduits under Aśoka, and repaired by the Western Kṣatrapa Rudradāman (inscription of 150 CE) and again under the Gupta Skandagupta in the mid-fifth century: more than seven centuries of use, traced in Section 8.2.

docs.title: 2.11.3 Aśoka’s edicts
docs.text: The edicts of Aśoka (r. c. 268–232 BCE) are the earliest datable Indian documents concerned with plants and animals. They record medical treatment for people and animals, the planting of medicinal herbs, roadside banyans and mango groves, the digging of wells, a list of animals not to be killed and a ban on burning forests without purpose (Singh 2008); their provisions are set out in Chapter 11. These measures belong within Aśoka’s policy of dhamma; they should not be read as a modern conservation programme or as “veterinary hospitals” in the modern sense, but they show a ruler taking public responsibility for the welfare of animals as well as people.

docs.title: 2.12.1 The landscapes of Saṅgam poetry
docs.text:
The earliest Tamil literature, the poems collected in the Saṅgam anthologies (roughly the early centuries CE; dates debated), classifies its subject matter by tiṇai, a term that combines the ideas of landscape, mode of life and poetic theme. Each of the five tiṇais of love poetry is associated with a type of country, its plants and animals, its people and their occupations, and a phase of love (Zvelebil 1973; Hart 1975). A. K. Ramanujan’s translations from the anthologies (Ramanujan 1985) are the most accessible way into the poems themselves. Table 2.2 gives a simplified summary.

Table 2.2. The five landscapes (tiṇai) of Saṅgam love poetry (simplified). Tiṇai Landscape Characteristic people and livelihoods kuṟiñci Mountains Hill people; millet fields guarded from parrots; honey gathering; hunting mullai Forest and pasture Herders (āyar, kōvalar); cattle; rain-fed millets marutam Riverine farmland Ploughmen (uḻavar); paddy fields, buffaloes, irrigation; towns neytal Seashore Fishers; fishing and salt-making pālai Parched land Not a fixed region but any land dried by heat; travellers and bandits

The scheme is a literary convention, not a geographical survey, and it should not be described as “agro-ecological zoning” in the modern sense. But it rests on a real observation: that the Tamil country contained distinct ecologies, each supporting a different way of life. In marutam poems the paddy fields, canals, buffaloes and wealthy farming households of the river valleys are part of the setting; in mullai poems the herders, their cattle and the rains; in kuṟiñci poems the girls who guard the millet (tiṉai) from parrots. Longer poems such as the Paṭṭiṉappālai and Maturaikkāñci describe the Kāvēri delta and the Pāṇḍya country with their fields, tanks, markets and ports. The Tamil kings’ patronage of irrigation is remembered in the tradition that the Cōḻa king Karikāla built the first dam across the Kāvēri, the Kallaṇai or Grand Anicut; the structure as it now stands was largely rebuilt in the nineteenth century (Chapter 8).

docs.title: 2.12.2 The Tirukkuṟaḷ on ploughing
docs.text:
The Tirukkuṟaḷ, a collection of 1,330 couplets on ethics, statecraft and love ascribed to Tiruvaḷḷuvar (proposed dates range from the early centuries CE to about 500 CE), devotes its chapter 104, Uḻavu (“Ploughing”), to agriculture. Its ten couplets (1031–1040) may be paraphrased as follows, after the translations of Pope (1886) and Tiruvalluvar (1990):

  • However the world may turn, it follows the plough; so, for all its toil, farming is foremost (1031).

  • Ploughmen are the linchpin of the world, for they support those who take up other work (1032).

  • Only those who live by ploughing truly live; all others follow behind them, eating by their favour (1033).

  • A land of prosperous ploughmen will see other kings bow before its own (1034).

  • Those who plough with their own hands never beg, and give to those who do (1035).

  • If the ploughman folds his hands, even ascetics who have given up desire cannot endure (1036).

  • If the ploughed soil is dried until a measure of it shrinks to a quarter of its weight, the crop will flourish without even a handful of manure (1037).

  • Manuring is better than ploughing; and after weeding, guarding the crop is better than watering it (1038).

  • If the owner does not visit his field, it will sulk like a neglected wife (1039).

  • The earth laughs to see those who sit idle, pleading that they have nothing (1040).

The chapter is a work of ethics, not a manual: its purpose is to establish the farmer’s dignity and the dependence of society on his labour. Yet couplets 1037 to 1039 reflect practical maxims about tilth, manure, weeding, watching over the crop and the owner’s personal attention to the land. The “ploughman” praised here is, in social terms, usually the landholding cultivator; the agricultural labourers of the Tamil country, many of them from communities later treated as untouchable, appear rarely in this literature (Chapter 18).

docs.title: 2.13 The Epics and the Early Land Grants
2.13.1 The epics
docs.text: The Mahābhārata and Rāmāyaṇa, composed over many centuries and reaching their present form in the early centuries CE, treat the prosperity of agriculture as a test of good kingship. In the Sabhāparvan of the Mahābhārata (2.5 in the critical edition), the sage Nārada questions Yudhiṣṭhira about his government, asking among other things whether large, full tanks have been built at intervals across his kingdom so that agriculture does not depend on rain alone, and whether farmers in distress are given seed and food and loans at a modest rate of interest. The Rāmāyaṇa contains a comparable catechism, and its account of Sītā’s birth from the furrow links the heroine to the earth and to ploughing. Such passages describe ideals of royal duty, but they show what was expected of a king: irrigation works, relief in hard times and protection of cultivators and cattle.

docs.title: 2.13.2 Land grants
docs.text:
From the early centuries CE, inscriptions begin to record grants of land. Cave inscriptions at Nasik in Maharashtra record gifts of fields and villages by Sātavāhana kings and their contemporaries to Buddhist monks, with privileges that exempted the donated land from entry by royal officials and from royal claims such as the right to dig for salt. In Bengal, copper-plate inscriptions of the Gupta period record the purchase of land for religious gifts, giving prices and measuring land in units such as kulyavāpa and droṇavāpa, named after the quantity of seed needed to sow it (Singh 2008).

From the fourth and fifth centuries, grants of land and villages to brahmins (agrahāra, brahmadeya) multiplied across India. They brought new land under the plough, extended Brahmanical institutions into frontier and forest regions, and transferred to the grantees rights over the produce and labour of the cultivators. Grant documents name fields, wet and dry land, trees, tanks, wells, pastures and boundaries, and so become an important source for the history of cultivation. Their significance for the agrarian order of early medieval India is discussed in Chapter 18.

docs.title: 2.14 The Agricultural Year and Its Festivals
docs.text:
Throughout this period the agricultural year was shaped by the monsoon, with a main sowing at the onset of the rains and, where water allowed, a second crop in the cool season. Texts divided the year into six seasons and timed operations by the lunar months and the nakṣatras (Chapter 3; for the astronomy, Volume 12). The terms kharīf and rabī for the monsoon and winter crops are Arabic in origin and belong to the revenue usage of the Sultanate and Mughal periods.

Many of India’s festivals mark points in the agricultural year, though most are attested in their present form only from later periods. In the Tamil country Poṅkal, in the month of Tai (mid-January), celebrates the harvest and is followed by a day honouring cattle. In Assam the three Bihu festivals mark stages in the rice year; in Kerala, Onam is a harvest festival; in Punjab, Baisakhi marks the wheat harvest; in western Odisha, Nuakhai celebrates the new rice; and in coastal Odisha, during Raja Parba, the earth is held to be menstruating and ploughing is suspended for three days. These observances express the importance of the agricultural cycle in social and religious life. Claims that they encode precise agronomic knowledge should be treated with caution.

docs.title: 2.15 Towards the Treatises
docs.text: By the middle of the first millennium CE, the elements of the later agricultural literature were in place: a crop repertoire combining winter and summer crops of local, south-west Asian, African and East Asian origin; the zebu ox and plough as the basis of tillage; tanks, wells and channels for irrigation; a body of weather lore and calendrical rules; and state and religious institutions with an interest in land and its produce. Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā in the sixth century gathers much of this lore, including the rain-forecasting chapters (21–28), the chapter on finding groundwater (54) and the chapter on trees (55) (Bhat 1981). These are discussed in Chapters 3, 8 and 4, where the specialised treatises of the following centuries are also examined.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Agriculture in South Asia began at Mehrgarh around 7000 BCE with barley, wheat, goats, sheep and locally domesticated zebu cattle, and cotton was in use there by the sixth or fifth millennium BCE. Archaeobotany has shown that farming in the subcontinent drew on several independent centres of domestication — the southern Deccan, Gujarat, the Ganga plain and the Indus region — as well as on crops from south-west Asia, Africa (from about 2000 BCE) and East Asia. Harappan farmers combined winter and summer crops in regionally varied systems, ploughed with the ard, and kept zebu cattle, buffalo, sheep and goats, but no securely identified domestic horse. Neolithic cattle-keepers of the southern Deccan grew native pulses and millets. The Vedic texts record the plough, the furrow and the crops of the north, and the Upaniṣads reflect on food; Buddhist, Jain and Brahmanical texts reveal both the importance of agriculture and the low status of the labour of ploughing. The Arthaśāstra, Aśoka’s edicts, the Sudarśana reservoir, the Tamil anthologies and the Tirukkuṟaḷ, the epics and the early land grants show agriculture as a central concern of states, religious institutions and poets by the early centuries CE.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Fuller (2006) is the essential synthesis of archaeobotanical evidence, and Fuller (2011) a shorter statement of the argument for multiple centres of domestication. Meadow (1996) treats the domestication of animals in the north-west. Possehl (2002) and Kenoyer (1998) describe the Indus civilisation. Singh (2008) provides a reliable general history of the whole period, and Gopal and Srivastava (2008) a detailed survey of the textual and epigraphic evidence for agriculture; Sharma (1980) remains fundamental on labour and the śūdra. For the Tamil poems, Hart (1975) on their setting and Ramanujan (1985) for translations.

docs.title: Chapter 3: Kṛṣi-Parāśara, Rain Forecasting and the Agricultural Treatises
docs.text:
Sanskrit learning produced only a handful of works devoted to field agriculture. The best known is a short verse manual called the Kṛṣi-Parāśara, “Agriculture according to Parāśara”. It is often presented as an ancient compendium of farming science; the published text is shorter, later and more practical than that (Section 1.5). This chapter describes what the Kṛṣi-Parāśara contains, as far as the editions of Majumdar and Banerji (1960) and Sadhale (1999) allow. It then sets the text beside the older and fuller rain lore of Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā, the rain records of the Arthaśāstra, and the weather sayings of the regional languages. A section asks what such forecasting could and could not achieve. The chapter ends with the other agricultural treatises of medieval India and a brief look at farming books written elsewhere in the pre-modern world.

These treatises have to be read against the society that produced them, which is described more fully in Chapter 18. By the time the Kṛṣi-Parāśara was written, land grants to brahmins, temples and monasteries had spread settled rice farming across eastern and southern India, and the grantees held rights over the produce and labour of the cultivators (Section 18.3). The texts assign agriculture to the vaiśya and discourage the higher varṇas from ploughing, while much of the actual work was done by śūdra peasants, by dependent labourers, many of them from castes later treated as untouchable, and by women (Section 18.2). The farming manuals speak for the landholder who supervised this work, not for those who did it, and the reader should keep that in mind throughout this chapter and the next.

docs.title: 3.1 The Text, Its Attribution and Its Date
3.1.1 Editions
docs.text:
The Kṛṣi-Parāśara first became widely available to scholars in the edition and English translation of Girija Prasanna Majumdar and Sures Chandra Banerji, published by the Asiatic Society in its Bibliotheca Indica series in 1960 (Majumdar and Banerji 1960). Majumdar, a botanist with a long interest in Sanskrit plant literature, had earlier translated the Upavanavinoda (see Chapter 4). In 1999 Nalini Sadhale published a further text and translation, with notes, as the second of the Agri-History Bulletins of the Asian Agri-History Foundation (Sadhale 1999). These two editions are the basis of everything said about the text in this chapter. Where they leave a point uncertain, it is left uncertain here.

The text is short: a few hundred verses of simple, mostly unadorned Sanskrit, with no commentary. It reads as a working manual for a landholding householder rather than as a learned treatise. Its language is sometimes irregular, and some of its technical words for tools and operations are rare. Both features suggest a regional text written for practical use.

docs.title: 3.1.2 Who was “Parāśara”?
docs.text: The name Parāśara belongs, in the epics and Purāṇas, to a Vedic seer, the father of Vyāsa, to whom the Viṣṇu Purāṇa and several other works are traditionally ascribed. A Parāśara was also cited as an early authority on astral science and omens: Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā and its tenth-century commentary by Utpala refer to older works on rain and portents ascribed to sages such as Garga and Parāśara (Bhat 1981). Placing a farming manual under the name of a famous seer was a way of giving it authority. It tells us nothing about the actual author, who is unknown. The attribution to Parāśara should be treated as traditional, in the same way as the attribution of the Arthaśāstra to Kauṭilya.

docs.title: 3.1.3 Date and place
docs.text:
Some modern accounts place the text in the Gupta period or even earlier, but there is no evidence for this. Majumdar and Banerji (1960) placed its composition between about 950 and 1100 CE; other scholars have argued for a later date. The text cannot be dated precisely, and any date before the late first millennium CE should be regarded as unsupported.

Its place of origin is more securely indicated. The agriculture it describes is centred on wet rice: nurseries, transplanting, standing water in the fields and its drainage. The sequence of operations fits the monsoon regime of the lower Gangetic plain, and part of its vocabulary is eastern Indian.
