For these reasons the text is generally assigned to Bengal or a neighbouring region of eastern India (Majumdar and Banerji 1960; Sadhale 1999). It belongs, then, to the same broad world as the Pāla and Sena kingdoms, whose copper-plate land grants record villages, fields, ponds and rice lands in some detail (see Chapter 18).

Scholarly Note: What the Kṛṣi-Parāśara does not contain

Much that circulates under the name of the Kṛṣi-Parāśara is not in the published text. It does not contain:

  • a recipe for kuṇapajala, the fermented liquid manure made from animal remains. That preparation belongs to the Vṛkṣāyurveda of Surapāla and to the Upavanavinoda (Chapter 4);

  • a classification of twelve soils, a “soil-testing section” using earthworms, or a description of petrichor;

  • pesticide formulas using tobacco or custard apple. Both plants came from the Americas and reached India only after 1500;

  • tables of cloud names, wind directions or animal signs with numbered verses;

  • a division of the year into kharīf, rabī and zāid seasons, which are Perso-Arabic revenue terms (Section 9.12), or recommendations of particular rice varieties for deep water or uplands.

On such attributions in general, see Section 1.5.

docs.title: 3.2 The Praise of Agriculture
docs.text:
The text opens, after the customary invocation, with a praise of agriculture. One of its verses begins kṛṣir dhanyā kṛṣir medhyā jantūnāṃ jīvanaṃ kṛṣiḥ, “agriculture is blessed, agriculture is pure, agriculture is the life of creatures” (Majumdar and Banerji 1960; Sadhale 1999). These verses praise agriculture as the means of life of all creatures and set it above other ways of earning a living. Even learned men, the text suggests, depend on food, and food depends on the farmer. The theme is old: the Ṛgvedic gambler is told to give up dice and plough his field, and the Tamil Tirukkuṟaḷ gives a whole chapter to the ploughman as the linchpin of the world (Sections 2.7 and 2.12).

The Kṛṣi-Parāśara addresses a householder who owns land and cattle and is expected to watch over the work himself. Its warm praise of farming stands in contrast to the normative literature, which was more ambivalent about the plough (Section 2.9).

docs.title: 3.3 What the Text Covers
docs.text: The contents may be summarised under the headings that both editors recognise. The order below follows the logic of the farming year rather than the exact sequence of the verses.

docs.title: 3.3.1 Forecasting the year’s rain
docs.text:
Rain is the first concern of the text, and forecasting takes up a large part of it. The methods are those of the astral sciences (jyotiṣa) applied to the farmer’s needs.

The rulers of the year. Each year, in this system, has a planetary “king” and “minister”, fixed by an arithmetical rule applied to the number of the Śaka year; the minister is the fourth planet counted from the king. The character of the rains, and so of the harvest, is predicted from these rulers: some planets as king are said to bring abundant rain, others scanty rain or drought (Majumdar and Banerji 1960; Sadhale 1999). The same idea survives in the annual almanacs (pañcāṅga) of many Indian regions, which still announce the “king” and “minister” of the coming year.

The cloud of the year. The text names four kinds of cloud, āvarta, saṃvarta, puṣkara and droṇa, and gives a simple arithmetical rule, applied to the number of the year, for finding which of them governs a given year. Each cloud is associated with a different quality of rain, from patchy or scanty to abundant. These four are the classic cloud names of Sanskrit literature; they are not meteorological cloud types in the modern sense of forms such as cumulus or stratus. Kālidāsa’s Meghadūta, near its beginning, addresses the cloud-messenger as born in the famous lineage of the Puṣkaras and Āvartakas.

Observations in particular months. Beside these calendrical rules the text prescribes observations of wind, cloud, rain and sky on fixed days of particular months, from which the rain of the coming season is to be inferred. What is seen in the months before the rains is read as a sign of what will follow during the monsoon. The underlying idea, that the weather of one season is “carried” into another, is shared with the doctrine of the “pregnancy” of clouds in the Bṛhatsaṃhitā (Section 3.4).

The quantity of rain. The text also treats the amount of the year’s rain, reckoned in traditional measures, and how it is to be known. Here too it stands close to the older astral literature, in which rainfall was measured by collecting it in a vessel of standard size (Sections 3.4 and 3.5).

The rain lore of the Kṛṣi-Parāśara is less detailed than Varāhamihira’s, and much of it is clearly derived from the same tradition. Its distinctive contribution is to place these forecasts at the head of a manual of field operations. For its author, judging the year’s rain was the first thing a cultivator needed to do.

docs.title: 3.3.2 Cattle and the cattle shed
docs.text: Draught cattle were the farmer’s capital, and the text gives them close attention (Sadhale 1999). It describes the cattle shed: where it should be built, the need to keep it clean and to remove dung and urine, and the protection of animals from damp and disease. It also gives rules for the care of the animals, and prescribes auspicious times and rites connected with them. The tone is that of a householder protecting valuable property. Livestock husbandry in general, including the veterinary literature, is treated in Chapter 13.

docs.title: 3.3.3 Manure
docs.text: The text gives a seasonal routine for cow-dung manure: in Māgha the dung heap is to be dug out, then dried in the sun and broken up, laid in a pit in each field in Phālguna, and spread at sowing time (Majumdar and Banerji 1960; Sadhale 1999). The text warns that a crop grown without manure will bear no fruit. It does not offer a theory of soil fertility, and it does not describe the elaborate fermented preparations of the horticultural texts. Its manure is the ordinary farmyard manure of a mixed rice-and-cattle economy. Soil and manuring are discussed more fully in Chapter 7, and the later scientific study of Indian manuring in Section 10.7.

docs.title: 3.3.4 The plough
docs.text: One of the most frequently cited passages of the Kṛṣi-Parāśara names the parts of the plough and gives their dimensions in traditional units such as the hasta (cubit), vitasti (span) and aṅgula (finger-breadth). Among the parts named are the īṣā, the long pole or beam joining plough to yoke, and the yuga, the yoke itself. Several of the other names are rare words whose exact reference is uncertain, and the two editors do not always agree on them; they are not listed here. The plough described is the light wooden ard drawn by a pair of oxen, with an iron share, that remained the standard implement of Indian farming until the twentieth century (Randhawa 1980). The passage is valuable to historians of technology precisely because it is so plain: it records a real tool, not an idealised one. The parts of such a plough are shown in Figure 7.1, and the history of the plough in India is traced in Chapters 2 and 7.

docs.title: 3.3.5 Seed
docs.text: The text gives rules for collecting seed from the harvest, drying it and storing it so that it remains fit for sowing. Seed is to be kept dry and free from damage, and seed of poor quality will not give a good crop (Majumdar and Banerji 1960; Sadhale 1999). The text also prescribes rites and auspicious times for taking out the seed and beginning to sow. The wider history of seeds, landraces and their storage is treated in Chapter 9.

docs.title: 3.3.6 Sowing, transplanting, weeding and drainage
docs.text:
The heart of the practical section concerns rice. The text describes sowing, raising seedlings, and transplanting them into flooded fields during the rains. It insists on timely weeding, and it gives instructions for the management of water in the field: water is to be kept in the field while the crop needs it and drained out at the proper stage so that the grain can ripen (Majumdar and Banerji 1960; Sadhale 1999). This attention to letting water out of the field, as well as holding it in, is characteristic of a deltaic region where too much water was as great a danger as too little.

No yields, seed rates or spacings are given that could be converted into modern figures, and the text times its operations by lunar months and nakṣatras rather than by named crop seasons.

docs.title: 3.3.7 Harvest, threshing and storage
docs.text: The text closes the agricultural cycle with the harvest, the preparation of the threshing floor, threshing, and the storage of grain. These operations, too, are linked to auspicious times and to rites performed on the threshing floor. The details are practical rather than technical, and the text says nothing about methods of preserving stored grain against insects. Farmers’ storage practices are described in Section 9.14.

docs.title: 3.3.8 Rites of the farming year
docs.text:
Throughout the text practical instruction is interwoven with ritual. The first ploughing of the season, the first sowing and the bringing in of the harvest are all accompanied by offerings and observances, and auspicious lunar days and nakṣatras are prescribed for each operation. The text also describes a festival associated with the month of Pauṣa, the Puṣyayātrā (Majumdar and Banerji 1960; Sadhale 1999). Rites of this kind are typical of agrarian societies, and similar harvest festivals are still celebrated across eastern India. Agricultural festivals more generally are discussed in Chapter 2.

These rites were not decoration. For the author they were as much part of farming as ploughing and weeding: success depended on correct timing, and correct timing was understood in astral terms. A modern reader may separate the observational from the ritual parts of the text. Its author did not.

Cross-Reference: The nakṣatra calendar

The Kṛṣi-Parāśara, like all Indian agricultural texts, times its operations by lunar months, lunar days (tithi) and the twenty-seven or twenty-eight lunar mansions (nakṣatra). The structure of this calendar, its relation to the solar year and the seasons, and the history of the pañcāṅga are treated in Volume 12, Khagola Jyotiṣa. Because the lunar months drift against the solar year and the nakṣatra positions have shifted with the precession of the equinoxes, a nakṣatra named in a medieval text cannot be turned into a fixed modern calendar date without calculation.

docs.title: 3.4 Rain Forecasting in the Bṛhatsaṃhitā
docs.text:
The fullest Sanskrit account of rain forecasting is not in a farming manual but in the Bṛhatsaṃhitā of Varāhamihira, a sixth-century astronomer-astrologer associated with Ujjain in the Avanti region. The Bṛhatsaṃhitā is a compendium of the “natural” branch of astral science (saṃhitā): omens, portents, the signs of good and bad harvests, gems, animals, architecture and the care of trees. Varāhamihira repeatedly cites earlier authorities, and his chapters on rain record a body of lore that was already old in his time. The standard English translation is that of Bhat (1981), whose chapter numbering is used here.

Eight consecutive chapters deal with forecasting rain (Table 3.1). Two other chapters touch farming directly: chapter 54, on finding groundwater (dakārgala), treated in Chapter 8, and chapter 55, on the care of trees (vṛkṣāyurveda), treated in Chapter 4.

Table 3.1. The rain-forecasting chapters of Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā (chapter numbers as in (Bhat 1981)). Ch. Title Subject 21 Garbhalakṣaṇa Signs of the “conception” of the clouds in the cool season 22 Garbhadhāraṇa The sustaining of the cloud-embryos and the signs that they will yield rain 23 Pravarṣaṇa The first rains, and the measurement of rainfall 24 Rohiṇīyoga Forecasts from observations when the moon is in conjunction with Rohiṇī 25 Svātiyoga Forecasts from observations when the moon is in Svāti 26 Āṣāḍhīyoga Forecasts from observations at the Āṣāḍha full moon 27 Vātacakra Forecasts from the direction of the wind 28 Sadyovarṣaṇa Signs of immediate rain

docs.title: 3.4.1 The “pregnancy” of the clouds
docs.text:
The central idea of these chapters is that the rains of the monsoon are “conceived” months earlier, in the cool season, and “born” when their time comes. The conception season begins in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa (November–December). An “embryo” (garbha) formed when the moon stands in a particular nakṣatra is said to be delivered as rain about 195 days later, when the moon is again in that nakṣatra (Bhat 1981). Six and a half months after the cool season brings us to the beginning of the rains, so the scheme links each day of winter to a day of the coming monsoon.

The forecaster was to watch the sky on the days of conception. Favourable signs include gentle winds from the north, north-east or east, a clear sky with soft, glossy clouds, haloes around the sun and moon, and mild thunder and lightning. Unfavourable signs, such as meteors, dust storms, thunderbolts and planetary eclipses, are said to destroy the embryo. An embryo accompanied by all five signs of wind, rain, lightning, thunder and cloud is expected to bring abundant rain. If heavy rain falls during the period of pregnancy itself, the embryo is thought to be lost, “miscarried” before its time (Bhat 1981).

The scheme is elegant and internally consistent, and it reflects an awareness that the seasons are connected. It is also, in its working detail, a calendrical construction. There is no known physical mechanism by which the weather on a given winter day determines the rain on a particular day half a year later, and there is no established evidence that forecasts made by this method have useful skill.

docs.title: 3.4.2 Measuring the rain
docs.text: The chapter on the first rains (pravarṣaṇa) contains one of the clearest pieces of quantitative method in the whole tradition. Rain is to be collected in a round vessel one hasta (cubit) across, and the amount is to be expressed by weight: fifty palas of collected water make one āḍhaka (Bhat 1981). A vessel of fixed aperture is the essential principle of every rain gauge. Varāhamihira uses the measurement to judge whether the first rain of the season is good or poor, as one input to his forecasts. It is not described as part of a continuous record kept over many years.

docs.title: 3.4.3 Conjunctions, wind and immediate signs
docs.text:
The next three chapters prescribe observations at particular moments of the lunar calendar: when the moon passes Rohiṇī, when it passes Svāti, and at the full moon of Āṣāḍha, just before the main rains. The appearance of the sky, the direction of the wind and the presence of clouds or rain at these moments are read as signs for the season. The chapter on the “wheel of winds” (vātacakra) forecasts the year’s rain from the direction of the wind on the Āṣāḍha full moon (Bhat 1981).

The last chapter of the group, on immediate rain (sadyovarṣaṇa), is the most down-to-earth. It lists signs that rain will come soon: the look of the sky at sunrise and sunset, the colour and movement of the clouds, and the behaviour of animals, such as ants carrying their eggs and frogs calling (Bhat 1981). These are the kinds of short-range signs that farmers everywhere have used, and they are closest to what modern observers would accept as genuine indicators of approaching rain.

docs.title: 3.5 The Arthaśāstra and the Recording of Rain
docs.text:
Rain measurement in India is attested still earlier in the Arthaśāstra, the treatise on statecraft ascribed to Kauṭilya. In its present form the text is composite and dates from roughly 50 BCE to 300 CE; the attribution to a minister of Candragupta Maurya around 300 BCE is traditional (Olivelle 2013). The Arthaśāstra is discussed as a whole in Volume 18, Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra; only its rain lore concerns us here.

In Book 2 the royal storehouse is to be equipped with a rain gauge (varṣamāna), a vessel with a mouth one aratni (cubit) wide (2.5.7; (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013)). The chapter on the superintendent of agriculture (sītādhyakṣa, 2.24), who managed the crown’s own farmland, then states the normal rainfall of different regions in the volume measure droṇa. The arid jāṅgala country is given sixteen droṇas, the wet ānūpa country half as much again; Aśmaka thirteen and a half, Avanti twenty-three; for the western regions (Aparānta), the Himalayan regions and lands watered by channels the amount is said to be unlimited (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013). The ancient droṇa cannot be converted reliably into millimetres of rain, so these figures cannot be compared directly with modern data. What matters is the practice: rain was measured at state storehouses, and normal amounts for different regions were known well enough to be written down.

The same chapter connects the forecasting of rain with the positions and movements of Jupiter and Venus and with changes in the appearance of the sun. It advises the superintendent to plan sowing according to the expected rain, choosing crops that need more or less water (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013). Here administrative record-keeping and astral forecasting stand side by side, as they do in Varāhamihira. The rest of the chapter on the superintendent is summarised in Section 2.11.1.

docs.title: 3.6 Folk Forecasting: Khanā, Ghāgh and Bhaḍḍarī
docs.text:
Alongside the Sanskrit texts, every farming region of India had, and still has, a stock of rhymed sayings about weather, seasons and crops. They were transmitted orally, among cultivators rather than scholars, and they were written down only in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries by local scholars and colonial collectors. Because they were oral, they are hard to date, and many versions of each saying exist. The examples below are described rather than quoted. No reliable critical edition exists from which a fixed wording could be cited, and inventing “typical” sayings would be no better than inventing verses.

Khanā. In Bengal the best-known body of such sayings is the Khanār vacan, “the sayings of Khanā”. Legend makes Khanā a learned woman astrologer, sometimes connected with the household of Varāhamihira himself, whose tongue was cut out because her predictions surpassed those of the men around her. The sayings ascribed to her are short Bengali couplets on the timing of ploughing and sowing, the signs of rain and drought, the right season for particular crops, the care of cattle and the management of the household. As recorded, their language is that of early modern Bengali; their origins may be older, but they cannot be dated. Similar collections exist in neighbouring regions, such as the sayings attributed to Ḍāk in Assam and Bengal.

Ghāgh and Bhaḍḍarī. In the Hindi-speaking north, weather and farming sayings are attributed to Ghāgh and to Bhaḍḍarī. Ghāgh is a figure of legend placed by different traditions in different centuries and regions. Bhaḍḍarī (Bhaḍalī in Gujarati and Rajasthani usage) is likewise legendary and is associated especially with weather prognostication. The sayings attributed to both deal with the signs of rain in the sky and in animal behaviour, the qualities of good and bad bullocks, the right moment for sowing, and the conduct of a sensible farmer. They circulate in Bhojpuri, Awadhi, Braj and Rajasthani forms.

It is notable that in Bengal the emblematic authority on weather and farming is a woman. Whatever the historical reality behind the legend, it reflects the fact that agricultural knowledge was carried by women as well as by men. Women did much of the work of seed selection, storage, transplanting and post-harvest processing (see Chapters 9 and 14).

These sayings differ from the Sanskrit texts in voice rather than in substance. They mix astral rules (rain on a particular nakṣatra, the weekday on which a month begins) with local observations of wind, cloud, dew, the behaviour of birds and insects, and the flowering of plants. Their value lies less in any single prediction than in what they show of farmers’ attention to their environment and of the way knowledge was condensed into memorable form.

docs.title: 3.7 What Could Such Forecasting Do?
docs.text:
A fair evaluation of this material must distinguish several kinds of rule that are mixed together in the texts, because they differ greatly in what they could achieve.

Calendrical and astrological rules predict the year’s rain from the planet that rules the year, from the cloud assigned to the year by arithmetic, or from the position of the moon on certain days. These rules have no physical basis. The number of the year cannot affect the monsoon, and a forecast derived from it can be right only by chance.

Long-range rules link observations in one season to rain in another, as in the doctrine of the pregnancy of the clouds. They rest on a sound intuition: the seasons are connected, and the state of the atmosphere in one season does influence the next. But the specific links proposed, from a particular winter day to a particular monsoon day, have no known mechanism. Modern long-range forecasting depends on large-scale patterns of ocean temperature and atmospheric pressure across the whole tropics, which no ground-level observer could have detected.

Short-range signs, such as rising humidity, the build-up of clouds, shifts of wind, haloes and the behaviour of insects, frogs and birds, can carry real information about weather in the next few hours or days. Farmers who read them well had a practical advantage. Such signs are local and short-lived, however. They can tell a farmer that rain is coming this afternoon, but not whether the monsoon will fail next year.

Measurement stands apart. The rain gauges of the Arthaśāstra and the Bṛhatsaṃhitā are genuine empirical instruments, and the regional figures of the Arthaśāstra show that measurements were used to describe normal conditions. There is no evidence, however, that continuous records were kept and analysed over long periods to test the forecasting rules.

The monsoon’s variability was a matter of life and death, and the failure of the rains brought repeated famines. Systematic seasonal forecasting began only in the 1880s, when H. F. Blanford of the newly founded India Meteorological Department issued forecasts based partly on Himalayan snowfall. In the early twentieth century his successor Gilbert Walker searched worldwide weather records for statistical predictors of the monsoon and in the process identified the Southern Oscillation, later understood as part of the El Niño system. The colonial famines of the late nineteenth century, when the rains failed and grain continued to be exported, showed that forecasting alone could not prevent catastrophe (Davis 2001). Even today seasonal monsoon forecasts have limited skill.

Debate: Did Indian rain lore anticipate monsoon science?

For: the texts treat rain as part of a seasonal system, measure rainfall with standard vessels, and record observations of wind and cloud; some short-range signs they list are physically meaningful.

Against: the core predictive rules are astrological; the long-range links have no mechanism and no demonstrated skill; there is no evidence of the systematic testing of predictions against records that defines a forecasting science.

Assessment: the texts deserve to be read as a serious attempt to bring order to the most important uncertainty in farmers’ lives. They are part of the history of meteorology, as similar weather lore is in Europe and China. They did not anticipate the physical understanding of the monsoon, and nothing is gained by claiming that they did.

docs.title: 3.8 Other Agricultural Treatises
docs.text: The Kṛṣi-Parāśara is not alone. A small number of other works, in Sanskrit and in the regional languages, deal wholly or partly with agriculture and plant care; their dates, as far as they can be established, are given in Table 1.2 (Chapter 1). Those concerned mainly with trees and gardens are discussed further in Chapter 4.

docs.title: 3.8.1 The Kāśyapīya Kṛṣisūkti
docs.text: The Kāśyapīya Kṛṣisūkti, “Kāśyapa’s verses on agriculture”, is attributed to the sage Kāśyapa. Like the Kṛṣi-Parāśara it is a Sanskrit verse text, but it comes from the south of India. Its date is uncertain; its editor proposes the later first millennium CE, but the evidence is slight (Ayachit 2002). The text gives particular attention to rice, the dominant crop of the river deltas and tank-irrigated lands of the peninsula, and to the management of water. It places agriculture within a framework of royal responsibility and religious merit, in which the ruler is expected to promote cultivation. Ayachit’s translation made the text accessible, but it has received far less scholarly study than the Kṛṣi-Parāśara. Its relation to the irrigation history of south India (see Chapter 8) remains to be worked out.

docs.title: 3.8.2 The Lokopakāra
docs.text: The Lokopakāra (“For the benefit of the people”) of Cāvuṇḍarāya, written in Kannada around 1025 CE, is an early encyclopaedic work in Kannada. It brings together practical knowledge on topics such as astrology and omens, house-building, water-finding, cookery, perfumes, remedies and the care of plants, and an English translation was published by the Asian Agri-History Foundation (Ayangarya 2006). Its plant-care section belongs to the vṛkṣāyurveda tradition and is described in Section 4.1.5. The Lokopakāra matters for the history of agricultural knowledge because it shows Sanskrit technical material being recast in a regional language for a lay readership.

docs.title: 3.8.3 The Mānasollāsa
docs.text: The Mānasollāsa, also called Abhilaṣitārthacintāmaṇi, was composed in 1131 CE at the court of the Western Cālukya king Someśvara III. It is an encyclopaedia of royal life in five sections of twenty chapters each, covering the acquisition and protection of the kingdom and the king’s enjoyments and pastimes (Shrigondekar 1925). Several parts concern plants and animals: the laying out of gardens, with plant-care instructions of the vṛkṣāyurveda type; horses and elephants; dogs and hunting; birds; fishing; and a celebrated section on cookery. The text describes the agriculture and husbandry of the court rather than of the village, but it shows how much practical knowledge of plants and animals was expected of a cultivated king. Its material on animals is used in Chapters 15 and 17, and its cookery in Chapter 14.

docs.title: 3.8.4 Other sources
docs.text: Agricultural material is also scattered through the Purāṇas, notably the Agni Purāṇa, which has chapters on the care of trees and of animals; through the dharmaśāstra literature on land, tillage and its rules; and through inscriptions recording irrigation works and land grants. From the thirteenth century onward, Persian sources from the Sultanate and Mughal courts add much on crops, revenue and gardens; they are discussed in Chapter 18. Agricultural verse also exists in the regional languages, though it has received little critical study. In Tamil, the Ēr eḻupatu (“Seventy on the plough”), traditionally ascribed to the poet Kampaṉ, praises the plough and the cultivating Veḷḷāḷar; in Malayalam, the Kṛṣigīta, a verse work of uncertain, probably early modern date, presents the rice farming of Kerala as teaching given by Paraśurāma. Both are works of praise and of caste and regional identity as much as manuals, and their dates and attributions are traditional. For most of Indian history, however, agricultural knowledge was transmitted by practice and by word of mouth rather than in writing. The treatises are a small and socially narrow window onto it.

docs.title: 3.9 Farming Books Elsewhere
docs.text:
It can be helpful to set the Indian treatises beside agricultural writing from other pre-modern societies, provided the comparison is descriptive rather than competitive.

In the Roman world, Cato, Varro and above all Columella, whose De re rustica in twelve books was written in the first century CE, wrote for owners of estates worked largely by enslaved labourers. Columella covers soils, vines, olives, livestock, bees and gardens, and the management of the estate’s workforce. In China, Jia Sixie’s Qimin yaoshu (“Essential techniques for the common people”), compiled in the sixth century, is a long and systematic manual of field crops, vegetables, trees, animal husbandry and food processing, including fermentation; it quotes many earlier works. In al-Andalus, Ibn al-ʿAwwām of Seville compiled his Kitāb al-filāḥa (“Book of agriculture”) in the twelfth century, drawing on earlier Arabic, Greek and Andalusi sources; it is especially rich on irrigated gardens and fruit trees. The Byzantine Geoponika, compiled in the tenth century, is an anthology of older Greek agricultural writing.

Beside these, the Indian works have a distinctive profile. The Kṛṣi-Parāśara is very short and addressed to a single householder. The Indian texts are composed in verse for memorisation, closely tied to astral science and ritual, and concerned with rice and the monsoon rather than with the vine and the olive. The tree and garden texts discussed in the next chapter are, by contrast, closely modelled on medicine. Each tradition reflects its own ecology, economy and learned culture. None of these works records the whole agricultural knowledge of its society, and the cultivators whose practice they describe, enslaved estate workers in Italy, peasants in China and India, mostly left no writings of their own.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The Kṛṣi-Parāśara is a short Sanskrit verse manual, attributed by tradition to the sage Parāśara, probably composed in Bengal or eastern India around 950–1100 CE or somewhat later. After praising agriculture, it forecasts the year’s rain and then gives a householder’s rules for cattle, manure, the plough, seed, the cultivation of rice, the harvest and the rites of the year. Its rain lore draws on the older tradition recorded in Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā and the Arthaśāstra, which also measured rainfall; the oral sayings of Khanā, Ghāgh and Bhaḍḍarī carry the same mixture of astral rule and local observation into the vernaculars. Measurement and short-range signs had real value; the astrological and long-range rules did not. The Kāśyapīya Kṛṣisūkti, the Lokopakāra and the Mānasollāsa show that agricultural writing in India was limited in volume but varied in region, language and audience.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: The text and translation of Majumdar and Banerji (1960) remains the basic edition of the Kṛṣi-Parāśara; Sadhale (1999) offers a convenient translation with notes. Varāhamihira’s rain chapters can be read in Bhat (1981), and the Arthaśāstra’s chapter on the superintendent of agriculture in Kangle (1965) and Olivelle (2013). Ayachit (2002) translates the Kāśyapīya Kṛṣisūkti and Ayangarya (2006) the Lokopakāra. Gopal and Srivastava (2008) sets these texts in the wider history of early Indian agriculture, and Randhawa (1980) provides a broad survey.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Vṛkṣāyurveda: The Science of the Life of Trees
docs.text:
Vṛkṣāyurveda, “the science of the life of trees”, is the Sanskrit name for a body of knowledge about growing and tending trees, shrubs, creepers and garden plants. Its name and much of its method come from medicine (āyurveda). Plants are treated as living bodies that must be nourished, can fall ill, and can be cured. The tradition is represented by a single chapter in an encyclopaedia, a few chapters in the Purāṇas, one surviving specialised treatise, sections of medieval encyclopaedias and anthologies, and a late compilation. Its literature is therefore small. This chapter describes the texts, the ideas about plant life on which they rest, and the main topics they treat. It deals separately with the fermented liquid manure called kuṇapajala, with the literary and horticultural notion of plant “cravings” (dohada), and with the marvels the texts claim to produce. What the gardens produced, and what Indian culture made of their flowers, scents and betel, is the subject of Chapter 5. Plant classification is treated more fully in Chapter 6, and medicinal plants in Chapter 12 and in Volume 13, Āyurveda.

The word itself is old. The Arthaśāstra (2.24.1) requires the superintendent of agriculture to know the science of agriculture and the science of plant life (vṛkṣāyurveda), or to be assisted by people who do (Section 2.11.1). Nothing survives of any treatise of that period, but the term shows that a recognised body of knowledge about the care of plants existed by the early centuries CE.

docs.title: 4.1 The Texts
docs.text: The principal sources are the Bṛhatsaṃhitā (ch. 55), the Agni Purāṇa, Surapāla, the Lokopakāra, the Mānasollāsa, the Upavanavinoda and the Viśvavallabha; their approximate dates are given in Tables 1.1 and 1.2 (Chapter 1). For several of them the dates are disputed.

docs.title: 4.1.1 Bṛhatsaṃhitā, chapter 55
docs.text: The oldest surviving systematic account is chapter 55 of Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā (6th century), titled Vṛkṣāyurveda (Bhat 1981). It is short, but most of the topics of the later texts are already present in it. It recommends planting trees by houses, gardens and water bodies, and describes the preparation of the soil. It lists trees that can be raised from cuttings, gives seasons for transplanting, and prescribes the spacing of trees and a watering schedule. It then sets out the symptoms of disease and their treatment, ways of making a barren tree bear, and treatments of seeds before sowing (Section 4.3). Varāhamihira’s chapter is the model on which several later texts drew, directly or indirectly. For the Bṛhatsaṃhitā more generally, and for its rain-forecasting chapters, see Chapter 3; for chapter 54 on finding groundwater, see Chapter 8.

docs.title: 4.1.2 The Agni Purāṇa and other Purāṇas
docs.text: The Agni Purāṇa, an encyclopaedic Purāṇa of uncertain and composite date, contains a short chapter on the care of trees. Much of it parallels the Bṛhatsaṃhitā. Chapter numbers differ between editions and are not given here. Several Purāṇas also praise the planting of trees as a meritorious act and prescribe rites for consecrating new gardens and trees. A widely quoted verse of the Matsya Purāṇa (chapter 154 in the usual numbering, within the story of Pārvatī and Śiva), spoken by the goddess Pārvatī when she adopts an aśoka sapling as her son, ranks a single tree as the equal of ten sons. Such passages tell us more about the religious value placed on tree-planting than about techniques. They help explain why wealthy patrons founded gardens and groves, and why treatises on their care were written (see also Chapter 11).

docs.title: 4.1.3 Planting as merit and as policy
docs.text:
The planting of useful trees was also an act of public policy long before any surviving treatise: Aśoka’s second Rock Edict and seventh Pillar Edict record the planting of medicinal herbs, roadside banyans and mango groves (Chapter 11). Later kings, queens, merchants and temple authorities continued the practice, and inscriptions of many periods record the gift of gardens, groves and roadside trees together with tanks and wells. The vṛkṣāyurveda texts served people who undertook such works. Their praise of tree-planting as a source of religious merit, which can seem conventional, reflects a real social institution.

Folk practice carried the same values in other forms. In many parts of India a pīpal (aśvattha, Ficus religiosa) and a neem (Azadirachta indica) are planted side by side and their union is celebrated as a “marriage” of the two trees. The tulasī plant is ceremonially married to Viṣṇu in the annual tulasī-vivāha. Such customs express the idea that trees are persons with kinship and life-cycles of their own.

docs.title: 4.1.4 Surapāla’s Vṛkṣāyurveda
docs.text:
The only surviving independent treatise of any length is the Vṛkṣāyurveda of Surapāla, edited and translated by Nalini Sadhale as the first of the Agri-History Bulletins of the Asian Agri-History Foundation (Sadhale 1996). Surapāla describes himself as a physician (vaidya) in the service of a king named Bhīmapāla. This king has not been securely identified, and the text is usually dated, with some uncertainty, to the tenth or eleventh century CE. A Pāla connection in eastern India has been suggested but is not proven. The text is a verse work of a few hundred stanzas. Its standpoint is a physician’s. It covers the praise of trees and the merit of planting them, the choice of land, the classification of plants, seeds and their treatment, planting, watering, nourishment, the protection of plants from external harm, the diagnosis and cure of their diseases, a series of “marvels”, and the layout of gardens.

Two features make Surapāla’s text especially important. First, it shows how thoroughly the categories of human medicine were carried over to plants, as discussed below. Second, it contains the classic account of kuṇapajala (Section 4.3.6). What it does not contain is listed in Section 1.5; for its contents the reader should rely on Sadhale’s translation.

docs.title: 4.1.5 The Lokopakāra and the Mānasollāsa
docs.text: Two encyclopaedic works of the eleventh and twelfth centuries, described in Section 3.8, include plant-care sections in the vṛkṣāyurveda manner. The Kannada Lokopakāra of Cāvuṇḍarāya (c. 1025 CE) gives one of its chapters to the care of trees and garden plants, which its English translation makes accessible (Ayangarya 2006). The chapter follows the order already familiar from Varāhamihira: the choice and preparation of the ground, the trees auspicious near a house, the treatment of seeds and cuttings, planting, watering by season, nourishing applications of dung, oil-cake, milk and similar substances, the protection of trees against insects and disease by pastes and fumigation, and procedures for making trees flower or fruit out of season or bear fruit of unusual size, colour or taste. Much of this is shared with Surapāla, and it is not known whether either author drew on the other or both on a common source. The Lokopakāra is the earliest surviving treatment of the subject in a Dravidian language, and it carries the knowledge of the Sanskrit garden texts to readers who did not read Sanskrit. Its terms for plants and operations are partly Kannada, which makes it a valuable witness to the vocabulary of gardeners in the Deccan. The Mānasollāsa of Someśvara III (1131 CE) treats the laying out and tending of a garden among the king’s enjoyments (Shrigondekar 1925).

docs.title: 4.1.6 The Upavanavinoda
docs.text: The Upavanavinoda, “Delight of the garden”, is a section on arbori-horticulture in the Śārṅgadharapaddhati, an anthology of Sanskrit verse on many subjects compiled by Śārṅgadhara in 1363 CE. This Śārṅgadhara is not the author of the medical Śārṅgadhara-saṃhitā. G. P. Majumdar edited and translated the section in 1935, with notes on the plants named (Majumdar 1935). The Upavanavinoda covers much the same ground as Surapāla, from the praise of trees and the choice of soil to planting, watering, nourishment, diseases and marvels. The two texts share a good deal of material, including a description of kuṇapajala. As an anthology section, it gathers older verses rather than presenting the views of a single author.

docs.title: 4.1.7 The Viśvavallabha
docs.text: The Viśvavallabha of Cakrapāṇi Miśra, composed in Mewar in the later sixteenth century, is a late compilation; its author is associated with the court of Mahārāṇā Pratāp, and Nalini Sadhale has translated it (Sadhale 2004). It is a short verse work in a sequence of chapters that moves from water to plants. It begins, as Varāhamihira’s dakārgala does, with the signs of underground water — trees, termite mounds, soils and stones — and with the digging of wells and tanks (Section 8.10). It then turns to the garden: the kinds of land, the choice of trees for particular places, the treatment of seeds before sowing, planting and the spacing of trees, watering, manures and nourishing liquids, the protection of plants from pests and disease, and a closing set of marvels like those of Surapāla. Much of the content closely parallels the Bṛhatsaṃhitā and the older vṛkṣāyurveda material, so that the work is most useful as evidence of what a scholar at a Rajput court in the sixteenth century thought worth keeping from that tradition, and of its continued practical interest in an arid kingdom where wells and orchards mattered greatly. Its author should not be confused with Cakrapāṇidatta, the eleventh-century Bengali commentator on the Caraka-saṃhitā, and no separate vṛkṣāyurveda by a “Cakrapāṇi” is known.

docs.title: 4.1.8 The disputed “Vṛkṣāyurveda of Parāśara”
docs.text:
A work entitled Vṛkṣāyurveda and attributed to Parāśara has been published in modern editions. It is often presented as the foundational text of Indian botany, dated to the early centuries CE or earlier, and credited with an advanced classification of plants and with descriptions of the internal structure of leaves. These claims cannot be accepted as they stand.

Debate: The “Parāśara” Vṛkṣāyurveda

The claim: an ancient sage Parāśara composed a botanical treatise that classified plants by their flowers and described the internal anatomy of leaves, anticipating modern botany.

The difficulties: the manuscript basis of the published text has not been set out in a critical edition that other scholars can check; its date is unknown; its technical vocabulary and some of its descriptions have no parallel in the securely dated texts; and the name Parāśara was attached to several works of very different periods, including the medieval Kṛṣi-Parāśara (Chapter 3).

Assessment: until a proper critical study is available, the work should be treated as of uncertain authenticity and date. It should not be cited as evidence for ancient Indian botanical knowledge, and statements that it “anticipated Linnaeus” or described cells are unsupported.

docs.title: 4.2 Plants as Living Beings
docs.text: The vṛkṣāyurveda texts rest on a premise widely shared in Indian thought: plants are living beings (jīva) with some form of awareness. This premise appears in several traditions with different emphases.

docs.title: 4.2.1 Brahmanical sources
docs.text:
The Manusmṛti, in its account of creation, lists the kinds of plants and then says of them:

Manusmṛti 1.49

tamasā bahurūpeṇa veṣṭitāḥ karmahetunā antaḥsaṃjñā bhavanty ete sukhaduḥkhasamanvitāḥ “Enveloped by darkness of many forms, the result of their past actions, these beings have inner awareness and experience pleasure and pain.”

The verse places plants at the bottom of a hierarchy of rebirth. They are beings born into a dull, “dark” form as a result of past deeds, yet still conscious and capable of pleasure and pain (Olivelle 2005). The surrounding verses (1.46–48) give one of the early Sanskrit classifications of plants, discussed in Chapter 6.

The Mahābhārata’s dialogue between Bhṛgu and Bharadvāja (12.177 in the critical edition), in which Bhṛgu infers the five senses of trees from their behaviour, makes the same point in argument. Jain thought classes plants as one-sensed living beings (ekendriya) (Tatia 1994), and the Buddhist monastic code forbids monks to destroy plant life because lay people held plants to be alive. These views are discussed in Chapter 6.

docs.title: 4.2.2 Āyurveda and the vṛkṣāyurveda texts
docs.text: The medical texts classify plants by form, habitat and use, and they treat plants as bodies made of the five elements (pañcabhūta), with tastes (rasa) and qualities that affect the human body (see Chapter 6 and Volume 13). The vṛkṣāyurveda authors went a step further and treated the plant itself as a patient. Its body is governed, like a human body, by the three doṣas, vāta, pitta and kapha, and it can be diagnosed and treated accordingly. In Surapāla this is a practical framework, not a metaphysical claim (Sadhale 1996).

docs.title: 4.2.3 Modern plant physiology: J. C. Bose
docs.text:
In the early twentieth century the physicist Jagadis Chunder Bose (1858–1937) turned from research on electromagnetic waves to plant physiology. Using sensitive instruments of his own design, he recorded electrical responses of plant tissues to mechanical, electrical, thermal and chemical stimuli. He argued that these responses resembled those of animal nerve and muscle. His Plant Response as a Means of Physiological Investigation (1906) set out these results (Bose 1906), and later works described further instruments such as the crescograph for recording growth. Bose was open about his conviction that living and non-living matter, plants and animals, form a continuum. That conviction drew on his own cultural background as well as on his experiments.

Bose’s work was controversial in his lifetime, and some of his interpretations were not accepted. His central observation, that plants generate and propagate electrical signals, is now part of mainstream plant physiology. Action potentials in sensitive plants and in the Venus fly-trap are well documented, and electrical and chemical signalling within plants is an active field of research. None of this shows that plants have minds or feelings in the human sense. Nor does it vindicate the claims, popular since the 1970s, that plants respond to human emotions, prayers, mantras or music. Those claims have not been established by reliable experiment. The vṛkṣāyurveda texts should be read as belonging to their own philosophical world, not as anticipations of modern plant physiology.

docs.title: 4.3 The Topics of the Texts
docs.text: The following account draws chiefly on Bṛhatsaṃhitā 55 (Bhat 1981), Surapāla (Sadhale 1996) and the Upavanavinoda (Majumdar 1935). Details are given only where they are secure. The texts are not identical, and a statement made in one should not be assumed to hold for all.

docs.title: 4.3.1 Classes of plants
docs.text: Surapāla, following earlier usage, divides plants into four classes. Vanaspati are trees that bear fruit without visible flowers, such as the figs. Druma are trees with flowers and fruit. Latā are creepers, and gulma are shrubs (Sadhale 1996). The scheme is practical: it groups plants by habit, which determines how they are planted and tended. The fig family’s lack of visible flowers is a correct observation, since fig flowers are enclosed within the fruit-like syconium. But there is nothing in the text to suggest that its authors understood fig pollination, and the classification should not be read as an anticipation of modern taxonomy. The history of plant classification in India, from the Vedic and dharmaśāstra lists to the medical lexicons, is treated in Chapter 6.

docs.title: 4.3.2 Choosing the land and the site
docs.text:
The texts begin practical instruction with the land. They use the classical division into jāṅgala (dry, open country), ānūpa (wet, marshy country) and sādhāraṇa (intermediate) land, familiar from the medical texts (Zimmermann 1987). They describe good and bad soils by colour, texture and other qualities, and they recommend preparing the ground before planting (Sadhale 1996; Majumdar 1935). Varāhamihira advises softening the soil and enriching it before planting (Bhat 1981). The broader history of Indian soil concepts is treated in Chapter 7.

The choice of site was not only agronomic. The texts discuss which trees should be planted near the house and in which directions. Following the vāstu literature, they regard certain trees, for instance thorny ones and those with milky sap, as unsuitable near a dwelling. Auspicious trees were to be planted first in a new garden. Such rules combine considerations of shade, safety and convenience with omen lore, and they cannot be neatly separated.

docs.title: 4.3.3 Seeds, cuttings and propagation
docs.text:
The texts describe propagation from seed, from cuttings and from bulbs or rootstocks. Seeds were selected and treated before sowing. The treatments described include soaking in milk, smearing with ghee or cow-dung, and fumigating with the smoke of various substances; the details differ between the texts (Bhat 1981; Sadhale 1996). Some of these treatments are intended to hasten germination, others to protect the seed.

Varāhamihira lists trees that can be raised from cuttings smeared with cow-dung. Among them are the jackfruit, the aśoka, the banana, the rose-apple (jambū), the pomegranate, the grape-vine and the citron (Bhat 1981). Propagation by cuttings and by suckers or divisions of the rootstock is well within the experience of any gardener, and the lists are plausible.

Scholarly Note: Did the texts describe grafting?

It is often said that the vṛkṣāyurveda texts describe cleft grafting, budding, approach grafting and air-layering in the modern sense, but no such systematic account is found in the editions. A few passages have been read as referring to the insertion of a cutting into another plant, or to the joining of plants. But the wording is brief and open to more than one interpretation, and the translators do not present a systematic account of grafting. Grafting was certainly practised in India at later periods, notably for the mango; its history in the earlier period remains to be established. This volume does not credit the Sanskrit texts with grafting techniques that they do not clearly describe.

docs.title: 4.3.4 Planting and spacing
docs.text: Pits are to be dug, prepared and filled with good soil before planting, and young plants protected from sun, wind and animals until established (Sadhale 1996; Majumdar 1935). Varāhamihira gives seasons for transplanting. He also prescribes a spacing between trees: twenty hastas is best, sixteen middling, and twelve the minimum. Trees planted too close, so that their roots touch and intertwine, are said to bear poorly (Bhat 1981). The hasta or cubit was roughly the length of a forearm. These are the distances of a tree garden or orchard, not of a field.

docs.title: 4.3.5 Watering through the seasons
docs.text: Varāhamihira’s watering rule is simple. Newly planted trees are to be watered morning and evening in the hot season, on alternate days in the cold season, and in the rains whenever the soil has dried (Bhat 1981). Surapāla and the Upavanavinoda elaborate on this, adjusting watering to the season, the age of the plant and its kind, and warning against both excess and deficiency (Sadhale 1996; Majumdar 1935). The rule that water should be matched to the season and to the plant is sound horticultural advice, though the texts do not quantify it.

docs.title: 4.3.6 Nourishment and kuṇapajala
docs.text:
The texts recommend a range of nourishing applications. Varāhamihira prescribes watering a tree that fails to fruit with milk, cooled after being boiled with horse gram, black gram, green gram, sesame and barley, to bring abundant flowers and fruit (Bhat 1981). The later texts add manures and liquid preparations of various kinds.

The best known of these is kuṇapajala. The name means “carrion water” (kuṇapa, corpse or carrion; jala, water). In the description given by Surapāla, and in similar terms by the Upavanavinoda, the remains of animals, flesh, fat and marrow, are boiled in water. The liquid is then mixed with further ingredients such as oil-cake, milk and pulses, and left to ferment for some days before being applied to plants (Sadhale 1996; Majumdar 1935). Versions differ in their ingredients, and no single standard recipe can be extracted from the texts; none is given here. The texts recommend the preparation for nourishing trees and promoting flowering and fruiting.

Kuṇapajala is a horticultural preparation of the tree and garden texts. It does not appear in the Kṛṣi-Parāśara, and there is no evidence that it was a standard practice of field agriculture. Its essential ingredient is animal remains, which distinguishes it from modern preparations made only from cow dung and urine, such as the jīvāmṛta of natural farming (Section 20.5). Fermented animal and plant residues are a recognised class of organic manure, and it is unsurprising that such a liquid would feed plants; the effects of any particular modern version are a matter for field trials. Rotting animal matter also carries a risk of pathogens and attracts flies and scavengers, and anyone experimenting with such preparations today should follow modern guidance on handling animal by-products.

docs.title: 4.3.7 Diseases and their treatment
docs.text:
Here the medical model is most visible. Varāhamihira notes that trees exposed to cold, wind and hot sun fall ill. The signs are pale or yellow leaves, the failure of new shoots to grow, the drying of branches and the oozing of sap. The treatment he gives is first to cut away the affected part with a knife, then to apply a paste of viḍaṅga (Embelia ribes), ghee and mud, and to water the tree with milk mixed with water (Bhat 1981).

Surapāla develops this into a fuller scheme (Sadhale 1996). He distinguishes harm from outside, such as insects, frost, wind, fire, lightning, injury by animals and people, from internal disorders arising from the three doṣas. Each doṣa disorder is recognised by its signs, and the treatment follows the logic of human therapeutics. Oily and nourishing applications counter vāta; cool, sweet substances counter pitta; and pungent, bitter or drying preparations counter kapha. Pastes, washes, fumigation and special waterings are all used. The framework allowed the gardener to sort a wide range of symptoms into a small number of types and to choose a treatment by analogy.

Some modern writers have argued that the three doṣa categories correspond to water stress, heat stress and fungal disease. The correspondence is loose at best. The doṣa scheme is a classification of symptoms in the language of humoral medicine, not a theory of causes in the sense of modern plant pathology. The texts knew nothing of fungi, bacteria or viruses as agents of disease. Their treatments are best read as what they are: the empirical and theoretical practice of medieval gardeners, worth studying in its own terms.

docs.title: 4.3.8 Dohada: the cravings of plants
docs.text:
Dohada originally meant the cravings of a pregnant woman, which in Indian custom were to be satisfied for the sake of the child. In Sanskrit poetry the term was transferred to trees. Poetic convention held that certain trees would burst into flower only when their particular “craving” was satisfied, usually by a beautiful woman. The aśoka blossoms when kicked by a young woman’s foot, and the bakula when sprinkled with wine from her mouth. Other trees respond to an embrace, a glance, a song or a laugh. Kālidāsa’s play Mālavikāgnimitra turns on the ritual of the aśoka’s dohada, which the heroine performs. In the Meghadūta the exiled yakṣa describes the aśoka and the bakula in his garden as longing for his wife’s foot and mouth. These are literary conventions (kavisamaya). They were part of courtly culture and may have been enacted in garden festivities, but they are not horticultural observations.

In the horticultural texts the word acquires a more technical sense. Dohada there refers to special nourishing treatments applied to a tree to induce or increase flowering and fruiting, using substances such as milk, honey, ghee, flesh, fish and various plant products (Sadhale 1996; Majumdar 1935). The two senses coexist. Gardeners of royal and wealthy households worked within a culture in which the poetic notion of the tree’s longing was well known, and their manuals recast it as a matter of feeding the tree what it “desired”.

docs.title: 4.3.9 Marvels
docs.text: Both Surapāla and the Upavanavinoda include a section on marvels (adbhuta), procedures said to produce extraordinary effects (Sadhale 1996; Majumdar 1935). They include making a tree flower or fruit out of season, changing the colour of flowers or the taste and fragrance of fruits, making seeds sprout and grow with unusual speed, and producing unusual forms of growth. These are the claims of the texts, and they are reported here as such. Some may reflect real effects of nutrition, pruning or watering on the timing of flowering. Others, such as changing the colour of a flower by watering it with dyed water, are not borne out by plant physiology. There is no reason to suppose that the authors tested them systematically. Such sections were also entertainment for patrons, akin to the marvels of other medieval garden literatures.

docs.title: 4.3.10 Gardens
docs.text:
The vṛkṣāyurveda texts were written for the owners of gardens: kings, nobles, temples, monasteries and wealthy householders. Sanskrit literature distinguishes several kinds, among them the udyāna or upavana (pleasure garden or park), the ārāma (grove or orchard, also used of monastic parks) and the garden attached to the royal women’s quarters, so prominent in court drama. Such gardens combined fruit trees, flowering trees and shrubs, creepers trained on bowers, ponds and tanks with lotuses, and pavilions. The texts’ advice on spacing, on the placing of trees around the house and the water, and on fragrant and ornamental plants serves this kind of garden. Trees that Āyurveda values as medicines, such as neem, bilva, āmalakī and harītakī, appear among those to be planted and tended, and several of them, notably the aśoka, the bilva and the aśvattha, were valued as auspicious garden and temple trees; but the texts give them no special cultivation rules, and their medicinal uses belong to Volume 13 and Chapter 12. The Mānasollāsa describes a royal garden as one of the king’s enjoyments (Shrigondekar 1925). The Persianate garden tradition, with its walled, quartered chārbāgh, arrived later and is discussed in Chapter 18 (Moynihan 1979).

The people who actually did the work rarely appear in these texts. Gardening and the supply of flowers and garlands were the hereditary occupation of particular communities, known in Sanskrit as mālākāra (“garland-makers”) and in the modern languages by names such as Mālī. Their practical knowledge was transmitted within families and is largely unrecorded. The treatises represent the learned, written side of a craft whose main bearers were not authors (see Section 5.2).

docs.title: 4.4 Reading Vṛkṣāyurveda Today
docs.text:
The vṛkṣāyurveda texts are valuable historical documents. They show that by the late first millennium CE there was in India a written tradition of horticulture that drew on long practical experience. They record sensible practices such as soil preparation, propagation by cuttings, adequate spacing, seasonal watering, manuring and the cutting out of diseased wood. They also show how the conceptual tools of medicine were used to organise knowledge about plants. The same texts contain ritual prescriptions, omen lore and marvels. For their authors these were not separate from the practical advice, and a modern reader should not pick out the practical parts and present them as the whole.

Several cautions follow from the state of the sources. The number of texts is small, and only Surapāla’s is a substantial independent treatise. The identification of many plant names is uncertain, and different translators identify the same Sanskrit name with different species. Where modern experiments on traditional preparations have been carried out, they must be judged on their own merits, by the ordinary standards of agricultural research. Their results tell us about the modern preparation, not about what a medieval author knew.

The revival of interest in these texts since the 1990s, led in large part by the editions of the Asian Agri-History Foundation, has made them accessible to farmers and gardeners as well as historians. Some organic growers have adopted preparations inspired by them. That is a legitimate modern development, discussed in Chapter 20. But it should not be confused with the historical question of what the texts say, which can be answered only by reading them in critical editions and translations.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Vṛkṣāyurveda, the science of the life of trees, is attested as a term in the Arthaśāstra and survives in a small group of texts, from chapter 55 of the Bṛhatsaṃhitā (6th century) and Surapāla (c. 10th–11th century) to the Upavanavinoda (1363) and the Viśvavallabha (16th century); the so-called Vṛkṣāyurveda of Parāśara is of disputed authenticity. Resting on the widely shared view that plants are living beings, the texts treat the plant as a patient and deal with land, propagation, spacing, watering, nourishment (including the animal-based kuṇapajala), diseases classified by the doṣas, dohada, marvels and gardens. Bose’s experiments belong to modern plant physiology and do not confirm the texts’ metaphysics. Read critically, the texts document a real horticultural tradition written for garden owners and resting on the unrecorded skill of gardeners.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Sadhale (1996) translates Surapāla’s Vṛkṣāyurveda, and Majumdar (1935) the Upavanavinoda. Varāhamihira’s chapter on trees is in Bhat (1981). For Bose’s experimental work see Bose (1906). Ayangarya (2006) and Sadhale (2004) translate the plant sections of the Lokopakāra and the Viśvavallabha. Randhawa (1980) surveys horticulture within the general history of Indian agriculture.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Gardens, Flowers and Aromatics
docs.text: The garden texts of the previous chapter teach how to raise and tend plants; they say little about what the gardens produced or what was done with it. This chapter turns from the treatises to the products. Flowers were needed every day for worship, adornment, welcome and festivity; they were grown and strung by particular communities and, in the south, in temple gardens supported by endowments. Fragrant woods, roots, resins and flowers, and a few animal products, were the materials of a perfumery that Varāhamihira already treats as a branch of learning and that survives in the attar distilleries of Kannauj. The betel leaf and the areca nut, grown in specialised gardens, made the quid that was offered at every social occasion. The botanical identity of many of the Sanskrit names involved is uncertain, and the chapter gives the usual identifications with that caution. Plants valued chiefly as medicines are treated in Chapter 12, and the sacred trees in Chapter 11.

docs.title: 5.1 Flowers in Indian Culture and Cultivation
docs.text:
Many of the trees, shrubs and creepers that the vṛkṣāyurveda texts teach the gardener to tend (Chapter 4) were grown for their flowers. Flowers (puṣpa) were needed every day and in quantity: for worship, for personal adornment, for garlands given in welcome and in honour, for the decoration of houses and festivals, and as the raw material of perfumes. In the common Hindu form of worship with five offerings (pañcopacāra), the deity receives scent (gandha), flowers (puṣpa), incense (dhūpa), a lamp (dīpa) and food (naivedya). Three of the five thus come from the garden and the perfumer. The eightfold worship (aṣṭaprakārī pūjā) of many Jain temples likewise includes sandalwood paste, flowers and incense, although some Jain communities avoid offering fresh flowers out of concern for the life in them. Flowers are offered at Buddhist shrines, and garlands and sheets of roses are laid on the graves of Sufi saints. The demand for flowers in India has therefore always been large, steady and seasonal. It supported specialised growers, garland-makers and sellers (Section 5.2).

This section surveys some of the flowers that matter most in Indian culture. The botanical identity of Sanskrit flower names is often uncertain. A single name may have been applied to different plants in different regions and periods, and one plant may have many names, some of them poetic epithets. Table 5.1 gives the usual identifications, which should be read with that caution. The sacred trees valued chiefly for themselves rather than for their flowers, such as the aśvattha, the banyan and the bilva, are treated in Chapter 11.

Table 5.1. Some flowers of Sanskrit literature and their usual identifications. Identifications of older names are often uncertain. The poets’ flower of the moon mallikā Arabian jasmine, Jasminum sambac Hindi mogrā, bela; Tamil malli mālatī, jāti Usually Jasminum grandiflorum Identity of mālatī debated yūthikā Jasminum auriculatum Hindi juhī campaka Magnolia champaca (syn. Michelia champaca) Not the American frangipani, also called “champa” aśoka Saraca asoca Not the avenue tree Polyalthia longifolia bakula Mimusops elengi Small flowers that keep their scent when dry kadamba Usually Neolamarckia cadamba The name may cover more than one tree pārijāta, śephālikā Night jasmine, Nyctanthes arbor-tristis The mythical pārijāta is not necessarily this plant ketakī Screw-pine, Pandanus odorifer Source of kewṛā water and attar

docs.title: 5.1.1 Lotus and water-lily
docs.text:
No flower is more important in Indian culture than the lotus. The Sanskrit names padma, kamala, aravinda, paṅkaja (“mud-born”) and many others denote the sacred lotus, Nelumbo nucifera. Its large pink or white flowers and round leaves stand above the water on long stalks. The English word “lotus” is also used for the water-lilies (Nymphaea), whose leaves and flowers usually float on the surface. In Sanskrit these are utpala, especially the blue nīlotpala, and kumuda, the white water-lily that opens at night. The two genera are not closely related; botanists place Nelumbo in a family of its own, far from the water-lilies. Sanskrit poets also kept them apart. By convention the kamala opens to the sun and closes at dusk, the kumuda opens at moonrise, and the two are paired as the flowers of day and night.

The lotus is everywhere in Indian religious art. Lotus medallions cover the railings of the early Buddhist stūpas at Bharhut and Sanchi. There the goddess Śrī-Lakṣmī is shown on a lotus, bathed by two elephants, in the motif later called Gaja-Lakṣmī. In Hindu iconography Brahmā is born from a lotus that rises from Viṣṇu’s navel, and Lakṣmī holds lotuses in her hands. Hindu, Buddhist and Jain images alike stand or sit on lotus pedestals. Because the plant rises clean from the mud, it became a symbol of purity in the midst of worldly life. The Bhagavad Gītā (5.10) compares the person who acts without attachment to a lotus leaf, which water does not wet. The water-repellent surface of the lotus leaf is real, and botanists now speak of the “lotus effect”. The Gītā uses an everyday observation as a moral image; it does not offer a theory of surfaces.

Lotuses and water-lilies were grown in the tanks and ponds of gardens, palaces and temples, and the garden texts include water plants among those to be planted. The lotus was also a food plant. Its rhizome (bisa, mṛṇāla) and seeds have long been eaten, and both are still sold in Indian markets (Achaya 1998). The lotus stem is a familiar vegetable in Kashmir, where it is called nadru. The puffed “fox nut” of north Indian snack foods, makhānā, is often called a lotus seed but comes from a different water plant, the prickly water-lily Euryale ferox. It is cultivated in the ponds of Mithila in north Bihar, much of it by the Mallāh, a community of boatmen and fishers.

docs.title: 5.1.2 Jasmines
docs.text:
The jasmines (Jasminum) are the flowers of the garland and of the hair. Sanskrit literature distinguishes several kinds by name, but the names are hard to pin to species. Mallikā is generally identified with Jasminum sambac, the “Arabian” jasmine. Despite its English name it is a plant of South and Southeast Asian cultivation, a shrub with intensely fragrant white flowers, single or double, that open in the evening (Hindi mogrā or bela, Tamil malli). Mālatī and jāti are usually taken to be the large-flowered jasmine, J. grandiflorum (Hindi camelī), though other identifications of mālatī have been proposed. Yūthikā is the juhī, J. auriculatum. Kunda, a flower of the cold season whose whiteness poets compare to teeth and to the moon, is commonly identified with a jasmine such as J. multiflorum, but the identification is not certain.

Jasmine is grown commercially on small plots, mostly by smallholders. The buds are picked early in the morning, much of the picking being done by women, so that they open on the day of sale. Buds are strung tightly on thread to make the hair ornaments called veṇī or gajrā and the garlands of temples and weddings. In Tamil Nadu jasmine strings are still sold by the muḻam, the length of a forearm, the same unit as the hasta by which Varāhamihira measured the spacing of trees (Section 4.3). The jasmine of the Madurai region is especially prized and has been registered as a geographical indication.

docs.title: 5.1.3 Flowering trees
docs.text:
The campaka, Magnolia champaca (formerly Michelia champaca), is a tall evergreen tree with fragrant cream, yellow or orange flowers. It was planted in gardens and by temples, and its flowers were worn in the hair and used in perfumes. A familiar poetic convention holds that bees do not visit the campaka. The name “champa” is now also given in many Indian languages to the frangipani or temple tree (Plumeria). This is a small tree of tropical America, brought to India after 1500, which is now planted around temples, tombs and cemeteries across the country. Older texts that mention the campaka cannot refer to it.

The aśoka, Saraca asoca, is a small evergreen tree with dense clusters of orange to scarlet flowers. Its name means “without sorrow”. It is the tree whose blossoming, in poetic convention, is brought on by the touch of a young woman’s foot (Section 4.3.8). In the Rāmāyaṇa Sītā is held captive in Rāvaṇa’s aśoka grove in Laṅkā. The true aśoka should not be confused with the tall, narrow Polyalthia longifolia. That tree is widely planted along avenues and is often called “ashoka” today, but it has inconspicuous flowers and no place in the classical literature. Because the bark of Saraca asoca is collected for medicinal use, the tree has become scarce in the wild in parts of its range (see Chapter 12).

The bakula (Mimusops elengi, Tamil makiḻam) bears small, star-shaped cream flowers. They keep their fragrance for a long time after drying and are strung into garlands. In poetic convention the bakula flowers when sprinkled with wine from a woman’s mouth. The kadamba, usually identified with Neolamarckia cadamba, has globular orange flower-heads that open with the rains. It is the tree of the monsoon in Sanskrit poetry and of Kṛṣṇa’s youth in Vraja (Chapter 11). As with many tree names, kadamba may have been applied to more than one species.

The pārijāta of everyday use is the night jasmine, Nyctanthes arbor-tristis, also called śephālikā (Hindi harsiṅgār, Bengali śiuli). Its white flowers with orange tubes open at night and fall at dawn, carpeting the ground beneath the tree. Fallen flowers are gathered for worship, and the orange corolla tubes were used as a yellow-orange dye. The name also belongs to a mythical tree, one of the treasures that emerged at the churning of the ocean and which grew in Indra’s paradise. In the Harivaṃśa and the Viṣṇu Purāṇa Kṛṣṇa carries it off from heaven for his wife Satyabhāmā. The mythical pārijāta need not be the night jasmine. Some texts and regions give the name to the coral tree (Erythrina), and the identification varies.

Other flowers have special ritual uses. The red hibiscus (japā, Hibiscus rosa-sinensis) is offered to Kālī and other goddesses, especially in Bengal. According to a Purāṇic story, the fragrant ketakī (screw-pine, Pandanus odorifer) may not be offered to Śiva, because it once bore false witness on behalf of Brahmā. The oleander (karavīra, Nerium oleander), red or white, is widely offered in worship, although every part of the plant is poisonous.

docs.title: 5.1.4 Newcomers: marigold, tuberose and the rose
docs.text:
Some of the flowers most closely associated with India today are not Indian in origin. The marigold, which supplies most of the orange and yellow garlands of temples, weddings, festivals and funerals, belongs to the genus Tagetes, native to Mexico and Central America. The large African marigold (T. erecta) and the smaller French marigold (T. patula) both came from the Americas. Their English names are misnomers. They reached India after 1500, most probably through Portuguese and other European shipping, and became indispensable within a few centuries. They are easy to grow, flower over a long season, and are cheap. The marigold (Hindi gendā) is now among the most widely grown flower crops in India. Since the plant was unknown in India before the sixteenth century, “marigold” in translations of older Sanskrit texts is a mistranslation. The tuberose (Polianthes tuberosa, Hindi rajnīgandhā), whose night-scented white spikes are used in garlands and perfumery, is also Mexican in origin. Its history in India likewise begins after contact with the Americas.

The rose has an older but similar history. Wild roses grow in the Himalaya, and Sanskrit lexicons contain names such as śatapatrī, “hundred-petalled”, that some lexicographers take to mean a rose. But śatapatra is also a name of the lotus, and the rose has no place in classical Sanskrit poetry comparable to that of the lotus or jasmine. The rose became a garden flower of the first rank in India through the Persianate world. In Persian poetry the rose (gul) and the nightingale (bulbul) are the central images of love. In the gardens of the Sultanate and Mughal periods (Chapter 18) roses were planted in quantity, among them the damask rose (Rosa damascena), the rose of perfumers. The Hindi gulāb comes from Persian gul-āb, “rose-water”, a name transferred from the distillate to the flower. Rose-water, rose attar and gulkand, a preserve of rose petals in sugar, became part of the courtly culture of northern India. Rose growing for distillation became established around particular towns, among them Kannauj and Ghazipur in Uttar Pradesh and Pushkar in Rajasthan. The naturalistic flowering plants carved and inlaid in Mughal buildings of Shāh Jahān’s reign, including the Taj Mahal, show how important flowers had become in imperial imagery.

docs.title: 5.1.5 Flowers in poetry
docs.text:
Flowers form a large part of the conventions of Sanskrit poetry (kāvya). Kāma, the god of love, shoots arrows made of flowers. In a commonly cited list the five arrows are the lotus (aravinda), the aśoka, the mango blossom (cūta), the navamallikā jasmine and the blue water-lily (nīlotpala). Each season has its flowers. Spring (vasanta) brings the mango blossom, the aśoka, the red kiṃśuka (palāśa, Butea monosperma) and the bees maddened by them. The rains bring the kadamba and the ketakī; autumn brings the lotus-filled ponds and the saptacchada (Alstonia scholaris); the cold season brings the kunda and the lodhra. The Ṛtusaṃhāra, a poem on the six seasons attributed to Kālidāsa (the attribution has been doubted), is built around such pairings. The bee (bhramara, ṣaṭpada) drawn from flower to flower is the stock image of the fickle lover. The birds that accompany these flowers in poetry, the haṃsa, the cakravāka and the kokila, are discussed in Chapter 17.

The Tamil tradition has its own system. The five landscapes (tiṇai) of Saṅgam love poetry (Chapter 2) take their names from characteristic flowers or plants. Kuṟiñci is usually identified with Strobilanthes kunthiana, a shrub of the southern hills that flowers en masse only once in about twelve years. Mullai is a jasmine. Neytal is usually taken to be a water-lily, and marutam and pālai are trees whose identifications are debated. The poems use the flowers to signal both a landscape and a phase of love. These conventions are literary, but they rest on close acquaintance with real plants: their seasons, habitats, colours and scents.

docs.title: 5.2 Garland-makers, Flower Markets and Temple Gardens
docs.text:
Behind the flowers of worship and poetry stood the people who grew, picked and strung them. The Sanskrit mālākāra, “garland-maker”, names a recognised occupation in Sanskrit literature and appears often in Buddhist and Jain narrative literature, where garland-makers sell flowers in the market and offer them to the Buddha or to Jain teachers. In the modern languages the corresponding communities are known by names such as Mālī (in much of northern and western India), Mālākār (in Bengal and Assam) and Phūlmālī. Like other occupational groups they were ranked within the caste order. Their position varied by region, generally among the cultivating and service castes, below the landholding castes for whom they often worked. The Mālīs were also market gardeners, growing vegetables as well as flowers on irrigated plots near towns. The social reformer Jotirao Phule (1827–1890) came from a Mālī family of Pune whose surname is said to derive from their work supplying flowers (phūl). He made the condition of the cultivating and labouring castes central to his critique of caste. In Bengal Mālākār craftsmen also make the white śolā-pith ornaments used on images of deities and at weddings (see Volume 17, Śilpa–Kāru).

Flowers were sold daily in town markets, and the flower-seller is a stock figure of Sanskrit and vernacular literature. Large wholesale markets, such as Mallick Ghat beside the Howrah Bridge in Kolkata and the Dadar market in Mumbai, open before dawn and continue an old pattern, linking the growers of the surrounding countryside with retailers outside temples and in residential streets. The volume of flowers used in temples has itself become a problem, since used offerings are often thrown into rivers; some temples and private enterprises now collect them for composting or for making incense. In Delhi, the festival of the flower-sellers, Phūlwāloṃ kī Sair, honours this trade. Large fans of flowers (paṅkhā) are carried in procession and offered both at the Sufi shrine of Quṭb al-Dīn Bakhtiyār Kākī and at the Yogmāyā temple in Mehrauli. According to the usual account the festival began in the early nineteenth century, in the reign of the Mughal emperor Akbar Shāh II, in fulfilment of a vow; it was revived after Independence.

Temples needed a constant supply of flowers, leaves and garlands, and many maintained their own flower gardens, called nandavana (Tamil nantavaṉam), after Nandana, the garden of Indra’s heaven. South Indian temple inscriptions of the Cōḻa, Pāṇḍya, Vijayanagara and later periods frequently record endowments for this purpose: grants of land or money to maintain a flower garden, to pay gardeners and garland-makers, to dig or maintain a well or tank to water the garden, or to supply a fixed quantity of flowers and garlands for daily worship and festivals. Flower-growing was thus an institution with its own staff and revenues, alongside the temple’s kitchens and lamps. Temple gardens also figure in devotional tradition. According to the hagiographies of the Tamil Vaiṣṇava saints, Periyāḻvār tended a garden at Srivilliputtur and made garlands for the god there. His daughter Āṇṭāḷ, who was found as an infant in the garden, secretly wore the garlands before they were offered. Hence her epithet Cūṭikkoṭutta Cuṭarkkoṭi, “the radiant creeper who gave (the garland) after wearing it”. Toṇṭaraṭippoṭi Āḻvār is likewise said to have kept a flower garden for the temple at Srirangam. These are hagiographical traditions, not historical records, but they show how closely the work of the garden was bound up with devotion.
