The vṛkṣāyurveda texts say little about flower farming as a trade; their concern is the garden of a patron. But their advice applied equally to temple and market gardens, and some of their marvels, such as changing a flower’s colour or scent (Section 4.3.9), were plainly aimed at the flower garden.

docs.title: 5.3 Perfumery and Aromatics
docs.text: Scent mattered greatly in Indian culture. In the Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika philosophical schools smell (gandha) is the distinctive quality of earth, one of the five elements, and in ordinary life fragrance marked purity, festivity, wealth and the divine presence. Bad smells marked impurity and death. Perfumes were used on the body, in the hair, on clothes, in the mouth, in the house and in worship. Many of their ingredients came from plants grown in gardens or gathered from forests, and some came from animals. James McHugh’s study of smell in Indian religion and culture is the best general guide to this subject (McHugh 2012). The ingredients mentioned in the texts and their trade across the Indian Ocean also concern Volume 19, Vāṇijya and Samudra, and the history of distillation concerns Volume 14, Rasāyana.

docs.title: 5.3.1 Gandhayukti: the art of combining scents
docs.text:
The Sanskrit term for perfumery is gandhayukti, “the combining of scents”. Lists of the sixty-four arts (kalā) expected of a cultivated person, such as the list in the Kāmasūtra, include it. Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā has a chapter of that name (Bhat 1981). It gives preparations for scenting the hair, the body, the mouth and clothes, and for incense to perfume the house, compounded from a set of aromatic ingredients in stated proportions. Historians of mathematics have noticed this chapter because in one passage Varāhamihira counts how many different perfumes can be made by combining ingredients drawn from a fixed set, an early instance of combinatorial reasoning in Sanskrit. The chapter is a reminder that the Bṛhatsaṃhitā, the source of the oldest systematic vṛkṣāyurveda (Section 4.1.1), treated the garden and the products made from it as one field. Later, more specialised works on perfumery survive in Sanskrit manuscripts, and McHugh discusses this literature (McHugh 2012).

At the Mughal court perfumery was organised as a department of the imperial household. Abū’l-Faẓl’s Āʾīn-i Akbarī describes the imperial perfumery, lists perfumes and their prices, and gives the composition of several compound scents (Abū’l-Faẓl 1873).

docs.title: 5.3.2 Sandalwood
docs.text:
Sandalwood (candana, Santalum album) is the pre-eminent Indian aromatic. The tree is small and evergreen, native to the dry forests of the southern peninsula, especially Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. It is a hemiparasite: although it has green leaves, its roots attach to the roots of neighbouring plants and draw water and nutrients from them. Young plants therefore need host plants to grow well, a fact that long frustrated attempts to raise sandalwood in pure plantations. The fragrant part is the heartwood and the roots of mature trees, from which the essential oil is distilled. In Sanskrit poetry sandalwood is malayaja, “born on the Malaya mountains” of the southern Western Ghats, and its paste was smeared on the body in the hot season for its cooling feel. Sandal paste marks the forehead in worship, sandalwood is burned on funeral pyres by those who can afford it, and Parsis offer sticks of sandalwood to the sacred fire. The red sanders (raktacandana, Pterocarpus santalinus) of the southern Eastern Ghats is an unrelated tree. Its wood is red and nearly odourless, and it is valued for dye and for timber.

Sandalwood was traded from south India to the Middle East, East Asia and Europe for many centuries. In Mysore it became a state monopoly: Tipu Sultan is said to have declared it a royal tree, and under the later Mysore government and British rule its felling and sale were tightly controlled. In 1916, when the First World War cut off the export of sandalwood to Germany for distillation, the Mysore government set up its own sandalwood oil factory at Bangalore, and a soap factory soon followed; its sandalwood soap became widely known. Watt’s Dictionary gives a full account of the sandalwood trade and its regulation in the late nineteenth century (Watt 1889).

In the twentieth century wild sandalwood declined sharply. The causes were over-exploitation, large-scale smuggling encouraged by state control and high prices, the loss of forest habitat, and a disease called spike, now attributed to a phytoplasma. Santalum album has been listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. Since the early 2000s Karnataka and Tamil Nadu have relaxed the rules that made all sandalwood the property of the state, in order to encourage growing on private land. Meanwhile, plantations of Indian sandalwood in northern Australia have become a major source of supply. Sandalwood is often cited as a case in which a state monopoly, intended to protect a valuable resource, contributed to its depletion by giving the people on whose land the trees grew no reason to protect them.

docs.title: 5.3.3 Agarwood, musk and camphor
docs.text:
Agaru (agarwood, aloeswood, the ʿūd of Arabic perfumery) is the resin-laden heartwood of trees of the genus Aquilaria. In India the chief source is A. malaccensis (syn. A. agallocha) of the north-eastern forests. Healthy wood is pale and scentless. The dark, fragrant resin forms only in response to wounding and infection by fungi, so that only a small proportion of trees in the wild contain it. In Sanskrit poetry agaru smoke scents palaces and the hair of women, and kṛṣṇāguru, “black agaru”, is a mark of luxury. Assam, and the town of Hojai in particular, is the main Indian centre of agarwood distillation and trade. Wild trees have been heavily over-harvested, and Aquilaria species are listed in Appendix II of CITES, which regulates international trade. Growers in Assam and elsewhere now cultivate the trees and induce resin formation artificially.

Musk (kastūrī, also mṛganābhi, “deer’s navel”) is an animal product. It is the secretion of a gland in the abdomen of the male musk deer (Moschus spp.) of the Himalaya. The gland was removed from deer that were hunted for it, and musk was among the most precious ingredients of Indian, Persian, Arab and Chinese perfumery. The image of the musk deer roaming the forest in search of a scent that comes from its own body is a familiar one in Hindi devotional poetry, often attributed to Kabīr. Musk deer are now protected under Indian wildlife law, and international trade in musk is controlled under CITES (see Chapter 16). Modern perfumery uses synthetic musks.

Camphor (karpūra) is burned in the āratī lamp, especially in south Indian temples, and was a prized ingredient of courtly betel quids. Two different natural products are involved. The camphor of early Indian Ocean trade came largely from Dryobalanops aromatica, a tall tree of Sumatra and Borneo in whose trunk crystals of borneol form; it is known in Hindi as bhīmsenī kapūr. The common camphor of later trade was obtained by distilling the wood of the camphor laurel, Cinnamomum camphora, a tree of China, Taiwan and Japan. Neither tree is native to India. Most camphor sold today is synthetic, made from turpentine. Camphor is poisonous if swallowed, particularly to children (see the safety note in Section 5.4).

docs.title: 5.3.4 Vetiver
docs.text: Vetiver (uśīra; Hindi khas) is a tall, tufted grass, Chrysopogon zizanioides (syn. Vetiveria zizanioides), with a deep, dense mass of fragrant roots. In north India the roots were woven into screens (khas kī ṭaṭṭī) hung in doorways and windows in the hot season and kept wet. Air blowing through them was cooled by evaporation and scented. The roots are distilled for an essential oil, and khas attar and the more concentrated rūḥ-i khas are products of Kannauj. The Hindi word khaskhas, for poppy seed, is unrelated and should not be confused with khas. Because its roots go deep and its clumps form dense hedges, vetiver has also been promoted since the late twentieth century for soil and water conservation on slopes and field boundaries (see Chapter 7).

docs.title: 5.3.5 The attar distillers of Kannauj
docs.text:
The word attar (Arabic and Persian ʿiṭr, “perfume”) denotes in India a natural perfume made by distilling flowers, herbs, spices or woods. The distillate is traditionally collected in a base of sandalwood oil. Kannauj, on the Ganga in Uttar Pradesh and an ancient city (Kānyakubja) that was the capital of the Maukharīs, of Harṣa and later of the Gurjara-Pratihāras, is the best-known centre of the craft and is often called India’s perfume capital. Local tradition gives its perfumery a very long history. The reliable record, however, belongs mainly to the Mughal and later periods, and the industry in its present form took shape in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Kannauj perfume has been registered as a geographical indication.

The Kannauj method is known as deg-bhapkā, after its two main vessels (Figure 5.1). Flowers or other raw material are loaded with water into a large copper still (deg), set into a brick hearth and fired with wood or cow-dung cakes. The lid is sealed with clay. The vapour passes through a bamboo pipe into a copper receiver (bhapkā) that already contains sandalwood oil and stands in a tank of cool water. The aromatic vapour condenses into the oil, which absorbs the scent. The still is recharged with fresh flowers and the process repeated, often over several days, until the oil is saturated. The perfumed oil is then separated from the water. It was traditionally stored in bottles of leather (kuppī) that allowed residual water to escape.

Figure 5.1. The deg-bhapkā method of the attar distillers of Kannauj, schematic and not to scale. Flowers and water are heated in a sealed copper still; the vapour passes through a bamboo pipe into a copper receiver standing in cool water, where it condenses into a charge of sandalwood oil (Section 5.3.5).

The range of Kannauj attars reflects the flowers and aromatics of north India. They include rose (gulāb), several jasmines (camelī, motiyā, bela), kewṛā from the screw-pine (much of it grown and distilled in the Ganjam district of coastal Odisha), henna flowers (hinā), vetiver (khas) and compound attars such as shamāmā, made from many herbs and spices. The most remarkable is miṭṭī attar, “earth attar”. It is distilled from discs of baked clay to capture the smell of rain on dry earth, the smell that is everywhere associated with the first monsoon showers. The industry has faced severe pressures: the scarcity and cost of sandalwood oil, the competition of synthetic perfumes, and the substitution of cheaper base oils. It survives on a reduced scale, supplying attars for personal use, for religious purposes and as flavourings for tobacco and pān products.

docs.title: 5.3.6 Rose attar and the Mughal court
docs.text: Rose-water made by distillation was an old product of the Persian world and was familiar in India long before the Mughals. Rose attar, the essential oil of the rose, has a more famous story. Jahāngīr records in his memoirs that the attar of roses was discovered in his reign by the mother of his wife Nūr Jahān. According to him, she noticed an oily film on the surface of rose-water as it was being prepared and collected it. The emperor rewarded her and gave the perfume his own name (Thackston 1999). Later retellings credit Nūr Jahān herself, sometimes with the oil collecting on the surface of a rose-water bath. The story should be read as court tradition. An emperor’s memoirs are good evidence that the discovery was claimed and celebrated at his court. They are not proof that rose oil had never been separated before, and the history of rose oil in the wider Persian and Ottoman world is a separate question.

docs.title: 5.3.7 Incense
docs.text: Incense (dhūpa), burned in worship of many faiths and in homes, is made mostly from plant resins and aromatic woods and roots: guggulu (Commiphora wightii, see Chapter 12), the resin of the sāla tree (Shorea robusta, Hindi rāl), the resin of the Indian frankincense tree (śallakī, Boswellia serrata), benzoin (lobān, widely burned in Muslim households and at Sufi shrines; in India the name usually denotes the resin of Southeast Asian Styrax trees, although Arabic lubān means frankincense), sandalwood, agaru, and roots such as jaṭāmāṃsī. The incense stick (agarbattī, a name usually explained as “agaru wick”) is made by coating a thin bamboo stick with a paste of charcoal, a binding material and aromatics. The rolling is commonly done by hand, as piece-rate home-work, much of it by women. Bengaluru and Mysore are major centres of the industry, which is discussed further in Volume 17, Śilpa–Kāru. Burning incense produces fine smoke particles, and heavy indoor use is a recognised source of indoor air pollution.

docs.title: 5.4 Tāmbūla: Betel Leaf and Areca Nut
docs.text:
The chewing of betel quid, tāmbūla (Hindi pān, from Sanskrit parṇa, “leaf”), has been a part of Indian social life for well over a thousand years. It is shared with much of South and Southeast Asia and parts of the Pacific. The basic quid has three ingredients. The leaf is that of the betel vine (Piper betle, nāgavallī; Tamil veṟṟilai). The nut, commonly called betel nut, is the seed of the areca palm (Areca catechu, pūga, guvāka; Hindi supārī). The lime (cūrṇa) is slaked lime made by burning shells or limestone. A paste of kattha (catechu, khadira), the concentrated extract of the heartwood of Senegalia catechu (syn. Acacia catechu), is often added, together with spices such as cardamom and clove and, in the courtly quid, camphor (Achaya 1998).

Tāmbūla was offered to guests and at the end of meals. It was given by a king to a courtier as a mark of favour, and the Hindi idiom bīṛā uṭhānā, “to take up the betel roll”, means to accept a challenge. Betel leaves and areca nuts are offered in Hindu worship and play a part in betrothal and marriage rites; in south India tāmbūlam is given to guests as they leave a ceremony. In Assam tāmol-pān, areca and betel, are offered as the first gesture of hospitality. The medical texts discuss the quid as a digestive and a breath freshener after meals. Those claims belong to Volume 13 and are not endorsed here (see the safety note below).

docs.title: 5.4.1 The betel garden
docs.text:
The betel vine is a perennial creeper of the pepper family. It is grown for its leaves, which must be tender and unblemished. It is propagated from stem cuttings and needs shade, humidity, shelter from wind and frequent watering. In north and eastern India it is grown in enclosed structures known in Hindi as barejā or barej. These are low frames of bamboo, reed and thatch, open to light but closed against sun and wind, under which the vines are trained on reed or split-bamboo supports along raised beds and drainage trenches. In south India and in the homegardens of Kerala and the Konkan, vines are often trained on the trunks of areca palms or on live supports such as Sesbania and Erythrina, so that the two components of the quid grow together (see Chapter 10). Watt’s Dictionary records the cultivation and trade of betel and areca as they were in the late nineteenth century (Watt 1889).

Betel cultivation was the hereditary occupation of specific castes. Colonial ethnographers recorded them as the Bārui of Bengal and the Barai of northern India; many Barai use the surname Caurasiyā. The sellers of the prepared leaf were the Tamolī or Tāmbolī, whose name derives from tāmbūlika, “betel-seller”. These occupational identities, like others, were never as rigid as the census categories implied, and many members of these communities have long done other work. But the association of particular castes with the barejā reflects how specialised betel growing was. It required capital for the structure, continuous labour and a careful knowledge of the vine’s needs.

The areca palm, probably of Southeast Asian origin, is grown on a large scale in coastal and hill Karnataka, Kerala, Assam and the north-east. India is one of the world’s largest producers and consumers of areca nut. Tobacco, introduced from the Americas from the sixteenth century onwards (see Chapter 9), was soon added to the quid in many regions. In the late twentieth century packaged mixtures of areca, lime, flavourings and tobacco, sold as gutkhā and pān masālā, spread rapidly. They greatly increased the consumption of areca and tobacco among the young and the poor.

Areca nut, betel quid, camphor and oleander

The International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies betel quid with or without tobacco, and areca nut itself, as carcinogenic to humans (IARC Working Group on the Evaluation of Carcinogenic Risks to Humans 2004). Habitual chewing is a major cause of oral cancer in South and Southeast Asia and of oral submucous fibrosis, a disabling, precancerous scarring of the mouth. The addition of tobacco increases the risks further. This section describes the cultural history of tāmbūla; nothing in it should be taken as a recommendation to chew betel quid, areca or pān masālā. Camphor is poisonous if swallowed, and small amounts can cause seizures in children. Camphor tablets used for worship should be kept out of their reach. All parts of the oleander (karavīra) are poisonous and must not be eaten. Attars, essential oils and incense are not medicines, and no therapeutic claims are made for them in this chapter.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Gardens supplied the flowers of worship and poetry — the lotus and water-lilies, the jasmines, the campaka, aśoka, bakula, kadamba and pārijāta, and after 1500 the American marigold and tuberose and the Persianate rose. They were grown, strung and sold by Mālī and other garland-makers and, in the south, in temple flower gardens supported by endowments. Perfumery, which Varāhamihira treats as the art of gandhayukti, drew on sandalwood, agarwood, musk, camphor, vetiver and flowers, and survives in the deg-bhapkā distilleries of Kannauj; several of its raw materials have been depleted by over-exploitation. Betel leaf and areca nut, grown by specialised castes, make the tāmbūla quid, central to Indian sociability, but areca nut is a recognised human carcinogen.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: McHugh (2012) is the essential study of perfume and smell in Indian religion and culture. Achaya (1998) covers the history of betel, flowers used as food and many aromatics, and Watt (1889) records the cultivation and trade of sandalwood, betel and areca in the late nineteenth century. For the Mughal perfumery and flower lists see Abū’l-Faẓl (1873).

docs.title: Chapter 6: Ordering the Plant World: Classification in Indian Traditions
docs.text:
Every community that lives with plants sorts them: into trees and grasses, food and poison, plants of the wet field and plants of the dry scrub. What differs from one tradition to another is the purpose of the sorting and the criteria used. The Indian sources discussed in this chapter classify plants for several distinct purposes. Vedic poets praise plants and name them in ritual; the Dharmaśāstra places them in a hierarchy of living beings shaped by karma; the physicians order them by growth habit, by the parts that are used, and above all by their taste and action on the body; the lexicographers of the nighaṇṭu tradition collect their names; Jain and Buddhist monastic thinkers ask whether plants are alive and how far they may be harmed; and farmers, herders and forest communities sort them in the languages of everyday work. None of these systems was an attempt at a universal natural taxonomy of the kind that European botany developed from the seventeenth century, and it is unhelpful either to judge them by that standard or to claim that they “anticipated” it.

The chapter follows these strands roughly in chronological order, then turns to the encounter between Indian plant knowledge and European botany, from Hortus Malabaricus to the colonial economic dictionaries, and ends with a historically framed comparison with Linnaean taxonomy. The Vṛkṣāyurveda texts, with their own short classifications, are treated in Chapter 4; medicinal plants as plants are the subject of Chapter 12; and the therapeutic doctrine of dravyaguṇa belongs to Volume 13, Āyurveda.

docs.title: 6.1 The Vedic Vocabulary of Plants
docs.text:
The Ṛgveda (core c. 1500–1200 BCE) does not offer a classification in any formal sense, but it already has a stable set of words for kinds of vegetation. Oṣadhi (later also auṣadhi) denotes herbs and plants in general, especially those valued for healing, and in time gives the ordinary word for medicine, auṣadha. Vanaspati, “lord of the forest”, is a large tree; in ritual contexts the word can also denote the wooden sacrificial post and the tree-deity. Vṛkṣa is the ordinary word for tree. Vīrudh denotes plants that spread or grow up, usually understood as creepers, shrubs and smaller growth; it is especially frequent in the Atharvaveda, where oṣadhayo vīrudhaḥ often appear together as a phrase for the whole world of healing plants (Whitney 1905).

The longest Vedic poem addressed to plants is the Oṣadhisūkta, Ṛgveda 10.97, a hymn spoken by a healer in praise of the plants he uses. It opens:

Ṛgveda 10.97.1

yā oṣadhīḥ pūrvā jātā devebhyas triyugam purā manai nu babhrūṇām ahaṃ śataṃ dhāmāni sapta ca “The plants that were born of old, three ages before the gods — I shall now call to mind the hundred and seven domains of the brown ones.”

The “hundred and seven” is a poetic count, not a census, and the “domains” (dhāman) are the plants’ seats or forms; translators differ on how to render the word (Jamison and Brereton 2014). Later in the hymn the plants are addressed as those that bear fruit and those that are fruitless, those without flowers and those that flower. This is the earliest Indian text to contrast plants by the presence or absence of visible flowers and fruit, a contrast that reappears in every later scheme. It is a poet’s inclusive list, however, not a set of defined classes.

The Atharvaveda names many more individual plants than the Ṛgveda, and several hymns are addressed to particular plants used against disease or in rites of protection and love, among them kuṣṭha, a Himalayan root that later became an important article of trade (Chapter 12) (Whitney 1905). The identification of most Atharvavedic plant names with modern species is uncertain, and the same caution applies to the most famous Vedic plant, soma, whose botanical identity remains unresolved after two centuries of debate.

Two further ideas from the late Vedic period frame later thinking. First, the Upaniṣads classify living beings by their mode of birth. The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (6.3.1) names three origins of beings — from an egg, from a living individual, and from a sprout (udbhijja) — and the Aitareya Upaniṣad adds a fourth, the sweat-born (svedaja) (Olivelle 1998). Plants are thus the “sprout-born” (udbhijja), a term that the Dharmaśāstra and the medical texts take up. Second, the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (6.11) uses a tree as an image of the living self: struck at the root, the stem or the top, a great tree bleeds sap but lives on, because it is pervaded by the living self (jīva); when life leaves one branch, that branch withers, and when it leaves the whole tree, the tree withers (Olivelle 1998). The passage is a teaching about the self, not a botanical observation, but it shows that a tree could be taken as a paradigm of a living being.

docs.title: 6.2 Manu: Plants among the Immobile Beings
docs.text:
The Mānava Dharmaśāstra (Manusmṛti, c. 2nd c. CE) gives the earliest compact classification of plants in Sanskrit. In its account of creation (1.43–49) it lists beings by mode of birth — born from a caul (jarāyuja), from an egg, from sweat, and from a sprout — and then describes the sprout-born. All of them are immobile (sthāvara) and grow from seed or from a cutting (bījakāṇḍaprarohin). Within them Manu distinguishes the classes set out in Table 6.1 (Olivelle 2005).

Table 6.1. Kinds of plants in Manusmṛti 1.46–48 (after Olivelle (2005)). Term Description in the text oṣadhi Plants that die when their fruit ripens, bearing many flowers and fruits (annual herbs, including the cereals) vanaspati Plants that bear fruit without flowers vṛkṣa Plants that bear both flowers and fruit guccha, gulma Clumps and bushes of various kinds tṛṇa The various kinds of grass pratāna, vallī Spreading plants and climbers

The criteria are visible life-history traits: whether the plant dies after fruiting, whether it has visible flowers, and whether it is a tree, a clump, a grass or a climber. The “fruit without flowers” class fits trees such as the banyan, the pipal and the cluster fig, whose minute flowers are hidden inside the fig and are not seen by the casual observer; modern readers commonly make this identification, although the text names no examples.

Manu then adds that plants, enveloped in darkness as a result of past actions, nonetheless have inner awareness and feel pleasure and pain (1.49; the verse is quoted in Section 4.2), and elsewhere teaches that wrongdoing can lead to rebirth as an immobile being (Olivelle 2005). This is a doctrine about karma and consciousness, not plant physiology, but it helps to explain why later Brahmanical, Jain and Buddhist writers felt obliged to state a position on whether plants feel.

The same question is argued at length in the Mahābhārata, in a dialogue between the sages Bhṛgu and Bharadvāja in the Śāntiparvan (12.177 in the critical edition). Bhṛgu argues that trees have all five senses: they wither in heat and so must feel touch; their fruits and flowers fall at the sound of wind and thunder, so they must hear; a creeper finds its way round a tree, so it must see; they flourish with good and bad odours, so they must smell; and they drink water through their roots, so they must taste. The argument is a philosophical one, built from everyday observations, and is best read as such. When the question of plant feeling returned in the early twentieth century with J. C. Bose’s experiments on plant responses, it was as modern plant physiology, which can settle nothing about these older arguments (Section 4.2.3).

docs.title: 6.3 The Medical Schemes of Caraka and Suśruta
docs.text:
The physicians had the most practical reason to classify plants, since they had to find, collect and prepare them. At the start of the Caraka-saṃhitā (Caraka’s redaction c. 100 BCE–200 CE, completed by Dṛḍhabala in the 4th–5th c. CE) all substances used in therapy are divided by origin into three kinds: those from animals (jāṅgama), from the earth, that is, minerals (pārthiva), and from plants (audbhida, “sprouted”) (Sharma 1981). The plant substances are then divided into four classes, and the Suśruta-saṃhitā (layered, early centuries BCE to c. 3rd–5th c. CE) gives a closely parallel fourfold division of immobile beings in its own first chapter (Bhishagratna 1907). Table 6.2 sets them side by side.

Table 6.2. The fourfold division of plants in the first chapters of the Caraka- and Suśruta-saṃhitā (Sūtrasthāna). Caraka Suśruta Term Defined as Term Defined as vanaspati bearing fruit (without flowers) vanaspati without flowers, bearing fruit vānaspatya bearing flowers and fruit vṛkṣa bearing flowers and fruit oṣadhi ending with the ripening of the fruit oṣadhi ending with the ripening of the fruit vīrudh spreading (creepers) vīrudh spreading or bushy (pratānavatī, stambinī)

The two schemes are versions of the same idea and agree closely with Manu. They differ mainly in vocabulary (Caraka’s vānaspatya where Suśruta has vṛkṣa) and in Suśruta’s subdivision of vīrudh into spreading plants and plants that form clumps or bushes; neither author argues with the other on the point. Figure 6.1(a) shows how Caraka’s four classes sit within his division of all therapeutic substances. Later works keep the four classes with small variations; Surapāla’s Vṛkṣāyurveda, for example, opens with its own fourfold division adapted to the gardener’s needs (Chapter 4).

Figure 6.1. Two Indian classifications of plants as hierarchies: (a) Caraka’s division of therapeutic substances by origin, with his four classes of plants (Table 6.2); (b) the Jain classification of living beings by the number of their senses, in which plants are one-sensed beings (Section 6.7). After Sharma (1981), Tatia (1994) and Dundas (2002).

What matters more in practice is that both physicians immediately move from these life-form classes to lists of usable parts and to groupings by action. Caraka lists the products that are taken from plants: roots, bark, heartwood, exudates (niryāsa), stalks, expressed juice, young shoots, alkaline preparations (kṣāra), latex (kṣīra), fruits, flowers, ash, oils, thorns, leaves, buds, tubers and sprouts (Sharma 1981). He also gives short lists of plants used for their roots and of plants used for their fruits. The plant’s growth habit is thus a first orientation; the working categories of the physician are the part used and its effect.

Life form, part and action

Indian medical texts use three different kinds of category for plants, which should not be confused: (1) life-form classes (vanaspati, vṛkṣa/vānaspatya, vīrudh, oṣadhi, and in other texts gulma, latā, tṛṇa); (2) the part used (root, bark, leaf, flower, fruit, seed, heartwood, exudate and so on); and (3) groups by action or property (Caraka’s fifty groups of ten, Suśruta’s named gaṇas, classes by taste). Only the first resembles a botanical classification; the third is the one physicians used most.

docs.title: 6.3.1 Groups by action
docs.text: The fourth chapter of Caraka’s Sūtrasthāna arranges five hundred drugs, most of them plants, into fifty groups of ten (mahākaṣāya), each defined by an action such as “life-promoting” (jīvanīya), “nourishing” (bṛṃhaṇīya) or “scraping” (lekhanīya) (Sharma 1981). Suśruta, in the Sūtrasthāna chapter on the collection of drugs, gives a different set of groups (gaṇa), each named after its first member, such as the vidārigandhādi group (“the group beginning with vidārigandhā”) or the āragvadhādi group (“beginning with āragvadha”, the Indian laburnum, Cassia fistula) (Bhishagratna 1907). The “-ādi” convention, naming a group after its first member, was inherited by the nighaṇṭus and is still used. These groupings bring together plants that have nothing in common botanically and separate close relatives; that is their purpose. They are discussed further in Chapter 12 and, as therapeutics, in Volume 13, Āyurveda.

docs.title: 6.4 Classification by Taste and Potency
docs.text:
The most distinctive principle of Āyurvedic dravyaguṇa (“substances and their qualities”) is that every substance, plant or otherwise, can be characterised by a small set of properties: its taste (rasa), of which there are six — sweet (madhura), sour (amla), salty (lavaṇa), pungent (kaṭu), bitter (tikta) and astringent (kaṣāya); its qualities (guṇa), such as heavy or light, oily or dry; its potency (vīrya), usually reduced to two, heating (uṣṇa) or cooling (śīta); its post-digestive taste (vipāka); and, for effects that cannot be predicted from these, its specific power (prabhāva) (Sharma 1981; Wujastyk 2003). The nighaṇṭus record these properties for each plant alongside its synonyms.

For the history of plant classification the significance of this system is that it gives a way of sorting plants that cuts entirely across their form: neem leaf, the bark of a forest tree and a rhizome can all be “bitter and cooling”. The six tastes were a central organising principle of the physician’s knowledge, and taste was an important means of recognising and testing plant material in the market. Attempts to match the six tastes with particular classes of modern phytochemicals are a modern overlay on the texts. The doctrine itself, and the relations between taste, potency and the doṣas, are treated in Volume 13, Āyurveda.

docs.title: 6.5 Land, Season and Collection
docs.text:
Indian medical texts consistently relate plants, animals and people to the kind of land they come from. Three kinds of land (deśa) are distinguished: jāṅgala, dry, open country with sparse trees and thorny vegetation; ānūpa, marshy, well-watered country; and sādhāraṇa, land of a middling or mixed kind. Francis Zimmermann’s study The Jungle and the Aroma of Meats shows how this triad, which applies to landscapes, game animals, water and people as much as to plants, organises a whole medical ecology (Section 1.6; (Zimmermann 1987)). The triad is thus not a plant classification in its own right but a framework in which the qualities of plants are partly explained by the qualities of the land in which they grow.

The texts draw practical conclusions. Drugs should be collected from land of the proper kind, free of ant-hills, cremation grounds, saline patches and other defects; plants should be mature, undamaged by insects, fire or frost; and particular parts should be gathered at particular seasons (Sharma 1981; Bhishagratna 1907). These rules are the closest the medical tradition comes to a field manual for collectors. The triad is not a map of modern climatic zones, and the collectors’ rules are best read in the physicians’ own terms rather than as chemistry.

docs.title: 6.6 The Nighaṇṭu Tradition: Names, Synonyms and Identities
docs.text:
The largest body of Sanskrit writing about individual plants is lexical. Sanskrit lexicons (kośa) and the medical glossaries called nighaṇṭu list each plant under a head name followed by its synonyms, and the medical ones usually add its properties and actions. The general lexicon Amarakośa (mid-first millennium CE; date uncertain) already has a section on forests and herbs (vanauṣadhivarga) that gives synonym sets for hundreds of trees and herbs. The medical nighaṇṭus include the Dhanvantari-nighaṇṭu (usually placed in the late first or early second millennium CE), the Madanapāla-nighaṇṭu (fourteenth century), the Rāja-nighaṇṭu of Narahari (late medieval; its date is disputed), and the drug section of Bhāvamiśra’s Bhāvaprakāśa (sixteenth century), which remains the most widely used in teaching today. The dates of almost all these works are debated; Meulenbeld (1999) surveys the evidence.

Most nighaṇṭus organise their entries into chapters (varga) named, like Suśruta’s gaṇas, after the first plant: the Bhāvaprakāśa, for instance, has a harītakyādi and a guḍūcyādi varga, as well as chapters on flowers, fruits, grains and vegetables. The principles of grouping are mixed: some chapters are defined by use (grains, vegetables, aromatics), some by part (flowers, fruits), and some only loosely by property. The Bhāvaprakāśa also takes in new plants: it is among the first Sanskrit medical works to describe the disease it calls phiraṅga (“the Frankish disease”, syphilis) and to admit imported drugs such as copacīnī, the China root (a Smilax), reflecting the trade of the Portuguese period.

docs.title: 6.6.1 How Sanskrit plant names work
docs.text:
Sanskrit synonyms are usually descriptive. A name may describe the plant’s form (maṇḍūkaparṇī, “frog-leaf”; pṛśniparṇī, “spotted leaf”; śatamūlī, “hundred-rooted”), its smell (aśvagandhā, “smelling of horse”), its habitat (jalaja, “water-born”), a property (tiktā, “bitter”; amṛtā, “immortal” or “deathless”), a use, or a mythological association. A single plant may therefore carry a dozen or more names, and one name may be applied to several plants that share the feature described. Poetic synonyms add another layer: turmeric (haridrā) is also called niśā and rajanī, both meaning “night”; and the similar-sounding dāruharidrā, “tree-turmeric”, is an entirely different plant (Berberis aristata).

This system was well suited to a tradition in which names were learnt with the plants themselves, from teachers and collectors, and in which a synonym also served as a short description. It becomes a problem when texts travel across regions and centuries. Āyurvedic pharmacognosy has a recognised category of “controversial drugs” (sandigdha dravya), plants whose classical name is applied to different species in different regions. Well-known examples are brāhmī (Bacopa monnieri in the Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, in Kerala practice and in much of the country, but Centella asiatica, the classical maṇḍūkaparṇī, in Bengal and parts of north India; Section 12.3.8); śaṅkhapuṣpī (variously Convolvulus pluricaulis, Evolvulus alsinoides and Clitoria ternatea); rāsnā (Pluchea lanceolata in the north, other species elsewhere, including Alpinia and the orchid Vanda); and pāṣāṇabheda (“stone-breaker”), a name given to several unrelated plants. Some of these differences are old regional traditions in their own right; others are substitutions that arose when the original plant became scarce or unknown. The practical consequences for identity, trade and adulteration are discussed in Chapter 12.

docs.title: 6.7 Plants and Life: Jain, Buddhist and Tamil Views
6.7.1 Jain classification of one-sensed beings
docs.text:
Jain thought gives plants a precise place in a classification of all living beings (jīva) by the number of their senses. Umāsvāti’s Tattvārthasūtra, the standard summary of Jain doctrine accepted by both major Jain traditions, divides embodied souls into immobile (sthāvara) and mobile (trasa) beings. The immobile beings are the earth-bodied, water-bodied and plant-bodied (vanaspati) souls, to which the Digambara recension of the text adds fire-bodied and air-bodied beings, while the Śvetāmbara recension counts fire and air among the mobile beings. All of them possess only one sense, touch. Mobile beings range from two-sensed creatures such as worms (touch and taste) through three-sensed creatures such as ants and four-sensed creatures such as bees and flies, to five-sensed beings, which include most larger animals and humans (Tatia 1994).

Within plant life Jain texts distinguish plants in which each body is the dwelling of a single soul (pratyeka) from those in which a single body is shared by innumerable souls (sādhāraṇa). Roots and tubers such as onion, garlic, potato and carrot are counted among the second kind (anantakāya, “having infinite bodies”), and the avoidance of these foods by observant Jains follows from this classification (Tatia 1994). The classification also had consequences for agriculture, since ploughing and clearing destroy earth-bodied and plant-bodied beings (Section 2.10). The Jain scheme is a moral and soteriological ordering of life, but it is also one of the earliest systematic classifications of all living things by a single, explicitly stated criterion (Figure 6.1b).

The Tattvārthasūtra is a summary. The fuller treatment of plant-bodied beings is in the Śvetāmbara canon, above all in the Prajñāpanā (Prakrit Paṇṇavaṇā), one of the subsidiary canonical texts (upāṅga), traditionally ascribed to Śyāmārya (Dundas 2002). Its first section, on the kinds of living beings, divides the plant-bodied into those with a separate body for each soul (patteya, Sanskrit pratyeka) and those in which a body is common to many souls (sāhāraṇa, sādhāraṇa), and then lists the kinds of plants with an individual body under twelve heads, usually given as trees (rukkha), clusters (guccha), shrubs (gumma), creepers (layā), climbers (vallī), jointed plants such as sugarcane and bamboo (pavvaga), grasses (taṇa), valaya (a class whose sense commentators explain in different ways), green herbs (hariya), annual crop plants that die after fruiting (osahi), water plants (jalaruha) and fungi (kuhaṇa). Each class is illustrated with long lists of named plants, and trees are further divided into those with a single seed in the fruit, such as the mango, and those with many seeds, such as the pomegranate. Several of these heads coincide with the life-form classes of Manu and the physicians; others, such as the jointed plants, the water plants and the fungi, reflect the monk’s concern to recognise every form in which life might be harmed. A similar list appears in the Uttarādhyayana (chapter 36). The canonical lists deserve the attention of historians of botany, and they have not yet been studied as fully as the Sanskrit medical schemes.

docs.title: 6.7.2 Buddhist monastic rules
docs.text: Early Buddhism did not regard plants as sentient beings within the round of rebirth. Its monastic rules nevertheless protect them. The Pāli Vinaya prescribes a penance for a monk who destroys vegetation (bhūtagāma); according to the story attached to the rule, it was introduced after lay people complained that monks who cut trees were harming “one-faculty life”, reflecting a widespread belief that trees are alive. The explanation attached to the rule lists five kinds of propagule (bījagāma) — plants propagated from roots, from stems, from joints, from cuttings, and from seeds — a classification by mode of propagation that would have been familiar to any gardener. Schmithausen (1991) has argued that early Buddhist texts reflect an older Indian view in which plants were regarded as at least borderline sentient, and that Buddhist doctrine gradually defined them out of the class of beings that can be reborn while monastic practice continued to treat them with restraint.

docs.title: 6.7.3 Tamil grammar
docs.text: The Tamil grammar Tolkāppiyam, in its chapter on usage (Marapiyal), classifies beings by the number of their senses, from one to six, the sixth being the mind, which humans possess. Grasses (pul) and trees (maram) are placed among the one-sensed beings, having touch alone. The same chapter, as usually interpreted, distinguishes pul from maram according to whether the hard part of the stem is on the outside or the inside, so that palms, whose stems lack an inner core of heartwood, are grouped with the grasses rather than with the trees. The scheme is independent in its language and categories, though it shares the sense-based principle with Jain thought; its relationship to Jain and Sanskrit sources is a matter of scholarly debate.

docs.title: 6.8 Folk and Tribal Classifications
docs.text:
Most of India’s plant knowledge has never been written in Sanskrit. Every Indian language has its own everyday categories of plant life: in Hindi, for example, peṛ (tree), jhāṛī (bush), bel (creeper) and ghās (grass); in Tamil, maram (tree), ceṭi (small plant or shrub), koṭi (creeper) and pul (grass). These life-form terms, together with a large number of names for individual kinds of plant, correspond closely to what ethnobiologists working across the world have described as the typical structure of folk classifications: a small number of broad life-form categories, a large number of “generic” names for the kinds that matter locally, and finer distinctions for the most important ones, such as crop varieties (Berlin 1992). The finest distinctions are usually drawn where livelihoods depend on them — among rice landraces, cultivated millets, fodder grasses, or the trees that yield fruit, timber and leaf fodder (Chapter 9).

Adivasi and other forest-dwelling communities hold detailed knowledge of wild plants for food, medicine, fibre, dyes, poisons and ritual. Jain (1991), compiled from decades of ethnobotanical fieldwork by S. K. Jain and his colleagues, records a vast number of such vernacular names and uses across India. Two cautions apply. First, such compilations record names and uses, not the full classificatory systems of the communities concerned, which have been studied in depth for only a few groups. Second, sweeping generalisations about the “classification system” of a whole community should be treated with caution unless they rest on published fieldwork. Tribal knowledge of plants, sacred groves and land is treated on its own terms in Volume 23, Jana–Jāti, and sacred groves in Chapter 11.

docs.title: 6.9 Indian Plant Knowledge and European Botany
docs.text: From the sixteenth century European physicians, merchants and administrators in India depended on Indian informants to learn the names and uses of plants. The Portuguese physician Garcia da Orta’s Colóquios dos simples e drogas da Índia (Goa, 1563), a dialogue on the drugs of India, drew openly on conversations with Indian and other Asian physicians and traders.

docs.title: 6.9.1 Hortus Malabaricus
docs.text:
The most important single work of this encounter is Hortus Indicus Malabaricus, published in twelve volumes at Amsterdam between 1678 and 1693 under the direction of Hendrik Adriaan van Rheede tot Drakenstein, the Dutch East India Company’s commander in Malabar. It describes and illustrates, with large copperplate engravings, the plants of the Malabar coast, mostly with their uses. Its content rested on Indian knowledge. The principal informant was the Ezhava physician Itty Achuden of the Kollatt family, whose testimony in Malayalam is printed in the first volume, and three Konkani brahmin physicians, Ranga Bhat, Vinayaka Pandit and Appu Bhat, who drew on palm-leaf manuscripts; the Carmelite missionary Matthaeus of St Joseph and Dutch and other European scholars took part in the work of description and editing. Plant names are given in Latin and in Indian languages, including Malayalam in its own script (Manilal 1980).

Grove (1995) has argued that the arrangement and descriptions of Hortus Malabaricus owe much to the Ezhava physicians’ own ways of grouping plants, so that a south Indian folk-medical classification passed, through the book, into European botany. Whatever weight one gives to that argument, the book’s influence is not in doubt: Linnaeus and his successors used it as a primary source on tropical Asian plants, and a number of Malayalam plant names survive, latinised, in modern scientific names. The work stands as an example of how “European” botany of the period was built on Asian expertise that was often unacknowledged in later accounts.

docs.title: 6.9.2 The colonial botanists
docs.text:
In the late eighteenth century the East India Company established the botanic garden at Calcutta (1787). William Roxburgh (1751–1815), its superintendent from 1793, worked first in the Northern Circars and then at Calcutta; his Plants of the Coast of Coromandel and his posthumously published Flora Indica were built on years of observation, on drawings by Indian artists whom he employed, and on the vernacular names supplied by local informants. William Jones, the Orientalist, urged botanists to retain Sanskrit plant names where they could. Whitelaw Ainslie’s Materia Indica (1826) recorded drugs with their names in several Indian languages. J. D. Hooker’s Flora of British India (1872–1897) provided the first comprehensive Linnaean flora of the subcontinent (Arnold 2000).

By the end of the century the Linnaean system had become the official language of plant knowledge in India. George Watt’s Dictionary of the Economic Products of India (1889–1893) organised a vast amount of information about useful plants by Latin binomial, but recorded under each entry the vernacular names, uses and trade data gathered from district officers and local informants across the country (Watt 1889). K. R. Kirtikar and B. D. Basu’s Indian Medicinal Plants did the same for medicinal plants, giving Sanskrit and vernacular names for each species (Kirtikar and Basu 1935). These works made Indian names searchable through Latin binomials, and they remain indispensable for anyone trying to identify a plant named in a Sanskrit or vernacular source. They also fixed particular identifications, sometimes on slender evidence, which later writers have repeated as if they were certain; the modern identification of a Sanskrit plant name is often only as good as the colonial dictionary on which it ultimately rests.

docs.title: 6.10 Indian Schemes and Linnaean Taxonomy
docs.text:
Carl Linnaeus’s Species Plantarum (1753) established the consistent use of two-word names (genus and species) and arranged plants in an explicitly “artificial” system based on the number and arrangement of stamens and pistils. Before Linnaeus, European botanists had used descriptive Latin phrase-names, often several words long, which functioned in much the same way as descriptive Sanskrit synonyms: a name was also a short description. Within a few decades the “natural” systems of Antoine-Laurent de Jussieu (1789) and Augustin Pyramus de Candolle grouped plants by overall similarity in many characters; after Darwin, classification was reinterpreted as a record of descent; and present-day systems, such as that of the Angiosperm Phylogeny Group, are based largely on molecular evidence of evolutionary relationship.

Set against this history, the Indian schemes look less like rivals and more like answers to different questions. The life-form classes of Manu, Caraka and Suśruta are comparable to the broad life-form categories found in folk classifications everywhere and to the trees, shrubs and herbs of ancient Greek botany: they sort plants by habit and life history, not by relationship. The physicians’ groupings by action and by taste, like the nighaṇṭu chapters, are deliberately functional and bring unrelated plants together. The Jain, Buddhist and Tamil schemes classify plants among living beings for moral and philosophical purposes. None of them aimed at a single, universal, hierarchical system of names, and none needed one, because knowledge was transmitted within communities of practitioners who could show each other the plants.

The Linnaean system’s strength is precisely that it is detachable from use and locality: a binomial name refers to the same species in Kerala, Kashmir and Uppsala. That strength was a product of European science’s particular needs — to catalogue plants arriving from all over the world in herbaria far from where they grew — and of colonial and commercial networks. Indian names, by contrast, carry information about use, property and local recognition that a binomial does not. The two are complementary tools, and the practical task today, in pharmacognosy, ethnobotany and the documentation of traditional knowledge (Chapter 20), is to connect them reliably: to establish, plant by plant and region by region, which species a given Sanskrit or vernacular name actually refers to.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Indian traditions classified plants for many purposes. The Vedic hymns supplied a basic vocabulary (oṣadhi, vanaspati, vīrudh, vṛkṣa) and the Upaniṣads the idea of plants as “sprout-born” living beings. Manu and the physicians Caraka and Suśruta defined a small set of life-form classes based on visible flowering, fruiting and habit, but the physicians’ working categories were the part used and the plant’s action and taste. The nighaṇṭus collected descriptive synonyms whose richness created lasting problems of identity. Jain, Buddhist and Tamil thinkers placed plants in classifications of living beings by their senses, with real consequences for diet, monastic life and attitudes to farming. Folk and tribal classifications, still only partly documented, follow the life-form and generic structure found across the world. In the colonial period Indian knowledge, transmitted through informants such as Itty Achuden, entered European botany through Hortus Malabaricus and was later recast in Linnaean terms by Roxburgh, Watt and their successors. The Indian schemes are best understood as functional and philosophical classifications in their own right, not as precursors of Linnaeus.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Olivelle (2005) for Manu’s account of plants; Zimmermann (1987) on land, plants and medicine; Meulenbeld (1999) on the nighaṇṭu literature and its dating; Tatia (1994) and Dundas (2002) for the Jain classification of living beings; Sivarajan and Balachandran (1994) on the plant sources of Āyurvedic drugs and the “controversial drugs”; Schmithausen (1991) on plants in early Buddhism; and Manilal (1980) on Hortus Malabaricus and its Indian contributors.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Soil, Tillage and Implements
docs.text:
Farmers everywhere know their soils intimately, and Indian farmers were no exception. Yet the written record of that knowledge is thinner and more scattered than is often supposed. No surviving Sanskrit text is a treatise on soils in the way the Bṛhatsaṃhitā has chapters on rain or on finding groundwater. What we have instead is a vocabulary of land spread across Vedic hymns, grammar, lexicons, statecraft, medicine and architecture; a handful of practical instructions on manure in the agricultural texts; and a much larger body of practice—names for soils, ways of feeding and protecting them—that was recorded mainly by colonial officials, ethnographers and agronomists from the nineteenth century onwards. This chapter keeps these layers apart. It first sets out what the texts say about land, then what farmers did to keep it fertile and in place, how salinity became a large problem in the canal era, and how modern soil science classifies India’s soils. The second half of the chapter turns from the soil to the work done on it: the plough and its history, the implements used to prepare the seedbed, to sow, weed, reap, thresh and winnow, the draught animals and village artisans on whom these tools depended, the mechanisation of the twentieth century, and the division of field work by caste and gender.

The Kṛṣi-Parāśara does not classify soils at all (Chapter 3), and no Sanskrit text matches its colour words for soils with the soil orders of modern science.

docs.title: 7.1 Words for Land in Early Texts
7.1.1 Vedic vocabulary
docs.text:
The Ṛgveda already distinguishes cultivated land from the rest of the landscape. The field is kṣetra, and a whole hymn (RV 4.57) is addressed to the “Lord of the Field” (kṣetrasya pati) together with the plough, the ploughshare and the furrow (sītā) (Jamison and Brereton 2014). The word urvarā denotes arable or fertile land; winning or possessing urvarā is among the goods for which the poets pray, alongside cattle, sons and water. The earth as a whole (bhūmi, pṛthivī) is celebrated at length in the Pṛthivī Sūkta of the Atharvaveda (AV 12.1; Section 2.7), which praises the earth’s fertility, its plants and its waters; but it is a hymn, not a description of soils.

Barren and saline ground also has a name. Ūṣa is saline earth, and land impregnated with it is ūṣara. In the Brāhmaṇa accounts of setting up the sacred fires, saline earth is one of the materials ritually gathered and laid down, along with sand, gravel and the earth thrown up by moles—an indication that these different kinds of earth were recognised and named, even if the context is ritual rather than agricultural. In later Sanskrit ūṣara becomes the standard word for land on which nothing will grow, and the word survives in north Indian usage as usar (Section 7.7).

docs.title: 7.1.2 Grammar and lexicon
docs.text:
Pāṇini (c. 4th c. BCE) records a productive way of naming fields after the crops for which they are suited. His rules on secondary derivatives (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.2.1–4) form words such as vraiheya and śāleya (“a field fit for vrīhi / śāli rice”), yavya (“fit for barley”), tilya or tailīna (“fit for sesame”), māṣīṇa (“fit for black gram”) and maudgīna (“fit for green gram”). The grammar thus preserves a classification of land by use: what mattered was what a field would grow.

The Sanskrit lexicon Amarakośa (first millennium CE; its date is uncertain, though often placed around the sixth century) gathers land-words in its section on the earth. It glosses urvarā as land rich in every kind of crop, gives ūṣa as saline earth and ūṣara for land containing it, and lists terms for desert (maru, dhanvan), dry ground (sthala) and the field (kṣetra, kedāra). Like Pāṇini, it reflects the vocabulary of educated speakers rather than a farmers’ manual, but it shows that fertile, saline, desert and dry land were standard categories.

docs.title: 7.1.3 The Arthaśāstra
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra (composite, c. 50 BCE–300 CE; see Volume 18, Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra) approaches land as an administrator does. In Kangle’s and Olivelle’s translations, the village accountant (gopa) is to record the land of each village by category: cultivated and uncultivated (kṛṣṭa, akṛṣṭa), dry land and wet, embanked fields (sthala, kedāra), gardens and orchards, groves, enclosures, forest, house sites, shrines, irrigation works, cremation grounds and so on (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013). The distinction between sthala, land depending on rain, and kedāra, bunded fields that hold water (above all for rice), runs through later Indian agrarian vocabulary.

The chapter on the superintendent of agriculture (sītādhyakṣa, Book 2, chapter 24) adds a finer, practical grading of micro-sites. As Kangle renders it, land struck by river foam (the edges of a river bed) suits creeper fruits such as gourds; the margins of overflow channels suit long pepper, grapes and sugarcane; the surroundings of wells suit vegetables and root crops; the edges of moist beds suit green herbs; and the ridges between beds suit fragrant and medicinal plants. This is a classification by moisture and position in the landscape, the kind of judgement every gardener makes, and it is one of the few passages in early Sanskrit prose that matches particular crops to particular ground. The chapter does not set out a system of manures; its other contents are summarised in Section 2.11.1.

docs.title: 7.2 Land, Ecology and Medicine: Jāṅgala and Ānūpa
docs.text:
The most developed classification of land in Sanskrit comes from medicine, not agriculture. Āyurvedic texts divide country (deśa) into jāṅgala, ānūpa and sādhāraṇa. Jāṅgala land is dry and open, with sparse thorny trees, hard soil, clear skies and wind; it is considered healthy, and its animals (antelope, deer and game birds) yield the light meats the physicians prized. Ānūpa land is marshy and well watered, with dense vegetation, rivers and lakes, heavy air and the diseases of phlegm and wind. Sādhāraṇa is the balanced, intermediate type. Francis Zimmermann’s classic study showed that this is an ecological theory linking landscape, animals, food and bodily humours (Section 1.6; (Zimmermann 1987)). Caraka uses the scheme when advising where medicinal plants should be gathered and where patients fare best (Sharma 1981).

The plant-science texts borrowed the same frame. Surapāla’s Vṛkṣāyurveda (c. 10th–11th c.) describes land as ānūpa, jāṅgala and sādhāraṇa, judges ground by its colour and other qualities, and names trees suited to each kind; it also explains the ailments of trees as disorders of vāta, pitta and kapha, with treatments to match (Sadhale 1996). The Upavanavinoda of the Śārṅgadharapaddhati (1363) has a comparable section on judging ground for a garden (Majumdar 1935). These works apply Āyurvedic categories to plants and to the land they grow in; they do not classify soils themselves into vāta, pitta and kapha types. The Vṛkṣāyurveda tradition, including its fermented plant-feeds such as kuṇapajala, is treated in Chapter 4.

Classifying land by what it does

Across the early sources land is classified by use and by water: what it will grow (Pāṇini’s crop-fields), whether it holds water (sthala and kedāra), where it lies in relation to a river or well (the Arthaśāstra), whether it is saline (ūṣara), and whether the country as a whole is dry or marshy (jāṅgala, ānūpa). This is closer to a modern “land capability” assessment than to a soil taxonomy, and it is better described in those terms than as an anticipation of pedology.

docs.title: 7.3 Judging the Ground: Tests in Bṛhatsaṃhitā and Vāstu Texts
docs.text:
The physical tests of soil that do appear in Sanskrit belong to architecture. Varāhamihira’s chapter on building (vāstuvidyā, Bṛhatsaṃhitā 53 in Bhat’s numbering) and the later vāstu manuals tell the builder how to examine a house site (Bhat 1981). A pit is dug and then refilled with the same earth: if earth is left over, the site is excellent; if it just fills the pit, it is middling; if it falls short, the site is poor. A loose soil that cannot be packed back is thus judged inferior, a sensible test of compaction and bearing capacity for a building. A pit may also be filled with water and checked after an interval to see how much has drained away. Beyond these tests, ground is judged by colour, smell and taste, and by the plants growing on it; Varāhamihira assigns soils of different colours and tastes as suitable for the houses of the different varṇas, white for brahmins, red for kṣatriyas, yellow for vaiśyas and dark for śūdras, a reminder that these tests were embedded in a social hierarchy as well as in practical judgement.

Two cautions follow. First, these are tests of a building site, not of agricultural fertility; they should not be presented as “traditional soil testing for crops”. Second, they do not amount to a systematic analysis of agricultural soils. Farmers certainly looked at, handled and smelled their soil, and in saline tracts a salty crust or taste was an obvious warning; but these were the ordinary judgements of experience, and they are best described as such.

Varāhamihira’s separate chapter on finding underground water (dakārgala, Bṛhatsaṃhitā 54) also reads the ground, using plants, termite mounds, the colour of soil and stones as signs of water at a given depth. It is discussed in Chapter 8.

docs.title: 7.4 Farmers’ Soil Vocabularies
docs.text:
Every farming region of India has its own names for soils, usually based on texture, colour, moisture behaviour and the crops they carry, and many of these entered English through revenue settlements and district gazetteers. A few are especially well established.

  • In the Ganga–Yamuna Doab and much of north India, cultivators distinguish matiyār (stiff clay), dumaṭ or domaṭ (loam) and bhūr (light sand), terms that colonial settlement officers adopted for assessing revenue.

  • In Bundelkhand, the heavy black soils are mār and kābar, the lighter brown soils paṛuā, and the thin, stony upland soils rākaṛ.

  • The black cotton soils of the Deccan were known to British observers as regur, a word taken from Telugu (regaḍa); in Tamil Nadu the black-soil country of the south is called karisal.

  • In Tamil literature the agricultural lowland of paddy fields is the marutam landscape, one of the five tiṇai of Saṅgam poetry (Chapter 2).

Such vocabularies are local and practical. A word like mār carries knowledge of how the soil behaves—that it cracks when dry, holds moisture for a winter crop, and becomes unworkable when wet—which no colour term alone conveys. They do not map neatly onto Sanskrit words or onto modern soil orders, and attempts to force them into a single pan-Indian scheme lose exactly the local precision that makes them valuable.

docs.title: 7.5.1 Manure in the agricultural texts
docs.text: The Kṛṣi-Parāśara, a late text probably from Bengal, is the clearest early Sanskrit witness to deliberate manuring. It treats cow dung as the essential fertiliser: dung is to be accumulated in a pit or heap through the cold season, dried and broken up, and carried to the field to be laid down in small heaps before sowing, with the text insisting that crops without manure do not prosper (Majumdar and Banerji 1960; Sadhale 1999). This fits its wider concern with the cattle shed and the welfare of cattle, which are the source of both draught power and manure (Chapter 3). The Vṛkṣāyurveda texts go further in prescribing special preparations for trees and gardens, including the fermented kuṇapajala; those recipes belong to horticulture and are treated in Chapter 4.

docs.title: 7.5.2 Manuring in practice
docs.text:
For the field crops of ordinary farmers the evidence comes mainly from the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, when officials and agronomists described what they saw. The most important single witness is the agricultural chemist John Augustus Voelcker, consulting chemist to the Royal Agricultural Society of England, whom the Secretary of State sent to India in 1889 to advise on the application of agricultural chemistry. He toured the provinces until 1891, and his Report on the Improvement of Indian Agriculture (1893) is the most careful contemporary assessment of Indian farming practice (Voelcker 1893). Voelcker concluded that Indian cultivators managed their land with considerable skill; that their mixed cropping, rotations and weeding were in many respects as good as British practice; that their implements were in general suited to their soils, cattle and means; and that the main obstacles to higher yields were not ignorance but shortages of water, manure, fuel and credit. The shortage of manure he traced above all to the burning of cattle dung as fuel for want of firewood. He also urged the government to employ trained scientists, a recommendation that bore fruit in the research institutions described in Section 19.4. Later chapters refer back to this account. The practices he and others recorded include the following.

Farmyard manure. Dung, urine-soaked litter and household sweepings were collected in pits and carried to the fields, often by women, who also made the dung cakes that competed with the fields for the same material. The best-manured land was usually the land closest to the village. Folding livestock. In the Deccan and the south, herders of sheep and goats were paid in grain or cash to pen their flocks overnight on a farmer’s field before sowing, so that the dung and urine were deposited directly on the soil. Such arrangements linked settled cultivators and mobile pastoralists in a long-standing exchange (Chapter 13). Tank silt. Where tanks were common, the silt that accumulated on the tank bed was dug out in the dry season and carted to the fields, at once restoring the tank’s storage and returning fine soil and organic matter to the land (Chapter 8). Green manure and leaf manure. Crops such as sunn hemp (Crotalaria juncea) and dhaiñcā (Sesbania species) were grown and ploughed in, especially before rice, and green leaves and twigs lopped from trees and shrubs (for example Pongamia pinnata) were trampled into puddled rice fields in the south and west. Oilcakes. The cake left after pressing oilseeds in the village oil mill (Chapter 14) was used as cattle feed and as manure for valuable crops such as sugarcane and tobacco; neem cake was valued as well for its insect-deterring properties (Schmutterer 1995). Ash and burning. Ash from household fires and burnt crop residues was spread on fields. In the Konkan and along the Western Ghats, the rāb method of preparing rice nurseries involved burning layers of branches, leaves, dung and grass on the seedbed before sowing. Legumes, rotation and fallow. Pulses were grown in rotation or as mixed crops with cereals, and land was rested when it could be spared. Farmers valued pulses because cereals did well after them; the biological explanation, nitrogen fixation by root-nodule bacteria, is a nineteenth-century discovery and should not be read back into the practice. Rotations and mixed cropping are discussed in Chapter 9.

Albert Howard drew on these practices of collecting and rotting wastes when he developed the “Indore process” of composting, a well-documented instance of Indian farm practice shaping a modern method (Section 10.7).

Debate: Sustainable by design?

It is tempting to describe these practices as a balanced system that kept Indian soils fertile for millennia. The reality was more uneven. Manure was scarce and unequally distributed; the fields of landholders near the village received it, while distant and poorer fields often did not. Many soils were farmed at low yields precisely because nutrients were not replaced, and the burning of dung for fuel was a response to a shortage of wood that had its own ecological history (Chapter 11). The practices recorded here are best understood as ingenious responses to constraints, not as a finished science; their value for today’s agriculture has to be tested, not assumed (Chapter 10).

docs.title: 7.6 Holding Soil and Water in Place
docs.text:
On the plains the commonest conservation structure was the earthen field bund. Bunds hold rainwater on the field long enough to soak in, keep rice fields flooded, and stop topsoil washing away in heavy monsoon storms. In the black-soil country of the Deccan, bunds and small embankments across gentle slopes conserved the moisture on which the post-monsoon crop depended. In the Thar the khadin, an earthen embankment built across a slope to pond runoff, turns the silt and moisture left behind into a cultivable field (Chapter 8).

In the hills the characteristic solution is the terrace. Bench terraces with earth or dry-stone risers are cut into slopes throughout the Himalaya, from Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand to Sikkim, and along parts of the Western Ghats. In the North-East, the Angami Nagas build irrigated rice terraces on steep hillsides, and the Apatani of the Ziro valley in Arunachal Pradesh farm a levelled, bunded and canal-fed valley floor in which rice is grown together with fish. The zabo system of the Chakhesang Nagas links protected forest above, water-harvesting ponds and cattle yards with rice fields below, so that runoff carries manure down to the crops (Agarwal and Narain 1997). These are the work of communities whose knowledge is discussed further in Volume 23, Jana–Jāti.

Shifting cultivation (jhūm in the North-East, with many local names elsewhere) handles fertility in a different way: forest is cleared and burned, cropped for one or two years, and then left to regrow for a long fallow during which the soil recovers. Where fallows are long it can be a stable system; where population pressure or land loss shortens them, soils degrade. Colonial and post-colonial states often condemned it wholesale. It is treated in Chapter 10.

docs.title: 7.7 Saline and Alkaline Land: Ūṣara, Usar and Reh
docs.text:
Saline and alkaline soils occur naturally in the semi-arid parts of north and west India, where evaporation draws dissolved salts to the surface and leaves a white or grey crust. Villagers in the Ganga plain call such land usar (from Sanskrit ūṣara) and the salt efflorescence reh. Some communities made use of it: saline earth was a source of salt and saltpetre, and specialised castes such as the Nonias of north India worked it. For cultivation, however, usar was largely written off, used at most for grazing.

The problem became much larger in the nineteenth century. The great canals of the Doab and Punjab (Chapter 8) delivered water without adequate drainage; in many tracts the water table rose, land became waterlogged, and reh spread over fields that had previously been cultivated. Colonial officials recognised the problem by the 1870s, and historians of the canal regime have treated waterlogging and salinisation as among its most serious ecological costs (Kumar 1983; Ludden 1999). Farmers’ remedies—flushing salts with water where drainage allowed, adding manure, growing tolerant crops—were limited, and large-scale reclamation of sodic soils with gypsum and drainage is a twentieth-century development. Salinity in irrigated land remains a major problem in north-western India today.

docs.title: 7.8 Modern Soil Science and the Indian Soil Groups
docs.text:
Scientific soil survey in India began under colonial rule and was developed after independence by the Indian Council of Agricultural Research and its soil survey institutions. The broad grouping now taught in Indian schools and used in general surveys is summarised in Table 7.1. Internationally, these soils are also described in the categories of the United States Department of Agriculture’s Soil Taxonomy (for example, many black soils as Vertisols), but the correspondence between the two systems is approximate.

Table 7.1. The major soil groups of India in the standard modern classification (simplified). Group Main occurrence and origin Characteristic properties and uses Alluvial Indo-Gangetic and Brahmaputra plains, coastal plains and deltas; river-deposited sediments Generally fertile, from sandy to clayey; the basis of the rice and wheat agriculture of the plains Black (regur) Deccan plateau of Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and adjoining areas; mainly weathered basalt Clay-rich, swelling when wet and cracking deeply when dry; retain moisture; cotton, sorghum, pulses and post-monsoon crops Red and yellow Much of peninsular and eastern India; weathered crystalline rocks Usually light-textured and low in nutrients; millets, pulses, groundnut, and rice where irrigated Laterite High-rainfall uplands: Western Ghats, Odisha, parts of the North-East Strongly leached, rich in iron and aluminium; plantation crops such as cashew, tea, coffee and rubber, with manuring Arid (desert) Rajasthan and adjoining dry regions Sandy, low in organic matter; productive where water is available Saline and alkaline Patches in dry regions, poorly drained irrigated land and coasts Salt crusts and sodic conditions; require drainage and reclamation Peaty and marshy Waterlogged coastal tracts, e.g. Kuttanad in Kerala and parts of the Sundarbans High in organic matter, often acidic Forest and mountain Himalaya and other hill ranges Thin and variable, depending on slope and vegetation

This grouping is a modern scientific construction based on parent material, climate and laboratory analysis. It is useful to know it, both because it describes the ground on which Indian agriculture actually takes place and because it shows how the old local vocabularies relate to the landscape: regur, karisal, mār and kābar all name variants of the black soils, while bhūr and dumaṭ describe textures within the alluvium. But there is no basis for equating particular Sanskrit colour words with particular modern soil orders, and no evidence that the Sanskrit texts possessed a soil taxonomy comparable to this one.

docs.title: 7.9 The Plough
docs.text:
Cross-Reference: Field work elsewhere in this volume

The Kalibangan field and the Vedic hymns to the plough are discussed in Chapter 2; the plough passage and the farming rites of the Kṛṣi-Parāśara in Chapter 3; water-lifting devices in Chapter 8; seeds and mixed cropping in Chapter 9; draught breeds in Chapter 13; and husking, grinding and grain storage in Chapter 14. The sections that follow concentrate on the implements and the work done with them.

docs.title: 7.9.1 The Indian ard
docs.text:
Until well into the twentieth century almost all ploughing in India was done with an ard: a plough that cuts a furrow and stirs the soil but, having no mouldboard, does not turn it over. The common form was made by the village carpenter, almost entirely of wood. A pointed body carried the share at its tip; a single handle rose from it for the ploughman to grip and to press the point into the ground; and a long pole ran forward from the body to the yoke (Figure 7.1a). The share, a pointed iron bar or small iron blade fixed to the point of the body, was the one part that had to be renewed regularly by the smith. The yoke lay across the necks of a pair of bullocks, in front of the zebu’s hump, against which the animals pushed. In many wet-rice tracts and on heavy soils buffaloes replaced bullocks, and in western Rajasthan a plough was often drawn by a single camel. The whole implement was cheap, could be made and mended in the village, and was light enough to carry on the shoulder to a distant field.

Figure 7.1. Two Indian field implements, schematic and not to scale. (a) The wooden ard: the body, tipped with an iron share, runs in the soil; the handle rises from it, and the pole joins it to a yoke carried on the necks of a pair of bullocks (Section 7.9 and Table 7.2). (b) The multi-tube seed drill of the Deccan: tines on a bullock-drawn frame open the rows, and seed dropped into the bowl runs down bamboo tubes into them (Section 7.11).

Because the ard does not invert the soil, a field was ploughed several times, often in different directions, until the clods were broken and the surface reduced to a fine tilth; criss-cross ploughing of this kind is what the Early Harappan field at Kalibangan preserves. How often a field was ploughed depended on the crop, the soil and the farmer’s means. Land for wheat or sugarcane was usually worked more thoroughly than land for rain-fed millets, and the farmer who could plough often, and at the right moment, was the farmer who owned his own bullocks. In the rice country of the east and south the plough was also driven through standing water to churn the field into soft mud before transplanting. This puddling buries weeds, levels the field and reduces the loss of water through the soil.

Ploughs differed from region to region in weight, length of pole and shape of body and share, according to the soil and the animals available: light ploughs for the small cattle of the eastern rice country and for narrow hill terraces, and, on the black soils of the Deccan, where the ordinary plough was used sparingly (Section 7.10), occasionally a heavy plough drawn by several pairs to break the ground deeply and root out persistent weeds. In shifting cultivation the burnt clearing was sown with a digging stick and worked with the hoe, and the plough had no part (Chapter 10). Table 7.2 lists some common field implements with representative regional names.

Table 7.2. Some common implements of Indian field work, with representative names. Names vary greatly from region to region; those given are examples, not a complete list. Implement Representative names Use Plough Sanskrit lāṅgala, sīra, hala; Hindi hal; Tamil ēr, kalappai Cuts furrows and stirs the soil without turning it over Ploughshare Sanskrit phāla; Hindi phāl Iron point or blade fixed to the wooden body Yoke Sanskrit yuga; Hindi juā Joins the pair of draught animals and carries the pole Plough-pole Sanskrit īṣā Joins the body of the plough to the yoke Levelling plank Hindi pāṭā, Punjabi suhāgā; Bengali mai Breaks clods, levels and firms the surface, covers broadcast seed Blade harrow Marathi and Hindi bakhar; Telugu guntaka Shallow working of black soils; cutting weeds; loosening the surface Spade, mattock Sanskrit kuddāla; Hindi kudāl, phāvṛā; Tamil maṇveṭṭi Digging, earthwork, bunds and channels Hand hoe Hindi khurpā, khurpī Weeding and loosening soil around plants Sickle Sanskrit dātra, lavitra; Hindi hãsiyā, darāntī Reaping Threshing floor Sanskrit khala; Hindi khalihān; Tamil kaḷam Hard, dung-plastered floor on which the crop is threshed Winnowing basket Sanskrit śūrpa; Hindi sūp; Tamil muṟam Separating grain from chaff and dust Cart Sanskrit anas (Vedic), śakaṭa; Hindi gāṛī; Tamil vaṇṭi Carrying manure, silt, harvest and goods

docs.title: 7.9.2 Archaeological evidence
docs.text:
The ploughed field at Kalibangan and the terracotta plough model from Banawali (Section 2.4) show that the ard was in use in the north-west by the third millennium BCE. No metal ploughshare is known from Harappan sites, and the working point of the Harappan plough was presumably of hard wood. The cutting tools of the earliest farmers were blades of flint and chert; at Neolithic Mehrgarh the excavators reported a sickle made of such blades set with bitumen in a wooden haft. Harappan metal tools of copper and bronze include axes, chisels and knives (Kenoyer 1998).

Iron changed the farmer’s equipment, though more slowly than was once believed. Iron sickles, hoes and axes are found at sites of the first millennium BCE in the Ganga plain and in the megalithic burials of the Deccan and the south.
