Iron ploughshares are rarer in the early levels, and when they became common is debated (Chapter 2) (Allchin and Allchin 1982; Singh 2008). For the medieval centuries the sources say little about field implements; the technical changes that historians of the period emphasise, such as the spread of the geared water-wheel, lie in water-lifting and in crops rather than in tillage (Chapter 8) (Habib 2008).

docs.title: 7.9.3 Words for the plough
docs.text:
The Ṛgveda has two words for the plough, sīra and lāṅgala, together with the share (phāla), the yoke (yuga), the pole (īṣā), the goad (aṣṭrā), the furrow (sītā) and the ploughman (kīnāśa) (Jamison and Brereton 2014). Lāṅgala has often been regarded as a loanword into Vedic from a non-Indo-European language of the subcontinent; an Austroasiatic origin was proposed by Jean Przyluski, but the question remains open. In later Sanskrit hala becomes the ordinary word, and the plough becomes the emblem of Balarāma, Kṛṣṇa’s elder brother, called Haladhara and Halāyudha, “plough-bearer” and “he whose weapon is the plough”. In parts of north India women keep a day associated with him, Hal Ṣaṣṭhī (Hal Chhaṭh), on which custom requires them to avoid food grown on ploughed land.

The parts of the plough were familiar enough to serve as a metaphor: the Buddha’s spiritual plough in the Kasibhāradvāja Sutta (Chapter 2) names the yoke and plough (yuganaṅgala), the pole (īsā), the binding strap (yotta), and the share and goad (phāla, pācana) (Sutta Nipāta 1.4, v. 77). The Amarakośa, in its section on the vaiśya, gives lāṅgala, hala, godāraṇa (“that which tears the earth”) and sīra as synonyms for the plough, explains īṣā as the shaft of the plough and sītā as the track it leaves, and gives dātra and lavitra for the sickle. In Tamil the plough is ēr, and the ploughing praised in the Tirukkuṟaḷ’s chapter Uḻavu is the work of the uḻavar, the ploughmen of the marutam landscape.

The administrative texts treat implements as stores to be managed, as in the Arthaśāstra’s rules for the crown farms (Section 2.11.1). The Kṛṣi-Parāśara, centuries later, names the parts of the plough and gives their dimensions; its passage is discussed in Chapter 3.

docs.title: 7.10 Preparing the Seedbed: Planks, Harrows and Hoes
docs.text:
After the plough, or in place of it, came lighter operations to break clods, level the field, kill weeds and conserve moisture. The most widespread implement for this was the levelling plank, a heavy beam of wood (Hindi pāṭā, Punjabi suhāgā) dragged across the field by a pair of bullocks while the driver stood on it to add his weight. The plank crushes clods, smooths the surface and presses it firm, which slows the drying of the soil beneath; drawn over a field after broadcast sowing, it also covers the seed. In Bengal a ladder-like frame, the mai, served the same purpose, and in puddled rice fields plank or ladder levelled the mud so that water would stand evenly.

On the black soils of the Deccan, Malwa and Gujarat the characteristic implement was not the plough but the blade harrow, called bakhar in Marathi and Hindi and guntaka in Telugu: a horizontal iron blade fixed between two wooden legs and drawn by bullocks so that it slides just below the surface, cutting the roots of weeds and loosening the top layer without bringing up moist soil from below. Black soils swell when wet and crack deeply as they dry, and so partly till themselves; what the farmer needed was to break the crust, control weeds and prepare a shallow seedbed. In many black-soil districts the blade harrow was therefore worked over the field repeatedly each season, while deep ploughing was done only at intervals of some years. Narrower versions of the same blade were used to weed between the rows of growing crops (Section 7.12).

Hand tools did the work that animals could not. The spade or mattock (Sanskrit kuddāla; Hindi kudāl and phāvṛā; Tamil maṇveṭṭi, the “mamoty” of Anglo-Indian usage) built and repaired bunds, cut channels, dug manure pits and lifted silt from tank beds (Section 7.5), and it was the main tillage tool on plots too small, steep or stony for a team. The small hand hoe, the khurpā or khurpī, was the most widely used implement of all for weeding and for loosening soil around plants.

docs.title: 7.11 Sowing
docs.text:
The simplest method of sowing was broadcasting: scattering seed by hand over the prepared field and covering it with the plank. Small millets, many pulses and much rice in the east were sown in this way, as are the relay crops sown into standing rice before its harvest (Chapter 9). Seed could also be dropped by hand into the furrow behind the plough, so that the next furrow covered it, or fed through a bamboo tube tied to the plough, which delivered it to the moist bottom of the furrow; in the Punjab the two methods are called kerā and porā. Placing seed deep mattered most for crops sown on stored moisture after the rains, when the surface had already dried.

The fullest development of this idea was the multi-tube seed drill of the Deccan and other parts of south and west India (Figure 7.1b). A wooden frame carries several tines, each with a hollow bamboo tube behind it; the tubes join at the top in a wooden bowl, into which the sower, walking behind, drops seed by hand, so that it runs down into the rows opened by the tines. A pair of bullocks draws the drill. Often a second, single-tube drill followed to sow a different crop in some of the rows, which is how the alternate-row mixtures of the Deccan, such as sorghum with pigeon pea, were laid out (Chapter 9). Row sowing saves seed, places it at an even depth, and leaves lines between which the crop can be weeded with a bullock hoe. The drill has many regional names and forms.

European observers in the late eighteenth century wrote admiring accounts of these drills, several of which were collected by Dharampal (1971). It is sometimes claimed that the Indian drill was the model for the seed drill of the English agriculturist Jethro Tull (1701). There is no good evidence of such a transmission, and seed drills were invented more than once: a seeding plough with a funnel and tube appears on Mesopotamian seals, and multi-tube drills were used in China from the Han period. The Indian drill is best appreciated in its own right, as an implement well suited to the dry farming of the black-soil country.

In dibbling, a hole is made with a pointed stick and a few seeds are dropped in and covered. It is slow but economical of seed, suits ground that cannot be ploughed, and is the main method of sowing in shifting cultivation. Transplanting, finally, was the defining operation of wet-rice farming. Seed was sown thickly in a nursery bed; after some weeks the seedlings were pulled, tied in bundles, carried to the puddled field and pressed by hand, a few at a time, into the mud. The Kṛṣi-Parāśara describes this sequence (Chapter 3). Finger millet was also transplanted in parts of the south, as were tobacco, chillies and many vegetables. Transplanting needs much labour in a short time, and in most of India it has been done largely by women (Section 7.16).

docs.title: 7.12 Weeding and Interculture
docs.text:
The Tirukkuṟaḷ names weeding, with manuring and guarding the crop, among the farmer’s essential tasks, and the Kṛṣi-Parāśara insists on timely weeding (Chapters 2 and 3). In practice most weeding was done by hand. Workers squatted in the field and worked through it with the khurpī, cutting weeds below the surface and loosening the soil; in rice fields weeds were pulled and pressed back into the mud to rot. This slow, back-breaking work was done mostly by women and hired labourers, and in many regions it was one of the main sources of wage work for women from landless households.

Where crops were sown in lines, bullocks could do part of the work. Light bullock hoes, essentially narrow blade harrows set to pass between the rows, were drawn through the standing crop to cut weeds and loosen the surface. This interculture was one of the main advantages of drill sowing, and the drill, the blade harrow and the bullock hoe together made up a coherent system of dry farming.

Broadcast rice in parts of eastern and central India was treated in a striking way. When the crop was some weeks old and the field held water, it was ploughed across with the ordinary plough and then levelled. This operation, called biāsī in Chhattisgarh and neighbouring regions (“beushening” in older English writing), uproots weeds and thins and redistributes the rice plants, which recover in the soft mud; it substitutes for transplanting where labour or water is too scarce for a nursery.

docs.title: 7.13.1 Reaping
docs.text: Grain crops were reaped with the sickle, a curved iron blade on a short wooden handle, its edge often finely toothed, used by a reaper who squats or bends low and grasps a handful of stalks before cutting. Cereals were generally cut low, because straw was valuable as fodder, thatch and fuel; pulses and some other crops were pulled up by hand. The crop was tied in sheaves, dried in the field and carried to the threshing floor by head-load or cart. Households without enough labour of their own hired reapers, who in much of India were paid in kind with a share of the sheaves they cut, and in many villages the poor were allowed to glean the fields afterwards. In the twentieth century the wheat and rice harvests of Punjab and Haryana came to depend on labourers who migrated seasonally from eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.

docs.title: 7.13.2 Threshing
docs.text: The threshing floor (Sanskrit khala, Hindi khalihān, Tamil kaḷam) was a patch of level ground beaten hard and plastered with cow dung and water, which dried to a smooth, clean surface. The Kṛṣi-Parāśara gives rules and rites for preparing and using it (Chapter 3). Wheat, barley, sorghum and many other grains were threshed by treading. The sheaves were spread in a circle around a stout wooden post in the middle of the floor (Sanskrit methi or medhi); a line of bullocks, tied abreast to the post, was driven round and round over the crop, while workers with forks turned the straw, until the grain had been trodden out and the straw broken. In the wheat country the broken straw, bhūsā, was itself a valued fodder. Rice was often threshed by beating handfuls of stalks against a plank, a stone or the floor, or by treading; pulses, mustard and other small seeds were beaten out with sticks.

docs.title: 7.13.3 Winnowing
docs.text: On a day with a steady breeze a worker stood on a stool or platform and poured the threshed mixture slowly from a basket held at head height, so that the heavier grain fell to the floor while the wind carried the chaff aside. The grain was then cleaned further in the winnowing basket (Sanskrit śūrpa, Hindi sūp, Tamil muṟam), a shallow basket of split bamboo or reed, open at one end, in which grain is tossed so that chaff, dust and small stones are separated from it. The śūrpa appears among the implements of the Vedic ritual (Chapter 14), and Gaṇeśa is called Śūrpakarṇa, “he whose ears are like winnowing baskets”. Husking and grinding are discussed in Chapter 14, and the storage of grain and seed in Chapters 9 and 14.

docs.title: 7.13.4 Dividing the harvest
docs.text: The threshing floor was also where the harvest was divided. Before the grain left the floor, shares were measured out to the landholder, the tenant or sharecropper, and the village artisans and servants—carpenter, smith, potter, barber, washerman and others—who were paid in grain at harvest for their services through the year (Wiser 1936). Under the Mughal revenue system one form of crop-sharing consisted precisely in dividing the heaps of grain on the threshing floor between the cultivator and the state (Habib 1999).

docs.title: 7.14 Draught Animals, Carts and Village Artisans
docs.text:
The basic unit of power on the Indian farm was the pair of bullocks. The plough, the plank, the blade harrow, the drill, the cart, the leather bucket of the well (Chapter 8) and the oil press (Chapter 14) were all built for a pair, and several of the best-known Indian cattle breeds were valued above all for draught (Chapter 13). A pair had to be fed all year, although much of its work was concentrated into a few weeks of ploughing, sowing and threshing. Holdings were commonly described in terms of ploughs, and the household with its own pair was in a different position from the one without. Smallholders who could not keep a pair joined with neighbours, borrowed or hired a team, or paid for ploughing in labour, and so often ploughed and sowed late. Landless labourers owned no draught animals at all.

The bullock cart is as old as the plough in the subcontinent: terracotta models of carts with solid wheels are common at Harappan sites (Kenoyer 1998). The Vedic ox-cart is the anas, distinct from the horse-drawn chariot (ratha); the common later word is śakaṭa. Most later carts had spoked wheels made by the carpenter and fitted with iron tyres by the smith. On the farm the cart carried manure and tank silt to the fields and the harvest to the threshing floor and market. Over long distances the grain trade depended, until the railway age, on the pack-bullock caravans of the Banjārās, which also supplied armies (Habib 1999).

The village carpenter and smith made and maintained almost the whole stock of implements. The carpenter shaped plough, yoke, plank, harrow frame, drill and cart from local wood; the smith forged and sharpened the share, the harrow blade, the sickle, the hoe and the spade, and before each season shares and sickles were brought to him to be re-pointed. In much of India these artisans were paid not for each job but with a customary share of grain from each household at harvest, an arrangement Wiser (1936) described as part of the north Indian jajmānī system. Rope-makers, potters and leather-workers supplied the rest: ropes and tethers, pots, and the leather of buckets, straps and whips. The leather-workers’ trade, indispensable to an agriculture of bullocks, was also a mark of their exclusion (Chapter 18).

docs.title: 7.15.1 Colonial attempts at improvement
docs.text:
From the first half of the nineteenth century British officials, missionaries and improving landholders tried to introduce European ploughs and harrows, and the experimental farms of the later nineteenth century tested many imported designs. Most of these trials failed. Heavy iron ploughs needed larger animals than most Indian cultivators possessed, cost far more than a wooden plough, and could not be repaired in the village. Voelcker (Section 7.5.2) saw a place for light improved implements introduced with care for particular purposes, but not for wholesale replacement.

In the early twentieth century provincial agricultural departments promoted light iron ploughs, some with small mouldboards for burying weeds or green manure, and Indian manufacturers began to make them. The best known was Laxmanrao Kirloskar, who began making iron ploughs in the first decade of the century and soon afterwards established his works at Kirloskarwadi, in what is now Maharashtra. Adoption was slow and uneven, and the wooden plough remained the ordinary implement of most Indian farmers until the 1960s, and in many regions long after.

docs.title: 7.15.2 Tractors, threshers and combines
docs.text:
After independence a Central Tractor Organisation used tractors to reclaim land overgrown with deep-rooted grasses in central and northern India, but the mechanisation of ordinary farming began with the Green Revolution of the late 1960s and 1970s (Chapter 20). Tractor manufacture in India began around 1960, and in the irrigated regions of Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh tractors bought with institutional credit spread rapidly, for ploughing and seedbed preparation and, with a trailer, for haulage in place of the bullock cart. In the rice regions small two-wheeled power tillers came into use. By the early twenty-first century India had become one of the world’s largest producers and markets for tractors, and many small farmers hired a tractor and driver for each operation.

Mechanical threshers spread in the wheat country at the same time. They did in hours what treading did in days and produced the chopped bhūsā that farmers wanted for fodder, but they also caused many serious injuries to hands and arms caught in the feeding chutes, and the Dangerous Machines (Regulation) Act of 1983 was passed to regulate their safety. Combine harvesters, which reap and thresh in one operation, became common in Punjab and Haryana from the 1980s, often owned by contractors who moved with the harvest from region to region. Because combines leave standing stubble and loose straw, and the interval between the rice harvest and wheat sowing is short, many farmers in the north-west took to burning the rice residue in the field, which contributes to severe air pollution across the region in late autumn. Machines that sow wheat directly through the residue have been promoted as an alternative; the problem remains unsolved.

docs.title: 7.15.3 The effects of mechanisation
docs.text:
A review of the evidence by Hans Binswanger in 1978 found little clear evidence that tractors had substantially raised yields or cropping intensity in South Asia, and concluded that their main effect had been to replace bullocks and human labour (Binswanger 1978). Others have argued that in irrigated areas the speed of tractor ploughing helps farmers fit two crops into a year. The distributional effects are less disputed. Mechanisation reduced the demand for the labour of attached ploughmen, harvest workers and the women who had threshed and winnowed, and it favoured larger farmers and the contractors who hired out machines. It also changed the place of cattle in the farm economy (Chapter 13). In rain-fed regions, on small and scattered holdings and in the hills, the bullock and the wooden plough remained in use much longer, and in some places they still are.

Debate: Were India’s implements “primitive”?

Colonial writers often called the Indian plough a primitive implement that merely scratched the soil, and the judgement recurs in modern development writing. Those who studied it closely, Voelcker above all, took a different view: the ard, the plank, the blade harrow and the drill formed a set of cheap, locally repairable tools matched to small cattle, thin purses and soils that often did not need deep inversion. Neither view should be pressed too far. The old implements were well adapted to the constraints under which most cultivators worked, but they were also limited by them: they demanded great quantities of human and animal labour, the timing of operations depended on access to a team, and the poorest households had no team at all. They are best judged against those constraints, and contempt and nostalgia are equally out of place.

docs.title: 7.16 Who Did Which Work
docs.text:
The tools of field work were divided by caste and by gender. Ploughing was the central operation of the farming year, yet it was hedged with restrictions. Following the Manusmṛti’s disapproval of the plough (Section 2.9), in much of India brahmins, and in some regions other high-caste landholders, did not handle the plough themselves. The work fell to tenants and attached ploughmen, often from castes treated as untouchable or from Adivasi communities: the halvāhā of north India, whose name means “ploughman”, and the Dubla hāli farm servants of south Gujarat studied by Breman (1974) are examples (Chapter 18).

Women were almost everywhere in South Asia barred by custom from ploughing, and in many regions from touching the plough at all; Agarwal (1994) discusses this taboo and the use made of it in arguments against women’s independent rights in land. Ester Boserup argued that societies using the plough tended to restrict women’s field work more than those that cultivated with the hoe (Boserup 1970), and Alberto Alesina, Paola Giuliano and Nathan Nunn found that descendants of societies that traditionally used the plough hold less equal views about women’s roles today (Alesina et al. 2013). Both are broad comparative arguments, which India, with its great regional variety, fits only in part.

Exclusion from the plough did not mean exclusion from the field. Transplanting and weeding rice were in most regions largely women’s work, and the songs women sang while transplanting form a large oral literature in many Indian languages. Women did much of the harvesting, gleaning, threshing, winnowing and cleaning of grain, carried head-loads and manure, and made the dung cakes that competed with the fields for it (Section 7.5); in shifting cultivation they often did much of the hoeing and sowing. Most of this work was done with hand tools—the khurpī, the sickle and the sūp—rather than with the animal-drawn implements controlled by men. Mechanisation has altered this division without abolishing it: threshers, combines, rice mills and herbicides took over many tasks for which poor women had been paid, while the work that remains unmechanised, above all transplanting and weeding in small fields, is still largely theirs.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Early Indian texts classify land by fertility and salinity (urvarā, ūṣara), by the crop it will bear (Pāṇini), by whether it holds water (sthala, kedāra), by micro-site (the Arthaśāstra) and by the dry or marshy character of a country (jāṅgala, ānūpa); the physical soil tests of Sanskrit are tests of building sites. The Kṛṣi-Parāśara gives the clearest early instructions on manuring with cow dung, but most of what we know about fertility management, bunds and terraces comes from farmers’ practice recorded since the nineteenth century. Canal irrigation spread waterlogging and reh, and modern soil science’s groups have no exact counterpart in the Sanskrit sources. The soil was worked with the ard, a wooden plough with an iron share, and a set of cheap, locally made implements — plank, blade harrow, seed drill, hoes, sickle, threshing floor and winnowing basket — maintained by village carpenters and smiths paid in grain. Colonial attempts to replace them largely failed; tractors, threshers and combines spread with the Green Revolution. Throughout, field work was divided by caste and gender: ploughing was barred to brahmins by custom and to women almost everywhere, while transplanting, weeding and much of the harvest fell to women and to labourers of low status.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Zimmermann (1987) on jāṅgala and ānūpa; Kangle (1965) and Olivelle (2013) for the Arthaśāstra; Sadhale (1999) for the Kṛṣi-Parāśara; Voelcker (1893) for Indian farming practice and implements in the late nineteenth century; Agarwal and Narain (1997) for terraces and water-harvesting structures; and Habib (2008) for the history of agricultural technology in medieval India.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Water: Tanks, Canals, Wells and Communities
docs.text: Indian agriculture has always had to manage a seasonal abundance of water and a long seasonal scarcity. Over most of the subcontinent the bulk of the year’s rain falls in the few months of the south-west monsoon, and much of it runs off quickly; the rest of the year is dry, and the monsoon itself is uncertain in its timing and amount (see Volume 19, Vāṇijya and Samudra, on the monsoon, and Chapter 3 on rain forecasting). Almost every Indian irrigation technique is a way of holding monsoon water back—in a tank, behind a weir, in the soil, or underground—or of lifting stored water from a well or river when it is needed. This chapter surveys those techniques and the institutions that sustained them, from the earliest textual references to the colonial canals and the recent decline and partial revival of community systems. The emphasis is on what can be documented in texts, inscriptions, surviving works and field studies.

docs.title: 8.1.1 Before and in the Veda
docs.text:
The Harappan cities were careful managers of water: Mohenjo-daro had a very large number of brick-lined wells and covered drains, and Dholavira in Kachchh had large stone-cut reservoirs for storing seasonal runoff (Kenoyer 1998; Possehl 2002). Whether Harappan farmers practised canal irrigation on any scale is debated; much of their agriculture probably relied on rainfall and on the flooding of rivers (Chapter 2).

The Ṛgveda knows both natural and artificial water. A hymn to the Waters speaks of waters that are heavenly or that flow, khanitrimā uta vā yāḥ svayaṃjāḥ, “those that are dug and those that arise of themselves” (RV 7.49.2; (Jamison and Brereton 2014)). The well (avata) appears in the same collection: one late hymn (RV 10.101), addressed to the priests as if they were farmers, uses the image of a well with a strap and bucket, drawing water that does not run dry, alongside the yoking of ploughs. The word kulyā, a channel or ditch, also occurs in Vedic texts. These references show that dug channels and wells were familiar, but they do not describe irrigation systems, and nothing in the Vedic corpus supports claims of large-scale hydraulic works.

docs.title: 8.1.2 Buddhist and Jain traditions
docs.text: Early Buddhist and Jain texts are set in a landscape of rice fields divided by bunds and fed by channels. A well-known story in the later Buddhist commentarial tradition tells how the Śākyas and the Koliyas, neighbouring peoples on either side of the river Rohiṇī, quarrelled over the waters of a weir across the river during a drought, and how the Buddha made peace between them. Whatever its historicity, the story assumes that dividing river water between communities was a familiar cause of conflict.

docs.title: 8.1.3 The Arthaśāstra
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra (composite, c. 50 BCE–300 CE) gives the earliest sustained treatment of irrigation as a matter for the state; for the text as a whole, see Volume 18, Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra. Its key term is setu, which covers dams, embankments and the reservoirs they create. In the chapter on settling the countryside (Book 2, chapter 1) the king is told to have irrigation works built, either with water available on the spot (sahodaka) or with water brought from elsewhere (āhāryodaka), and to help others who build them by providing land, roads, timber and implements (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013). In Book 7, when weighing one strategic advantage against another, the text judges a work with its own water source better than one depending on water brought from elsewhere, and among the former, the one that irrigates the larger crop.

Several other passages concern water. The chapter on the superintendent of agriculture (2.24) fixes a water rate graded by the way the water reaches the field (Section 2.11.1), and the rain gauge and regional rainfall norms are discussed in Section 3.5. In Book 3, the rules on property and damage grant remissions of tax for a number of years to those who construct new irrigation works or restore abandoned ones, the remission being longer for new works; they treat privately built works as property; and they impose fines on those who breach embankments or obstruct another’s water. Whether these rules describe actual Mauryan administration or the ideal of later theorists is uncertain, but they show that by the early centuries CE, Sanskrit political thought treated irrigation works as both a royal responsibility and a form of property.

docs.title: 8.1.4 Merit and patronage
docs.text: From the Dharmaśāstra and Purāṇic literature onward, the building of wells, tanks, stepwells and gardens is classed as pūrta, a work of public merit that, with sacrificial and charitable works (iṣṭa), earns religious reward. Thousands of inscriptions across India record the digging or repair of a tank or well by a king, queen, merchant, temple, village assembly or individual, often with a grant of land or revenue for its upkeep. This ideology of merit was one important reason why so much hydraulic infrastructure was built by patrons outside the central state; it does not mean that the resulting water was shared equally (Section 8.5).

docs.title: 8.2 The Sudarśana Lake at Girnar
docs.text:
The best-documented early irrigation work in India is the Sudarśana lake at Girnar, near Junagadh in Saurashtra, known from inscriptions on the same boulder that carries a set of Aśoka’s major rock edicts. The Sanskrit inscription of the Western Kṣatrapa ruler Rudradāman, dated to year 72 of the Śaka era (150 CE), records that the lake had been constructed under Candragupta Maurya by his provincial governor, the vaiśya Puṣyagupta, and that under Aśoka the Yavana king Tuṣāspha had furnished it with conduits. A great storm had then burst the dam and emptied the lake. Rudradāman, the inscription says, had it rebuilt, stronger than before, from his own treasury and without oppressing the people with taxes, forced labour or levies, through his minister Suviśākha, a Pahlava who governed the province (Singh 2008). The lake was breached again three centuries later; an inscription of the Gupta emperor Skandagupta on the same rock records its repair in the mid-fifth century by Cakrapālita, son of the provincial governor.

These records are valuable precisely because they are not idealised prescriptions. They show a single reservoir maintained for more than seven centuries under three successive powers—Maurya, Kṣatrapa and Gupta—and the provincial officials who served them, with all the risks of breaching and neglect that such works faced. They also show irrigation as royal propaganda: Rudradāman’s boast of having avoided forced labour (viṣṭi) is a reminder that such labour was the normal way in which large works were built.

A second early record comes from Odisha. The Hāthīgumphā inscription of the Kaliṅga king Khāravela (1st c. BCE) says that he brought into his capital a canal first opened by a “Nanda king” long before; the interval is read differently by different scholars, so the age of the canal is uncertain.

docs.title: 8.3.1 What a tank is
docs.text:
Across the drier parts of the peninsula, from Tamil Nadu through Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana into the Deccan, the characteristic irrigation work is the tank: Tamil ēri, Kannada kere, Telugu cheruvu. A tank is made by throwing an earthen embankment across a shallow valley or the line of a seasonal stream. Monsoon runoff collects behind the bund; one or more sluices let water out to the fields below as the crop requires; and a surplus weir carries off excess water in heavy rain so that the bund is not overtopped. In many areas tanks are arranged in chains or cascades along a drainage line, so that the surplus of one feeds the next (Figure 8.1). Tanks also serve for drinking water, bathing, washing, cattle, fish and the recharge of nearby wells, and the silt deposited on their beds is a valued manure (Chapter 7).

Figure 8.1. The south Indian tank (Tamil ēri, Kannada kere, Telugu cheruvu), schematic and not to scale. (a) Tanks built in a chain along a drainage line: each earthen bund holds back runoff, sluices release water to the fields below, and surplus weirs pass excess water on to the next tank. (b) A section through one bund. After the descriptions in Section 8.3.

docs.title: 8.3.2 Tanks in inscriptions
docs.text: The epigraphic record of tanks in south India is enormous. Pallava, Pāṇḍya, Cōḻa, Cālukya, Hoysala, Kākatīya and Vijayanagara inscriptions record the construction and repair of tanks, the grant of land whose income was to pay for annual desilting and bund repair, and disputes over water. In Karnataka and Andhra, grants known as daśabandha (Telugu dasavanda, “one-tenth”) rewarded those who built or maintained tanks with a share of the land or produce they irrigated. Large tanks associated with particular rulers include the great reservoir at Gaṅgaikoṇḍacōḻapuram, the capital built by the Cōḻa king Rājendra I in the eleventh century. Such works were important, but most tanks were small, local and anonymous.

docs.title: 8.3.3 The Uttaramērūr inscriptions
docs.text:
The most detailed evidence for the local management of tanks comes from two inscriptions of the Cōḻa king Parāntaka I, of 919 and 921 CE, at Uttaramērūr near Kanchipuram. They set out the rules by which the sabhā, the assembly of this brahmadeya (a village granted to brahmins), was to choose its executive committees (vāriyam). Candidates were nominated by ward and chosen by lot, slips bearing their names being drawn from a pot (kuḍavōlai). Among the committees were an annual committee, a garden committee and a tank committee (ēri-vāriyam) responsible for the village’s tanks (Singh 2008).

The inscriptions are justly famous as evidence of elaborate local self-government, but they are sometimes described too generously as a “village democracy”. Eligibility was limited to men of a certain age who owned taxable land and a house on their own site and had Vedic learning; the assembly was that of brahmin landholders, and the cultivators and labourers who worked the land had no voice in it. The tank committee managed water on behalf of landholders.

docs.title: 8.3.4 Cōḻa and Vijayanagara landscapes
docs.text:
Under the Cōḻas (9th–13th c.) the Kāvēri delta was irrigated mainly by channels taking off from the river and its branches, while the drier uplands around it depended on tanks. Inscriptions show temples acting as major investors in, and managers of, irrigation, receiving endowments of land and lending money for tank works.

Kathleen Morrison’s archaeological study of the region around Vijayanagara, the capital of the empire of that name (14th–16th c.), shows how varied irrigation could be within a single landscape (Morrison 1995). Close to the Tungabhadrā river, weirs (anicuts) diverted water into long channels that fed irrigated fields; away from the river, reservoirs behind embankments held runoff; and on the uplands, dry farming and small run-off fields persisted. Morrison argues that agricultural intensification around the city was achieved through this mix of strategies, each with different costs and risks, rather than through a single type of “hydraulic” system directed by the state.

docs.title: 8.4 The Grand Anicut on the Kāvēri
docs.text:
In south India a weir across a river that diverts water into irrigation channels is called an anicut (from Tamil aṇaikkaṭṭu). The most celebrated is the Grand Anicut, Tamil Kallaṇai (“stone dam”), near Tiruchirappalli at the head of the Kāvēri delta, which regulates how the river’s water is divided between the Kāvēri proper and its northern branch, the Kollidam (Coleroon). Tradition attributes the original work to the early Cōḻa king Karikāla (early centuries CE), and later Cōḻa-period traditions credit him with embanking the Kāvēri. No contemporary inscription confirms the attribution, and the date of the earliest structure is not known; but an old masonry weir certainly existed at the site before the colonial period (Figure 8.2).

Figure 8.2. The Grand Anicut (Kallaṇai) on the Kāvēri near Tiruchirappalli. Tradition attributes the original weir to the Cōḻa king Karikāla; the structure seen today is largely the product of nineteenth-century rebuilding and later works. Photo: Beckamrajeev, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The structure visible today is largely the work of the nineteenth century. In the 1830s and 1840s the Madras engineer Arthur Cotton studied the old weir, built a new regulating work (the Upper Anicut) across the Kollidam upstream, and rebuilt and raised the Grand Anicut itself, with further modifications by later engineers. Cotton is said to have learned from the old anicut how to found a masonry weir on a sandy river bed, and he went on to build the great anicut across the Godāvarī at Dowleswaram (begun 1847), which transformed irrigation in the Godāvarī delta; a similar work on the Kṛṣṇā followed in the 1850s. The Grand Anicut thus belongs to two histories at once: a long Tamil tradition of river diversion, and the colonial irrigation engineering that built on it.

docs.title: 8.5 Tanks, Caste and Community
docs.text:
Tanks are often presented as the model of community water management, and in an important sense they were. Their upkeep depended on collective labour by the villagers who used them, known in Tamil as kuṭimarāmattu (roughly, “maintenance by the cultivators”): desilting the bed, repairing the bund, clearing the channels. Water was distributed through village functionaries such as the Tamil nīrkaṭṭi, who opened sluices and turned water from field to field in an agreed order, often paid in grain at harvest. Rules for sharing in scarcity, closing the sluices, and timing the crop were made and enforced locally.

But “community” did not mean equality. David Mosse’s study of tank systems in the Ramanathapuram and Sivaganga region of Tamil Nadu shows that tanks were embedded in political systems of kingship, temple honour and caste rank (Mosse 2003). Rights to water, the order in which fields received it, and the duty to perform the labour of maintenance were tied to caste status: dominant landholding castes controlled tanks and took the first and best water, while the actual digging, desilting and watering were frequently done by Dalit labourers and by low-ranked service castes, including the water-turners themselves. Mosse also shows that the colonial state, by treating tanks as revenue-producing property and taking over their maintenance, weakened the older political arrangements that had sustained them, without creating effective new ones.

Exclusion from water was also enforced in everyday life. Across much of India, Dalits were barred from using village wells and tanks used by the upper castes, and separate wells were the norm. In 1927 B. R. Ambedkar led a large assembly of Dalits to drink from the public Chavdar tank at Mahad in Maharashtra, a landmark of the movement against untouchability. Any account of traditional water management that celebrates community must also record whom the community excluded.

Water institutions

Most Indian irrigation systems were neither purely state works nor purely “community” works. Kings and temples financed large tanks and channels; village assemblies and dominant landholders managed them; customary officials—the nīrkaṭṭi in Tamil Nadu, the kohli of the Kangra kuhls, the watermen of the Maharashtra phads—regulated day-to-day distribution; and the heavy labour fell largely on lower castes. These institutions were often durable and effective, and also hierarchical.

docs.title: 8.6 Kashmir: Suyya’s Works
docs.text: One of the few accounts of a named hydraulic engineer in pre-modern India comes from Kalhaṇa’s Rājataraṅgiṇī, the Sanskrit chronicle of the kings of Kashmir completed in 1148–49. In its fifth book Kalhaṇa describes the works of Suyya, a man of humble origins who served King Avantivarman (r. c. 855–883). According to Kalhaṇa, the valley suffered from floods because the Vitastā (Jhelum) was choked by rocks where it leaves the valley, and Suyya had the bed cleared—famously, by throwing money into the river so that villagers would dig out the obstruction while searching for coins. He is said to have built stone embankments, moved the confluence of the Vitastā and the Sindhu, reclaimed land from the marshes, protected villages with circular dykes, and fixed the allotment of irrigation water to villages; Kalhaṇa adds that the price of rice fell greatly as a result (Stein 1900). The town of Sopore (Suyyapura) is named after him. The account is a court chronicle written three centuries after the events, and its details cannot be checked independently, but it is a rare literary description of drainage and river training in medieval India.

docs.title: 8.7 Stepwells
docs.text:
The stepwell—Sanskrit vāpī, Gujarati vāv, Hindi and Rajasthani bāolī or bāvaḍī—is a well reached by a long flight of steps descending through a series of landings and pavilions to the water, so that people can reach the water whatever its level. Stepwells are concentrated in Gujarat and Rajasthan, where groundwater lies deep and fluctuates greatly with the seasons. The form is attested in the later first millennium CE (the Chand Baori at Abhaneri in Rajasthan is commonly dated to the eighth or ninth century), and the great Gujarati examples date from the eleventh to the sixteenth century (Jain-Neubauer 1981).

The Rani-ki-Vav at Patan, built in the later eleventh century and traditionally associated with Queen Udayamatī in memory of the Caulukya king Bhīma I, is the most elaborate, with hundreds of sculptures on its walls; it was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2014. The stepwell at Adalaj near Ahmedabad bears an inscription of 1499 recording its construction by a queen, Rūḍādevī, wife of a local Vāghelā chief. Many other stepwells were built under the Gujarat Sultanate and the Mughals, and the type was shared across religious communities.

Stepwells were primarily for drinking water, bathing and rest rather than irrigation, although some fed gardens. They were also social spaces, especially for the women who drew water, and cool places of retreat in the hot season. Their elaborate architecture made them works of conspicuous merit for their patrons, among whom queens and merchants are prominent. The stepped tank at Mohenjo-daro known as the “Great Bath” is a different kind of structure, and no stepwell of the Harappan period is known.

docs.title: 8.8 Regional Systems
docs.text:
India’s diversity of terrain and rainfall produced a correspondingly diverse set of local irrigation and water-harvesting systems. Many were documented systematically for the first time in the survey Dying Wisdom, edited by Anil Agarwal and Sunita Narain (Agarwal and Narain 1997), which did much to draw attention to them; some are summarised in Table 8.1, and Figure 8.3 locates them and the other works named in this chapter. Community water harvesting in tribal regions is treated more fully in Volume 23, Jana–Jāti.

Figure 8.3. Some irrigation works and water systems named in this chapter: the Sudarśana lake at Girnar; the stepwells of Patan, Adalaj and Abhaneri; the canal heads and towns of the north (Haridwar for the Ganges Canal, Hisar and Delhi for the Sultanate and Mughal canals); Mahad, where Ambedkar led the Chavdar tank satyagraha; the reservoirs and channels of Vijayanagara; the tanks of Uttaramērūr and Gaṅgaikoṇḍacōḻapuram; the Grand Anicut and Cotton’s anicut at Dowleswaram; and representative areas of the regional systems of Table 8.1. The kuhls of Kangra and the zabo of Nagaland lie outside the frame. Positions are plotted by latitude and longitude; the coastline is simplified, islands other than Sri Lanka are omitted, and no rivers or political boundaries are shown. Table 8.1. Selected regional water systems of India. docs.title: 8.8.1 Ahar–pyne of south Bihar
docs.text: The plains of south Bihar slope northward towards the Ganga, and their rivers run full in the monsoon and dry soon after. The ahar–pyne system exploits this. Pynes are channels that take water from the rivers in flood, or collect runoff, and lead it to ahars, reservoirs embanked on three sides with the fourth open to the slope. Water stored in the ahars, and the moisture in their beds, carries the rice crop through the end of the monsoon. Maintenance depended on landlord investment and on collective labour; the decline of both after the abolition of zamindari in the 1950s is widely blamed for the system’s deterioration (Agarwal and Narain 1997).

docs.title: 8.8.2 Phad of Maharashtra
docs.text: In the valleys of the Panjhra and neighbouring rivers of the Tapi basin, farmers built stone weirs (bandhara) to divert river water into main canals and smaller distributaries. The land commanded by each system was divided into blocks (phad), each of which grew a single crop in a given season, such as sugarcane or a grain crop, so that water could be delivered efficiently to the block as a whole. Water distribution and maintenance were organised by the irrigators through appointed watermen.

docs.title: 8.8.3 Kuhls of Kangra
docs.text: In the Kangra valley of Himachal Pradesh, gravity-flow channels called kuhls divert water from Himalayan streams to terraced rice fields. Mark Baker’s study shows that each kuhl is managed by the households it serves, under a watermaster (kohli) who organises the annual repair of headworks after the monsoon and the rotation of water between villages and fields; customary rules were written down by colonial settlement officers in the late nineteenth century and still carry weight (Baker 2005). Baker also traces how these institutions have adapted, or failed to adapt, to the spread of off-farm employment and state intervention.

docs.title: 8.8.4 The North-East
docs.text: In the zabo (“impounding water”) system of the Chakhesang Nagas of Kikruma and neighbouring villages, rainwater falling on protected forest above the fields is led into ponds, passes through cattle yards where it picks up manure, and is then channelled onto rice terraces, with fish sometimes reared in the fields. In the Khasi and Jaintia hills of Meghalaya, water from springs and streams is carried in bamboo pipes and progressively divided through smaller pipes and channels until it arrives, at a much reduced flow, at the base of individual plants, chiefly in betel-leaf and black pepper gardens. The system is often called “bamboo drip irrigation”; it shares the principle of delivering small quantities of water to each plant with modern drip irrigation, though it was developed independently (Agarwal and Narain 1997).

docs.title: 8.8.5 Rajasthan: kuṇḍs, johads and khadins
docs.text:
The Thar and its margins have very low and erratic rainfall, and water harvesting there aims first at drinking water. A kuṇḍ or kuṇḍī is an underground cistern, usually lined and covered with a dome, fed by a carefully prepared and often plastered catchment sloping towards it. In eastern Rajasthan, johads are crescent-shaped earthen embankments that hold monsoon runoff; their main benefit is often the recharge of downstream wells. From the 1980s the voluntary organisation Tarun Bharat Sangh, led by Rajendra Singh, revived the building of johads in Alwar district, an effort that became a model for water-harvesting campaigns elsewhere.

The khadin, associated by tradition with the Paliwal Brahmins of the Jaisalmer region, is a long earthen embankment built across the lower slope of a rocky catchment. Monsoon runoff collects behind it, depositing fine silt; when the water has soaked in or been drained, the moist bed is sown with a winter crop such as wheat or gram. The khadin is as much a soil-making device as a water-harvesting one (Chapter 7).

docs.title: 8.8.6 Surangam of the laterite coast
docs.text: In Kasaragod district of northern Kerala and the adjoining Dakshina Kannada district of Karnataka, farmers dig horizontal tunnels, called surangam or suranga, into laterite hillsides until they reach water-bearing strata; the water then flows out by gravity into a pit or tank, and is used for drinking and for areca nut and coconut gardens. The technique resembles the qanāt of Iran in principle, though a surangam is usually a single tunnel without the vertical shafts of a qanāt. How old the tradition is, and whether it is connected to West Asian practice, is not known; many existing tunnels are relatively recent.

docs.title: 8.9 Lifting Water
docs.text:
Where water lay below the level of the field—in a well, a river or a low tank—it had to be lifted. Irfan Habib’s survey of medieval Indian technology distinguishes several devices and traces their history (Habib 2008); the three main types are shown in Figure 8.4.

The swing-beam lever. The simplest device, a pivoted pole with a bucket at one end and a counterweight at the other (the shaduf of Egypt), is known in north India as ḍheṅklī or ḍhekulī, in Anglo-Indian usage in the south as the picottah, and by many other local names. Worked by one or two people, it lifts water a short height from shallow wells, tanks or streams. The rope-and-bucket lift. In western and northern India, a large leather bucket (charas in north India, mhoṭ or moṭ in Marathi) was drawn up from a deep well on a rope passing over a pulley by a pair of bullocks walking down an inclined ramp, then emptied into a channel. It could lift water from considerable depths but required continuous work by two men and two animals. The water-wheel. Sanskrit texts from the early centuries CE mention the araghaṭṭa and the ghaṭīyantra, “pot-machine”. In Habib’s reconstruction these were wheels carrying pots, either fixed to the rim or tied to a chain or garland of rope, turned directly by human or animal effort. The fully developed “Persian wheel” (Hindi rahaṭ), in which animals walking in a circle drive the pot-garland through right-angled gearing, spread in north India in the Sultanate period.

The emperor Bābur, writing in the 1520s, described the two methods he found in Hindustan: a wheel with a rope of pots, turned by an animal through a gear, in the Lahore and Dipalpur region; and the bullock-drawn bucket in the region of Agra and Bayana (Thackston 1996). In the Mughal period well irrigation of these kinds, rather than canals, watered most irrigated land in north India (Habib 1999).

Figure 8.4. Three ways of lifting water, schematic and not to scale. (a) The swing-beam lift, in which a counterweight balances a pot on a pivoted pole, raises water a short height from a shallow well, tank or stream. (b) The rope-and-bucket lift: a pair of bullocks walking down a ramp draws a large leather bucket up a deep well over a pulley. (c) The geared Persian wheel: an animal walking in a circle turns a horizontal wheel whose gearing drives a vertical wheel carrying a garland of pots. After Habib (2008) and the descriptions in Section 8.9.

Water-lifting was hard and continuous labour. A well with a charas could keep a team of men and bullocks occupied through the day in the dry season, and access to a well, which was expensive to dig and line, was itself a mark of a household’s standing. Wells were usually owned by landholding families, and their use, like the use of tanks, was governed by caste rules.

docs.title: 8.10 Finding Water: Varāhamihira’s Dakārgala
docs.text:
The fifty-fourth chapter of Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā (6th c. CE; Bhat’s numbering) is the dakārgala, a manual for finding groundwater for wells (Bhat 1981). Varāhamihira begins from the idea that water runs beneath the earth in channels (śirā) like the veins of the body, and that these can be located by surface signs. Most of the chapter is a list of such signs and their meanings: a particular tree, such as a jambū or an udumbara, growing in a dry place; an anthill beside a tree; the presence of certain creatures; the colour and texture of the soil; and the kind of stones met in digging. For each sign the text states in which direction from it, and at what depth (measured in puruṣa, a unit based on a man’s height), water will be found, and sometimes whether it will be sweet or brackish. It distinguishes ordinary country from desert regions, where the indications and depths differ.

The chapter is a remarkable document of systematic observation and of the importance attached to well-digging in Varāhamihira’s world. It is also a text of its time: the rules are stated as certainties, are mixed with astrological and omen material elsewhere in the Bṛhatsaṃhitā, and have not been tested as a set. That some plants indicate shallow groundwater is a reasonable general observation; that the particular depths and directions given in the text are reliable has not been shown. The dakārgala theme was continued in later works, among them the Viśvavallabha of Cakrapāṇi Miśra (16th c., Mewar), which also deals with water-finding (Section 4.1).

docs.title: 8.11 Canals of the Sultanate and Mughal Periods
docs.text: Canals drawing water from the great rivers of the north were built in the Delhi Sultanate. The most important builder was Fīrūz Shāh Tughluq (r. 1351–1388), whose canals from the Yamuna and the Sutlej carried water to his new city of Hisar and irrigated land along their courses (Raychaudhuri and Habib 1982). These canals fell into disrepair after his reign. Under Shāh Jahān, the Persian noble ʿAlī Mardān Khān re-excavated and extended the old Yamuna canal in the 1640s to bring water to the emperor’s new capital at Shāhjahānābād (Delhi); inside the Red Fort the water ran through the marble channel known as the Nahr-i Bihisht, “stream of paradise”. ʿAlī Mardān Khān is also credited with a canal bringing water from the Ravi to Lahore. These canals served cities and gardens first, but they also irrigated land along the way; their remains were later the starting point for British canal building in the Yamuna region (Habib 1999). Mughal water gardens are treated in Chapter 18.

docs.title: 8.12.1 From restoration to new canals
docs.text:
British irrigation in India began by restoring older works. The Western Yamuna Canal, on the line of the Tughluq and Mughal canals, was reopened in the early nineteenth century, and an Eastern Yamuna Canal followed. In the south, Arthur Cotton’s work on the Kāvēri, Godāvarī and Kṛṣṇā (Section 8.4) turned the deltas of the Madras Presidency into heavily irrigated rice country. In the north, the Ganges Canal, designed by Proby Cautley to take water from the Ganga at Haridwar into the Doab, was opened in 1854 and is often described as the largest irrigation canal of its time.

In Punjab, where large rivers cross dry plains, canal building after the 1880s created the “canal colonies”: wholly new agricultural settlements on former pasture and waste in the doabs between the Punjab rivers. The colonies made western Punjab one of the most productive wheat and cotton regions of Asia. Imran Ali has argued that they also served imperial interests—land was granted to favoured landholding castes, retired soldiers and loyal notables, while the “menial” castes who did much of the agricultural labour were largely excluded from proprietary grants, and the pastoral peoples who had used the land lost it (Ali 1988). David Gilmartin has set the canal colonies within a longer history of the Indus basin, in which the state’s control of water reshaped both the environment and the relationship between the state and the communities who used the rivers (Gilmartin 2015).

docs.title: 8.12.2 Costs and critics
docs.text: Canal irrigation brought gains in output and some protection against drought, but also serious costs. Seepage from unlined canals and the lack of drainage raised water tables; land became waterlogged and, as saline groundwater rose and evaporated, encrusted with reh (Chapter 7). Waterlogging was linked by contemporaries to an increase in malaria in canal tracts. Historians of the canal regime, notably Elizabeth Whitcombe in her work on the United Provinces, have documented these effects (Whitcombe 1972; Kumar 1983). Canal water was sold at rates set to make the works pay, and the government distinguished between “productive” works expected to earn a return and “protective” works built mainly against famine. Critics then and since have argued that investment went where it would yield revenue rather than where need was greatest, and that older systems such as the tanks of the south were neglected (Davis 2001; Ludden 1999). The Indian Irrigation Commission of 1901–03 reviewed the whole field after the famines of the late 1890s.

docs.title: 8.12.3 Independent India
docs.text: After independence, irrigation expanded rapidly through large multipurpose dams and canal systems, and, from the 1960s and 1970s onward, through private tubewells powered by electricity and diesel. Groundwater pumped by individual farmers has since become the main source of irrigation in much of the country, a shift whose consequences for aquifers are discussed in Chapter 20.

docs.title: 8.13 Decline and Revival of Tanks
docs.text:
Through the twentieth century, many tanks and other community systems decayed. The reasons were several. Colonial and post-colonial states took over formal responsibility for larger tanks but often did not maintain them; the authority of the local elites who had organised collective labour weakened with land reforms and changing village politics; the spread of private wells and tubewells gave the wealthier farmers an alternative and reduced their interest in common works; tank beds silted up and their catchments and supply channels were encroached upon by fields, roads and buildings, especially around growing towns. In many places the result was a vicious circle, in which a poorly maintained tank supplied less water, which further reduced the incentive to maintain it.

From the 1980s these trends provoked a revival of interest. Dying Wisdom and the work of voluntary organisations such as Tarun Bharat Sangh popularised traditional water harvesting (Agarwal and Narain 1997), and state and national programmes have funded the rehabilitation of tanks, often through water-users’ associations. Results have been mixed. Physical repairs are easier to fund than the social arrangements that kept systems working, and attempts to recreate “community management” have had to deal with the same inequalities of caste, land and gender that shaped the old systems (Mosse 2003). The lesson of the historical record is not that traditional systems were ideal and need only to be restored, but that their success depended on institutions—of authority, obligation and sharing—that have to be rebuilt in forms that are fair under present conditions.

Cross-Reference: Related chapters

Rain forecasting and the rain gauge: Chapter 3. Tank silt as manure, usar and reh: Chapter 7. Rice and other irrigated crops: Chapter 9. Groundwater and modern water policy: Chapter 20. Community water harvesting in tribal regions: Volume 23, Jana–Jāti.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Indian irrigation is, above all, the storage and lifting of monsoon water. The Arthaśāstra already treats irrigation works as a royal duty and a form of property, and the Sudarśana lake was maintained for more than seven centuries. Peninsular India relied on tanks, built by many kinds of patron and managed by village institutions; the river deltas on channels from anicuts such as the Grand Anicut; and other regions on a wide variety of local systems. Water was lifted by lever, leather bucket and wheel. Sultanate, Mughal and above all colonial canals expanded irrigation in the north at the cost of waterlogging and salinity, while community systems declined. Throughout, the management of water was bound up with caste and power, a fact that any revival must confront.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Agarwal and Narain (1997) for regional water-harvesting systems; Mosse (2003) on tanks, caste and the state in Tamil Nadu; Baker (2005) on the kuhls of Kangra; Morrison (1995) on Vijayanagara; Habib (2008) on water-lifting devices; Jain-Neubauer (1981) on stepwells; and Gilmartin (2015) on the Indus canals.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Crops and Seeds
docs.text: The fields of the subcontinent have never grown a single, fixed set of crops. Some plants were brought into cultivation within South Asia; many more arrived from south-west Asia, Africa, China, Southeast Asia and, after 1500, the Americas, and were then reshaped by generations of farmers into local varieties suited to particular soils, rains and tastes. This chapter surveys the principal crops: cereals, pulses, oilseeds, sugarcane, cotton, spices, fruits and vegetables. It then turns to the reckoning of seasons, to rotation and mixed cropping, and to the selection, treatment, storage and exchange of seed. Archaeobotanical evidence for the beginnings of farming is treated in Chapter 2; the processing of grain, oil and sugar in Chapter 14; and pests, livestock integration and trees on farms in Chapter 10.

docs.title: 9.1 A Region of Domestication and of Introduction
docs.text:
The Russian botanist N. I. Vavilov (1887–1943) placed the Indian region among the handful of world “centres of origin” of cultivated plants that he defined in the 1920s and 1930s. He credited it with rice, several pulses, sugarcane, the Old World cottons, the cucumber, a number of tropical fruits and several spices (Vavilov 1951). Vavilov’s method was to locate the regions where a crop showed the greatest varietal diversity and to treat these as its homeland. Later work showed that a centre of diversity need not be a centre of origin; a crop may become most varied far from where it was first domesticated, and several “centres” turned out to be broad zones rather than points (Harlan 1971). Vavilov’s scheme is therefore best read as a landmark in the history of crop science rather than as a current account of where crops began.

The present picture comes mainly from archaeobotany, whose evidence is set out in Chapter 2: in Dorian Fuller’s synthesis South Asia was not one centre but several, combining crops introduced from south-west Asia (from about 7000 BCE at Mehrgarh), from Africa (from about 2000 BCE) and from East Asia with local wild plants brought into cultivation in Gujarat, the southern Deccan, the Ganga plain and the north-west (Fuller 2006, 2011). The cultivated landscape that emerges is a mosaic of local domesticates and introductions, and it has stayed that way ever since. Table 9.1 summarises the probable origins of the principal crops by name.

Table 9.1. Probable origins of some major crops grown in India. “Origin” refers to the region where the crop was first domesticated, as far as current evidence allows; several entries remain under study (Fuller 2006, 2011; Achaya 1998). docs.title: 9.2 Grain Classes in the Texts
docs.text:
Sanskrit texts do not describe crops in the categories of modern botany, but they do group them. The earliest lists are ritual. Barley (yava) is the grain of the Ṛgveda, where the word can also mean grain in general; rice (vrīhi) is first named in the Atharvaveda, and wheat (godhūma) only in later Vedic texts. The Yajurveda’s camaka litany (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 18), in which the sacrificer asks for each good thing “and for me”, names among its foods rice, barley, beans (māṣa), sesame, mung, khalva, the millets priyaṅgu, aṇu and śyāmāka, wild rice (nīvāra), wheat and lentil. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad gives a compact list of ten cultivated grains:

Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.3.13

daśa grāmyāṇi dhānyāni bhavanti vrīhiyavās tilamāṣā aṇupriyaṅgavo godhūmāś ca masūrāś ca khalvāś ca khalakulāś ca “There are ten cultivated grains: rice and barley, sesame and beans, millet and panic, wheat, lentils, khalva and khalakula.”

The last two terms are of uncertain identity; they are usually taken to be pulses (Olivelle 1998). The word grāmya (“of the village”) sets these cultivated grains against āraṇya, wild foods gathered from the forest, such as nīvāra.

Pāṇini (c. 4th century BCE) has rules forming adjectives for a field suited to a particular grain, such as vraiheya (a field fit for vrīhi), śāleya (for śāli) and maudgīna (for mung): evidence that farmers matched land and crop in their everyday vocabulary. The Arthaśāstra’s chapter on the director of agriculture (Section 2.11.1) sorts crops by sowing time, a classification discussed in Section 9.12.

The fullest classical scheme is medical. The chapter on food and drink in the Caraka-saṃhitā (Sūtrasthāna 27) arranges foods in twelve groups (varga). The first two are grains: śūkadhānya, “awned grains”, the cereals (rice, barley, wheat and others); and śamīdhānya, “pod grains”, the pulses (mung, urd, horsegram, lentil, chickpea, pigeon pea and others), with sesame also treated in this group. In Caraka’s list of things that are best of their kind (Sūtrasthāna 25), red śāli rice is the most wholesome of the awned grains and mung of the pulses (Sharma 1981). The Suśruta-saṃhitā’s corresponding chapter (Sūtrasthāna 46) distinguishes śāli, ṣaṣṭika and vrīhi rices, then a class of “lesser grains” (kudhānya) comprising millets such as kodrava, śyāmāka and priyaṅgu, and then the pulses (Bhishagratna 1907). These are dietetic categories, concerned with how foods act on the body; they are not crop manuals, but they preserve a valuable record of which grains were known and how they were ranked (see Volume 13, Āyurveda).

Tamil literature offers a different, landscape-based frame. In the Saṅgam poems and the tiṇai scheme of the Tolkāppiyam, the marutam tract is the land of wet paddy fields (nel), while the hill country (kuṟiñci) is the land of dry millet (tiṉai) fields guarded against parrots; crops are part of a whole poetic ecology rather than a dietetic list (Chapter 2).

docs.title: 9.3.1 Origins
docs.text: Asian rice (Oryza sativa) has two main lineages, japonica, securely domesticated in the Yangtze basin of China, and indica, the dominant rice of India, whose history is debated. In Fuller’s model, local wild rice (Oryza rufipogon and O. nivara) was long cultivated in the middle Ganga plain before japonica arriving from the east hybridised with it after about 2000 BCE; early dates claimed for domesticated rice at Lahuradewa and elsewhere remain contested (Section 2.5; (Fuller 2011)). Rice cultivation spread through the Ganga plain in the first millennium BCE and became the staple of eastern and southern India.

docs.title: 9.3.2 Classical rice types
docs.text:
The texts distinguish rices by season, duration and quality. Śāli was the prestigious rice, generally a transplanted crop harvested in early winter (hemanta); Caraka names many kinds, among them raktaśāli (red), mahāśāli (“great”), kalama, dīrghaśūka (long-awned) and sugandhaka (fragrant) (Sharma 1981). Vrīhi usually denotes rainy-season rice ripening in autumn, rated in the medical texts as heavier and less wholesome than śāli. Ṣaṣṭika, “sixty-day” rice, was a quick-maturing type valued in diets for convalescents. Nīvāra, wild rice, was the food of forest ascetics in the epics and in Kālidāsa. Lexicons such as the Amarakośa add further names. The names do not map neatly onto modern varieties, and it would be a mistake to treat the medical texts’ lists as a census of rice diversity; they record the rices known to particular authors in particular regions.

Regional agrarian vocabularies preserve similar distinctions. In Bengal, rice crops are named by their seasons: āus (sown with the early rains and harvested in late summer or autumn), āman (the main transplanted crop, harvested in early winter) and boro (grown in the dry season on residual or lifted water). The Kṛṣi-Parāśara, which probably comes from eastern India and is centred on rice, gives instructions for raising seedlings, transplanting, weeding, draining the field and harvesting; the south Indian Kāśyapīya Kṛṣisūkti likewise devotes most of its agricultural material to rice (Majumdar and Banerji 1960; Sadhale 1999; Ayachit 2002). These texts are discussed in Chapter 3.

docs.title: 9.3.3 Landraces
docs.text:
Before the twentieth century, rice in India was grown as a very large number of landraces: farmer-maintained varieties adapted to particular water regimes, from upland fields watered only by rain to deep-water and floating rices of the deltas and the saline-tolerant rices of coastal Kerala, Goa and the Sundarbans. Grain colour (white, red, black), aroma, cooking quality, duration and ritual use all mattered to farmers. The rice scientist R. H. Richharia (1909–1996), director of the Central Rice Research Institute at Cuttack and later of a rice research institute at Raipur, reportedly assembled a very large collection of landraces from the Chhattisgarh region, and argued for breeding from local varieties rather than relying on imported high-yielding lines. Precise totals for the number of rice varieties “once grown” in India circulate widely but are not based on any agreed count.

Several regional landraces now carry Geographical Indication registrations, among them Navara and Palakkadan Matta in Kerala, Kalanamak in eastern Uttar Pradesh and Joha in Assam. The decline of landrace diversity after the Green Revolution, and the movements to conserve it, are discussed in Section 9.14.4 and Chapter 20.

docs.title: 9.4 Wheat and Barley
docs.text: Barley and wheat are the oldest crops of the subcontinent. At Mehrgarh, naked six-row barley dominates the early plant remains, with smaller amounts of wheat (Meadow 1996). In the Harappan civilisation, both were winter-sown staples of the Indus plains; Harappan sites also yield a distinctive short, round-grained bread wheat, often classed as Indian dwarf or “shot” wheat (Triticum aestivum subsp. sphaerococcum) (Weber 1999; Possehl 2002). In the Ṛgveda, yava is the grain that is ploughed, sown, reaped and threshed; later Vedic ritual uses barley in many offerings, and wheat gradually rises in importance in the first millennium BCE. In the north and north-west, barley and wheat have remained the main winter crops, sown after the monsoon on the moisture left in the soil or with well and canal water, and harvested in spring. Barley, which tolerates poorer and more saline soil, was long the grain of the less prosperous.

docs.title: 9.5 Millets
docs.text:
“Millet” is not a botanical group but a name for many small-grained grasses. India grows two kinds. The first are millets domesticated within South Asia, among them kodo (Paspalum scrobiculatum, Sanskrit kodrava), little millet (Panicum sumatrense), browntop millet (Urochloa ramosa) and Indian barnyard millet (Echinochloa frumentacea); śyāmāka refers to one or more of these small millets. At Rojdi in Saurashtra, small millets were the main crops in the Harappan period, a reminder that Harappan farming was not uniform (Weber 1991). The second are introductions. Foxtail millet (Setaria italica, usually identified with priyaṅgu) and broomcorn or proso millet (Panicum miliaceum, cīnaka, a name that itself suggests a connection with China) were domesticated in northern China. Sorghum (jowār), pearl millet (bājrā) and finger millet (rāgi, nācanī) are African domesticates that reached India around 2000 BCE (Fuller 2006). Some reported early finds of finger millet in India have been questioned on identification, but the African origin of all three is not in doubt.

Millets became the staple grains of the drier Deccan, Rajasthan, Gujarat and the southern uplands, and of many hill and forest communities. The medical texts rank them as kudhānya, “lesser grains”; in social terms, millet was often the food of the poor while rice and wheat were the grains of status, a ranking that shaped diets for centuries. In the twentieth century, irrigated rice and wheat displaced millets over large areas. Interest has revived because millets suit rain-fed farming on light soils, and the United Nations General Assembly, on India’s proposal, declared 2023 the International Year of Millets. The nutritional profile of millets varies a great deal by species; claims for them should be made species by species and from current nutritional data, not from tradition.

docs.title: 9.6 Pulses
docs.text:
Pulses (Caraka’s śamīdhānya; dvidala or vaidala, “split” grains, in other texts) are central to Indian food and farming. Several were domesticated within the subcontinent: mung (Vigna radiata, mudga), urd or black gram (V. mungo, māṣa), horsegram (Macrotyloma uniflorum, kulattha), moth bean (V. aconitifolia) and pigeon pea (Cajanus cajan, āḍhakī), whose wild relative grows in the Eastern Ghats (Fuller 2011). Lentil (masūra), chickpea (caṇaka), pea (kalāya) and grass pea (Lathyrus sativus, khesārī) came from south-west Asia; cowpea and the hyacinth bean from Africa. Grass pea is hardy and drought-tolerant, but heavy dependence on it in times of scarcity causes lathyrism, a crippling neurological disease, and its history shows how a “famine crop” can harm the poorest who rely on it.

Pulses are legumes, and their roots carry nodules in which bacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen. That growing legumes improves the following crop was known empirically to many farming peoples, in India as in the Roman world; the mechanism was demonstrated in Europe in the 1880s. Indian farmers commonly sowed pulses with cereals or after them, as discussed in Section 9.13. No surviving Sanskrit text, however, sets out a theory of rotation for soil fertility.

docs.title: 9.7.1 Oilseeds
docs.text: Sesame (Sesamum indicum, tila) was domesticated in South Asia from a wild relative and is found at Harappan sites (Fuller 2006). Its importance is preserved in language: Sanskrit taila, “oil”, means literally “that which comes from tila”. Sesame and its oil are prominent in ritual, especially in offerings to the dead. Mustards and rapeseed (Brassica species; sarṣapa, with white mustard called siddhārtha) became the oil crops of the northern plains and Bengal. Linseed (Linum usitatissimum, atasī, umā) is a south-west Asian domesticate; in India it was grown mainly for oil. Safflower (kusumbha) gave both an oil and a red dye. Castor (eraṇḍa), an African plant, supplied lamp oil and medicine. The coconut (nārikela) was the oil and food palm of the coasts, and niger (Guizotia abyssinica), an Ethiopian domesticate, was an oilseed of hill and forest farmers. Groundnut, now one of India’s main oilseeds, is an American crop (Section 9.11). The oil press (ghāṇī) and the castes who worked it are discussed in Chapter 14.

docs.title: 9.7.2 Flax and cotton
docs.text: Flax is the oldest plant fibre known to have been worked by humans; linen was woven in south-west Asia well before cotton, and Sanskrit kṣauma is often, though not certainly, understood as linen. Cotton, however, has a genuinely ancient history in South Asia. Mineralised cotton fibres preserved in a copper bead from a Neolithic burial at Mehrgarh, dated to around the sixth to fifth millennium BCE, are among the earliest evidence of cotton use anywhere (Moulherat et al. 2002), and cotton textiles are known from Mohenjo-daro (Kenoyer 1998). The Old World “tree cottons” (Gossypium arboreum, and the related G. herbaceum, whose earliest domestication may lie further west) were the cottons of India for millennia; cotton was independently domesticated in the Americas, and American upland cotton was promoted in India by colonial authorities in the nineteenth century. Since 2002 most of India’s cotton has been grown from hybrids carrying a gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt cotton), whose history and controversies are discussed in Section 20.9. Herodotus’ report of Indian trees that bore wool shows how Indian cotton struck the Greek world. Spinning, weaving and the cotton trade are treated in Volume 17, Śilpa–Kāru.

docs.title: 9.8 Sugarcane
docs.text:
The noble canes (Saccharum officinarum) were domesticated in New Guinea; the thin, hardy canes long grown in northern India (S. barberi) are thought to be hybrids between these and the wild S. spontaneum. Sugarcane (ikṣu) is named in the Atharvaveda and is a familiar crop in Sanskrit and Pali literature. What India gave the world was less the plant than the technology of making solid sugar. Indian texts of the early centuries CE distinguish grades of sugar product: the Arthaśāstra’s list of storehouse goods includes phāṇita, guḍa, matsyaṇḍikā, khaṇḍa and śarkarā, from thickened juice to crystalline sugar (Kangle 1965). Sanskrit śarkarā lies behind Persian shakar, Arabic sukkar and English “sugar”, and khaṇḍa behind “candy”. Chinese sources record that the Tang court sent envoys to Magadha in the seventh century to learn the method of sugar-boiling (Mazumdar 1998).

The Arthaśāstra ranks sugarcane as the least desirable crop for the state farms (Section 2.11.1). In the twentieth century the Sugarcane Breeding Institute at Coimbatore (founded 1912) crossed noble canes with S. spontaneum to produce hardier hybrid varieties that were grown far beyond India (Section 19.5.2). Jaggery-making and sugar-refining are treated in Chapter 14.

docs.title: 9.9 Spices
docs.text:
The Western Ghats are the home of black pepper (Piper nigrum, marica) and cardamom (Elettaria cardamomum, elā). Long pepper (Piper longum, pippalī), also a plant of the Indian region, was the older and more prized pepper in classical Indian pharmacology and was also traded westward. Ginger (Zingiber officinale; fresh ārdraka, dried śuṇṭhī) and turmeric (Curcuma longa, haridrā) are tropical Asian crops propagated from rhizomes; both have long histories of cultivation in South Asia. Not every “Indian spice” is Indian: true cinnamon is from Sri Lanka, while the Sanskrit tvak covers cassia barks as well; cloves are from the Moluccas and reached India by trade; cumin and coriander came from south-west Asia and the Mediterranean.

Black pepper was the principal Indian export to the Roman world, shipped from Malabar ports such as Muziris; the trade is treated in Volume 19, Vāṇijya and Samudra. Before the sixteenth century, the pungency of Indian cooking came from pepper, long pepper, ginger and mustard. The chilli (Capsicum) is a New World plant brought by the Portuguese in the sixteenth century; within a century or two it had become indispensable across the subcontinent.

docs.title: 9.10 Fruits and Vegetables
docs.text:
The mango (Mangifera indica, āmra), native to the region of north-eastern South Asia and Myanmar, is the fruit most celebrated in Indian literature. Other fruits of long South Asian cultivation include the jackfruit (panasa), jamun (jambū), Indian jujube or ber (badarī), Indian gooseberry (āmalakī), wood-apple (kapittha) and bael (bilva). Citrus fruits originated in the broad region of the eastern Himalayan foothills, north-east India, southern China and Myanmar. Bananas (kadalī) were domesticated in New Guinea and Southeast Asia but reached India early. Pomegranate (dāḍima) and grape (drākṣā) came from Iran and Central Asia, and the tamarind from tropical Africa, all in antiquity.

Among vegetables, the cucumber was domesticated in South Asia from a wild form of the Himalayan foothills, and the brinjal (vṛntāka) was domesticated in South or Southeast Asia. Gourds (bottle gourd alābu, ash gourd kūṣmāṇḍa, bitter gourd kāravella), yams, taro and leafy greens formed the everyday vegetable supply, much of it grown in kitchen gardens rather than fields. Many of the vegetables now thought typically Indian are later arrivals: the potato, tomato and chilli from the Americas, and cauliflower and cabbage from Europe in the colonial period. Medicinal plants are treated in Chapter 12 and Volume 13, Āyurveda.

docs.title: 9.11 Crops from the Americas and the Islamic World
docs.text:
The sixteenth century opened a new phase. Through Portuguese ports on the west coast and through overland trade, American crops entered India: maize, chilli, potato, tomato, tobacco, groundnut, pineapple, papaya, guava, custard apple, cashew, sweet potato and cassava among them (Achaya 1998; Randhawa 1980). They spread at very different speeds. Chilli and tobacco were adopted quickly; tobacco was being smoked at the Mughal court by the early seventeenth century, and Jahāngīr records in his memoirs that he tried to forbid it (Thackston 1999). Maize became a hill crop of the Himalaya and of parts of the north. The pineapple was known at the Mughal court. Cashew was planted along the western coast and later became a plantation and export crop.
