The potato and tomato became important only in the nineteenth century, when colonial administrators and missionaries encouraged them, and groundnut became a major field crop of the Deccan and Gujarat in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Cassava was promoted in Travancore in the nineteenth century and became a food of the poor in Kerala.

Debate: Pre-Columbian maize in India?

It is occasionally claimed that maize was grown in India before 1492, mainly on the basis of carved motifs on medieval temples that resemble maize cobs. Most archaeobotanists and art historians reject this: the motifs are more plausibly read as conventional ornaments (such as strings of pearls held by figures), and no maize remains have been found in any securely dated pre-Columbian Indian context.

A second current of introductions came through the Islamic world and the courts of the Sultanates and the Mughals. Persian and Central Asian fruits such as melons, grapes and new varieties of apricot and peach were cultivated in royal gardens, often with grafting; Bābur’s memoirs survey the plants of Hindustan, which he found wanting in the fruits of his homeland, and Jahāngīr describes fruits and grafts in his (Thackston 1996, 1999). The Mughal revenue system reorganised the agrarian calendar into two harvests and recorded crops in great detail (Section 9.12). In the colonial period, tea, coffee, rubber, cinchona and many other plantation crops transformed hill landscapes, with profound social and ecological effects. These histories are treated in Chapter 18.

docs.title: 9.12 Seasons and the Crop Calendar
docs.text:
Indian farmers grew crops in two main seasons long before the familiar terms kharīf and rabī existed. Those terms are Arabic in origin (kharīf, “autumn”; rabīʿ, “spring”) and entered Indian usage through Persian revenue practice under the Sultanates and the Mughals, which assessed land revenue harvest by harvest. Abū’l-Faẓl’s Āʾīn-i Akbarī tabulates revenue rates crop by crop for the rabī and kharīf harvests of the provinces (Abū’l-Faẓl 1873; Habib 1999). A third, minor summer season is called zāid (“additional”). These are not classical Sanskrit categories, and the Sanskrit agricultural texts do not use them. Figure 9.1 sets the three seasons and their main crops against the six seasons of the Sanskrit texts.

Figure 9.1. The two main crop seasons of northern India, with the minor summer season, set against the six seasons (ṛtu) of the Sanskrit texts. The kharīf crops are sown with the onset of the south-west monsoon and harvested in autumn; the rabī crops are sown after the rains on stored soil moisture or with well and canal water and harvested in spring. The terms are Perso-Arabic (Section 9.12). Months are approximate and vary from region to region; much of peninsular India, and the Tamil coast with its north-east monsoon rains in October to December, follows different calendars, and Bengal and Assam name their rice crops by season (āus, āman, boro; Section 9.3). Each ṛtu corresponds to a pair of lunar months, so its boundaries move against the solar months shown here.

Sanskrit texts reckon agricultural time in other ways. The year is divided into six seasons (ṛtu): vasanta (spring), grīṣma (summer), varṣā (rains), śarad (autumn), hemanta (early winter) and śiśira (late winter). The Taittirīya Saṃhitā already observes that the crop ripens twice a year (Section 2.7). Crops are also named by their seasons: vrīhi and ṣaṣṭika by the rains, śāli by early winter, barley by spring. The Arthaśāstra’s director of agriculture classifies crops by sowing time: early-sown crops (pūrvavāpa) such as śāli and vrīhi rice, kodo, sesame and millets; middle-sown crops (madhyavāpa) such as mung and urd; and late-sown crops (paścādvāpa) such as safflower, lentil, horsegram, barley, wheat, pea, linseed and mustard (Kangle 1965). In effect this is the monsoon-sown and winter-sown division under other names. The text also advises sowing crops that need more or less water according to the rainfall of the year. Detailed calendars tied to the lunar mansions (nakṣatra) appear in the Kṛṣi-Parāśara and in regional farmers’ sayings; they are discussed in Chapter 3 and, for the calendar itself, in Volume 12, Khagola Jyotiṣa.

docs.title: 9.13 Rotation, Mixed and Relay Cropping
docs.text:
The strongest evidence for how Indian farmers combined crops comes not from Sanskrit texts but from observers of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Voelcker (Section 7.5.2) singled out mixed cropping, the alternation of cereals with pulses and the keeping of fields free of weeds as matters in which British agriculture had little to teach Indian cultivators (Voelcker 1893), and Howard (Section 10.7) found mixed cropping one of the most striking features of their practice (Howard 1940). These observers had their own agendas (Voelcker defending the cultivator against official blame, Howard building a case against chemical fertilisers), but their descriptions are detailed and based on fieldwork.

Practices that these and later observers describe include:

  • Rotation, alternating cereals with pulses or oilseeds on the same land from one season or year to the next; for example, a monsoon cereal followed by chickpea, lentil or another winter pulse.

  • Mixed cropping, sowing two or more crops together in the same field, either mixed in the seed or in alternate rows. Examples include sorghum or pearl millet with pigeon pea and other pulses on the black soils of the Deccan; wheat or barley mixed with chickpea in the north; and lines of mustard sown through fields of wheat.

  • Relay cropping, sowing a second crop into a standing crop before it is harvested. In parts of eastern and central India, lentil, grass pea or linseed seed is broadcast into rice shortly before the rice harvest, so that it germinates on the residual moisture (the practice is called utera in Chhattisgarh and paira in Bihar and Odisha).

  • Intercropping of long- and short-duration crops, such as the classic Deccan combination of sorghum with pigeon pea: the cereal is harvested at the end of the rains, after which the slower pigeon pea grows on through the winter on stored soil moisture.

  • Composite multi-crop systems in particular regions, such as the akkaḍi sālu rows of Karnataka, in which lines of pulses and oilseeds are sown through finger millet, and the bārahnājā (“twelve grains”) of the Garhwal and Kumaon hills.

The advantages farmers sought were several: insurance against the failure of any one crop in an uncertain monsoon, a spread of labour and harvest over the year, food and fodder of several kinds from one field, and, in the case of pulses, a benefit to the following crop. Agronomists have since studied these systems experimentally. Results depend heavily on the crops, soils and rainfall concerned, and general statements that mixed cropping always controls pests or yields more than sole cropping are not supported. The sources also contain no figures on the extent of these practices, and none are given here.

docs.title: 9.14.1 Selection
docs.text: Every farming household that saved its own seed practised selection, choosing the heads, pods or fruits from which next season’s seed would come. The Kṛṣi-Parāśara has a short section on seed. As Majumdar and Banerji and Sadhale render it, the text advises gathering seed in the months of Māgha or Phālguna (late winter), drying it thoroughly in the sun, and keeping it so that it is not mixed with other seed; mixed or uneven seed, it says, gives a poor crop (Majumdar and Banerji 1960; Sadhale 1999). Many farmers’ practices of seed testing (floating seed in water and discarding what floats, or germinating a sample on a damp cloth before sowing) are recorded in modern surveys of farming practice; they are sensible tests, but they are not classical prescriptions.

docs.title: 9.14.2 Treatment before sowing
docs.text:
The earliest detailed prescriptions for treating seed are in the Arthaśāstra’s chapter on the director of agriculture (2.24; Section 2.11.1). As Kangle translates it, grain seeds are to be exposed to mist by night and heat by day for seven nights, and pulse seeds for a shorter period; cuttings of sugarcane and similar plants are to have their cut ends smeared with honey, ghee and hog’s fat mixed with cowdung; bulbous roots are to be smeared with honey and ghee; and hard-coated seeds (asthibīja) with cowdung (Kangle 1965). Whether these instructions describe practice on the royal farms or a learned author’s ideal is uncertain, as with much of the Arthaśāstra (see Volume 18, Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra).

The Vṛkṣāyurveda texts give many recipes for treating seeds of trees and garden plants before sowing, often with milk, ghee, honey and dung, and these are discussed in Chapter 4 (Sadhale 1996; Majumdar 1935).

docs.title: 9.14.3 Storage
docs.text:
Stored seed in a hot, often humid climate faces moisture, moulds, insects and rodents. Farmers’ storage practices, recorded across India in colonial and modern surveys, include:

  • drying seed thoroughly in the sun before storage;

  • storing it in earthen pots or jars with sealed mouths, in bins built of mud or of woven bamboo plastered with mud and dung, or in bundles and containers of straw;

  • mixing dried neem leaves, ash or sand with stored grain and seed;

  • keeping small seed lots in the kitchen roof or above the hearth, where smoke and warmth keep them dry;

  • in some dry regions, storing grain in lined underground pits.

Several of these practices are reasonable responses to the threats they address. Neem leaf and kernel contain compounds that deter or disrupt many storage insects (Schmutterer 1995), and keeping seed dry is the single most important factor in preserving its viability. Their effectiveness in any particular case depends on how they are carried out.

docs.title: 9.14.4 Exchange, landraces and conservation
docs.text:
Seed moved constantly: between neighbours, as part of marriage gifts, at fairs, along trade routes, and through the borrowing of seed from landlords and moneylenders at high rates of interest, a recurring source of indebtedness. In many communities, selecting and storing seed has been women’s work, and women’s knowledge of varieties has been an important, if little recorded, part of agricultural expertise. The result of continual selection and exchange was a large stock of landraces in every major crop: genetically diverse, locally adapted populations, rather than uniform varieties.

From the 1960s, the spread of high-yielding varieties of wheat and rice, bred for response to irrigation and chemical fertiliser, replaced landraces over large areas (Chapter 20). Collections of traditional varieties were made, partly in response, by national and international gene banks: the National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources in New Delhi, the International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics near Hyderabad (for sorghum, millets, chickpea, pigeon pea and groundnut) and the International Rice Research Institute in the Philippines, among others. Alongside these ex situ collections, farmers’ movements and non-governmental organisations have tried to keep landraces in cultivation. Examples include the Beej Bachao Andolan (“Save the Seeds” movement) in the Garhwal hills; the women’s groups of the Deccan Development Society in Telangana, which have promoted millet-based farming; Navdanya, founded by Vandana Shiva; and community seed banks in Odisha and elsewhere. Figures for their holdings vary widely between sources. The law on plant varieties and farmers’ rights, and the debates over patents on seeds and traditional knowledge, are discussed in Chapter 20 (Shiva 1991, 2001).

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: India’s crops have mixed origins. Wheat, barley, lentil and linseed came from south-west Asia; sorghum, pearl millet and finger millet from Africa; maize, chilli, potato, groundnut and tobacco from the Americas. Rice, several small millets, mung, urd, horsegram, pigeon pea, sesame, tree cotton, black pepper and cardamom have South Asian or partly South Asian origins, as archaeobotany has shown in revising Vavilov’s “centres”. Sanskrit texts group crops by ritual use, by sowing season (as in the Arthaśāstra’s early-, middle- and late-sown crops) and by dietetic value (Caraka’s awned grains and pod grains, Suśruta’s “lesser grains”); the categories kharīf and rabī come from Sultanate and Mughal revenue practice. The best evidence for rotation, mixed and relay cropping comes from colonial observers and later fieldwork. Seed was selected, treated (as the Arthaśāstra prescribes), stored with care, and exchanged, producing a large landrace diversity that the Green Revolution reduced and that gene banks and seed-saving movements now try to conserve.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Fuller (2006) is the standard synthesis of crop origins in South Asia. Achaya (1998) is a reference for the history of individual crops and foods. Randhawa (1980) gathers a great deal of material on the history of Indian agriculture, though it should be used critically. Voelcker (1893) remains the best contemporary description of Indian cropping practice in the late nineteenth century, and Habib (1999) covers crops and seasons in the Mughal period.

docs.title: Chapter 10: Agroecology: Pests, Livestock, Trees and Fallows
docs.text: “Agroecology” is a modern word for the study of farms as ecological systems: how crops, weeds, pests, livestock, trees, soil and water interact, and how farming practices shape those interactions. Applied to the Indian past, it is a useful lens, but it is also easily misused. Pre-modern farming in India, as everywhere, used no synthetic fertilisers or pesticides because none existed; that does not make it “organic farming” in the modern sense, nor does it make it sustainable or benign by definition. This chapter examines what the texts and the historical record actually show about the protection of crops and trees from pests, the integration of crops and livestock, the growing of trees on farms, shifting cultivation, the farming systems of the Himalaya and the North-East, and the making of manure. It ends with the ethical ideals often invoked in discussions of Indian ecological thought, and with their limits. Soils are discussed in Chapter 7, water in Chapter 8, forests and sacred groves in Chapter 11, and modern natural-farming movements in Chapter 20.

docs.title: 10.1 Protecting Crops and Trees in the Texts
10.1.1 Tree medicine
docs.text:
The fullest classical discussions of plant protection concern trees and garden plants rather than field crops, and are found in the Vṛkṣāyurveda tradition (Chapter 4). Varāhamihira’s chapter on trees in the Bṛhatsaṃhitā (chapter 55, 6th century CE) describes the signs of disease in trees and prescribes a simple course of treatment: the diseased part is cut away, the wound is dressed with a paste of viḍaṅga (Embelia ribes), ghee and mud, and the tree is sprinkled with milk and water (Bhat 1981). Surapāla’s Vṛkṣāyurveda (c. 10th–11th century CE) develops this into a fuller system. Following the logic of human medicine, it classifies the disorders of trees by the three doṣas and by external causes such as insects, frost, wind, fire and lightning, and its remedies include pastes applied to wounds, fumigation (dhūpana) with burning plant and animal substances, and sprinkling or watering with various liquids, among them the fermented preparation kuṇapajala (Sadhale 1996). The Upavanavinoda, a section of Śārṅgadhara’s anthology of 1363, follows the same pattern for the trees and flowering plants of the pleasure garden (Majumdar 1935).

These texts are valuable evidence of how learned gardeners thought about plant health: by analogy with the human body, through the categories of Āyurveda, and with close attention to symptoms such as yellowing leaves, failure to fruit and insect attack. They are not field manuals of crop protection, and the Kṛṣi-Parāśara as edited gives no recipes against pests.

docs.title: 10.1.2 Pests as calamities
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra treats rats as one of the great calamities against which a king must guard, alongside fire, flood, disease, famine, wild animals and snakes, and among the measures it lists is the release of cats and mongooses (Kangle 1965). Locust swarms, birds and wild animals in standing crops were a constant concern of farmers, and literature preserves the human side of crop protection. In the fourth canto of the Raghuvaṃśa, Kālidāsa pictures the women who guard the rice fields, sitting in the shade of the sugarcane and singing of the king’s fame; the Tamil poems of the hill country repeatedly describe girls on raised platforms in the millet fields, driving off parrots with rattles and slings. Field-watching from platforms, by day against birds and by night against deer, wild pigs and elephants, was work for women, children and the poor, and it remained a major part of the farming year in forest-edge villages into modern times.

docs.title: 10.2 Farmers’ Pest Practices
docs.text:
Most pest management in Indian agriculture was never written down in Sanskrit. It was carried in farmers’ practice and has been recorded, unevenly, in colonial reports and modern surveys. The commonly described practices include:

  • Neem. Leaves of the neem tree (Azadirachta indica, nimba) mixed with stored grain and seed; neem cake, the residue of oil pressing, worked into the soil; and, in more recent practice, water extracts of leaves or seed kernels sprayed on crops.

  • Ash and dust. Wood ash dusted on vegetable crops, especially cucurbits, against leaf-eating beetles and other insects; ash or fine sand mixed with stored pulses.

  • Smoke and fire. Smoke from smouldering heaps at the edge of fields, and fires lit at night, to drive off or attract and kill flying insects.

  • Birds as allies. Poles or branches set up in fields as perches for insect-eating birds such as drongos, and the retention of trees and hedges that shelter birds. Bird perches are now also recommended in integrated pest management programmes.

  • Border and trap crops. Rows of a different crop sown around or through the main crop, which may attract pests away from it or harbour their enemies; mixed cropping in general (Chapter 9).

  • Timing and choice of variety. Adjusting sowing dates to avoid periods of heavy pest attack, and keeping landraces known to withstand local pests and diseases.

  • Field sanitation and physical removal. Hand-picking of caterpillars and egg masses, removal of infested plants, and the burning or burial of crop residues.

Of these, neem has been studied most thoroughly. The seed kernel contains limonoids, of which azadirachtin is the most important, that act on many insects as feeding deterrents, as disrupters of moulting and growth, and as deterrents to egg-laying; their toxicity to mammals is low, though not nil, and they break down quickly in sunlight (Schmutterer 1995). Neem preparations are therefore genuinely useful, but their effect varies with the insect, the crop, the part of the tree used and the preparation; they act more slowly than synthetic insecticides; and they are not harmless to all beneficial insects. The disputes over patents on neem-based products are discussed in Chapter 20.

For the other practices, systematic evidence of effectiveness is patchy. Some, such as perches for insectivorous birds, rest on sound ecological reasoning and have experimental support in particular settings; others are untested, and each has to be judged on the evidence for it.

Health and Safety Note

Several plants used as traditional pest repellents are toxic to people and animals, among them tobacco, the latex of Calotropis (arka) and the seeds of Datura. Neem oil taken by mouth has caused serious poisoning in infants. Nothing in this chapter is a recipe; preparations of this kind should be handled only in line with current agricultural safety advice.

docs.title: 10.3 Crops and Livestock Together
docs.text:
Indian farming was, for most of its history, mixed farming: crops and animals depended on each other. Cattle and, in wet-rice areas, buffaloes pulled the plough, the cart, the water-lift and the cane-crusher. Their dung was the main manure of the fields, and also a fuel and a building material. In return, the fields fed them: straw of rice and wheat, the stalks (stover) of sorghum and pearl millet, the haulms of pulses and groundnut, and oil cake from the press. In dry regions sorghum stover could be as important a product as the grain, and farmers chose varieties with an eye to fodder as well as food. Trees on farms were lopped for leaf fodder in the dry season (Section 10.4).

The integration was never complete or frictionless. Much of the dung that might have manured the fields was dried into cakes and burnt for want of fuel wood, a shortage Voelcker regarded as a central constraint on Indian agriculture (Chapter 7). Grazing land and fallows were contested between cultivators and herders; and the care of animals followed lines of caste and gender. Women did much of the work of collecting dung, making dung cakes and cutting fodder. The removal of dead cattle and the working of hides fell to communities treated as untouchable, whose labour was essential to the agrarian economy and whose status was degraded by it (Chapter 13) (Ambedkar 1948; Wiser 1936).

Relations between settled farmers and mobile pastoralists also had a cooperative side: herders were paid to pen their flocks overnight on harvested fields, an exchange of manure for grazing described in Chapter 13.

In some wetland regions, fish were part of the same system. The Apatani of the Ziro valley in Arunachal Pradesh raise fish in their irrigated rice terraces; in the brackish coastal fields of Kerala, pokkāḷi rice grown in the monsoon season alternates with prawn and fish culture in the saline season; and in the khazan lands of Goa, reclaimed estuarine fields are managed with sluice gates for both salt-tolerant rice and fish. These are cases where a farming system makes use of seasonal changes in water and salinity rather than fighting them.

docs.title: 10.4 Trees on Farms: Agroforestry
docs.text: Growing trees and crops on the same land, now studied under the name of agroforestry, is very widespread in India (Nair 1993). The classical texts encourage the planting of trees, especially by roads, wells and tanks, as a meritorious act (Chapter 4), but the farming systems described below are known mainly from historical observation and modern study.

docs.title: 10.4.1 Homegardens
docs.text: The homegardens of Kerala are the best-studied example. Around each house, on plots that are often small, are grown together coconut and areca palms, jackfruit, mango, tamarind, banana, black pepper trained on trees, tubers such as yams and colocasia, vegetables, spices and medicinal plants, frequently with a cow, goats or poultry. The garden supplies food, fodder, fuel, timber and cash crops in a layered structure that resembles, in some respects, a forest (Kumar and Nair 2004). The homegarden is not a fixed “traditional” form: cassava, cocoa, rubber and other introductions of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries have been absorbed into it, and many gardens have been simplified as land has been subdivided or turned over to a single cash crop. Homestead gardens of other kinds are found across India, from the bamboo- and fruit-tree groves around Bengal villages to the kitchen gardens of north Indian households.

docs.title: 10.4.2 Trees in fields
docs.text: In the arid west of Rajasthan, the khejri tree (Prosopis cineraria) is deliberately kept in farmers’ fields. Crops such as pearl millet, moth bean and cluster bean are grown beneath it; its leaves are lopped for fodder, its pods (sāṅgarī) are eaten as a vegetable, and its wood is used for fuel. Khejri is a leguminous tree, and farmers in the region regard the soil under it as better for crops. It is protected with particular strictness by the Bishnoi community (Section 10.8 and Chapter 11). Elsewhere farmers retain or plant other useful trees in and around fields: the babul (Vachellia nilotica) on the black soils of the Deccan and Gujarat, valued for timber, pods and gum; the palmyra palm on field bunds in Tamil Nadu, tapped for sap and used for leaves and timber; the mahua (Madhuca longifolia) of central India, whose flowers are food and the source of a distilled liquor and whose seeds yield oil; and the tamarind, mango and neem in almost every region. Trees on bunds and boundaries mark property, provide shade for workers and animals, and break the wind; they also shade and compete with crops, and farmers manage them by lopping and spacing.

docs.title: 10.4.3 Tree crops under shade
docs.text: In the Western Ghats, several plantation crops are grown under a canopy of shade trees. In Kodagu (Coorg) and Chikmagalur, coffee is grown beneath retained forest trees and planted shade trees, on which pepper vines are trained; cardamom is grown under forest cover in the hills of Kerala, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. Coffee is not a traditional Indian crop: tradition credits the Sufi Baba Budan with bringing coffee seeds from Yemen in the seventeenth century, but plantations developed under British and Indian planters in the nineteenth century, often on land taken from forest. These shaded systems retain much more tree cover than open plantations do, and they have attracted the attention of conservationists, but their history is also one of forest clearance and of a plantation workforce recruited under harsh conditions.

docs.title: 10.5 Shifting Cultivation
docs.text:
Shifting cultivation (swidden, slash-and-burn) is practised in the hills of north-east India, where it is called jhūm, and has been practised in the Eastern Ghats (poḍu), in central India (bewar among the Baiga and other names elsewhere) and in the Western Ghats (kumri). A patch of forest or secondary growth is cut, the vegetation is dried and burnt, and the cleared land is cropped for one or two seasons, usually with a mixture of crops sown together: upland rice, millets, maize, pulses, vegetables, cotton, sesame and tubers. The plot is then left fallow so that the vegetation and the soil can recover, and the cultivators move on to another patch, returning after a cycle of years.

The ecology of shifting cultivation depends on the length of that cycle. Burning releases nutrients from the vegetation into the soil as ash; the fallow allows trees and bamboo to regrow, rebuilds soil organic matter and suppresses weeds; and the mixture of crops spreads risk and provides a varied diet. P. S. Ramakrishnan’s long-term studies of jhūm in Meghalaya showed that when cycles are long the system can sustain itself, but that as cycles are shortened by growing population, loss of land and other pressures, soil fertility declines, weeds increase and yields fall (Ramakrishnan 1992). Shifting cultivation is thus neither inherently destructive nor inherently sustainable; its effects depend on the cycle, the terrain and the wider pressures on the land.

Colonial forest departments were hostile to shifting cultivation, which they saw as a waste of timber and a challenge to state control of forests. From the late nineteenth century it was banned or restricted in many reserved forests; in the Central Provinces, the Baiga were confined to a reserved tract in which alone bewar was permitted (Gadgil and Guha 1992). These restrictions were part of the broader colonial transformation of forest rights (Chapter 11). Hostility continued after independence, when shifting cultivation was often described in official documents as primitive and wasteful and cultivators were encouraged to adopt settled terraces or plantations. More recent research has tended to stress the knowledge embodied in shifting cultivation, its crop diversity and the importance of secure land rights for those who practise it, while recognising that shortened cycles can cause real degradation (see also Volume 23, Jana–Jāti).

docs.title: 10.6 Farming in the Hills: The Himalaya and the North-East
docs.text: Hills and mountains cover a large part of India, from Kashmir and Ladakh along the Himalaya to Arunachal Pradesh, and south through the hills of Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram, Tripura and Meghalaya. Farming there contends with slope and erosion, short growing seasons at altitude, cold, heavy monsoon rain on the eastern ranges and, until recently, isolation from markets. Hill peoples answered these conditions with a range of systems that combine terraces, valley-floor rice, shifting cultivation, orchards, forest and livestock. Several have been described already: terraces in general (Section 7.6), the kuhls of Kangra, the zabo of the Chakhesang Nagas and the bamboo pipes of Meghalaya (Section 8.8), shifting cultivation (Section 10.5) and the transhumant herders of the western Himalaya (Chapter 13). The Apatani valley, the alder fallows of the Angami Nagas, the bamboo flowering and famines of Mizoram and the meltwater irrigation of Ladakh are treated in Volume 23 (Jana–Jāti). This section describes some of the other hill systems: the mixed farming of the central Himalaya, Kashmir, the orchards of the western Himalaya, Sikkim, and the rice valley of the Brahmaputra.

docs.title: 10.6.1 Terraces, forest and livestock in the central Himalaya
docs.text:
In Garhwal and Kumaon (Uttarakhand) and the adjoining hills of Himachal Pradesh, villages farm narrow bench terraces cut into the slopes. Two kinds of land are distinguished. Low terraces in the valleys and on gentle lower slopes, irrigated by small channels (gūl) led from streams, carry rice in the monsoon and wheat in the winter. The much larger area of upland terraces depends on rain alone and carries millets, pulses and other monsoon crops, followed where moisture allows by wheat or barley. Local terminology, such as talāun for the irrigated and upraun for the rain-fed land, records the distinction.

The fertility of these terraces has depended on the forest. Farmers lop oak (banj, Quercus leucotrichophora) and other trees for winter fodder, gather fallen leaves for bedding in the cattle sheds, and carry the mixture of dung and leaf litter down to the fields as manure, so that a village’s terraces are sustained by a much larger area of forest and grassland around them. Much of this work, from lopping and carrying fodder to spreading manure, is done by women. The link between forest, livestock and field explains why the reservation of Himalayan forests by the colonial forest department from the late nineteenth century, which restricted lopping, grazing and burning, was resented so strongly, and why protest in these hills, culminating in Chipko, took the form it did (Guha 1989); see Section 11.10.

On the rain-fed terraces the characteristic practice is the mixed sowing known as bārahnājā (“twelve grains”; Section 9.13). A single field may carry finger millet (maṇḍuā), barnyard millet (jhaṅgorā), foxtail millet, amaranth (rāmdānā), horse gram (gahat), rice bean, black soybean (bhaṭ), cowpea and other pulses and vegetables, sown together or in close succession; at higher altitudes buckwheat and naked barley take their place. The crops ripen at different times, differ in their tolerance of drought and pests, provide grain, pulses, greens and fodder from the same land, and spread the risk of failure. From the late 1980s farmers in the Henwal valley of Tehri Garhwal, among them Vijay Jardhari, organised the Beej Bachao Andolan (“save the seeds movement”) to collect and exchange local seeds and to defend mixed cropping against single cash crops promoted by development agencies. Since the 1970s large-scale migration of men to the plains and to the army has left many outlying terraces abandoned, and crop raiding by monkeys and wild boar (Section 16.11) has hastened their abandonment.

Grain from these terraces was traditionally ground in water mills (gharāṭ), in which a small stream led down a wooden chute turns a horizontal paddle wheel coupled directly to the upper millstone. Thousands of such mills once stood on the streams of Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh, usually owned by a family or a village and paid for with a share of the flour. Most were abandoned as diesel and electric mills spread, but since the 1990s improved designs with metal wheels, which can also drive small generators and other machines, have been promoted by government and voluntary agencies as a source of local, renewable power.

docs.title: 10.6.2 Kashmir: rice, saffron and floating gardens
docs.text:
The Kashmir valley, a flat alluvial basin drained by the Jhelum at about 1,600 metres, has been a land of irrigated rice since at least the period of Kalhaṇa’s chronicle, which records the drainage and irrigation works of Suyya in the ninth century (Section 8.6). Channels led from the side streams water terraced and level rice fields; maize, pulses and oilseeds were grown on the higher, unirrigated land. The fullest description of the agriculture of the valley before modern changes is The Valley of Kashmir (1895) by Walter Lawrence, who as settlement commissioner surveyed its land revenue. It records the cultivators’ varieties of rice, their calendar and their methods of irrigation and manuring, and is frank about the heavy exactions of the state and its officials under which they worked (Lawrence 1895).

Kashmir’s most famous crop is saffron (Crocus sativus; Sanskrit kuṅkuma). It is grown on the karewa, the raised plateaus of old lake deposits, above all around Pampore south-east of Srinagar. The saffron crocus is sterile and does not set seed; it is propagated by its corms, which are planted in well-tilled beds and left in the ground for several years. The flowers appear in October and November, and the three red stigmas of each flower are picked by hand and dried, so that a kilogram of saffron represents the labour of picking very large numbers of flowers. Kalhaṇa already counts saffron among the characteristic products of the valley in the description of Kashmir that opens his chronicle (Stein 1900), and the Āʾīn-i Akbarī describes the saffron fields (Section 18.7). How and when the plant reached Kashmir is uncertain. In recent decades the saffron area has shrunk under the pressure of urban building on the karewa and of irregular rainfall.

On the Dal and other lakes around Srinagar, cultivators grow vegetables on floating gardens (rādh): mats of reeds and water plants are cut, bound together, anchored with poles and covered with weed and mud dredged from the lake bed, and on them are grown cucumbers, melons, tomatoes and other vegetables. The gardens can be cut into sections and towed from place to place. They are one of the few Indian examples of a farming system built on the water itself, comparable in principle to the floating gardens of Myanmar’s Inle lake and of Bangladesh.

docs.title: 10.6.3 Orchards of the western Himalaya
docs.text: Fruit growing in the western Himalaya is old — the walnuts, apricots and almonds of Kashmir and Ladakh, the grapes of Kinnaur — but the orchard economy that now dominates much of Himachal Pradesh is modern. Small apple orchards were planted by Europeans in Kullu and around Shimla in the late nineteenth century. In 1916 Samuel Evans Stokes, an American who had settled at Kotgarh near Shimla, introduced varieties of the American Delicious apple, which proved well suited to the hills; from the middle of the twentieth century, as roads reached the valleys, apples became the main cash crop of Shimla, Kullu and Kinnaur districts. The change brought prosperity to many villages, but also dependence on a single crop, on market prices and on heavy spraying, and pressure on forests for packing cases until cardboard replaced wood.

docs.title: 10.6.4 Sikkim and the eastern Himalaya
docs.text:
In Sikkim and the Darjeeling hills the characteristic cash crop is large cardamom (Amomum subulatum), a native plant of the eastern Himalaya, distinct from the small cardamom of the Western Ghats (Section 9.9). It is grown in moist ravines and on shaded slopes under a canopy of trees, especially the Himalayan alder (Alnus nepalensis), whose roots fix nitrogen and whose leaf litter enriches the soil. Ecologists have described the alder–cardamom system as an efficient form of agroforestry that combines a valuable crop with continuous tree cover on steep land. Mandarin oranges, ginger, maize and terraced rice complete the farming of the lower and middle hills. From the late twentieth century the cardamom gardens suffered heavily from virus diseases, known locally as chirke and foorkey, and from the ageing of plantations, and production in Sikkim declined; replanting with healthy suckers and seedlings has been the main remedy.

Sikkim has also become a test case for organic farming policy. In 2003 the state government resolved to convert its agriculture to organic methods; chemical fertilisers and pesticides were progressively withdrawn, and in 2016 Sikkim was declared fully organic. Supporters point to the state’s small consumption of chemicals even before conversion, to the protection of its rivers and biodiversity and to the market value of an organic label; critics have pointed to lower yields of some crops, dependence on food from outside the state, and difficulties in certification and marketing. Independent, published assessments are still few, and the experiment is too recent for firm conclusions, and the general evidence on organic and natural farming is discussed in Chapter 20.

docs.title: 10.6.5 The Brahmaputra valley
docs.text:
The Brahmaputra valley of Assam is a rice country shaped by the river’s floods, which bring silt to the fields but can also destroy crops and villages. Assamese cultivators match their rice crops to the levels of the land and to the seasons of the flood. Āhu rice is sown in spring and harvested in summer, before or between floods. Sāli, the main crop, is transplanted during the monsoon and harvested in early winter. Bao, deep-water rice, is broadcast on low-lying land and grows with the rising water, its stems elongating as the flood deepens, to be harvested after the water falls. Boro rice is grown in winter on low wet land and harvested before the floods, now mostly with pumped water. The great Assam earthquake of 1950 raised the beds of many rivers with landslide debris and worsened the floods of the following years; from the mid-1950s the government built long earthen embankments along the Brahmaputra and its tributaries, which protected some land but, when breached, caused sudden and severe flooding and deprived the fields behind them of the silt that floods once brought. Among the many local varieties are glutinous bora rices used in festival foods, aromatic joha rices, and the komal sāul (“soft rice”) prepared from a glutinous variety, which can be eaten after soaking in cold water without cooking.

Wet-rice cultivation in the valley was greatly extended under the Ahom kings, who entered the Brahmaputra valley from upper Burma in the thirteenth century (1228 in the reckoning of their chronicles) and ruled much of Assam until the 1820s. The Ahom state was organised through the paik system: adult men were registered as paiks, grouped into units that served the state in rotation as soldiers and labourers, and received in return allotments of rice land. Paik labour built the embankments, raised roads (ālī) and tanks of the Ahom kingdom, and Amalendu Guha has argued that the state’s organisation of labour and land was central to the spread of settled wet-rice farming in the valley (Guha 1991). The system, like other systems of compulsory labour, bore heavily on those who served under it, and it was in decline before the British annexation.

Under colonial rule the valley acquired tea plantations on its higher ground (Section 18.8) and, from the early twentieth century, a large immigration of peasants from eastern Bengal who brought the low riverine and char lands under jute and rice. The valley is also the home of two of India’s native silks (Section 17.5): the golden muga silk of the moth Antheraea assamensis, reared outdoors by village households on som (Persea bombycina) and sualu (Litsea) trees, and eri silk from Samia ricini, reared indoors on castor leaves; because eri cocoons are usually spun after the moth has emerged, rather than reeled, the silk is produced without killing the pupa. In the Khasi hills of Meghalaya, potatoes introduced in the early nineteenth century became a major cash crop alongside the older areca, betel and orange gardens.

docs.title: 10.6.6 Manipur, Tripura and Mizoram
docs.text:
In the hills south of the Brahmaputra, the contrast between valley and hill is sharpest in Manipur. The Imphal valley, the heartland of the Meitei kingdom, is a basin of permanent wet-rice fields, among whose varieties is the black, aromatic, glutinous chak-hao used in festive dishes; the surrounding hills, home of Naga and Kuki peoples, were farmed largely by jhūm and terraces. The Meitei state, like the Ahom, drew on compulsory periodic labour from its male subjects (the lallup system) for public works, until the system was abolished under British supervision at the end of the nineteenth century. At the southern end of the valley lies Loktak lake, whose surface is partly covered by phumdi, floating mats of vegetation, soil and decaying organic matter. Fishing households build circular enclosures of phumdi (athaphum) in which fish gather and are harvested, and the largest continuous mass of floating vegetation forms the Keibul Lamjao National Park, the only home of the sangai, Manipur’s brow-antlered deer. Since a barrage at Ithai, built for the Loktak hydroelectric project in the 1980s, held the lake at a more constant level, the phumdi have thickened and spread, with consequences for fishing, farming on the lake margins and the sangai’s habitat that remain a matter of dispute.

In Tripura and Mizoram, where shifting cultivation was the main form of farming, the state has for decades tried to settle shifting cultivators on permanent holdings. In Tripura, programmes from the 1960s onward resettled jhūm families on rubber plantations, and the state became the second-largest producer of natural rubber in India after Kerala. In Mizoram a New Land Use Policy, in successive versions from the 1980s onwards, offered households support to move from jhūm to horticulture, wet-rice terraces, plantations and livestock. Evaluations have been mixed: incomes rose for some households, but the policies were costly, benefits were unevenly distributed, and many families continued to cultivate jhūm alongside the new enterprises. These experiences bear out a conclusion that P. S. Ramakrishnan drew from his long research in the region (Ramakrishnan 1992): that hill farming is changed most durably by building on what cultivators already know and do, rather than by replacing it wholesale.

Hill agriculture shows, perhaps more clearly than that of the plains, the interdependence of field, forest, water and livestock that runs through this chapter, and the value of crop diversity in uncertain environments. It also shows the limits of policies designed for the plains: the high-yielding packages of the 1960s (Chapter 19) did little for rain-fed hill terraces, and the hill states have increasingly turned instead to horticulture, spices and organic production.

docs.title: 10.7 Manure, Compost and the Indore Method
docs.text:
Manuring with dung, ash, oil cake, tank silt, leaf litter and the folding of animals is well attested in Indian agriculture. The Kṛṣi-Parāśara gives directions for collecting cow dung, letting it decompose and spreading it on the fields before sowing (Majumdar and Banerji 1960; Sadhale 1999), and the Vṛkṣāyurveda texts give recipes for nourishing trees, including kuṇapajala. These are discussed in Chapters 3, 4 and 7.

A documented case in which colonial science learned from Indian practice is the work of Albert Howard (1873–1947). Howard went to India in 1905 as Imperial Economic Botanist at Pusa in Bihar, where he worked with his wife Gabrielle Howard, also a botanist, on wheat and other crops. From 1924 to 1931 he directed the Institute of Plant Industry at Indore. There, with Yeshwant D. Wad, he worked out the “Indore process” of composting: vegetable wastes, cattle dung, earth soaked with urine from the cattle shed, wood ash and water were built into heaps or pits and turned at intervals until they had decomposed into humus. The method was published in 1931 (Howard and Wad 1931) and set out at length in An Agricultural Testament (Howard 1940).

Howard was explicit about his debts. He wrote that he had resolved to treat the cultivators of India as his teachers (Howard 1940), noted the mixed cropping and careful cultivation he observed in their fields, and drew also on the composting practices of East Asia. The Indore process was adopted on some plantations in India and elsewhere, and Howard’s writings became founding texts of the organic farming movement in Britain and beyond. His case also shows the limits of such learning. The Indore process was a systematisation by a colonial research station, not a traditional practice simply recorded; it demanded labour, water and organic material that many smallholders could not spare; and Howard’s insistence on humus was tied to a polemic against chemical fertilisers that later agronomists did not wholly accept. Contemporary natural-farming movements in India draw on a mixture of Howard’s ideas, older Indian practice and new formulations; they are discussed in Chapter 20.

docs.title: 10.8.1 Ideals
docs.text:
Indian texts and traditions offer several ideas that modern writers invoke in discussions of agriculture and the environment. The Vedic concept of ṛta, the order by which dawns return, seasons follow one another and sacrifices succeed, is often presented as an ecological principle. In the Vedic texts it is a cosmic and ritual order, closely linked with truth (satya); it is not a theory of ecosystems, though it does express a sense that human action must fit into a larger regularity. The Atharvaveda’s hymn to the Earth (12.1) addresses the earth as mother (12.1.12, quoted in Chapter 2) and includes a farmer’s or digger’s plea:

Atharvaveda 12.1.35

yat te bhūme vikhanāmi kṣipraṃ tad api rohatu mā te marma vimṛgvari mā te hṛdayam arpipam “What I dig out of you, O Earth, may that quickly grow back; O purifier, may I not strike your vital spot or your heart.”

The opening verse of the Īśā Upaniṣad, with its instruction to enjoy the world through renunciation and not to covet, is also frequently cited in this context; in the text, its subject is the Lord’s pervasion of the world and the renunciation of possessiveness, not the management of nature (Olivelle 1998).

The principle of non-injury (ahiṃsā) had direct consequences for attitudes to agriculture. Manu’s disapproval of the plough rests on the injury it does to the earth and its creatures (Section 2.9). The Buddhist monastic code forbids monks to dig the earth or destroy plant life, and later Jain lay codes list among trades to be avoided those that involve breaking the earth. These ideas did not stop anyone from farming. They expressed a hierarchy in which the people who actually ploughed were placed low, and in which the labour of cultivation was pushed onto śūdras and those below them (Sharma 1980).

The Bishnoi community of western Rajasthan, whose rules protect green trees, especially the khejri, and wild animals, has shaped a distinctive farming landscape in which trees and wildlife are tolerated in and around fields (Chapter 11, Section 11.8).

docs.title: 10.8.2 Limits
docs.text:
These ideals must be set against the historical record.

  • Agricultural expansion meant clearing forests. The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa’s legend of Videgha Māthava, in which the fire god burns his way eastward across the land, and the Mahābhārata’s burning of the Khāṇḍava forest to found Indraprastha both remember clearing by fire. Over three millennia, the Ganga plain and much of the peninsula were turned from forest and grassland to fields, a process that continued and accelerated under colonial rule (Gadgil and Guha 1992).

  • Farming systems did not prevent famine. Pre-modern and colonial India suffered recurrent famines when the monsoon failed. Mike Davis has argued that colonial revenue and market policies sharply worsened the impact of the droughts of the late nineteenth century (Davis 2001); economic historians such as Tirthankar Roy give more weight to the severity of the droughts, the low productivity of rain-fed farming and the slow growth of transport and credit, and note that famine mortality fell after 1900 as railways and relief improved (Roy 2011). On either view famine was not a colonial invention, and nothing in traditional practice guaranteed food security.

  • The labour was bound by caste. Much of the work of ploughing, transplanting, weeding, harvesting and herding was done by landless labourers, many of them from castes treated as untouchable, under relations of hereditary servitude or debt bondage that persisted into the twentieth century (Prakash 1990; Breman 1974). Women’s labour in the fields was essential and rarely matched by rights in land (Agarwal 1994). Any account of “sustainable” traditional agriculture must ask for whom it was sustained.

  • “Sustainability” is a modern frame. The idea of meeting present needs without compromising those of future generations was formulated in the international environmental debates of the late twentieth century. Pre-modern Indian practices can be studied for what they achieved and failed to achieve under that frame, but they were not designed to meet it, and texts should not be read as if they had anticipated it.

Debate: Was pre-colonial resource use prudent?

Madhav Gadgil and Ramachandra Guha argued that Indian caste society, by dividing occupations and resources among endogamous groups, reduced competition and encouraged the prudent use of local resources, and that colonial rule broke down these arrangements by asserting state control over forests and commons (Gadgil and Guha 1992). Their account of colonial forestry has been widely accepted; their picture of pre-colonial harmony has been criticised as idealised, since the same caste order rested on inequality and exclusion and did not prevent depletion of forests and soils. Studies of common-property institutions suggest that sustainable use of shared resources depends on specific rules, enforcement and local conditions rather than on culture in general (Agrawal 2001).

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The classical texts discuss plant protection mainly for trees and gardens: Varāhamihira, Surapāla and the Upavanavinoda treat tree disorders by analogy with human medicine, with pastes, fumigation and sprinkling. Field crop protection lived in farmers’ practice: neem, ash, smoke, bird perches, border crops, timing, resistant landraces and watching the fields, of which neem has the strongest scientific support (Schmutterer 1995). Indian farms were mixed systems in which cattle, dung, fodder and crop residues linked fields and animals, sometimes with fish in wet-rice and coastal systems, though fuel scarcity, contested grazing and caste-bound labour shaped how they worked. Trees on farms are widespread; shifting cultivation is sustainable or degrading according to its cycle; and the hill systems from Garhwal and Kashmir to Sikkim, Assam and Manipur show farming fitted closely to its terrain. Howard’s Indore method shows colonial science learning from Indian cultivators, with real limits. Ideals of ṛta, reverence for the Earth, ahiṃsā and the Bishnoi ethic are genuine parts of the tradition, but they coexisted with forest clearance, famine and caste-bound labour.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Schmutterer (1995) is the standard scientific work on neem. Nair (1993) introduces agroforestry, and Kumar and Nair (2004) reviews research on tropical homegardens. Ramakrishnan (1992) is a detailed study of shifting cultivation in north-east India; Guha (1989) links Himalayan forests to village agriculture, Lawrence (1895) describes the agriculture of Kashmir, and Guha (1991) the Ahom state and its rice economy. Howard (1940) gives Howard’s own account of the Indore method, and Gadgil and Guha (1992) is a provocative ecological history of India.

docs.title: Chapter 11: Forests, Sacred Groves and Sacred Trees
11.1 The Forest and the Village
docs.text:
Indian agriculture was won from the forest and always lived beside it. The fields of the Ganga plain, the Deccan and the southern deltas were cleared from woodland over many centuries; villages depended on neighbouring forests for fuel, fodder, leaf manure, timber, fibres, fruits, honey and medicines; and forest-dwelling peoples, who were often not farmers in the plough-based sense, were trading partners, subjects, soldiers and objects of suspicion for agrarian states. This chapter follows the forest through several kinds of evidence: early texts and the Arthaśāstra; the edicts of Aśoka; the community-protected patches of forest known as sacred groves; the cultural roles of particular sacred trees; the Bishnoi tradition of the Thar; and the modern history of forest law and forest protest, from colonial reservation to the Forest Rights Act of 2006.

Two cautions run through the chapter. First, reverence for trees and groves is real and old, but it is not the same thing as a conservation policy, and it has coexisted throughout Indian history with large-scale clearance, hunting and the expansion of cultivation. Second, the knowledge and institutions of forest peoples — Adivasi and other forest-dwelling communities — deserve treatment on their own terms; that treatment is given in Volume 23 (Jana–Jāti), and this chapter refers to it rather than duplicating it.

docs.title: 11.2.1 Araṇya and Grāma
docs.text:
Vedic literature contrasts the settled world of the village (grāma) with the wild space of the forest (araṇya). Domestic animals (grāmya paśu) are distinguished from wild ones (āraṇya paśu), and plants likewise from those of the wild. The forest was a place of danger and of power. A late hymn of the Ṛgveda (10.146) addresses Araṇyānī, the goddess of the forest: the poet describes the sounds heard at dusk in the woods, which make a lonely traveller imagine that someone is calling or that a cart is approaching, and praises the forest as fragrant, rich in food though untilled, and the mother of wild beasts, which does not kill unless another attacks (Jamison and Brereton 2014). The Atharvaveda’s Hymn to the Earth (12.1) asks that the earth’s hills, snowy mountains and forest be kindly to its people (Whitney 1905). The Āraṇyakas, “forest books”, take their name from the forest as a place for teaching rites and doctrines considered too dangerous or esoteric for the village.

The forest was also the place of the renouncer. In the Upaniṣads and in the early Buddhist and Jain literature, teachers and ascetics live in groves and forests outside settlements; the Buddha’s awakening took place under a tree, and his teaching was given in parks such as the deer park at Isipatana (Sarnath) and the Jetavana grove at Śrāvastī. The Buddhist monastic code counts the destruction of plant life (bhūtagāma) among the offences requiring confession, because laypeople regarded plants as possessing life; Jain ascetic rules, which recognise one-sensed life in plants, are stricter still (see Section 6.7).

docs.title: 11.2.2 Jāṅgala and Ānūpa
docs.text: Classical medicine divided land into dry, open jāṅgala, marshy ānūpa and an intermediate type (Section 1.6). Its ideal was not the forest at all but the healthy, game-rich jāṅgala savanna (Zimmermann 1987); that the English “jungle”, derived from this word, now names dense wet forest is a reminder that the vocabulary of Indian landscapes cannot be read through modern English.

docs.title: 11.2.3 Forests in the Epics and in Kāvya
docs.text: The epics are full of forests. The Pāṇḍavas and Rāma spend their exiles in forests; the Rāmāyaṇa’s Daṇḍaka forest is the frontier where Rāma encounters ascetics and rākṣasas; and the Mahābhārata narrates the burning of the Khāṇḍava forest by Agni with the help of Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna, with the slaughter of the creatures that tried to escape, after which the Pāṇḍava city of Indraprastha is founded in the region. Historians have often read the Khāṇḍava episode as a literary memory of forest clearance by fire, though it is a mythic narrative and cannot be dated or located as an event. Sanskrit poetry developed the idealised tapovana or hermitage grove, a place where animals are not hunted and ascetics live at peace with deer and trees; in the first act of Kālidāsa’s Abhijñānaśākuntala, King Duṣyanta, hunting a deer, is stopped by an ascetic who tells him that the animal belongs to the hermitage and must not be killed. Such scenes express an ideal of the protected forest; they are not descriptions of forest management.

docs.title: 11.3 The Forest in the Arthaśāstra
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra gives the fullest early account of how a state might use forests. The text is composite and in its present form dates from c. 50 BCE–300 CE (Olivelle 2013); its attribution to Kauṭilya, minister of Candragupta Maurya, is traditional. It should be read as a political treatise describing what a king ought to do, not as a record of Mauryan administration. Its treatment of law and statecraft is discussed in Volume 18 (Rājanīti and Dharmaśāstra).

In its chapter on the disposal of land not fit for cultivation (Book 2), the text recommends that the king set apart several kinds of forest (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013):

  • forests granted to brahmins for Vedic study, for the soma plant and for austerities, in which plants and animals are to be given safety;

  • a game forest (mṛgavana) for the king’s recreation, enclosed and stocked with animals rendered harmless, and areas in which animals are declared protected;

  • productive forests (dravyavana) for each kind of forest produce, with workshops for processing it;

  • elephant forests (hastivana, nāgavana) on the frontier, guarded by elephant-forest keepers.

The productive forests were under the superintendent of forest produce (kupyādhyakṣa), whose chapter lists the classes of material the state should obtain: hard timbers, bamboos, creepers, fibre plants, materials for ropes, leaves, flowers, medicinal substances, poisons, and animal products such as skins, bones, teeth, horns and hooves (Kangle 1965). Fines were laid down for damage to the state’s forests and for killing animals in protected areas; the superintendent of abattoirs was to prevent the slaughter of animals declared protected. The protection of elephants was the most emphatic: the text prescribes death for anyone who kills one, a rule that Trautmann (2015) explains by the Indian practice of capturing rather than breeding war elephants (Section 15.2; Volume 20, Yuddha).

Scholarly Note: The Āṭavika: Forest Peoples as the State Saw Them

The āṭavika is sometimes described in modern writing as a “forest superintendent”. This is a mistake. In the Arthaśāstra the āṭavikas are forest peoples and their chiefs, living in the aṭavī (wild forest) beyond or within the borders of the kingdom. The text regards them as a standing danger — they are listed among the troubles that can afflict a country — and at the same time as a resource: forest troops (āṭavikabala) appear among the kinds of troops a king may employ, and forest chiefs can be won over, set against enemies or used as guides (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013). Aśoka’s Thirteenth Rock Edict similarly addresses the forest peoples in his dominions, urging them towards his dhamma while reminding them of his power to punish (Singh 2008). The forest peoples’ own view of the forest is not recorded in these texts; for it see Volume 23.

The Arthaśāstra’s forest categories are sometimes presented as an ancient “protected-area system” that anticipated modern conservation. The resemblance is superficial. The text’s aim is the fiscal and military benefit of the king: forests are to be reserved because they supply revenue, timber, elephants and defensive cover, and the sanctuaries it mentions are royal or brahmanical preserves. Its value for a history of Indian forests lies precisely in showing how early a state could conceive of the forest as a resource to be classified, guarded and taxed.

Cross-Reference: Forest Peoples’ Knowledge

The ecological knowledge of Adivasi and other forest-dwelling communities — their classification and use of forest plants and animals, shifting cultivation, honey collection, fire management, and their own sacred groves and forest institutions — is the subject of Volume 23 (Jana–Jāti). Shifting cultivation as an agricultural system is discussed in Chapter 10; medicinal and useful forest plants in Chapter 12; and elephants and their forests in Chapter 15.

docs.title: 11.4 The Edicts of Aśoka
docs.text:
The inscriptions of Aśoka (r. c. 268–232 BCE) are the earliest datable Indian documents to concern themselves with animals and trees (Singh 2008). Their concern arises from Aśoka’s dhamma, with its emphasis on non-injury, rather than from anything like a modern ecological programme, but their provisions are concrete:

  • The First Rock Edict forbids animal sacrifice in the place of issue and reports that the slaughter of animals for the royal kitchen has been reduced to a few and would cease.

  • The Second Rock Edict states that the king has provided for medical treatment for humans and for animals, has had medicinal herbs, roots and fruits brought and planted where they did not grow, and has had wells dug and trees planted along roads for the use of animals and people.

  • The Fifth Pillar Edict, issued in the twenty-sixth year after Aśoka’s consecration, lists animals that are not to be killed — among them parrots, ruddy geese, wild geese, bats, tortoises, porcupines and squirrels, together with all four-footed animals that are neither used nor eaten — though several names in the list cannot be identified with certainty. It protects she-goats, ewes and sows that are with young or in milk; restricts the killing and sale of fish and the castration of animals on particular days; and forbids burning chaff that contains living creatures and setting fire to forests without purpose or in order to kill living beings.

  • The Seventh Pillar Edict records that banyan trees were planted along roads to give shade to animals and people, mango groves planted, and wells and rest-houses provided at intervals.

These measures were limited. Fishing and the killing of many animals remained lawful on most days, and the edicts did not prohibit hunting by others or the clearance of forest for agriculture. What they show is a ruler presenting the protection of named animals and the planting of useful trees as a duty of kingship — an idea that recurs in later royal inscriptions recording gifts of tanks, groves and roadside trees.

docs.title: 11.5.1 Names and Distribution
docs.text:
A sacred grove is a patch of vegetation, from a few trees around a shrine to many hectares of forest, that a community protects because it belongs to a deity, a spirit or the ancestors. Such groves are found throughout India, especially in the Western Ghats, the north-east, the central Indian Adivasi belt, the Himalaya and the Thar, and they have counterparts in West Africa, East Asia and elsewhere. They go by many local names (Malhotra et al. 2001; Gadgil and Vartak 1975):

  • devrāī in Maharashtra, Goa and the Konkan;

  • devarakāḍu (“the god’s forest”) in Karnataka, especially in Kodagu;

  • kāvu, including the serpent groves (sarpakkāvu), in Kerala;

  • kōvilkāṭu (“temple forest”) in Tamil Nadu;

  • oran in Rajasthan, a protected tract often dedicated to a local deity and used as common pasture;

  • sarnā among the Munda, Oraon and other communities of Jharkhand and adjacent regions, and jāherthān among the Santal;

  • law kyntang and law lyngdoh among the Khasi of Meghalaya, where the grove at Mawphlang is among the best known;

  • umanglai among the Meitei of Manipur.

There are many other names, and the same word may cover rather different institutions in different places.

How many sacred groves exist is not known. Estimates for India range from some tens of thousands to well over a hundred thousand, depending on what is counted (a single sacred tree, a shrine with a few trees, a large forest) and on how thoroughly particular states have been surveyed; the compilation by Malhotra et al. (2001) collected the state-level surveys then available and showed how uneven they were, so that precise national figures are not possible.

docs.title: 11.5.2 Deities, Rules and Management
docs.text:
Each grove is associated with a presiding power: a village goddess, a guardian deity such as the tiger-god Vāghobā of the Western Ghats or Aiyaṉār of Tamil Nadu, serpent deities in Kerala, a forest spirit, or the ancestors and deities of an Adivasi community. The rules that protect the grove vary greatly. In some, nothing may be removed, not even dead wood or fallen leaves; in others dead wood may be gathered, or fruits picked, or the grove opened for use at particular times. Hunting and cutting green trees are the most common prohibitions. Enforcement rests on belief that the deity will punish offenders with illness, crop failure or misfortune, on the authority of a priest or headman, and on community fines and sanctions. Periodic festivals, offerings and the maintenance of the shrine renew the grove’s status.

These institutions should not be idealised. Access to groves and to the rituals held in them is often governed by caste, clan and gender: some groves may be entered only by particular lineages or by men, and the priestly or managing roles are frequently hereditary. Grove rules are part of local systems of authority as well as of local ecology. Their governance is discussed for Adivasi communities in Volume 23.

docs.title: 11.5.3 What Ecologists Have Found
docs.text:
Scientific interest in Indian sacred groves dates above all from the work of Madhav Gadgil and V. D. Vartak, who surveyed groves in Maharashtra in the early 1970s. In a short paper of 1975 they reported that the groves preserved vegetation much less disturbed than the surrounding countryside, including large old trees, woody climbers and species that had become rare elsewhere, and argued for their continued protection (Gadgil and Vartak 1975). Later work in Kerala, Karnataka, Meghalaya, Manipur and elsewhere, brought together in the volumes edited by Ramakrishnan et al. (1998) and in Malhotra et al. (2001), has confirmed that many groves are refuges for plants and animals lost from the surrounding landscape, that some protect springs and stream heads, and that they can serve as seed sources for the regeneration of degraded land.

The findings are, however, heterogeneous. Groves differ enormously in size, condition and history. Some are fragments of old forest; others have been planted, are dominated by a few cultivated or sacred species, or are heavily used. A small grove isolated among fields cannot maintain populations of large animals, and edge effects, invasive plants such as Lantana camara and Chromolaena odorata, and grazing can degrade even well-protected patches. Ecologists have therefore moved away from treating sacred groves as untouched remnants of primeval forest towards studying each grove as a particular product of local history, belief and use.

Debate: Are Sacred Groves a Conservation Strategy?

It is often said that sacred groves were created to conserve biodiversity and that the rules surrounding them encode ecological knowledge. Gadgil and others have argued that religious sanctions can function as “prudent” rules of resource use, protecting resources whose value a community recognises. Critics reply that the motives recorded by the people who keep groves are religious and social — the deity’s anger, the honour of a lineage, the need for a place of worship — and that conservation, where it occurs, is often a by-product. Both positions can be true in different places. The safest conclusion is that sacred groves show how religious and customary institutions can protect patches of vegetation for long periods, not that they were consciously designed as conservation reserves (Gadgil and Guha 1992; Malhotra et al. 2001).

docs.title: 11.5.4 Threats and Protection
docs.text:
Sacred groves have been lost or reduced through the extension of cultivation and plantations, road building and urban growth, the decline of belief among younger people, and the conversion of the land to other uses when it becomes valuable. A frequently observed process is the replacement of an open-air shrine in a grove by a built temple: the deity is “Sanskritised”, trees are cleared for the building and its approaches, and the grove shrinks. State action has cut both ways. Colonial and post-colonial forest departments took many groves into government forest, which sometimes protected them and sometimes weakened the community authority that had kept them (Gadgil and Guha 1992).

Indian law now provides some instruments for their recognition. Amendments to the Wildlife (Protection) Act in 2002 created the categories of “community reserve” and “conservation reserve”; the Biological Diversity Act of 2002 allows state governments to notify “biodiversity heritage sites”; and the Forest Rights Act of 2006 (Section 11.11) allows communities to claim rights over forests they have traditionally protected. Several sacred groves have been brought under such provisions, but most remain protected, if at all, by custom alone.

docs.title: 11.6 Sacred Trees
docs.text:
Beyond the grove, particular species of tree are themselves sacred. Their protection is uneven — a sacred tree may stand in a field that has otherwise been cleared — but their cultural importance is very old. The following are among the most widely revered; their medicinal uses are discussed in Chapter 12 and in Volume 13 (Āyurveda).

Aśvattha (pipal, Ficus religiosa). Pipal leaves appear as a motif on Harappan seals and pottery (Kenoyer 1998). In Vedic ritual the upper fire-drill (araṇi) is to be made of the wood of an aśvattha growing on a śamī. The aśvattha is the Bodhi tree under which the Buddha attained awakening at Bodh Gaya, and is venerated by Buddhists as such. In the Bhagavad Gītā Kṛṣṇa declares himself “the aśvattha among all trees” (10.26), and the fifteenth chapter opens with the image of the cosmic aśvattha with roots above and branches below. Felling a pipal is widely regarded as a grave offence, and pipal trees are circumambulated, especially by women. Vaṭa or nyagrodha (banyan, Ficus benghalensis). In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (6.12) Uddālaka Āruṇi has his son Śvetaketu break open a banyan fruit and then a seed within it, to show that the great tree grows from an invisible subtle essence (Olivelle 1998). Married women in western and northern India worship the banyan in the Vaṭasāvitrī observance, which recalls Sāvitrī’s recovery of her husband from Yama; Śiva as teacher (Dakṣiṇāmūrti) is shown seated beneath a banyan; and the shade of large banyans has long served as a meeting place for village assemblies. Aśoka’s planting of banyans along roads has been noted above. Udumbara (cluster fig, Ficus racemosa). Its wood was used for ritual posts and implements in Vedic sacrifice. In Buddhist literature the udumbara “flower”, which is never seen because the fig’s flowers are hidden inside the fruit, became a simile for something extremely rare, such as the appearance of a Buddha. In Maharashtra the udumbara is associated with Dattātreya. Śamī (khejri, Prosopis cineraria). Besides its role in the Vedic fire-drill, the śamī is the tree in which the Pāṇḍavas, in the Mahābhārata, hid their weapons during their year of concealment at Virāṭa’s court; in parts of India it is worshipped on Vijayadaśamī. In the Thar it is a mainstay of farming: a leguminous tree that tolerates drought, its leaves are lopped for fodder and its pods eaten, and crops are grown beneath it. It is the tree at the centre of the Bishnoi tradition (Section 11.8). Bilva (bael, Aegle marmelos). Its trifoliate leaves are offered to Śiva, and the tree is commonly planted near Śiva shrines. Tulasī (holy basil, Ocimum tenuiflorum). Not a tree but a small aromatic herb, it is grown in courtyards on a raised platform (tulasī-vṛndāvana) and worshipped daily in many Vaiṣṇava households; its ritual marriage to Viṣṇu (tulasī-vivāha) is celebrated in the month of Kārttika. Kadamba (Neolamarckia cadamba). Its fragrant ball-shaped flower heads, which open with the rains, made it a tree of the monsoon in Sanskrit poetry, and it is closely associated with Kṛṣṇa’s youth in Vraja.

Other trees — the nimba (neem), the mango, the aśoka (Saraca asoca), the pārijāta, the coconut, and the palāśa (Butea monosperma) — have their own ritual roles in different regions. The Purāṇas and later ritual literature praise the planting of trees and the dedication of groves as works of merit, comparable to digging wells and tanks; a widely quoted Sanskrit verse, attributed in modern collections to different Purāṇas, promises that one who plants a pipal, a neem, a banyan, flowering trees, pomegranates, citrons and mangoes will not go to hell. Such merit literature encouraged planting near settlements; it was not an ecological design. Modern ecology recognises wild figs as important food sources for many fruit-eating birds and mammals, but that is a modern finding, not the reason for their veneration.

Bhagavad Gītā 15.1

ūrdhvamūlam adhaḥśākham aśvatthaṃ prāhur avyayam chandāṃsi yasya parṇāni yas taṃ veda sa vedavit “They speak of an imperishable aśvattha with roots above and branches below, whose leaves are the Vedic hymns; one who knows it knows the Veda.”

docs.title: 11.7 The Pañcavaṭī
docs.text: In the Rāmāyaṇa, Pañcavaṭī is the place in the Daṇḍaka forest, near the Godāvarī, where Rāma, Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa build a hut during their exile and from which Sītā is abducted; tradition locates it at Nashik. The name is usually explained as “five banyans”. In later religious practice the word came to denote a planting of five sacred trees, set out together near a temple, a house or a place of meditation. The lists of the five trees vary between texts, regions and communities. One frequently repeated set comprises the aśvattha, vaṭa, bilva, āmalakī (Phyllanthus emblica) and aśoka; others include the udumbara, nimba or other trees, and some take the name literally as five banyans. There is no single canonical pañcavaṭī. A planting of five long-lived trees creates shade and a small habitat for birds and insects; the texts present it as a sacred planting, not as an ecological one.

docs.title: 11.8 The Bishnoi
docs.text:
The Bishnoi community of western Rajasthan and adjoining regions follows the teachings of Jambhojī, also called Jambheśvara (1451–1536), who according to tradition founded the community in the Thar towards the end of the fifteenth century. The name is commonly explained from the twenty-nine (bīs + nau) rules of conduct that Jambhojī laid down. These include rules of personal purity and religious practice — such as filtering drinking water, daily bathing and abstention from intoxicants — together with prohibitions on cutting green trees and on killing animals, and an injunction to show compassion to all living beings. Bishnoi villages are known for their protection of the blackbuck and the chinkara, which can often be seen grazing close to Bishnoi fields, and for their care of khejri trees.

According to Bishnoi tradition, in 1730 soldiers of the ruler of Jodhpur came to the village of Khejarli to fell khejri trees for use in construction. A Bishnoi woman, Amṛtā Devī, clung to a tree and was killed, and her daughters and then many others followed; the tradition gives the number of the dead as 363. The ruler is said to have stopped the felling and issued an order protecting trees and animals in Bishnoi villages. The event is commemorated annually at Khejarli. Its details rest on community tradition rather than on contemporary documents, and they should be presented as such; but the Khejarli story has become one of the founding narratives of Indian environmentalism, and the Bishnoi themselves are a living example of a religious community whose rules protect trees and wild animals.

docs.title: 11.9 Colonial Forestry
docs.text:
The most profound change in the history of Indian forests came under British rule. Before the mid-nineteenth century, forests were cleared for cultivation, exploited for timber (notably Malabar teak for shipbuilding) and hunted over, but much forest land remained under the customary use of local communities. The expansion of the railways from the 1850s created an enormous demand for timber for sleepers and fuel, and the colonial state moved to assert control over forests as state property (Gadgil and Guha 1992).

A Forest Department was established in 1864 under the German forester Dietrich Brandis as the first Inspector General of Forests. The first Indian Forest Act was passed in 1865. The far more comprehensive Act of 1878 divided state forests into “reserved” forests, in which customary rights were largely extinguished or strictly regulated, “protected” forests, in which certain uses were permitted, and “village” forests. Within the administration there was debate over how far the rights of villagers should be recognised. K. Sivaramakrishnan’s study of eastern India has shown how forest policy was worked out regionally, through negotiation with local elites and the shifting categories of “forest” and “waste”, rather than imposed by a single plan (Sivaramakrishnan 1999). The overall outcome, as Gadgil and Guha (1992) argue, was a system that turned the customary use of forests by peasants, pastoralists and forest peoples into a privilege granted, and often withdrawn, by the state. The Indian Forest Act of 1927 consolidated this law and remains, with amendments, in force.

The consequences were far-reaching. Shifting cultivation was restricted or banned in many areas; grazing, lopping and the collection of forest produce were regulated or charged for; and commercially valuable species such as teak, sal and deodar were favoured in managed plantations at the expense of mixed forest used by villagers. Forest peoples lost access to land and resources on which their livelihoods depended. Resistance took many forms, from petitions and the breaking of forest rules to rebellions in which forest grievances played a large part, and the incendiary fires and protests in the Kumaon hills in the early 1920s. After the Kumaon disturbances, rules framed in 1931 allowed villages in Kumaon to form forest councils (van pañcāyat) to manage some forests as commons, an institution that still exists (Guha 1989).

Colonial rule also transformed the relationship with wild animals, through bounties on “vermin”, the shikār of British and princely elites, and game reserves that excluded local people; this history, and the extinction of the cheetah, are traced in Chapter 16 (Rangarajan 2001).

docs.title: 11.10 Chipko
docs.text:
The best-known Indian forest movement began in the Garhwal Himalaya (then in Uttar Pradesh, now Uttarakhand) in 1973.
