The regional breeds listed in Section 13.11 are the product of centuries of selection by herders and farmers, though the details of that selection were rarely written down. What ethnographers and animal scientists working with pastoral communities have recorded can be summarised under a few heads.

Individual knowledge of animals. Herders commonly know each animal in their herd individually, by name, by colour and markings, and by its mother. Names are often descriptive — of colour, horn shape, temperament or place of purchase — and are passed on, so that a herder can recite the female lines of the herd over several generations. Among the Toda of the Nilgiris, whose buffaloes are bound up with their religion, ethnographers since the early twentieth century have recorded that buffaloes are named and their descent remembered. This genealogical memory is the basis of selection: a good mother is expected to produce good daughters and bulls.

Selection of breeding males. Because a single bull, ram or male camel sires many offspring, herders paid particular attention to their choice. A breeding male was typically chosen from a mother of proven milk yield, hardiness or fertility, and judged by conformation, colour, gait and temperament; in many communities breeding males were shared within a lineage or village, and exchanged between herds to avoid inbreeding. A distinct and older institution was the release of a bull in a funerary rite (vṛṣotsarga): a young bull, branded and dedicated, was set free to roam and serve the village cows. Colonial officials, who called these animals “Brahmani bulls”, complained that they were often of poor quality; but where they were chosen well they served as village breeding bulls.

Breed as community identity. For many herding communities a breed is bound up with the community’s own identity: the Raika with particular camel breeds, the Maldharis of Banni with the Banni buffalo, Gaddi shepherds with their sheep and goats. Some breeds that herders had long recognised were only recently registered as distinct breeds by the national authority, the National Bureau of Animal Genetic Resources at Karnal — among them the Banni buffalo and the Kharai camel of Kachchh, which grazes on mangroves and swims between the coastal islands where they grow. Livestock breeds, like crop landraces (Chapter 9), are collective creations whose survival depends on the survival of the communities and grazing systems that made them.

docs.title: 13.10 Animal Shelters, Fairs and Markets
docs.text:
Two institutions illustrate the different ways in which Indian society cared for and traded in animals. The first is the animal shelter. In Gujarat and Rajasthan, Jain and Hindu merchant communities maintained pāñjarāpoḷs (piñjrāpoḷ) and gośālās, where old, sick and unproductive cattle and other animals were kept until they died a natural death, financed by charitable endowments and levies on trade. European travellers of the seventeenth century were struck by such institutions, which applied the ethic of non-injury to animals that had ceased to be economically useful. Many still exist. They are best understood as religious charities; they have never been able to house more than a small fraction of the cattle population, and the fate of unproductive cattle has always been a difficult question in an economy where slaughter of cows is forbidden or restricted.

The second institution is the animal fair. Great seasonal fairs, held at pilgrimage sites and river confluences, have for centuries been the main markets for cattle, horses, camels and elephants: the fair at Sonepur in Bihar, held at the full moon of Kārttika, was famous for its elephants and horses; that at Pushkar in Rajasthan for camels and cattle; and those at Nagaur and many other places for draught bullocks. At these fairs herders and breeders sold their young stock to cultivators, and the reputation of regional breeds was made and maintained. The fairs were also religious occasions, with bathing and worship, and centres of the exchange of information among herders, dealers and farmers.

docs.title: 13.10.1 The Decline of Draught Power
docs.text: For most of Indian history animals supplied nearly all the power used in agriculture. From the 1960s onwards, tractors, power tillers, electric and diesel pumps and mechanical threshers began to replace bullocks, first in the Green Revolution regions of the north-west and then more widely. The result has been a profound change in the place of cattle in the farm economy: male calves of indigenous breeds have lost much of their value, dairying has become the main reason for keeping cattle, and the old integration of draught animals, dung and crop residues described in Chapter 10 has weakened. Camels in Rajasthan, once essential for ploughing and transport, have declined steeply in number as their work has been taken over by vehicles. These changes have consequences for breeds, for pastoral communities and for the many people whose livelihoods depended on working animals.

docs.title: 13.11 Breeds
docs.text:
Over many centuries farmers and herders shaped distinct regional breeds of zebu cattle, buffalo, sheep and goat adapted to local climates, fodder and work. India’s national registry today recognises about fifty breeds of cattle and a smaller number of buffalo breeds, as well as many breeds of sheep, goats, camels and poultry. Some of the best known are listed in Table 13.1. Characterisations are general; productivity varies greatly with management.

Table 13.1. Some well-known Indian livestock breeds and their home regions. Breed Home region Main use Gir Saurashtra, Gujarat Milk Sahiwal Punjab (now largely Pakistan) Milk Red Sindhi Sindh Milk Tharparkar Thar desert Milk and draught Kankrej North Gujarat and Rajasthan Draught and milk Ongole Coastal Andhra Pradesh Draught and milk Hariana Haryana Draught and milk Hallikar and Amrit Mahal Southern Karnataka Draught Kangayam Western Tamil Nadu Draught Khillari Maharashtra and northern Karnataka Draught Murrah Haryana (buffalo) Milk Jaffarabadi and Surti Gujarat (buffalo) Milk

The Amrit Mahal breed was maintained for centuries by the rulers of Mysore, including Ḥaidar ʿAlī and Tipu Sultan, as draught cattle for the transport of artillery. Indian zebu breeds were exported in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries to the Americas, where they became the foundation of tropical cattle ranching: the Nelore of Brazil derives from Ongole cattle shipped from the Nellore region, and the American Brahman breed was developed from Gir, Kankrej, Ongole and other zebu stock. In India itself, the promotion of crossbreeding with European dairy breeds from the 1960s onwards, and the decline of draught use with mechanisation, have reduced many indigenous breeds; conservation programmes now seek to maintain them. The history of these state breeding efforts is the subject of the next section.

docs.title: 13.12.1 Hissar and the Army’s Cattle
docs.text:
Organised cattle breeding by the state in India began with the needs of the East India Company’s army, which depended on bullocks to draw its artillery and baggage. The government cattle farm at Hissar (now Hisar, in Haryana), founded in the early nineteenth century — its foundation is usually dated to 1809 — was established to breed draught bullocks and other transport animals for the army on the extensive grazing lands of the region. The farm worked with the local grey-white cattle of the Hariana tract, a breed valued for draught and for a reasonable yield of milk, and over the nineteenth and twentieth centuries it became the principal centre for the Hariana breed and a source of bulls distributed to villages for the improvement of local herds. In the south, the Amrit Mahal establishment of the Mysore rulers (Section 13.11) was taken over by the Company after the fall of Tipu Sultan in 1799 and maintained, with interruptions, for the bullocks of the Madras army. Draught power for the military, not milk, was the first object of the colonial state’s interest in Indian cattle.

Milk for British troops created a second institution. Because European soldiers were thought to need fresh milk and butter of assured quality, the army established its own dairy farms; the first of these Military Farms is said to have been opened at Allahabad in 1889, and they grew into a network of farms attached to cantonments across India. In the twentieth century the Military Farms were among the first establishments in India to keep large herds of European dairy cattle and their crosses, and after independence they took part, with the Indian Council of Agricultural Research, in developing the Frieswal, a cross between the Holstein-Friesian and the Sahiwal. The Military Farms have recently been wound up, their dairy role having long been overtaken by civilian supply.

docs.title: 13.12.2 Science, Surveys and the “Cattle Problem”
docs.text:
In the late colonial period the condition of Indian cattle became an object of official investigation. The rinderpest campaigns and the veterinary institutions described in Section 13.6 gave the state a veterinary service; quinquennial livestock censuses were begun in 1919; and the Royal Commission on Agriculture in India (1926–28) devoted much attention to cattle, fodder and dairying. Official opinion tended to hold that India had too many cattle of too poor a quality — that large numbers of underfed and “uneconomic” animals competed for limited fodder — and that improvement required the selection of good bulls, the castration or removal of poor ones, better fodder and, where possible, the culling of unproductive animals. The last point brought officials into conflict with Hindu sentiment against slaughter, and the “cattle problem” became a recurrent theme of debates on agricultural policy. Indian critics, for their part, pointed out that what officials called surplus cattle were often the working capital of poor households, which fed them on crop residues and roadside grazing that had no other use. The same argument was later made in anthropology by Marvin Harris, whose article “The cultural ecology of India’s sacred cattle” (1966) argued that the large number of cattle, the ban on slaughter and the use of dung, traction, milk and hides formed an adapted system in which few animals were in fact useless (Harris 1966). Harris’s thesis started a long debate. His critics questioned his figures and argued that religious and political values could not be reduced to ecological function (Simoons 1979). The debate is a reminder that the economics of Indian cattle cannot be read either from official complaints or from religious ideals alone.

The scientific institutions of dairying date from this period. An Imperial Institute of Animal Husbandry and Dairying was established at Bangalore in the 1920s; renamed the Imperial Dairy Research Institute in the 1930s, it became the National Dairy Research Institute after independence and moved its headquarters to Karnal in Haryana in the mid-1950s, keeping regional stations in the south and east. The Imperial (later Indian) Council of Agricultural Research, founded in 1929, came to coordinate research on animal husbandry as on crops.

docs.title: 13.12.3 Crossbreeding after Independence
docs.text:
After independence the improvement of cattle became part of national planning. The Key Village Scheme of the First Five-Year Plan (from 1952) set up centres for the selective breeding of local cattle with approved bulls and for artificial insemination, and later programmes extended artificial insemination widely. From the 1960s policy turned increasingly to crossbreeding the large population of non-descript (unclassified) cattle with European dairy breeds, chiefly the Jersey and the Holstein-Friesian, whose crossbred daughters could give much more milk under good feeding. A pioneering bilateral project, the Indo-Swiss project in Kerala begun in the 1960s, produced a crossbred population known as Sunandini from local cattle and the Brown Swiss and other European breeds. Frozen semen, liquid nitrogen and the dairy cooperatives of Operation Flood (Chapter 14) carried crossbreeding into villages throughout the country, especially in Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Punjab and other states with good markets for milk (George 1985). Official policy generally envisaged that recognised indigenous breeds would be bred pure in their home tracts while non-descript cattle were upgraded by crossing, but in practice the line was not always held.

The result has been a large increase in milk production, in which crossbred cows and, above all, buffaloes have played a central part, and a corresponding decline in the numbers and purity of many indigenous cattle breeds. Since the 2010s government policy has given new emphasis to indigenous breeds, notably through the Rashtriya Gokul Mission launched in 2014, with breeding centres for native cattle. The debate over the two approaches is summarised below.

Debate: Crossbred or Indigenous Cattle?

Advocates of crossbreeding point out that crossbred cows give substantially more milk than most indigenous cows under the same reasonable management, that they have allowed small farmers to earn a living from one or two animals, and that dairy income has been one of the most widely shared gains of Indian agriculture since the 1970s. Advocates of indigenous breeds reply that crossbreds need better feed, housing and veterinary care than poor households can provide; that they are more susceptible to heat stress and to some tropical diseases and ticks; that the male calves of crossbreds are of little use for draught; and that indiscriminate crossing has diluted breeds adapted over centuries to Indian climates and work, which may be valuable in a hotter future. Both sides have good arguments, and much depends on the region, the market and the resources of the farmer. One argument should be set aside: the claim that the milk of indigenous cows is uniquely health-giving because it contains only the “A2” form of the protein beta-casein, while that of European breeds is harmful, has not been established; a review by the European Food Safety Authority in 2009 found no established cause-and-effect relationship between the relevant milk peptides and disease (European Food Safety Authority 2009).

docs.title: 13.13 Other Livestock
docs.text:
Buffaloes became the principal dairy animal of northern and western India, valued for the high fat content of their milk; they are also the main draught animal of wet-rice cultivation in many regions. Sheep and goats supplied meat, milk, wool, skins and, through penning on fields, manure; goats are the livestock of the poor and of the drylands. Caraka’s dietetics compares the milks of different animals, and goat’s milk is described as light and easily digestible (Sharma 1981). Sheep, goats and wool, camels, and poultry and pigs are treated more fully in the sections that follow.

Dogs occupied an ambiguous place: they guarded herds and houses and hunted, and the Mahābhārata’s story of Yudhiṣṭhira refusing to enter heaven without the dog that had followed him is famous; but the dog was also a standard image of impurity, and the term śvapaca, “dog-cooker”, was used of the lowest outcastes. Several Indian hound breeds — the Mudhol hound of Karnataka and the Rajapalayam, Chippiparai and Kombai of Tamil Nadu — were developed for hunting and guarding.

docs.title: 13.14.1 Shepherds and Blankets of the Deccan
docs.text:
India’s sheep were, and mostly still are, animals of the drylands, kept for meat, manure and skins as much as for wool. Most Indian breeds produce coarse wool or hair rather than the fine fleece of the European Merino, and the wool of the peninsular breeds is largely coarse, hairy and dark. On the Deccan plateau sheep herding is the hereditary occupation of large shepherd castes — the Dhangar of Maharashtra, the Kuruba of Karnataka, the Kuruma and Golla of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana — many of whose members are now settled farmers or have left herding altogether. These communities have their own pastoral deities and shrines, such as Khandobā and Birobā in Maharashtra and Bīrappa and Mailāra in Karnataka, and their own histories of political and religious distinction: the Holkar rulers of Indore were of Dhangar origin, and the sixteenth-century Kannada poet-saint Kanakadāsa came from a Kuruba family.

The characteristic product of the Deccani shepherds was the rough woollen blanket, kambaḷi in Kannada (kambal in Hindi), ghongaḍī in Marathi, woven on simple looms from the black, brown and grey wool of the flock. Shepherd families sheared the sheep, spun the wool and wove the blankets themselves or through weaving sub-groups within the shepherd castes, and sold them at weekly markets and fairs. The blanket served the herder as cloak, rain cape, bedding and mat, and was carried by farmers and labourers throughout the Deccan. The trade has declined with competition from mill-made blankets and synthetic fibres, though it survives in particular centres and has been supported by craft cooperatives. The weaving of wool and its place among India’s textile traditions are treated in Volume 17, Śilpa–Kāru.

docs.title: 13.14.2 Rajasthan and the Himalaya
docs.text:
Rajasthan has long been India’s largest producer of wool, and its breeds — among them the Chokla, Magra, Marwari, Malpura, Jaisalmeri, Nali and Pugal — were selected by Raika and other herders in the Thar and its margins. Their fleece is mostly of the coarse “carpet” type, and Bikaner became the centre of a wool trade supplying spinning mills and the carpet-weaving industry of northern India, which also uses imported wool. In the twentieth century government farms and research institutes, including the Hissar farm and the Central Sheep and Wool Research Institute at Avikanagar in Rajasthan, crossed Indian sheep with Merino and other fine-wooled breeds in the hope of producing apparel wool; new crossbred strains such as the Hissardale were developed, but fine-wool crossbreeding never displaced the indigenous breeds in the hands of herders, who valued hardiness, mobility and meat at least as much as fleece.

In the western Himalaya, the wool of Gaddi and other hill flocks was spun and woven at home; the Gaddi’s characteristic dress, a long woollen coat (cola) bound at the waist with many turns of woollen rope (ḍorā), is made from it, as were the blankets and shawls of the Kullu and Kinnaur valleys.

docs.title: 13.14.3 Goats
docs.text: Goats are the livestock of the poorest households and of land too dry or broken for cattle; because they browse shrubs and trees and need little capital, they are often called “the poor man’s cow”. Regional breeds include the large Jamunapari of the Etawah region in Uttar Pradesh, the Beetal of Punjab, the Barbari, the Sirohi and Marwari of Rajasthan and the small Black Bengal, valued for meat and for its skin. Colonial and later forest officials regarded the goat as an enemy of the forest and sought to restrict its grazing (Section 13.9.3); the goat’s defenders argued that degradation had many causes and that the goat was blamed because its owners were poor and politically weak (Saberwal 1999).

docs.title: 13.14.4 Pashmina and the Kashmir Shawl
docs.text:
The most valuable fibre produced by any Indian animal comes from the goats of the Changthang plateau in eastern Ladakh, adjoining Tibet. To survive winters of extreme cold the Changthangi goat grows a fine, soft undercoat beneath its outer hair. The Changpa herders, who keep these goats together with sheep and yaks, collect the undercoat in spring by combing as the animals moult; the raw fibre is called pashm (Persian, “wool”), and the fabric woven from it is pashmina. Similar fibre came from goats in western Tibet and Central Asia, and for centuries the raw pashm of Ladakh and western Tibet was carried through Leh to Kashmir, where it was cleaned, spun by hand, very largely by women, and woven into shawls. By the treaty of Tingmosgang concluded between Ladakh and Tibet in the later seventeenth century, Ladakh secured control over the trade in raw pashm from western Tibet, and the Kashmir weavers’ supply of fibre was a recurrent concern of the rulers of Kashmir.

The Kashmir shawl was a luxury of the Mughal court: Abū’l-Faẓl records Akbar’s interest in shawls and the improvements he made to their manufacture (Abū’l-Faẓl 1873). Under the Afghan, Sikh and Dogra rulers of Kashmir the shawl industry was heavily taxed, and in the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries the shawl became a fashion in Europe, where its designs were imitated by mechanised weavers at Paisley in Scotland, in France and elsewhere. The European market collapsed in the 1870s, with grave consequences for the Kashmiri weavers (Maskiell 2002). A still finer fibre, shahtūsh, came from the Tibetan antelope or chiru (Pantholops hodgsonii), which, unlike the pashmina goat, had to be killed for it; the trade in shahtoosh is now banned under international and Indian law. Pashmina remains the livelihood of the Changpa herders and of the Kashmiri spinners and weavers, though many Changpa families have moved to settled life near Leh. The textile history of the shawl is treated in Volume 17.

docs.title: 13.15.1 The Raika and Their Camels
docs.text:
The one-humped dromedary is the animal of the Thar desert and of the drylands of Gujarat, Haryana and Punjab. It was bred above all by the Raika (Rabari), but also by other communities, including some Muslim pastoral groups of Kachchh and Sindh. According to a widely told Raika origin story, the god Śiva created the first camel to please Pārvatī and then created the first Raika to look after it; and the Raika, like many other Rajasthani communities, revere the folk hero Pābūjī, whose oral epic, sung by priest-bards before a painted cloth scroll, tells how he brought the first she-camels to Marwar. Camel breeding was thus not only an occupation but the core of a community’s identity.

Raika herds grazed on the common lands and village sacred groves (oran, Chapter 11) of western Rajasthan and moved with the seasons in search of browse. Researchers working with Raika breeders have reported that the community traditionally regarded the sale of female camels outside the community, and the sale of camel milk, as improper: milk was drunk by the herders and given away rather than sold, and it was male camels that were sold, chiefly at the great fairs such as Pushkar (Section 13.10). Breeders distinguish regional types, now recognised as breeds — the Bikaneri, Jaisalmeri, Marwari, Mewari and Kachchhi, and the Kharai of the Kachchh coast mentioned above — and select breeding males with care. The Indian Council of Agricultural Research maintains a research centre on the camel at Bikaner.

docs.title: 13.15.2 Work, War and Milk
docs.text:
For centuries camels carried the goods of the desert trade, drew ploughs in the sandy fields of the Thar, lifted water from deep wells and pulled carts in towns and villages. Their hair was made into ropes, bags and rugs, and their hides were worked; the Bikaner craft of decorating camel-hide vessels and lamps with gilded and painted designs (usta work) belongs to the craft history treated in Volume 17. Camels also served in war. The Bikaner Camel Corps, known as the Ganga Risala after Mahārājā Gaṅgā Siṃh of Bikaner (r. 1887–1943), served as one of the Imperial Service contingents of the princely states and was sent overseas, to China in 1900 and to Egypt during the First World War; mounted camel patrols remain in service with the Border Security Force on the Thar frontier. The military history of animals is treated in Volume 20, Yuddha.

Camel milk was a staple of the herders’ own diet, drunk fresh or soured; it is difficult to make into butter by traditional churning, which partly explains why it never entered the ghee-based dairy economy of settled India. In recent years camel milk has begun to be collected and marketed by dairies in Gujarat and Rajasthan, and claims have been made for its value in particular diseases; such claims are under investigation and should not be treated as established.

docs.title: 13.15.3 Decline and the Law of 2015
docs.text: The steep decline of camel numbers in Rajasthan over recent decades has been widely reported in successive livestock censuses. Its causes include the replacement of camels by tractors and motor vehicles, the loss of grazing to irrigation, enclosure and the restriction of grazing in forests and sanctuaries, and the declining interest of young people in a hard and poorly rewarded occupation. In 2014 the Government of Rajasthan declared the camel its state animal, and in 2015 it passed the Rajasthan Camel (Prohibition of Slaughter and Regulation of Temporary Migration or Export) Act, which banned slaughter and restricted the movement of camels out of the state. Breeders and organisations working with them have argued that the restrictions on sale and movement destroyed much of the market for male camels, which had been the herders’ main source of income, and so accelerated rather than halted the decline. The camel’s case illustrates a general point of this chapter: a breed survives only if the people who keep it can make a living from it.

docs.title: 13.16.1 Poultry
docs.text:
Chickens descend from the red junglefowl of the forests of South and Southeast Asia (Section 13.2). For most of Indian history they were kept in small numbers, scavenging around the house, by Adivasi, Dalit, Muslim and many other rural households, and often belonged to and were managed by women; eggs and birds supplied food, a little cash, and offerings in many Adivasi and village rituals. Many high-caste Hindu and Jain communities avoided domestic fowl and eggs as impure, and the chicken was in this sense a marker of caste and community as much as an economic resource. Since the 1970s an industrial poultry sector based on imported hybrid broiler and layer strains has grown very rapidly, and chicken has become the most widely eaten meat in India; the indigenous “desi” bird nevertheless remains important in tribal and poor households, where its hardiness and its meat, preferred by many consumers, give it a value beyond its low productivity. Among recognised indigenous breeds are the Kadaknath of the Jhabua region of western Madhya Pradesh, kept by Bhil and Bhilala households and known for its black skin and flesh, which has been granted a geographical indication.

The Aseel (Asil, from Arabic aṣīl, “of noble descent, pure-bred”) is a heavy, upright, hard-feathered game fowl bred in India for fighting. Aseel stock taken to Britain in the nineteenth century is thought to have contributed to the breed known as the Indian Game or Cornish, itself an ancestor of modern broiler chickens. Cockfighting has a long history in India: the list of arts in the Kāmasūtra includes the staging of fights between rams, cocks and quails. Today it is most prominent in the coastal districts of Andhra Pradesh, where fights are staged on a large scale during the Sankranti festival in January, with blades tied to the birds’ legs and heavy betting; it also survives in Tulu-speaking coastal Karnataka (kōri kaṭṭa), associated with local shrine festivals, and in parts of Tamil Nadu, Odisha and the North-East. Inciting animals to fight is an offence under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act of 1960, and courts have repeatedly directed the authorities to stop the Sankranti fights, with limited effect. The tradition thus sets the claims of local custom and festival against the law and the welfare of the birds.

docs.title: 13.16.2 Pigs
docs.text: Pigs, descended from the native wild boar, were kept across India by communities outside or at the margins of the caste order: by many Adivasi peoples of central and eastern India, by communities throughout the North-East, and by particular Dalit castes in the towns and villages of the north and elsewhere, for whom pig-rearing was both a livelihood and a further mark of the stigma attached to them by caste Hindus and Muslims, both of whom regarded the pig as impure. Village pigs were mostly small, dark, hardy scavengers that lived on waste and household refuse, and so also performed a sanitary function for which their keepers received little recognition. In the North-East, by contrast, pork is the most valued meat, pigs are fed with care on household and garden produce, and their slaughter marks marriages, funerals and the feasts by which households and lineages gain prestige; among several Naga and other hill peoples the semi-domesticated mithun (Bos frontalis), a bovine not milked but kept as wealth and slaughtered at the greatest feasts, holds a still higher place. Pig-keeping in the North-East suffered heavy losses from African swine fever, first reported in India in Assam in 2020.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: South Asia was a centre of animal domestication, above all of the humped zebu. In Vedic society cattle were wealth and were also sacrificed and eaten; the inviolability of the cow developed over the first millennium CE alongside, but distinct from, the ideal of vegetarianism, and became a mass political cause in modern times. The Arthaśāstra and Aśoka’s edicts show state management of herds and royal concern for animals. Most practical veterinary knowledge lay with herders and village healers and remains largely undocumented. Pastoral peoples created the regional breeds that are among India’s most valuable agricultural legacies, while forest law, enclosure and mechanisation have narrowed their livelihoods. The state bred cattle first for the army and then for milk, and crossbreeding raised yields while eroding indigenous breeds. Much of the livestock economy lay with shepherd castes, Adivasi, Dalit and other marginal communities, and the handling of dead cattle and hides was imposed on Dalits as a mark of exclusion.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: On domestication, Meadow (1996) and Fuller (2006); on the history of beef-eating and cow veneration, Alsdorf (2010) and Jha (2002), with Ambedkar (1948); on the Arthaśāstra’s herds, Kangle (1965) and Olivelle (2013); on the “cattle problem” and the sacred-cow debate, Harris (1966) and Simoons (1979); on pastoral peoples and ecology, Gadgil and Guha (1992) and Guha (1999), with Agrawal (1999) on Raika migration and Saberwal (1999) on Gaddi grazing; on the shrinking commons, Jodha (1986); on the Kashmir shawl, Maskiell (2002).

docs.title: 14.1 From Field and Herd to Kitchen
docs.text: Between the harvest and the meal lies a great body of practical knowledge. Milk has to be turned into products that keep in a hot climate; grain has to be threshed, husked, pounded, ground, parched or parboiled; oilseeds have to be crushed and cane juice boiled down; fruits, vegetables, fish and meat have to be dried, salted or pickled against the lean season. Most of this knowledge was carried by households — very largely by women — and by specialist castes of oil-pressers, confectioners and toddy-tappers, and only a small part of it was written down. This chapter follows it through dairying, fermentation, grain, oil, sugar and preservation, and then turns to the cookery texts and to the rules of purity that governed who might cook for whom. It draws throughout on the historical work of K. T. Achaya (Achaya 1994, 1998). Cattle and other livestock are treated in Chapter 13, the crops themselves in Chapter 9, and the dietetic and medical uses of foods in Volume 13, Āyurveda.

docs.title: 14.2 Milk in Early India
docs.text:
In the Ṛgveda cattle are the chief form of wealth, and milk (payas, kṣīra), curd (dadhi) and ghee (ghṛta) run through its imagery. The poets marvel that the cow, herself “raw”, holds “cooked” milk within her; they compare the dawns and the rain-clouds to milch cows and poetic inspiration to milking; ghee is the substance that makes the sacrificial fire blaze (Jamison and Brereton 2014). The history of the cow in Vedic society, including the sacrifice and eating of cattle and the later growth of cow veneration, is set out in Chapter 13; here the concern is with milk as food and ritual substance.

Dairy products were indispensable to the Vedic ritual. The daily agnihotra, offered morning and evening by the householder who maintained the sacred fires, was an offering of hot milk. Ghee (in ritual contexts usually called ājya) was poured into the fire in most offerings and was used to anoint the offering cakes and the implements. The Pravargya rite centred on the gharma, milk heated with ghee in a clay pot until it seethed. Another offering, the āmikṣā, was made by adding curd or sour milk to hot milk so that it separated into a solid curd and a liquid whey (vājina) — evidence that coagulation of hot milk with an acid medium was known in the Vedic period, even though later custom avoided deliberately “splitting” milk for food (Achaya 1994).

The churning of curd into butter supplied one of the great images of Indian literature. In the epic and Purāṇic myth of the churning of the ocean (samudramanthana), gods and demons use a mountain as the churning stick and a serpent as the rope, and draw out the nectar of immortality as a dairywoman draws butter from curd. The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (1.15) says that the self is to be found within oneself as oil is found in sesame seeds, ghee in curd, water in springs and fire in the fire-drills — an image that joins the dairy and the oil-press (Olivelle 1998). In the devotional literature of Kṛṣṇa, the butter-stealing cowherd god of Vraja, the dairy household becomes the setting of divine play.

docs.title: 14.3 The Classical Milk Products
docs.text:
Sanskrit texts from the late Vedic period onwards distinguish a sequence of products, each made from the one before: milk (kṣīra) is boiled and set as curd (dadhi); curd is churned to give fresh butter (navanīta) and buttermilk (takra); butter is heated to give ghee (ghṛta). The method is still used in Indian villages: the curd is churned with a wooden stick (Hindi mathānī) spun back and forth by a cord, and the butter is slowly heated until its water has evaporated and the milk solids have browned and settled, when the clear fat is poured off. Because it contains almost no water, ghee keeps for long periods without refrigeration; it was the form in which the surplus milk of the rainy season could be stored and traded. The Pali Vinaya allows Buddhist monks five “medicines” or tonics that could be stored and taken after noon — ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey and molasses — a list that shows which processed foods were valued for their keeping qualities.

Table 14.1 lists the principal terms. Their meanings shift between texts and periods, and some of the rarer ones are not clearly defined.

Table 14.1. Principal Sanskrit terms for milk and milk products (Achaya 1994, 1998). Term Meaning kṣīra, payas, dugdha Milk pīyūṣa Colostrum, the first milk after calving dadhi Curd (milk set with a starter) mastu The whey that separates from curd takra Buttermilk; Āyurvedic texts distinguish several kinds (ghola, mathita, udaśvit and others) by whether butter is removed and how much water is added navanīta Fresh butter churned from curd ghṛta, sarpis, ājya Ghee (clarified butter); ājya especially in ritual āmikṣā, vājina Vedic: the curd and whey obtained by adding curd or sour milk to hot milk kilāṭa, kūrcikā Milk solids obtained by heating or curdling milk; the exact preparations are not always clear pāyasa Rice boiled in milk, usually sweetened (Hindi khīr)

docs.title: 14.3.1 Khoa, Chhena and the Sweets of Bengal
docs.text:
Milk boiled down slowly in an open pan, with constant stirring, becomes a thick paste, khoa or māvā; reduced less far, with the skin repeatedly lifted, it gives rabṛī. Khoa, with sugar, is the base of many north Indian sweets such as peḍā and barfī. Whether the Sanskrit kilāṭa corresponds exactly to khoa is uncertain, but thickened milk sweets are old (Achaya 1998).

Milk deliberately curdled with an acid — lime juice, sour whey — and drained gives chhenā (chānā) in eastern India and, pressed into blocks, panīr in the north-west. Achaya argued that the old reluctance to “spoil” milk by splitting it held back the use of such acid-curd cheeses in Indian cookery, and that chhena-making in Bengal probably owed something to the Portuguese, who settled in the Hugli region in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries and made cottage cheese there; the great chhena sweets of Bengal — sandeś in its modern form, rasagollā and many others — appear to be developments of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries (Achaya 1994, 1998). The argument is plausible rather than proven. The origin of the rasagollā itself is contested between West Bengal, which credits a nineteenth-century Calcutta sweet-maker, and Odisha, which associates a related sweet with the Jagannātha temple at Puri. The word panīr is Persian, and the north Indian product is generally associated with Persianate cuisine.

docs.title: 14.4 Dairy in Āyurvedic Dietetics
docs.text:
Cross-Reference: Food and Medicine in Volume 13

The dietetic theory of Āyurveda — the classification of foods by taste and potency, the rules of seasonal diet, incompatible foods and the medicinal use of ghee, milk and fermented preparations — is treated in Volume 13, Āyurveda.

Āyurvedic dietetics gives milk products a large place. The Caraka-saṃhitā lists the milks of eight animals — sheep, goat, cow, buffalo, camel, elephant, mare and woman — and in its chapter on food and drink (Sūtrasthāna 27) devotes one of its twelve groups of foods to milk and milk products (gorasa), alongside groups for grains, pulses, meats, vegetables, fruits, wines and other drinks (madya), sugarcane products (ikṣu) and cooked preparations (kṛtānna) (Sharma 1981). Each product is described by its taste, potency and action on the three doṣas. Curd is hedged with restrictions — it is not to be eaten at night or heated, for example — while buttermilk is praised as a digestive. Ghee is valued as the vehicle of medicines: herbs are cooked in it to make medicated ghees, on the principle that ghee takes up the qualities of what is processed with it. Caraka also lists incompatible combinations of foods (viruddhāhāra), of which milk with fish is the most famous, and among the factors that determine the effect of food (Vimānasthāna 1) he gives a place to processing (karaṇa): cooking, soaking, churning or storage change a food’s qualities (Sharma 1981; Wujastyk 2003). These are the concepts of a medical system; the claims made for particular foods within it are claims about doṣas, not results of modern nutritional research.

Health and Safety Note

Traditional praise of dairy and fermented foods should not be read as medical advice. Ghee and butter are rich in saturated fat; claims that ghee lowers cholesterol or prevents heart disease, or that particular home-fermented foods cure illness, are not established by reliable evidence. Unboiled milk can transmit tuberculosis, brucellosis and other infections, and poorly stored grains and oilseeds can carry fungal toxins. Illicitly distilled liquor has repeatedly caused mass poisoning in India through methanol contamination, and mustard oil adulterated with the seed oil of the weed Argemone mexicana has caused outbreaks of epidemic dropsy. The consumption of pañcagavya is discussed, with a safety note, in Chapter 13.

docs.title: 14.5 Dairying Communities and Modern Cooperatives
docs.text:
In most of India milk was produced in small quantities by farming households, and the daily work of milking, setting, churning and making ghee fell mostly to women. Alongside them were castes and communities for whom cattle and dairying were a hereditary occupation and an element of identity: the Ahīr, Gvālā and Yādava groups of the north, who claim descent from Kṛṣṇa’s cowherd clan; the Gollas of Andhra and Karnataka; the Gavlīs of Maharashtra; the pastoral Rabārī, Maldhārī and Gujjar communities of the west and north-west; and the Toda of the Nilgiris, whose buffalo dairies are graded temples and whose dairymen are priests (Chapter 13). In towns, confectioners (the Halvāī of the north, the Moirā of Bengal) turned milk and sugar into sweets.

Modern organised dairying owes most to a cooperative. In the Kaira (Kheda) district of Gujarat, milk producers who sold to a private dairy at Anand holding the contract for Bombay’s milk supply complained of low and uncertain prices. With the encouragement of Vallabhbhai Patel and under the leadership of Tribhuvandas Patel, they formed the Kaira District Cooperative Milk Producers’ Union in 1946. Verghese Kurien, a dairy engineer who came to Anand in 1949, became its manager; the union learned to make milk powder from buffalo milk, and its products were sold under the brand name Amul. Its structure — village societies owned by the producers, which collect and test milk twice daily and pay according to fat content, federated into a district union that runs the processing plant — became known as the “Anand pattern”.

The National Dairy Development Board, set up at Anand in 1965 with Kurien as chairman, spread this pattern through Operation Flood, launched in 1970. The programme used the proceeds of sale of dairy commodities donated by the European Economic Community through the World Food Programme to build cooperative dairies in milk-producing districts and to link them to the cities in a national milk grid; by the end of the twentieth century India had become the largest milk producer in the world. Critics argued that donated commodities competed with local producers, and that urban consumers and better-off producers benefited more than the landless and women (George 1985). Its importance is nevertheless beyond dispute: it brought very large numbers of small producers, many of them households owning only one or two animals, into an organised market on their own terms.

docs.title: 14.6.1 Curd and Sour Gruels
docs.text: The simplest and most widespread fermentation is the setting of curd. Each household kept a little curd from one day to inoculate the next day’s milk — the practice microbiologists call back-slopping — so that household cultures of lactic acid bacteria were carried on, and sometimes given to new households, for long periods. Sour gruels made by fermenting rice water or cooked grain, called kāñjika or dhānyāmla in Sanskrit, are used in Āyurvedic preparations and as a sour base in cooking. In eastern India cooked rice left overnight in water (Odia pakhāḷa, Bengali pāntābhāt) is eaten in the hot season; in north India a sour fermented drink of black carrot and mustard (kāñjī) is made in winter; in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu fermented gruels of finger millet (ambali, kūḻ) are everyday foods of the poor.

docs.title: 14.6.2 Fermented Batters and the History of Idli
docs.text:
The steamed cakes (idli) and griddle pancakes (dosa) of south India are made from a batter of rice and black gram (Tamil uḷuntu, Hindi uṛad) soaked, ground and left to ferment overnight. Their early history calls for caution. Achaya noted that the Kannada Vaḍḍārādhane of Śivakoṭyācārya (920 CE) mentions iḍḍalige, and that the Lokopakāra of Cāvuṇḍarāya (c. 1025 CE) describes its preparation from black gram soaked in buttermilk, ground and seasoned — without rice, and without any mention of fermenting the batter; the Mānasollāsa (1131 CE) describes an iḍḍarikā also made from black gram (Achaya 1994, 1998; Shrigondekar 1925). Achaya therefore suggested that the fermented, steamed rice-and-pulse idli is a later development, and speculated that the technique might have come from Indonesia, where comparable fermented and steamed foods were made, at a time when south Indian dynasties had close contact with Southeast Asia. The early texts may simply not record a fermentation that cooks took for granted; the question is open.

Other fermented batters are regional: the ḍhokḷā of Gujarat, the appam of Kerala (traditionally leavened with palm toddy), the seli roṭī of the Nepali-speaking Himalaya. The jalebī, a fermented wheat batter fried and soaked in syrup, takes its name and probably its origin from the West Asian zalābiya (Achaya 1998). In the eastern Himalaya and the North-East, fermented soybean (kinema in Sikkim and Darjeeling, akhunī in Nagaland), fermented bamboo shoot, fermented leafy vegetables (gundruk) and fermented fish are central to diet and identity, with histories of their own largely outside the Sanskrit textual tradition.

docs.title: 14.6.3 Fermented Drinks and Alcohol
docs.text:
Alcoholic drinks have a long and well-documented history in India. The Vedic texts distinguish soma, the pressed plant juice of the great sacrifices, from surā, a fermented drink made from grain. Surā was offered in certain rites, notably the Sautrāmaṇī, and yet the texts already regard it with suspicion as a source of disorder. The Arthaśāstra places the manufacture and sale of liquor under a state superintendent (surādhyakṣa) who controls where it may be drunk and by whom; it names several kinds of drink — medaka, prasannā, āsava, ariṣṭa, maireya and madhu (the last made from grapes) — and describes the preparation of a ferment or starter (kiṇva) (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013). Caraka’s madya group lists many drinks by source and quality, and self-fermented medicinal preparations (āsava, ariṣṭa) remain part of Āyurvedic pharmacy (Sharma 1981).

At the same time Dharmaśāstra counts the drinking of surā among the gravest sins for brahmins (Olivelle 2005), and Buddhist and Jain ethics forbid intoxicants to monks and lay followers alike; for Jains, honey and fresh butter are also forbidden, along with alcohol and meat, because of the minute life believed to arise in them. The resulting pattern is not one of a “dry” civilisation but of drink regulated by caste, sect, gender and occasion. Palm toddy (tāḍī), the fermented sap of the palmyra, date and coconut palms, was tapped and sold by specialist castes — the Īḻavas of Kerala, the Nāṭārs of Tamil Nadu, the Īḍigas of Andhra and Karnataka, the Bhaṇḍārīs of the Konkan and others — many of whom were held to be of low rank precisely because of this work, and whose nineteenth- and twentieth-century reform movements often included a rejection of it. Many Adivasi communities brew rice beer (hanḍiyā in Jharkhand and Odisha, and many named beers in the North-East) with starter cakes of rice and plants, and distil a spirit from mahua flowers (Madhuca longifolia); these drinks have ritual and social roles that colonial and later excise laws often criminalised. When distillation began in India is debated; distilled spirits were certainly being made in the medieval period (see Chapter 18).

docs.title: 14.7.1 Pounding, Grinding and Parching
docs.text:
Grain must be freed from its husk and, for many uses, ground. The saddle quern, a flat lower stone on which grain is rubbed with a hand-held upper stone, is found at Neolithic and Harappan sites (Kenoyer 1998); the wooden mortar and pestle (ulūkhala and musala) and the winnowing basket (śūrpa) appear among the implements of the Vedic ritual, where rice for the offering cakes is husked before the fire. The rotary hand-mill (cakkī), two round stones of which the upper is turned by a peg handle, became the standard flour mill of the household in historical times; in the Himalaya, small water-driven mills (gharāṭ) ground the grain of whole villages. Husking rice with the pestle or, in Bengal and the east, with the foot-operated lever pounder (ḍhẽkī), and grinding wheat or millet at the hand-mill, were among the heaviest and most constant tasks of women. In Maharashtra the songs women sang at the grindmill (ovī) form a large oral literature. Power-driven rice and flour mills in the twentieth century relieved this labour, but also deprived many poor women who had husked rice for wages of their livelihood.

Several old preparations involve parching. Saktu (Hindi sattū) is flour of roasted barley or, later, of roasted gram, eaten mixed with water; the Ṛgveda (10.71.2) compares the wise who refine speech with their minds to men cleaning saktu through a sieve (Jamison and Brereton 2014). Parched or popped grain (lāja) is offered into the fire in the Hindu wedding rite and remains a common food as puffed rice (muṛī, kurmurā, pori). Flattened rice (pṛthuka; Hindi ciūṛā, Marathi pohe, Tamil aval) is made by soaking or parboiling paddy, heating it and pounding it flat while warm; it needs no further cooking, and the gift of a handful of flattened rice by the poor brahmin Sudāmā to his friend Kṛṣṇa in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa has made it the emblem of the humble offering.

docs.title: 14.7.2 Parboiling and Malting
docs.text: In much of eastern and southern India paddy is parboiled before husking: it is soaked, steamed or boiled, and dried, and only then milled. Parboiled grain is harder, breaks less in pounding and milling, keeps well, and has a texture and flavour preferred where it is eaten. Twentieth-century nutritional research found a further effect: some of the B vitamins, notably thiamine, migrate during parboiling into the grain, so that parboiled rice loses less of them in milling than polished raw rice. When the practice began is not known. Germinated grain was also used: sprouted, dried and ground finger millet (“ragi malt”) is a traditional food for infants in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, and malted grain was used in brewing, though early Indian brewing practice is imperfectly known.

docs.title: 14.7.3 Storage
docs.text: Grain was stored in large jars, in bins of unbaked clay or of wickerwork plastered with mud and dung (koṭhī), in underground pits in the drier regions and in granaries raised on posts in the wetter ones, often with neem leaves mixed in against insects (Chapter 12). The large buildings at Mohenjo-daro and Harappa long described as state granaries are now often interpreted as other kinds of public building (Kenoyer 1998; Possehl 2002). The storage of seed, as distinct from food grain, is treated in Chapter 9.

docs.title: 14.8 Oil Pressing
docs.text:
The commonest cooking and lamp oils of India were pressed from sesame (tila, from which comes the general Sanskrit word for oil, taila), mustard and rapeseed (sarṣapa), linseed (atasī), safflower (kusumbha), castor (eraṇḍa, used for lamps and as a purgative rather than for food) and, on the coasts, coconut (nārikela). Sesame was domesticated in South Asia and is found at Harappan sites (Fuller 2006). Groundnut, an American crop, became an important oilseed only from the nineteenth century (Chapter 9). The oil-cake left after pressing was fed to cattle and used as manure (Chapter 7).

The village oil mill, Hindi ghāṇī or kolhū, is a large mortar, usually cut from a tree trunk or built of stone, in which a heavy wooden pestle is turned by a bullock walking in a circle; the pestle grinds the seed against the side of the mortar, and the oil is drawn off while the cake remains. The same type of machine, with appropriate changes, was used to crush sugarcane. The ghāṇī is simple and can be made and repaired by village carpenters; the blindfolded bullock circling it all day became a proverbial figure of drudgery. The same mortar and pestle are also worked by machine (Figure 14.1).

Figure 14.1. An oil press (ghāṇī) with a stone mortar and a wooden pestle, here turned by a mechanical drive rather than by a bullock. The operator pushes the seed paste back towards the pestle, and the oil runs from a spout into the vessel below. Photo: Etan Doronne, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Oil-pressing was the hereditary occupation of particular castes: the Telī of north and central India, the Ghāñcī of Gujarat, the Gāṇiga of Karnataka, the Vāṇiyar (Vāṇiya Ceṭṭiyār) of the Tamil country, among others. Many of these communities also traded in oil and grain, and some rose to prosperity. Their ritual status was generally low. The Manusmṛti groups the oil-presser with the butcher, the tavern-keeper and the brothel-keeper as persons from whom a brahmin should not accept gifts (Olivelle 2005), and in Jain ethics the operation of mills and presses is one of the occupations forbidden to lay followers because of the destruction of small life it involves. In some regions the oil-pressers were divided according to whether they themselves worked the press or only traded in oil, the latter claiming higher standing.

In the twentieth century power-driven expellers and, later, solvent extraction and refining largely displaced the bullock ghāṇī, despite Gandhian programmes that promoted improved bullock presses for rural employment. “Wood-pressed” oils have recently returned as a premium product; the claims made for their nutritional superiority are largely untested.

docs.title: 14.9 Sugar and Jaggery
docs.text:
Sugarcane as a crop, the graded Sanskrit vocabulary of sugar products and the derivation of English “sugar” and “candy” from Sanskrit śarkarā and khaṇḍa are discussed in Chapter 9. The processing followed a sequence that remained recognisable into the twentieth century. Cane was cut and crushed in a press — at first a mortar-and-pestle mill of the kolhū type, later mills with two or three vertical wooden or iron rollers turned by bullocks — and the juice (ikṣurasa) was boiled in shallow iron pans over a furnace fed with the dried crushed cane (bagasse). Scum was skimmed off, often with the help of vegetable clarifying agents, and the juice thickened in stages: to a syrup or treacle (phāṇita); to a mass that set on cooling into blocks or balls of jaggery (guḍa, Hindi guṛ); and, when the thickened mass was allowed to crystallise and the molasses drained away, to a coarse granular sugar (khaṇḍa, khāṇḍsārī) and, by further purification, to white crystalline sugar (śarkarā). Large clear crystals grown slowly on threads in a concentrated syrup give rock-sugar (miśrī).

This knowledge travelled: the Tang court’s mission to Magadha to learn sugar-boiling (Chapter 9) was followed by Chinese developments of its own (Mazumdar 1998). The Hindi word cīnī for white sugar is usually taken to refer to China, suggesting that the exchange later ran in the other direction as well. Jaggery was also made from the sap of the date palm (Bengali nalen guṛ) and the palmyra (Tamil karuppaṭṭi). Bengal and the Gangetic plain were great sugar-producing regions in the Mughal and colonial periods (Chapter 18); in the twentieth century vacuum-pan factories took over refined sugar, while jaggery and khāṇḍsārī remained village industries.

docs.title: 14.10 Preservation
docs.text:
Much Indian food processing aimed at carrying food through the dry season or the monsoon. The main methods were:

  • Drying. Grains and pulses were sun-dried before storage. Pastes of pulses were shaped into small cakes and dried (vaḍī, Kannada sanḍige, Tamil vaṭakam) or rolled into thin wafers (pāpaḍ) for frying later. Unripe mango was sliced and dried and ground (āmcūr). Fish were sun-dried and salted on every coast and along the great rivers (Bengali śuṭkī, Tamil karuvāṭu), and dried meat (Sanskrit vallūra) is named in the lexicons.

  • Salting. Salt, from sea pans on the coasts and from inland lakes and rock deposits, was used for fish, for limes and other fruits, and in most pickles. Salt was taxed by states from the Arthaśāstra onwards, and the British salt monopoly was the target of Gandhi’s Salt March of 1930.

  • Pickling. Fruits and vegetables — mango, lime, gooseberry (āmalaka), bamboo shoot and many others — were preserved with salt, oil, spices and sometimes sour agents and the sun. The common modern word acār is Persian, but salted and spiced preserves of fruits are older.

  • Cooking in fat and sugar. Ghee, oil and sugar syrup were themselves preservatives: sweets made with khoa or chhena keep only briefly, but sweets fried in ghee and soaked in syrup, or sugar-based sweets with little water, keep for days or weeks, and preserves of fruits in syrup (murabbā, a word of Arabic origin that came through Persian) became popular under the Indo-Islamic courts.

These are empirical methods. Their effect can be described in modern terms — drying, salt and sugar lower the water available to micro-organisms, and acid and oil exclude many of them — without implying that they were designed on that basis; and in a monsoon climate their limits were real.

docs.title: 14.11 Texts on Food and Cookery
docs.text:
The Upaniṣads already make food a theme of philosophical reflection: in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad Bhṛgu first perceives that brahman is food (annaṃ brahmeti vyajānāt, 3.2; Chapter 2). Practical cookery, however, is recorded mainly in much later works and in incidental descriptions in poetry, narrative, temple inscriptions and travellers’ accounts (Achaya 1994).

The richest early account is the section on food in the Mānasollāsa of the Cālukya king Someśvara III (1131 CE), the encyclopaedia of royal enjoyments described in Chapter 3 (Shrigondekar 1925). It describes the king’s meal: rice, pulses and vegetables; meat, including pork, game and fish, roasted, fried or cooked in sauces; breads and fried cakes; sweets of milk, grain, jaggery and ghee; and drinks. Its frank treatment of meat at a Hindu court is a useful corrective to the assumption that “traditional” Indian food was everywhere vegetarian. A little earlier the Kannada Lokopakāra of Cāvuṇḍarāya (c. 1025 CE), a compendium of useful knowledge, includes a section on cookery as well as on plants (Ayangarya 2006).

Several later Sanskrit works are devoted to cookery or dietetics, though their dates and authorship are often uncertain. The Pākadarpaṇa is attributed to Nala, the epic king who, in the Mahābhārata, served in disguise as charioteer and cook to King Ṛtuparṇa; the attribution is legendary and the text is probably medieval. The Kṣemakutūhala of Kṣemaśarman, usually placed in the sixteenth century, combines cookery with Āyurvedic dietetics. The Bhojanakutūhala of Raghunātha, generally assigned to the later seventeenth century in Maharashtra, is a compilation on foods and their qualities drawn from earlier dietetic and culinary sources. K. T. Achaya summarises the contents of all three (Achaya 1994); they are described here from his account.

The Indo-Islamic courts produced their own culinary literature. The Niʿmatnāma, an illustrated Persian book of recipes compiled for the sultans of Malwa at Mandu around 1500, records the dishes, perfumes and remedies of a cuisine that combined Persian and Indian elements; it has been translated by Norah Titley (Titley 2005). The Āʾīn-i Akbarī describes Akbar’s kitchen and gives recipes for the imperial table, from vegetarian dishes to pulāʾo and meat preparations (Abū’l-Faẓl 1873). Through such kitchens, and the cooks and confectioners of the Sultanate and Mughal cities, much of what is now thought of as “Indian” food took shape.

docs.title: 14.12 Food, Purity and Caste
docs.text:
Food in India has never been only nourishment; it has also been a principal medium through which caste rank was expressed and enforced. The Dharmaśāstras set out at length whose food a brahmin may and may not accept, and treat the acceptance of food from those of low status as polluting (Olivelle 2005). In practice, rules of commensality — who may eat with whom, who may cook for whom, from whose hands one may take water — were among the most closely watched boundaries between castes, and anthropologists working in twentieth-century villages found that the ranking of castes could be reconstructed from the transactions of food among them (Marriott 1968).

A central distinction in north India was between kaccā food, cooked in water (boiled rice, lentils), which was highly vulnerable to pollution and was normally accepted only from one’s own caste or a higher one, and pakkā food, fried in ghee or oil, which was less vulnerable and could be accepted more widely — one reason why ghee-fried foods were served at feasts where several castes were present, and why brahmin cooks were widely employed. At the bottom of the order, Dalit communities were excluded from shared wells and kitchens, and the eating of beef or of the flesh of dead cattle, forced on some by poverty and by the work of removing carcasses, was made a mark of their exclusion (Chapters 13 and 18). Vegetarianism itself carried caste meanings: it was a mark of high status for brahmins and many trading castes, and was adopted by groups seeking higher rank, while the majority of Indians, then as now, ate meat or fish when they could.

These rules were never uniform. They varied by region and sect, were relaxed in some devotional movements and pilgrimage centres — the shared food of the Jagannātha temple at Puri is the classic example — and were challenged by Buddhist, Jain, Sikh, Bhakti, Islamic and modern reform movements. The common kitchen (laṅgar) of the Sikh gurdwaras, at which all sit together to eat, was a deliberate rejection of caste commensality. Urban life has weakened the rules in public, though they remain powerful in marriage and the home.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Dairy products were central to Indian food and ritual from the Vedic period, and medical and lexical texts record a graded vocabulary of milk products. Acid-curdled cheeses and the chhena sweets of Bengal appear to be comparatively recent, possibly owing something to Portuguese example; the twentieth century brought the Anand cooperative of 1946 and Operation Flood from 1970. Fermentation produced curd, sour gruels, batters whose early history remains uncertain, and alcoholic drinks regulated by state, caste and sect. Grain was pounded, ground, parched, flattened and parboiled, mostly by women; oil was pressed in the bullock ghāṇī by castes of low ritual rank; Tang China sought India’s sugar-making knowledge; and drying, salting, pickling and cooking in fat and sugar carried food through the year. Cookery texts from the Mānasollāsa to the Āʾīn-i Akbarī record court cuisines, while rules of purity made food an instrument of caste. The knowledge was real and largely unwritten; the medical virtues claimed for it belong to Volume 13 and to critical evaluation.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Achaya (1994) is the standard historical survey of Indian food, and Achaya (1998) a reference work on individual foods and terms. Mazumdar (1998) places Indian sugar technology in an Asian context. Shrigondekar (1925) edits the Mānasollāsa, and Abū’l-Faẓl (1873) translates the Āʾīn-i Akbarī. On dietetics see Sharma (1981) and Volume 13.

docs.title: Chapter 15: Elephants and Horses: Hastyāyurveda and Aśvaśāstra
15.1 Two Royal Animals
docs.text:
Of all the animals discussed in this volume, the elephant and the horse were the least connected with the peasant economy and the most closely connected with kings. Both were instruments of war and emblems of sovereignty; both had their own bodies of specialised knowledge, preserved in Sanskrit treatises on their selection, care, training and medicine; and both were sources of great expense to the states that maintained them. Their histories in India are nevertheless almost opposite. The Asian elephant is native to the subcontinent, and Indian kings obtained their elephants by capturing them from the wild rather than by breeding them. The horse was not native to most of South Asia, did not thrive in much of its climate, and for over two thousand years Indian rulers depended heavily on horses imported from Central Asia, Iran and Arabia. These contrasting histories shaped the knowledge traditions examined in this chapter (Trautmann 2015; Digby 1971).

Warfare with elephants and cavalry is treated in Volume 20 (Yuddha and Dhanurveda); this chapter concentrates on the animals themselves and on the knowledge of their keepers.

docs.title: 15.2 Elephants in Early India
docs.text: Elephants appear on the seals of the Indus civilisation, and their bones are found at Harappan sites, but there is no clear evidence that Harappans tamed them (Kenoyer 1998; Possehl 2002). The capture, taming and use of elephants for riding, work and war appear in the historical record in the Ganga valley in the first millennium BCE. Thomas Trautmann has argued that the military use of captive elephants was an Indian development, which spread from India to Southeast Asia, to the Achaemenid and Hellenistic kingdoms of the west and ultimately to Carthage (Trautmann 2015). Greek writers record that Seleucus I, after his war with Candragupta Maurya around 303 BCE, received five hundred elephants as part of the settlement, and that these animals played a part in the wars of his successors.

docs.title: 15.2.1 Capture Rather Than Breeding
docs.text:
Trautmann’s central observation is that Indian kings, with few exceptions, did not breed elephants in captivity. An elephant takes some fifteen to twenty years to reach working maturity, and a female in calf or nursing a calf cannot work; it was cheaper to capture adult animals from the wild and train them. The supply of war elephants therefore depended on the preservation of wild elephant populations and of the forests in which they lived. This, Trautmann argues, gave Indian kings a direct interest in protecting forests and forest peoples, who were the capturers and first trainers of elephants (Trautmann 2015).

The Arthaśāstra reflects exactly this interest. It provides for elephant forests (nāgavana) at the frontiers of the kingdom, under a superintendent with a staff of guards, and treats the killing of an elephant there as a capital offence. Its chapters on the superintendent of elephants describe the stables, the rations, the staff — physicians, trainers, grooms, cooks, guards — and the classes of trained elephant: those under training (damya), those trained for war (sāṃnāhya), those for riding (aupavāhya) and the vicious (vyāla) (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013). Like the rest of the Arthaśāstra, these chapters describe an administrative ideal; their dating follows that of the text as a whole (c. 50 BCE–300 CE in Olivelle’s analysis).

docs.title: 15.3 The Literature of Elephant Science
docs.text: The body of Sanskrit knowledge about elephants is called gajaśāstra or hastividyā; its medical branch is hastyāyurveda or gajacikitsā. Its two best-known texts are the Hastyāyurveda ascribed to the sage Pālakāpya and the much shorter Mātaṅgalīlā of Nīlakaṇṭha.

docs.title: 15.3.1 Pālakāpya’s Hastyāyurveda
docs.text:
The Hastyāyurveda is a large work in prose and verse, printed in 1894 in the Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series (Pālakāpya 1894). It is framed as a dialogue between the sage Pālakāpya and King Romapāda of Aṅga, whose capital was Campā in the eastern Ganga plain. In the legend Pālakāpya was born of an elephant mother and grew up among elephants in the forest; when Romapāda’s men captured the wild herd, the sage followed it to the court and there taught the king the knowledge of elephants and their diseases.

The work is divided into four sections (sthāna) with a total of 160 chapters:

  • Mahārogasthāna, on the major diseases;

  • Kṣudrarogasthāna, on the minor diseases;

  • Śalyasthāna, on surgery, chiefly the extraction of foreign bodies such as arrows and spear-heads and the treatment of wounds;

  • Uttarasthāna, the “later section”, on matters such as feeding, bathing, oiling, regimen by season and general care.

Disease is explained, as in human Āyurveda, through the three doṣas and the other categories of Āyurvedic physiology, and the treatments — oils, decoctions, purgation, enemas, fumigation, bleeding, surgery and dietary regimen — correspond closely to those of human medicine (Volume 13). The work also contains a great deal of mythology, auspicious and inauspicious marks, and ritual.

The date of the Hastyāyurveda is uncertain. The legend of Pālakāpya is old, and elephant physicians are mentioned in the Arthaśāstra; but the text as printed is a compilation that presupposes developed Āyurvedic doctrine, and it is best placed somewhere in the first millennium CE, with the possibility of later additions (Meulenbeld 1999). Older claims that it is a work of the third century BCE or earlier have no basis.

docs.title: 15.3.2 The Mātaṅgalīlā
docs.text:
The Mātaṅgalīlā (“The Sport of Elephants”) of Nīlakaṇṭha, a short work of uncertain date, probably from Kerala, was translated by Franklin Edgerton under the title The Elephant-Lore of the Hindus (Edgerton 1931). It is a compact handbook in verse that summarises the tradition: the myth that the first elephants were born from the shell of the cosmic egg from which the sun emerged, and the legend that elephants once had wings and flew until they were cursed by a sage whose tree they had broken; the auspicious marks of good elephants; the classes of elephant — in the commonest scheme, bhadra, manda and mṛga, with a mixed class (saṅkīrṇa) — distinguished by build, proportions and temperament; the stages of life; the signs and stages of musth (mada); the methods of capture; and the qualities of a good elephant-keeper. Edgerton’s translation remains the most accessible introduction to the subject for readers without Sanskrit. It should not be confused with the Hastyāyurveda, which is a different and much larger work. Figure 15.1 sets the divisions of the two texts beside the working classes of the Arthaśāstra’s stables.

Figure 15.1. Three ways of ordering knowledge about elephants: the four sections of Pālakāpya’s Hastyāyurveda, the classes of elephant in the Mātaṅgalīlā (with literal glosses of their names), and the working classes of the Arthaśāstra’s elephant stables. After Pālakāpya (1894), Edgerton (1931) and Kangle (1965); see Section 15.3.

docs.title: 15.3.3 Other Sources
docs.text: Elephant lore is also found in the Bṛhatsaṃhitā (on the marks of elephants), in Purāṇas such as the Agni Purāṇa, which has chapters on the treatment of elephants and horses, and in the Mānasollāsa (Section 3.8), whose sections on royal pleasures include the training and sports of elephants (Shrigondekar 1925). A number of later elephant treatises survive in manuscript, many of them unpublished.

docs.title: 15.4.1 Methods of Capture
docs.text: The texts and later observers describe several methods of capture. Elephants were driven into concealed pits; noosed from the backs of trained elephants; lured by tame females used as decoys; or, in the largest operations, driven by lines of beaters into a stockade — the kheddā of Bengal, Assam and Mysore. The British officer G. P. Sanderson, who conducted kheddā operations for the Mysore government in the 1870s, left a detailed account of the method and of the skills of the forest people on whom it depended (Sanderson 1878). The capturers and first trainers were very often members of forest communities, a fact that the Sanskrit texts acknowledge only indirectly.

docs.title: 15.4.2 The Mahout
docs.text: The trained elephant was managed by a rider and keeper — in Sanskrit hastipaka, hastyārohaka or mahāmātra, whence the modern “mahout” (Hindi mahāvat). The keeper controlled the animal with voice commands, pressure of the feet behind the ears and the goad (aṅkuśa). The Mātaṅgalīlā lists the qualities of a good keeper: knowledge of the elephant’s nature and moods, patience, courage and kindness (Edgerton 1931). In practice the craft was learned by apprenticeship, often within families or communities of hereditary mahouts, and much of it was never written down. Mahouts in Kerala, Karnataka, Assam and Sri Lanka still use command vocabularies inherited from these traditions.

docs.title: 15.4.3 Musth
docs.text:
All the elephant texts give careful attention to musth (mada), the periodic state in adult males marked by secretion from the temporal glands, dribbling of urine and heightened aggression. The texts describe its stages and its signs and prescribe changes of diet and restraint during it; they also treat the flow of mada as a sign of vigour and therefore of value in a war elephant. Modern research has shown that musth is associated with greatly raised levels of testosterone and plays an important part in the reproductive competition of bulls (Sukumar 2003). The traditional descriptions of its outward signs are accurate observations; their physiological explanations are those of Āyurveda.

Health and Safety Note

The treatments described in the elephant and horse treatises are reported here as historical evidence of what the texts prescribe. Several involve purgatives, bleeding, cautery or substances that are toxic in quantity, and none has been tested by modern veterinary science. They are not a guide to the care or treatment of animals. Sick animals should be seen by a qualified veterinarian; the care of captive elephants in particular is a specialised field governed in India by law and by veterinary guidelines.

docs.title: 15.5 Elephants, Kings and Empires
docs.text:
In the ideal of the Indian army as four-limbed (caturaṅga) — infantry, cavalry, chariots and elephants — the elephant was the most prestigious arm and the king’s own mount (Figure 15.2). The Delhi Sultans, whose cavalry came from the Persianate north-west, quickly adopted the elephant as well, obtaining animals by capture, purchase and tribute from Bengal, Odisha and the forests of central India; Simon Digby showed how the control of the supply routes for war-horses and elephants shaped the politics of the Sultanate (Digby 1971). The Mughals maintained very large elephant establishments, and the Āʾīn-i Akbarī records Akbar’s elephant stables in detail — the classes of elephants, their rations and the numbers of attendants assigned to each (Abū’l-Faẓl 1873; Gommans 2002). Bābur, a newcomer from Central Asia, recorded in his memoirs his first impressions of the Indian elephant and its uses (Thackston 1996).

Elephants also served in ceremony and religion. They carried kings and images in procession, were kept by temples, and in Kerala remain central to temple festivals (pūram); the Dasarā procession at Mysore is another famous example. Ivory was worked into a variety of objects from early times (see Volume 17).

Figure 15.2. The building known as the “Elephant Stables” in the royal centre of Vijayanagara (Hampi), Karnataka, 15th–16th centuries: a row of domed chambers, each large enough for an elephant, on either side of a central pavilion. Photo: iMahesh, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 15.6 The Elephant in Religion and Art
docs.text: The elephant’s place in Indian religion and art is older and wider than its use in war. In Vedic and epic mythology Indra rides the white elephant Airāvata, born from the churning of the ocean, and elephants of the quarters (diggaja) support the world at its eight directions. The elephant-headed Gaṇeśa, remover of obstacles, became from the Gupta period onwards one of the most widely worshipped deities of India. The motif of Gajalakṣmī, the goddess Lakṣmī lustrated by two elephants pouring water over her from pots held in their trunks, appears on early Buddhist monuments such as the railings of Bharhut and Sanchi and on coins, and remained a symbol of prosperity and royal fortune. In Buddhist tradition Queen Māyā dreamed of a white elephant entering her side before the Buddha’s birth, and the Jātaka stories include tales in which the Bodhisattva is born as an elephant. The great rock-cut elephants of Mamallapuram and the elephant friezes of temple plinths across the south show how closely the animal was tied to the image of royal and divine power.

docs.title: 15.7 Colonial Capture and Protection
docs.text: Under colonial rule the capture of wild elephants continued on a large scale, now organised by forest departments and private contractors for the army, the timber industry and sale. Two methods were especially important: the kheddā stockade drive, practised in Mysore, Assam and Bengal, and melā shikār in Assam, in which riders on trained elephants pursued and noosed wild animals. Large numbers of captured elephants died in the process or soon afterwards. At the same time the government recognised that unrestricted killing threatened the supply: the Madras presidency protected wild elephants by law in 1873, and the Elephants’ Preservation Act of 1879 extended protection more widely, while still permitting capture under licence and the killing of animals declared dangerous (Rangarajan 2001; Sukumar 2003). Working elephants hauled timber in the forests of the Western Ghats, Assam and Burma well into the twentieth century. The great elephant fairs, of which the Sonepur fair at the confluence of the Gaṇḍak and the Ganga in Bihar was the most famous, were for long the main markets for captive elephants; the sale of elephants has since been restricted by wildlife law.

docs.title: 15.8 Elephants Today
docs.text: The Asian elephant (Elephas maximus) is classified as endangered. India holds the largest share of the remaining wild population, but its range has been greatly reduced and fragmented by agriculture, roads, mining and settlement, and conflict between elephants and farmers — crop raiding on one side, the killing of elephants on the other — is now among the most serious conservation problems in the country (Sukumar 2003). The Government of India launched Project Elephant in 1992 to protect elephant habitat and corridors. Large numbers of elephants also live in captivity, in temples, with private owners and in forest departments, where their welfare — chaining, inadequate exercise, unsuitable diets, the stress of festivals — has become a matter of legal and public concern. Raman Sukumar’s ecological work has combined field biology with the history of the human–elephant relationship and is the starting point for modern study (Sukumar 2003).

docs.title: 15.9.1 Archaeology and the Ṛgveda
docs.text: No securely identified domestic horse has been found at Mature Harappan sites. Claims for horse remains at a few Harappan and late Harappan sites have been disputed by specialists, and the earliest widely accepted evidence for domestic horses in South Asia belongs to the second millennium BCE (Meadow 1996; Possehl 2002). Claims that Harappan terracotta figurines represent horses have not been accepted. In the Ṛgveda, by contrast, the horse (aśva) and the light chariot with spoked wheels are everywhere: in the racing and warfare of gods and men, in the hymns to the sacrificial horse (Ṛgveda 1.162 and 1.163), and in the names of deities such as the Aśvins (Jamison and Brereton 2014). The contrast is one of the main pieces of evidence in the debate over the relationship between the Indus civilisation and the speakers of Vedic Sanskrit (see Volume 1).

docs.title: 15.9.2 The Horse Sacrifice
docs.text:
The aśvamedha, the horse sacrifice performed by a king claiming paramount sovereignty, is described at length in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa and the ritual sūtras. A consecrated stallion was allowed to wander for a year, guarded by armed men, and then sacrificed. Several historical kings, from the Śuṅga Puṣyamitra to the Gupta Samudragupta, claimed to have performed it. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad opens with a meditation that identifies the sacrificial horse with the cosmos (Olivelle 1998):

Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.1.1

uṣā vā aśvasya medhyasya śiraḥ “The dawn, clearly, is the head of the sacrificial horse.”

The passage goes on to identify the horse’s eye with the sun, its breath with the wind and its body with the year. It is a ritual and contemplative identification.
