The Ṛgveda already gives the Sun a chariot drawn by seven mares (1.50.8), an image that later mythology and temple art developed; the number seven belongs to a widespread pattern of Vedic symbolism and is not an observation of the colours of sunlight.

docs.title: 15.10 Horses and the Horse Trade
docs.text: Much of the subcontinent is poorly suited to breeding horses: the humid climate of the south and east, the lack of suitable grazing, and diseases took a heavy toll, and Indian-bred horses were generally regarded as inferior to imported ones. The arid north-west — Sindh, Punjab, Rajasthan, Kathiawar — and the Deccan plateau were partial exceptions, and these regions developed their own horse-breeding traditions (Gommans 2002). For the most part, however, Indian states obtained cavalry horses by import: overland from Central Asia and Afghanistan through the passes of the north-west, and by sea from the Persian Gulf and Arabia to the ports of Gujarat, the Konkan, Malabar and the Coromandel coast (Digby 1971). Late-thirteenth-century observers, among them Marco Polo, described the large sums spent by south Indian kings on imported Arabian horses, many of which soon died; in the sixteenth century the horse trade through Goa was a vital interest of the Vijayanagara kings. Sanskrit horse texts reflect this situation in their lists of horses by country of origin, which name the north-western regions (Sindhu, Kamboja, Bāhlīka/Balkh) and Persia among the best sources.

docs.title: 15.11.1 Śālihotra and the Horse Texts
docs.text:
In Sanskrit tradition the founder of horse science (aśvaśāstra, aśvāyurveda) is the sage Śālihotra, and the name became so closely associated with horse medicine that in Hindi and Urdu a horse doctor is still called a sālotrī. The epic tradition also associates expert knowledge of horses with Nakula, one of the five Pāṇḍavas. A number of works circulate under Śālihotra’s name, in different recensions; like the Hastyāyurveda, they presuppose developed Āyurvedic doctrine, and in their surviving forms they are medieval. Older claims that Śālihotra wrote in the third century BCE or earlier rest on tradition alone. Other horse treatises include the Aśvacikitsita ascribed to Nakula, the Aśvavaidyaka of Jayadatta, and horse sections in the Agni Purāṇa and in Someśvara’s Mānasollāsa (Shrigondekar 1925; Meulenbeld 1999).

Śālihotra material was adapted into Persian from the Sultanate period onwards, and Persian versions known as Sālotar circulated widely; illustrated Persian horse books were produced at Mughal and regional courts. These works combined Indian material with the hippology of the Islamic world, which had its own rich tradition. The English word “farrier”, which is sometimes said to derive from Śālihotra, in fact comes through French from Latin ferrarius, “worker in iron”, and has nothing to do with Indian horse science.

docs.title: 15.11.2 Contents of the Horse Treatises
docs.text:
The horse treatises cover broadly similar ground:

  • the mythical origin of horses — from the churning of the ocean, which produced the divine horse Uccaiḥśravas, and the legend that horses once had wings;

  • the classification of horses by place of origin, colour, build and temperament, and their auspicious and inauspicious marks, among which the position of hair whorls (āvarta) is particularly important — a feature shared with Arab and Persian hippology;

  • judging age by the teeth, and the qualities of a good horse for war, riding and display;

  • stable construction, grooming, feeding and exercise, and regimen by season;

  • the diseases of horses, explained through the doṣas, and their treatments by oils, decoctions, fumigation, bleeding, cautery and surgery.

Like the elephant texts, they record a long experience of keeping horses and contain accurate descriptions of external signs. Their medical theory is Āyurvedic, and their treatments are of historical interest only (see the safety note above).

docs.title: 15.12 The Horse in Indian Art and Culture
docs.text:
Because horses were costly and associated with kings and warriors, they became potent symbols. The Sun god Sūrya is shown driving a chariot drawn by seven horses, and the thirteenth-century Sun temple at Konark in Odisha was conceived as his colossal stone chariot, with carved wheels and rearing horses. Equestrian figures of warriors and heroes appear on memorial stones (vīrakal) of the Deccan and the south, and the terracotta horses offered to village guardian deities such as Aiyaṉār in Tamil Nadu, and in the Bankura region of Bengal, are among the best-known forms of Indian folk art. Rajput and Mughal painting produced a rich tradition of equestrian portraits, and Mughal and Deccani artists painted individual horses from the royal stables with the same care as they gave to the emperors’ elephants. The great animal fairs at Pushkar and Sonepur (Section 13.10) were also horse markets.

The keeping of horses also involved specialist communities: grooms (sāīs), horse-dealers, farriers and horse-doctors, whose skills, like those of mahouts, were learned within families. Many of the dealers who brought horses from Central Asia and Afghanistan in the Mughal period were Afghans and Central Asians, while the grooms and keepers in Indian stables were drawn from local service communities (Gommans 2002).

docs.title: 15.13 Horse Breeds and Horse Cultures
docs.text:
Several distinctive horse and pony breeds are recognised in India today: the Marwari of Rajasthan and the Kathiawari of Gujarat, both with their characteristic inward-curving ear tips; the Manipuri pony, ridden in the Manipuri game of sagol kangjei, from which British officers in Manipur and Cachar learned modern polo in the mid-nineteenth century; and the hill ponies of the Himalaya — Spiti, Zanskari and Bhutia. Their histories are poorly documented before the modern period, and claims that particular modern breeds descend from horses named in Sanskrit texts cannot be verified. The Marathas, whose light cavalry dominated eighteenth-century warfare, bred horses in the Bhīmā valley of the Deccan (the Bhīmthaḍī horse), a breed that has become rare (Gommans 2002).

Under colonial rule the army established stud farms to breed remounts; the estate at Pusa in Bihar, where the agricultural research institute was founded in 1905, had earlier been a government stud. Modern veterinary education in India began in the late nineteenth century, partly to serve the army’s horses and the cattle of the countryside (see Chapter 13).

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Elephants and horses were the animals of kings. The elephant, native and wild-caught, gave rise to a knowledge tradition — Pālakāpya’s Hastyāyurveda, the Mātaṅgalīlā, the Arthaśāstra’s elephant forests — rooted in the forest and in the skills of capturers and mahouts, and its supply depended on preserving the forests where elephants lived. The horse, largely imported and expensive, gave rise to the aśvaśāstra literature ascribed to Śālihotra, which travelled into Persian as Sālotar and met the hippology of the Islamic world. Both traditions are medieval in their surviving texts, both applied the framework of Āyurveda to animals, and both preserve careful observation alongside myth and ritual. Today the elephant is an endangered species whose survival depends on reconciling it with farmers; the Indian horse breeds are a small but distinctive heritage.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Trautmann (2015) is the essential historical study of elephants and kings; Edgerton (1931) translates the Mātaṅgalīlā; Sukumar (2003) covers elephant biology and conservation. For horses and the horse trade see Digby (1971) and Gommans (2002); for the medical literature, Meulenbeld (1999).

docs.title: Chapter 16: Wild Animals: Hunting, Protection and Conservation
16.1 Wild Animals beside the Field
docs.text:
The farmers whose knowledge this volume describes never worked in a landscape empty of wild animals. Deer and antelope grazed their crops, wild pigs rooted in their fields, elephants raided their millet and paddy, wolves, leopards and tigers took their goats and cattle, and monkeys stripped their orchards. Wild animals were also food, a source of skins, horns, ivory and medicines, objects of worship and fear, and the quarry of kings. The history of wild animals in India is therefore part of agrarian history: the expansion of cultivation over thousands of years was also the contraction of wild habitat, and the long story of hunting, from the ritual and royal hunts of the texts to the colonial war on “vermin”, was in large part a story about who controlled the land and its produce.

This chapter follows the larger wild mammals of South Asia from rock art and the Harappan seals, through texts on medicine, statecraft and ethics, to the royal, Mughal and colonial hunt and the rise of modern wildlife protection. Elephants are treated in Chapter 15, birds (including falconry) in Chapter 17, and forests, sacred groves and the Bishnoi in Chapter 11; this chapter refers to them rather than repeating them.

One caution runs throughout. Texts that forbid killing, kings who protected particular animals and communities that revere particular species are an important part of this history, but they are not evidence of an ancient “conservation policy” in the modern sense. They coexisted, often in the same courts and the same centuries, with enthusiastic hunting and with the steady clearance of forest for the plough.

docs.title: 16.2 Early Evidence: Rock Art, Seals and Names
16.2.1 Hunters in Rock Art
docs.text: The oldest images of Indian wild animals are the rock paintings of central India, above all those of the rock shelters of Bhimbetka near Bhopal, a World Heritage Site. Their dating is debated, but the earliest layers are generally assigned to the Mesolithic. They show deer, wild cattle, boar, elephants, rhinoceros and big cats, often in scenes of hunting with bows, spears and traps, and later layers add horses, riders and armed warriors (Singh 2008). The animal bones from Mesolithic and early Neolithic sites, and from the earliest levels at Mehrgarh, show that hunting of gazelle, deer, wild cattle, wild pig and the onager long continued alongside the first herding and farming (Chapter 2).

docs.title: 16.2.2 The Harappan Seals
docs.text: The square stamp seals of the Mature Harappan civilisation (c. 2600–1900 BCE) are carved with animals. The most frequent is the one-horned animal usually called the “unicorn”, which is not a real species; but the seals also show, with great naturalism, the zebu bull, the water buffalo, the elephant, the rhinoceros and the tiger (Kenoyer 1998; Possehl 2002). On a famous seal from Mohenjo-daro a seated, horned figure is surrounded by an elephant, a tiger, a rhinoceros and a buffalo, with deer or antelopes below the seat. John Marshall identified the figure as a “proto-Śiva” in his aspect as Paśupati, lord of animals; that identification is now widely doubted, and the meaning of the scene is unknown. The presence of these animals on seals does not mean that they were domesticated; it does show that the rhinoceros and the tiger lived in or near the Indus plains and that they mattered to the people who made the seals.

docs.title: 16.2.3 Names in the Vedic and Later Texts
docs.text:
The Ṛgveda knows many wild animals, mostly as images in hymns: the lion (siṃha), an image of terrifying strength; the wolf (vṛka), the archetypal enemy of the herds; the bear (ṛkṣa); the wild boar (varāha); the monkey (kapi); and the elephant, called the “beast with a hand” (mṛga hastin) (Jamison and Brereton 2014). The word mṛga originally meant any wild beast, as opposed to domestic animals (paśu); only later did it come to mean above all the deer and antelope, so that the king of beasts, the lion, is mṛgarāja or mṛgendra, and hunting itself is mṛgayā, “the pursuit of wild animals”. The tiger (vyāghra) is not mentioned in the Ṛgveda but appears in the Atharvaveda and later Vedic texts, and its skin is spread for the king in the royal consecration; scholars have often linked its arrival in the texts with the movement of Vedic culture east into the forested Ganga valley, though the argument from silence is not conclusive.

Some of the commoner Sanskrit and Tamil names are listed in Table 16.1. Identifications are often uncertain, because the same word could denote different animals in different periods and regions.

Table 16.1. Some names of wild mammals in Sanskrit and Tamil, with their usual identifications. Term Identification Notes mṛga wild animal; deer General sense “wild beast” in early texts; later chiefly deer and antelope. siṃha, mṛgendra lion The Asiatic lion, once widespread in north-western and central India. vyāghra; Tamil puli tiger Absent from the Ṛgveda; prominent from the Atharvaveda onwards. dvīpin, citraka leopard; cheetah Dvīpin is usually the leopard; citraka (“spotted”) can mean the leopard or the cheetah, and is the source of Hindi cītā. hastin, gaja; Tamil yāṉai elephant See Chapter 15. khaḍga, gaṇḍa rhinoceros The Indian one-horned rhinoceros. mahiṣa buffalo Wild and domestic water buffalo are not always distinguished. gavaya, gaura wild cattle Identifications (gaur, gayal, nilgai) are uncertain and disputed. varāha, sūkara; Tamil paṉṟi wild pig Also the boar incarnation of Viṣṇu. vṛka wolf The enemy of the herds in Vedic imagery. ṛkṣa, bhalluka; Tamil karaṭi bear Chiefly the sloth bear. kapi, vānara, markaṭa monkey Including langurs and macaques. kṛṣṇasāra, eṇa, hariṇa; Tamil māṉ antelope, deer Kṛṣṇasāra is the blackbuck, whose range was held to define land fit for Vedic ritual. śṛgāla, gomāyu jackal A stock figure of cunning in the fables. tarakṣu hyena The striped hyena.

The blackbuck had a special place. The Manusmṛti (2.23) defines the land fit for sacrifice as the country where the black antelope roams by nature (Olivelle 2005), and the skin of the black antelope was used in Vedic ritual and by students and ascetics. A wild animal thus served as the boundary marker of a ritual geography — a reminder that the open plains of northern and western India, the jāṅgala of the medical texts, were once antelope country.

docs.title: 16.3 Animals in Āyurvedic Classification
docs.text:
The fullest systematic classification of wild animals in classical Sanskrit is found not in a work of natural history but in the dietetic chapters of the medical compendia, because meat was an important part of Āyurvedic diet and therapy. Caraka’s chapter on food and drink (Sūtrasthāna 27) groups the animals whose flesh may be eaten into eight classes according to their habitat and manner of feeding (Table 16.2) (Sharma 1981). Suśruta (Sūtrasthāna 46) divides meats first into those of dry-land (jāṅgala) and wet-land (ānūpa) animals and then subdivides each (Bhishagratna 1907).

Table 16.2. The eight classes of animals whose meat is discussed in the Caraka-saṃhitā (Sūtrasthāna 27), with examples. After Sharma (1981) and Zimmermann (1987). Class Meaning Examples prasaha those that seize their food Predators such as the lion, tiger, leopard, wolf, hyena and jackal, and birds such as hawks, crows and vultures. bhūmiśaya those that lie in the ground Burrowing animals such as the porcupine and the monitor lizard. ānūpa marsh animals Large animals of wet country: buffalo, rhinoceros, boar, elephant. vāriśaya water-dwellers Fish, tortoises, crabs. vāricara those that move on water Water birds: geese, ducks, cranes. jāṅgala dry-land animals Deer and antelope. viṣkira scatterers Birds that scratch and scatter their food: quails, partridges, peafowl, junglefowl. pratuda peckers Birds that peck: pigeons, parrots and others.

Francis Zimmermann’s study of these chapters showed that they rest on an ecological picture of the subcontinent (Zimmermann 1987). Each kind of land (deśa) has its characteristic animals, and the qualities of an animal’s flesh reflect those of its habitat: the meat of the antelope and the deer of the dry, open jāṅgala is light, wholesome and the best for general use, whereas that of the heavy, slow animals of the marshy ānūpa is heavy and productive of phlegm. The ideal landscape of Āyurveda was a dry savanna rich in game (Chapter 1). The scheme is dietetic, not zoological — it groups the lion with the crow because they feed alike — but it rests on careful attention to where and how animals live. The therapeutic uses of meats and of other animal products in Āyurveda are discussed in Volume 13 (Āyurveda).

Health and Safety Note

The medical texts prescribe the meat, fat, horn, bile and other products of many wild animals. These prescriptions are described here as historical evidence. Many of the animals concerned are now protected by law, and the hunting of them and the possession of or trade in their parts are criminal offences under the Wild Life (Protection) Act; illegal trade in animal parts for medicine is one of the main threats to species such as the tiger, rhinoceros and pangolin. Nothing in this chapter is a recommendation to use any animal product as medicine.

docs.title: 16.4 Mṛgayā: Hunting as Royal Sport and Royal Vice
16.4.1 The Arthaśāstra
docs.text:
The literature of statecraft treated the hunt with a mixture of approval and suspicion. The Arthaśāstra (composite, c. 50 BCE–300 CE) provides for an enclosed game forest (mṛgavana) for the king’s recreation, stocked with animals whose claws and teeth have been removed or which have otherwise been rendered harmless, and for forests in which animals are given safety; killing or injuring animals in protected forests is fined (Chapter 11, Section 11.3) (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013).

In its discussion of the vices (vyasana) of the king, the Arthaśāstra stages a debate on whether hunting or gambling is the worse. An earlier teacher holds that hunting is worse, because it exposes the king to robbers, enemies, wild beasts, forest fires, falls, losing his way, hunger and thirst, and so to the loss of life. The text’s own view is that gambling is worse, and it credits hunting with real benefits: exercise, the reduction of phlegm, bile, fat and sweat, practice in hitting moving and stationary targets, and knowledge of the behaviour of animals when angry or afraid (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013). Hunting is thus treated as a kind of military training, a theme taken up in Volume 20 (Yuddha and Dhanurveda).

docs.title: 16.4.2 The Law Books and the Epics
docs.text:
The Manusmṛti (c. 2nd century CE) is less indulgent. Among the ten vices of a king that arise from desire, it names hunting first, and it counts hunting with drinking, gambling and women as the four most ruinous of them (Olivelle 2005). Its argument that meat cannot be obtained without injury to living creatures applies to the hunt as to the slaughterhouse, though Manu still permits meat in many circumstances.

The epics are full of hunting, and many of their decisive misfortunes begin with it. In the Rāmāyaṇa, King Daśaratha as a young man, hunting by night beside the Sarayū, shoots at a sound he takes for an elephant drinking and kills the son of a blind ascetic couple; the dying father’s curse, that Daśaratha too will die grieving for a son, is fulfilled when Rāma goes into exile. In the Mahābhārata, Pāṇḍu shoots a deer in the act of mating, which turns out to be a sage who had taken that form, and is cursed to die if he ever approaches his wives. In these stories the hunt is a royal privilege whose excess brings disaster.

docs.title: 16.4.3 Hunting in Kāvya
docs.text:
Kālidāsa’s Abhijñānaśākuntala opens with a hunt. King Duṣyanta, in his chariot, pursues a blackbuck which flees, turning its neck to look back at the chariot, until hermits of Kaṇva’s forest stop him: the deer belongs to the hermitage and must not be killed (Chapter 11). In the second act the king’s general praises hunting in terms that closely echo the Arthaśāstra — it takes off fat, makes the body light and fit, teaches how animals behave in fear and anger, and gives the archer practice at moving targets — while the jester, worn out by the chase, complains of its hardships.

Classical Tamil poetry, by contrast, knows hunting mainly as the life of the hill people of the kuṟiñci landscape, who hunted boar and deer, gathered honey and guarded their millet fields against parrots and elephants (Chapter 2). Across south India, hero-stones (naṭukal, vīragal) commemorate men who died defending cattle from raiders or fighting tigers and boar, and the dynastic emblem of the Hoysaḷas of Karnataka showed their legendary founder Saḷa killing a tiger (or, in some versions, a lion).

docs.title: 16.4.4 The Mānasollāsa
docs.text: The most detailed Sanskrit account of the royal hunt is in the Mānasollāsa of Someśvara III (Section 3.8; (Shrigondekar 1925)). Its fourth book, on the king’s entertainments (vinoda), treats hunting at length among the other pleasures of the court: the varieties of hunting, the keeping and training of hunting dogs and the methods used for particular kinds of game. It describes an ideal of courtly life rather than particular hunts. Falconry and the Śyainikaśāstra are discussed in Chapter 17 (Section 17.3).

docs.title: 16.5 The Ethics of Killing: Aśoka, Buddhists and Jains
16.5.1 Aśoka
docs.text: The edicts of Aśoka (r. c. 268–232 BCE), whose provisions on animals and trees are summarised in Chapter 11 (Section 11.4), are the earliest datable Indian texts to criticise hunting. The Eighth Rock Edict states that in the past kings went out on pleasure tours (vihārayātrā) in which there was hunting and other such amusements, but that Aśoka, ten years after his consecration, set out for Sambodhi — the place of the Buddha’s enlightenment — and since then has made tours of dhamma instead, meeting ascetics and brahmins and instructing the people of the countryside (Singh 2008). The First Rock Edict adds that where once many hundreds of thousands of animals were killed each day for the royal kitchen, only three are now killed — two peafowl and a deer, and the deer not always — and that even these will cease. The edicts present the giving up of the royal hunt as a mark of a reformed king; they did not forbid others to hunt.

docs.title: 16.5.2 Buddhist Teaching
docs.text:
The first of the five precepts of the Buddhist lay follower is to refrain from taking life (pāṇātipātā veramaṇī). The discourses list trade in living beings and in meat among the wrong livelihoods for a lay disciple (Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.177). The position on meat was more nuanced: monks, who lived on alms, were allowed to accept meat unless they had seen, heard or suspected that the animal had been killed specifically for them; the monastic code forbade them the flesh of certain animals, including humans, elephants, horses, dogs, snakes and the large carnivores — lions, tigers, leopards, bears and hyenas. Some later Mahāyāna texts, such as the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, condemn meat-eating outright.

The Jātaka stories of the Buddha’s former births, many of them older folk tales, frequently cast the Bodhisattva as an animal who sacrifices himself for others (Cowell 1895). In the Nigrodhamiga Jātaka (no. 12) the Bodhisattva is a king of deer who offers his own life in place of a pregnant doe chosen for the royal kitchen, and so moves the king of Benares to grant safety to deer and then to all creatures; in the Mahākapi Jātaka (no. 407) a monkey king makes a bridge of his own body for his troop to escape the king’s archers; in the Chaddanta Jātaka (no. 514) a six-tusked elephant king allows a hunter to saw off his tusks. Several of these stories were carved at Bharhut and Sanchi and painted at Ajanta. They are moral fables, not natural history, but they show a sustained effort to imagine animals as moral subjects, and the hunter in them is usually the villain. The Pañcatantra, by contrast, a collection of animal fables for the instruction of princes, probably composed in the early centuries CE and later carried through Middle Persian into Arabic as Kalīla wa Dimna, uses its lion king and scheming jackal ministers as types of human character; it is evidence of attitudes to power rather than of zoological knowledge (Olivelle 1997).

docs.title: 16.5.3 Jain Teaching
docs.text:
Jainism made non-injury (ahiṃsā) the first and most comprehensive of its vows. Jain doctrine classifies living beings by their number of senses and distinguishes mobile (trasa) from immobile (sthāvara) beings (Tatia 1994). The mendicant renounces all injury; the layperson renounces at least the intentional killing of mobile beings, which rules out hunting, fishing and occupations that involve killing. Jain communities have maintained animal shelters (pāñjarāpoḷ, “pinjrapole”) for aged, injured and unwanted animals, especially in Gujarat and Rajasthan, and Jain teachers sought, with varying success, to persuade rulers to proclaim days on which no animal might be killed (amāri). Jain sources credit the twelfth-century Caulukya king Kumārapāla of Gujarat, a patron of the scholar Hemacandra, with such prohibitions, and record that the Śvetāmbara monk Hīravijaya obtained from Akbar orders forbidding slaughter on certain days, including the Jain festival of Paryuṣaṇa. The scope and enforcement of such orders are hard to judge.

Scholarly Note: Ideals and Practice

The ethic of non-injury was real and influential. It shaped the diet of large sections of Indian society, inspired royal proclamations from Aśoka to Akbar, and sustains today the animal shelters of Jain communities and the protective practices of groups such as the Bishnoi. But it did not end hunting. Kings who patronised Buddhist and Jain monks continued to hunt; the Arthaśāstra and the Mānasollāsa treat the hunt as a royal art; and the killing of animals that damaged crops or took livestock was accepted almost everywhere. The relation between ideal and practice in this field is a long negotiation, not a story of a lost conservationist golden age (Alsdorf 2010).

docs.title: 16.6 Hunting and Gathering Peoples
docs.text:
Alongside the royal hunt there was the hunting of those for whom it was a livelihood. Many communities of forest and hill — among them the Chenchus of the Nallamala hills, the Bhils and Gonds of central India, the Santals of the Chotanagpur plateau and the Irulas of Tamil Nadu — lived wholly or partly by hunting, trapping and gathering. Specialist hunting and trapping castes, such as the Pārdhīs of western and central India and the Baheliyas of the north, served villages and courts as catchers of birds and animals (Chapter 17). The Sanskrit texts rank the hunter (vyādha, lubdhaka) low, and under colonial rule many such groups were classified as “criminal tribes” under the Act of 1871.

Royal and colonial hunters depended on their knowledge of tracks, calls and seasons: the trackers, beaters and trappers of the shikār, the capturers of elephants and cheetahs, and the informants of colonial naturalists came mostly from these communities and were rarely named (Rangarajan 2001). Some communal hunts survive in modified form, such as the annual ritual hunts (sendra) of the Santals, now contested by forest officials. In the 1970s the Irulas, traditional catchers of snakes and rats, formed a snake catchers’ cooperative that extracts venom for the manufacture of antivenom. Forest peoples also worship the animals they live among, as with tiger deities such as Vāghobā in Maharashtra, or seek protection from them, as from the Sundarbans goddess Bonbibi, invoked by Hindu and Muslim honey-gatherers and fishers against the tiger. These traditions are treated more fully in Volume 23 (Jana–Jāti).

docs.title: 16.7.1 The Ring Hunt and the Royal Chase
docs.text:
The Turkish and Mongol traditions brought by the Delhi Sultans and the Mughals placed the hunt at the centre of royal life. The historian Baranī presents the long hunting expeditions of Sultan Balban (r. 1266–1287) as exercises that kept his cavalry in readiness, much as the Arthaśāstra had treated hunting as training. The most spectacular form of the Central Asian hunt was the qamargha, a ring hunt in which thousands of beaters, sometimes whole armies, gradually closed a circle many miles across, driving the game into an ever smaller space where the ruler and his nobles killed it. Abū’l-Faẓl records that in 1578 Akbar, during a great qamargha near Bhera in the Punjab, was overcome by a spiritual experience and ordered the hunt stopped and the trapped animals released — an episode he presents as a sign of the emperor’s spiritual elevation. The Āʾīn-i Akbarī justifies Akbar’s hunting as more than pleasure, an occasion for learning about the condition of the country and its people, and describes a variety of methods used at court, among them hunting with trained cheetahs and with tame decoy antelopes (Abū’l-Faẓl 1873).

Bābur, who came to India from Kabul in 1526, recorded the animals of his new country with a naturalist’s curiosity, among them the rhinoceros, which he hunted in the jungles near Peshawar — evidence of how far west the species still ranged in the early sixteenth century (Thackston 1996). His great-grandson Jahāngīr (r. 1605–1627) was the most passionate hunter of the dynasty and the most careful recorder of animals. His memoirs note the game he and his household killed, with tallies broken down by species; record with pride that the empress Nūr Jahān shot tigers from an elephant’s howdah; and contain detailed observations of animal behaviour and of rare animals brought to the court (Thackston 1999). Near Lahore, at Sheikhupura, he built a tower over the grave of a favourite antelope, Mansraj, and forbade the hunting of deer in the area; the Hiran Minar still stands. Mughal painting is a major source for the appearance of wild animals in the period (Chapter 17).

Mughal and later princely courts also kept menageries of local and exotic animals, a tradition continued by the public zoological gardens of the nineteenth century, such as that at Alipore in Calcutta (1876).

docs.title: 16.7.2 The Cheetah
docs.text:
The cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus) once ranged across the open plains and scrublands of northern, western and central India and the Deccan, where it hunted blackbuck and gazelle. Its history in India has been reconstructed by Divyabhanusinh (1995). Trained cheetahs were used for coursing antelope from before the Mughal period, and the practice reached its height at the Mughal court. The animal, hooded, was carried on a cart or on horseback close to a herd of blackbuck, unhooded and released for a short, explosive chase; when it brought down its prey it was rewarded with a share of the meat. Akbar kept very large numbers of cheetahs, ranked in grades with their own keepers, and the Āʾīn-i Akbarī describes their management in detail (Abū’l-Faẓl 1873). Jahāngīr records as a remarkable event the birth of a litter of cheetah cubs in captivity in his own establishment, observing that this had not happened before even though his father had kept so many (Thackston 1999).

That remark points to the heart of the problem. As with the elephant (Chapter 15), coursing cheetahs were not bred but captured from the wild, generally as adults that had already learned to hunt, so that every hunting establishment was a continuous drain on the wild population. Divyabhanusinh argues that this long-standing capture, combined with the shrinking of the grasslands and of the blackbuck herds on which the cheetah depended and with the bounties paid on it as a predator in colonial times, drove it to extinction. By the early twentieth century Indian princes who wanted to continue coursing had to import cheetahs from Africa. The last reliable records of wild cheetahs in India date from the late 1940s — a widely reproduced photograph shows three young cheetahs shot by the Maharaja of Koriya in 1947 — and the species was declared extinct in India in 1952. The Asiatic cheetah now survives only in Iran, in very small numbers (Divyabhanusinh 1995).

docs.title: 16.8 Colonial Shikār and the War on “Vermin”
docs.text:
British rule transformed the scale and meaning of hunting (Rangarajan 2001). The shikār — the hunting of tigers from elephant back or from platforms (machān) over a tethered bait, with lines of beaters driving the animal towards the guns — became a central ritual of colonial and princely power. Viceroys, governors and visiting royalty were entertained with great tiger shoots, such as the one held for King George V in the Nepal Terai in 1911; British officers hunted wild boar on horseback with spears (“pig-sticking”) as a test of nerve and horsemanship, contested in competitions such as the Kadir Cup near Meerut; and Indian princes competed in the size of their tiger tallies, some of which ran into hundreds.

Alongside the sport went a systematic campaign of extermination. From the 1870s the colonial government paid rewards for killing tigers, leopards, wolves, bears, wild dogs and other animals classed as “vermin” or “dangerous animals”. Officials justified the bounties as protection for human life and livestock — wolves, tigers and leopards did kill large numbers of people and animals in some districts — and as a means of extending and securing cultivation. Mahesh Rangarajan’s study of the bounty records shows that tens of thousands of tigers and well over a hundred thousand leopards and wolves were killed for reward in the half-century after 1875 (Rangarajan 2001); his study of the Central Provinces traces how the campaign against “dangerous” animals was tied to the colonial drive to extend settled cultivation into forest country (Rangarajan 1996). At the same time, the Arms Act of 1878 restricted the ownership of guns by Indians, and some historians have argued that the combination of disarmed villagers and protected game reserves left cultivators more exposed to crop damage in some areas.

The consequences can be traced species by species. The Asiatic lion, once found across much of north-western, northern and central India, was shot out of nearly all its range during the nineteenth century, surviving only in the Gir forest of Saurashtra. The Indian rhinoceros, which Bābur had still found near Peshawar, had by the late nineteenth century vanished from the Indus basin and most of the Ganga plain, surviving in the floodplains of the Brahmaputra, north Bengal and the Nepal Terai. The cheetah disappeared. The swamp deer (barasiṅghā), the wild buffalo, the gaur and the blackbuck lost much of their range to cultivation, drainage and guns. Clearance for cultivation, plantations and railways probably did more lasting damage than hunting, but the two worked together.

Colonial law began to protect some animals while their numbers were falling. The Elephants’ Preservation Act of 1879 restricted the killing of wild elephants — valuable to the state as working animals, much as they had been to the kings of the Arthaśāstra — and the Wild Birds and Animals Protection Act of 1912 provided for closed seasons and protection of specified species. Forest departments regulated hunting through licences and game rules in reserved forests, which had the effect of reserving the animals for officials and sportsmen while excluding local hunters (Chapter 11, Section 11.9).

docs.title: 16.9 The Beginnings of Conservation
docs.text:
Modern wildlife conservation in India grew partly out of the hunting culture itself. The Bombay Natural History Society, founded in 1883, brought together hunters, naturalists and collectors; its Journal published notes from all over the subcontinent, and its Mammal Survey of India in the 1910s and 1920s documented the distribution of species. Many early conservationists were hunters alarmed at the decline of game.

Princely states created and protected some of the most important wildlife areas. The Nawabs of Junagadh protected the last lions of Gir from about the beginning of the twentieth century, restricting their shooting to rare, closely controlled occasions; a well-known story credits the Viceroy Lord Curzon, who declined an invitation to shoot a lion around 1900, with encouraging this policy. Princely hunting preserves became the cores of several later national parks: Travancore created a game sanctuary around the Periyar lake in 1934, and Jaipur’s preserve at Ranthambhore later became a tiger reserve. Such preserves often protected animals at the expense of neighbouring cultivators. In Assam, the Kaziranga area was declared a reserved forest in 1908, largely to protect the rhinoceros, and later became a game sanctuary; it became a national park in 1974 and a World Heritage Site in 1985.

In 1936 the United Provinces established India’s first national park in the sub-Himalayan forests of the Ramganga valley, named the Hailey National Park after the Governor, Sir Malcolm Hailey. Among those who helped to define its boundaries was Jim Corbett (1875–1955), born at Naini Tal, who had become famous for hunting man-eating tigers and leopards in Kumaon and Garhwal at the request of the government and the villagers who suffered from them. His books, beginning with Man-Eaters of Kumaon (1944), joined accounts of these hunts to a deep knowledge of the forest, and in later life he turned from shooting to photography and to warning of the tiger’s decline (Corbett 1944). After independence the park was renamed, first Ramganga and then, in the 1950s, Corbett National Park.

docs.title: 16.10.1 From the Board for Wildlife to Project Tiger
docs.text:
The Indian Board for Wild Life was constituted in 1952 to advise the central and state governments, and new sanctuaries and national parks were declared in the following decades, including the Gir sanctuary in 1965. But the 1950s and 1960s were a period of rapid decline. The clearing of forest and grassland for agriculture, the spread of firearms, the trade in skins and the opening of former princely preserves all reduced wildlife populations. The General Assembly of the International Union for Conservation of Nature, meeting in New Delhi in 1969, drew attention to the plight of the tiger; tiger hunting was banned in India in 1970.

The Wild Life (Protection) Act of 1972 provided for the first time a national legal framework. It prohibited the hunting of animals listed in its schedules, regulated trade in wild animals and their products, and set out procedures for declaring sanctuaries and national parks. Later amendments tightened it and, in 2002, created conservation and community reserves (Chapter 11). India joined the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) in 1976. In the early 1970s the tiger replaced the lion as India’s national animal.

Project Tiger was launched on 1 April 1973, with nine tiger reserves — among them Corbett, Kanha, Manas, Ranthambhore, Similipal and the Sundarbans — under the direction of Kailash Sankhala, with the strong personal support of the Prime Minister, Indira Gandhi. A count in 1972 had put the number of tigers in India at fewer than two thousand. The project’s model was a core area free of human use within a buffer zone of regulated use. The pugmark census of its early decades was shown by the ecologist K. Ullas Karanth and others to be unreliable, and was replaced by camera trapping and statistical sampling. In 2005 it emerged that the Sariska Tiger Reserve in Rajasthan had lost all its tigers to poachers, a shock that led to the report of a Tiger Task Force and to the creation of the National Tiger Conservation Authority in 2006. The official all-India estimates since 2018, based on camera trapping, have put the number of tigers at around three thousand or more; the figures have been welcomed as evidence of recovery and also questioned on methodological grounds.

Project Elephant followed in 1992 (Chapter 15, Section 15.8). The campaign against a hydroelectric dam in Kerala’s Silent Valley, in which the lion-tailed macaque became a symbol, ended with the declaration of a national park there in 1984.

docs.title: 16.10.2 The Lions of Gir and the Question of Translocation
docs.text:
The Asiatic lion (Panthera leo leo, formerly P. l. persica) has recovered under protection from a very small population in the early twentieth century to several hundred animals, according to the censuses of the Gujarat Forest Department, and lions now range well beyond the Gir protected area into the farmland and coasts of Saurashtra. Recovery has brought conflict over livestock and the resettlement of many families of the Maldhārīs, pastoralists who lived with their buffaloes and cattle in settlements inside Gir, from the 1970s onwards.

Because the whole wild population lives in one region, conservation biologists have long argued that a second population should be established elsewhere, as an insurance against epidemic disease or natural disaster; an outbreak of canine distemper virus that killed a number of Gir lions in 2018 lent weight to the argument. From the 1990s the Kuno–Palpur sanctuary in Madhya Pradesh was prepared as a second home for the lion, and villages were relocated out of it. The Gujarat government, which regarded the lion as a symbol of the state, resisted the transfer. In 2013 the Supreme Court ordered that lions be translocated to Kuno, but the order was not carried out.

Debate: The Cheetah at Kuno

On 17 September 2022 eight cheetahs brought from Namibia were released into enclosures in the Kuno National Park, Madhya Pradesh, followed in 2023 by twelve from South Africa, under a government plan to establish the species in India seventy years after its extinction. Supporters argue that the cheetah can serve as a flagship for India’s neglected grasslands and open forests and restores a lost member of the fauna. Critics, including several Indian and international biologists, have questioned whether Kuno and the proposed additional sites are large enough and hold enough prey for a free-ranging population; whether African cheetahs, a different subspecies from the extinct Asiatic animal, can be called a “reintroduction”; whether conflict with leopards, people and livestock outside the park can be managed; and whether the project diverted attention and resources from the translocation of lions to Kuno ordered by the Supreme Court. Several imported adults and cubs born in India died in the first years, which supporters attributed to the expected difficulties of any introduction and critics to flaws in design. The outcome remains uncertain.

docs.title: 16.11 Wild Animals and Farmers
docs.text:
For most Indian farmers the most important fact about wild animals is the damage they do. Crop raiding is as old as agriculture: the Tamil poems of the hill country already picture watchers guarding millet against elephants, boar and parrots, and the watch-platform (machān), the night fire, the drum and the sling remain familiar in the fields. Today the most serious crop raiders are elephants, wild pigs, nilgai (Boselaphus tragocamelus, the “blue bull”, which many villagers will not kill because its name associates it with the cow), several species of deer, and rhesus and bonnet macaques. Elephants, which raid paddy, sugarcane, banana and stored grain and can destroy houses, kill people in India every year and are themselves killed by electrocution, poisoning and trains; conflict with farmers is now one of the main obstacles to their conservation (Sukumar 2003). Livestock predation by lions in Saurashtra, tigers and leopards in central India and the Himalaya, wolves in the Deccan grasslands and snow leopards in the high mountains imposes heavy costs on herders, who are often among the poorest people in their regions.

Responses combine guarding, trenches, walls and electric fences, early-warning systems for elephants, and compensation schemes run by state forest departments, often criticised for low payments and long delays. Section 62 of the Wild Life (Protection) Act allows the central government to declare an animal vermin in a specified area for a specified period, and this power has been used in recent years at the request of states — in 2015–16, for example, by notifications of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change for wild pigs and nilgai in parts of Bihar and for rhesus macaques in parts of Himachal Pradesh — each time provoking controversy. Research by Vidya Athreya and colleagues in the sugarcane country of western Maharashtra showed that leopards live and breed in dense rural landscapes far from any forest, mostly unseen (Athreya et al. 2013), and that capturing “problem” leopards and releasing them elsewhere tended to increase attacks on people rather than reduce them (Athreya et al. 2011). Such findings have encouraged a shift from removal towards coexistence.

Some agricultural landscapes are themselves important habitats. The blackbuck, chinkara and nilgai of the north-western plains, the wolves and Indian foxes of the Deccan, and many birds live among fields and on the grazing commons that official classifications long labelled “wastelands”. Where communities such as the Bishnoi protect wild animals on religious grounds, blackbuck and chinkara graze close to the fields (Chapter 11, Section 11.8).

docs.title: 16.12 Conservation and Displacement
docs.text:
The protected-area model adopted in India, as in much of the world, rested on the idea that wildlife is best protected by removing people. Villages were relocated out of national parks and tiger reserves — from Kanha, Sariska, Kuno and many other areas — and the rights of those who remained to graze, collect forest produce or cultivate were curtailed. Pastoral groups such as the Maldhārīs of Gir and the Van Gujjars of the Rajaji area in the Uttarakhand foothills, and Adivasi communities in central and southern India, bore much of the cost. Relocation has sometimes been voluntary and fairly compensated, in other cases coercive and impoverishing (Rangarajan 2001; Gadgil and Guha 1992).

The Forest Rights Act of 2006 (Chapter 11, Section 11.11) recognised the rights of forest dwellers within protected areas and laid down that “critical wildlife habitats” could be made inviolate only through a defined process with the informed consent of the people affected. The relationship between that Act and the Wild Life (Protection) Act remains contested in courts and in practice.

Debate: Inviolate Areas or Shared Landscapes?

One school of conservationists, many of them field biologists working on large mammals, argues that wide-ranging, conflict-prone animals need large areas free of human use, as the tiger’s recovery in some reserves shows. Another, represented by ecologists and historians such as Madhav Gadgil and Mahesh Rangarajan and by advocates of forest rights, argues that exclusion has been unjust to forest dwellers, has made them hostile to conservation, and ignores the long coexistence of people and wildlife in Indian landscapes; they emphasise community-managed reserves, the knowledge of local people and the protection of wildlife outside parks (Gadgil and Guha 1992; Rangarajan 2001). Most participants accept both that some areas need strict protection and that conservation cannot succeed without the support of those who live with wild animals; the disagreement is about the balance.

These questions of the rights and knowledge of forest communities are treated more fully in Volume 23 (Jana–Jāti).

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Wild animals have been part of the Indian agrarian world since the hunters of the rock shelters and the seal-carvers of the Indus cities. Vedic and classical texts named many wild mammals, and Āyurveda classified them by habitat and manner of feeding. Hunting (mṛgayā) was both a royal art, praised as training in the Arthaśāstra and by Kālidāsa and elaborated in the Mānasollāsa, and a royal vice in Manu and the epics, while Aśoka, the Buddhists and the Jains made the renunciation of killing a moral ideal that coexisted with the hunt rather than replacing it. The Mughals raised cheetah coursing to its height; capture, the loss of grasslands and colonial bounties drove the cheetah to extinction in India by about 1950. Colonial shikār and the war on “vermin” devastated tigers, leopards and wolves, and the lion and rhinoceros survived only in refuges. Conservation grew from naturalists’ societies, princely preserves and the first national park (1936), and after independence the Wild Life (Protection) Act of 1972 and Project Tiger built a network of protected areas — at heavy cost to farmers living with crop raiders and predators and to forest dwellers displaced from parks.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Rangarajan (2001) is the best introduction to the history of wildlife in India, and Rangarajan (1996) studies forests, hunting and bounties in the Central Provinces in detail. For the cheetah see Divyabhanusinh (1995); for the Āyurvedic classification of animals and landscapes Zimmermann (1987); for Mughal hunting and natural history Thackston (1999); for elephants and human–elephant conflict Sukumar (2003); and for the ecological history of Indian land use Gadgil and Guha (1992).

docs.title: Chapter 17: Birds, Insects, Reptiles and Aquatic Life
17.1 Knowledge of Smaller and Wilder Creatures
docs.text: Beyond the cattle of the farm and the elephants and horses of the court lay a much larger world of animals that Indians observed, named, hunted, protected, used and wrote about: birds, insects, snakes and other reptiles, frogs, fishes, shellfish, turtles, crocodiles and river dolphins. Knowledge about them was rarely gathered into a single treatise. It is scattered across Vedic hymns, the Arthaśāstra and the edicts of Aśoka, medical and gemmological texts, the omen literature, court poetry and the memoirs of Mughal emperors — and, above all, it lived in the practice of fowlers, falconers, silk-rearers, lac-cultivators, honey-hunters and fisherfolk, most of whose knowledge was never written down. This chapter surveys these sources, separating, as far as possible, what was observed from what was conventional or mythical.

docs.title: 17.2 Birds in Vedic and Classical Literature
17.2.1 Vedic Birds
docs.text:
Birds appear in the Ṛgveda chiefly as images and messengers. The falcon or eagle (śyena) brings the soma from heaven (Ṛgveda 4.26–27); a pigeon (kapota) that has entered the house is treated as a messenger of Nirṛti, the goddess of destruction, in a hymn to avert its evil (10.165); pairs of ruddy shelducks (cakravāka) and geese (haṃsa) appear in similes (Jamison and Brereton 2014). In a famous riddle hymn two birds sit on one tree:

Ṛgveda 1.164.20

dvā suparṇā sayujā sakhāyā samānaṃ vṛkṣam pari ṣasvajāte tayor anyaḥ pippalaṃ svādv atty anaśnann anyo abhi cākaśīti “Two birds, companions joined together, embrace the same tree. One of them eats the sweet fig; the other, not eating, looks on.”

The verse, taken up again in the Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad (3.1.1), was read in later tradition as an image of the individual self and the witnessing self. Its value here is as a reminder that birds in Vedic poetry are usually symbols; the ornithological content is incidental. The Vedic haṃsa, for example, is often a solar or spiritual image rather than a particular species.

docs.title: 17.2.2 Poetic Conventions and Real Birds
docs.text: Classical Sanskrit poetry developed a repertoire of bird conventions (kavisamaya): the haṃsa that can separate milk from water; the pair of cakravākas condemned to spend each night apart and calling to each other across the river; the cātaka that drinks only raindrops falling from the clouds; the cakora that feeds on moonlight; the peacock (mayūra) that dances at the approach of rain clouds, declared India’s national bird in 1963; the kokila (koel) whose call announces spring. Some of these conventions rest on real observation. The haṃsa of the poets is most probably the bar-headed goose, a winter visitor that leaves the plains for Central Asia in spring — the “departure of the geese for Mānasa” of the poets. The ruddy shelduck does live in pairs and calls loudly at dusk. The pied cuckoo, often identified with the cātaka, arrives in northern India with the monsoon. Others — the milk-separating swan, the moon-drinking cakora — are poetic fancies. K. N. Dave’s Birds in Sanskrit Literature is the standard attempt to identify the birds named in the texts, and shows both how rich the vocabulary is and how uncertain many identifications remain (Dave 1985).

docs.title: 17.2.3 Protected Birds
docs.text: Lists of birds also appear in administrative and legal contexts. Aśoka’s fifth Pillar Edict (c. 242 BCE; Chapter 11) exempts from killing, among other creatures, parrots, mynas, ruddy shelducks, wild geese and pigeons (Singh 2008). The Arthaśāstra, in its chapter on the superintendent of slaughterhouses, likewise protects a list of birds and animals, including geese, cranes, ruddy shelducks, peacocks, parrots and mynas, mostly birds valued for their beauty, their song or their auspiciousness (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013). These are early examples of legal protection for named animals; their selection reflects royal, religious and aesthetic preferences rather than ecological criteria.

docs.title: 17.3 Omens, Hunting and Court Natural History
17.3.1 Bird Omens
docs.text: The interpretation of omens from the calls, flight and behaviour of birds and animals (śakuna) was an important branch of Indian divination. Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā devotes a group of chapters to it, describing how the direction, time and quality of a bird’s cry predict success or failure on a journey or undertaking (Bhat 1981); later handbooks of śakuna elaborated the system. The omen literature preserves a great many bird names and some acute observations of behaviour, but its purpose was divination, not natural history.

docs.title: 17.3.2 The Mṛgapakṣiśāstra
docs.text: Modern accounts often cite a Mṛgapakṣiśāstra (“Treatise on Beasts and Birds”) ascribed to a Jain author named Haṃsadeva and dated to the thirteenth century, which describes the appearance, habits and temperament of many animals and birds. The work is known only through a twentieth-century publication with an English version; its manuscript basis has not been properly described, and its date and authenticity are uncertain. Some scholars regard it as a late compilation. Until a critical study is available it should not be used as evidence for medieval Indian zoology.

docs.title: 17.3.3 Falconry and Fowling
docs.text: Hawking was a royal sport across the Persianate and Indian worlds. A Sanskrit treatise on falconry, the Śyainikaśāstra, edited and translated by Haraprasad Shastri (Shastri 1910), is ascribed to a king Rudradeva of Kumaon; it classifies hunting birds, describes their training and care and treats hunting as a royal pleasure with its own ethics. Falconry flourished at the courts of the Delhi Sultans and the Mughals, whose falconers (mīr-shikār) formed a specialised service. Fowling with nets, snares, decoys and lime was practised by specialist communities — the Pārdhī of western and central India, the Bahelia of the north and many others — whose knowledge of bird behaviour was intimate and largely unwritten, and who were stigmatised under colonial law as “criminal tribes”.

docs.title: 17.3.4 Jahāngīr and the Painters
docs.text: The Mughal emperor Jahāngīr (r. 1605–1627) recorded in his memoirs many careful observations of animals and birds: he noted, for example, the breeding behaviour of a pair of sarus cranes kept at court, including the sharing of incubation between male and female, and described birds and animals brought to him from distant lands (Thackston 1999). He had his painters, above all Ustād Manṣūr, record birds, animals and flowers with a precision unmatched in earlier Indian art. These paintings and notes are among the most valuable documents of pre-modern natural history in India.

docs.title: 17.4.1 Modern Ornithology
docs.text: Scientific ornithology in India took shape in the colonial period, notably through Allan Octavian Hume, who founded the journal Stray Feathers (1872), and through the Bombay Natural History Society, founded in 1883. Sálim Ali (1896–1987) made the study of Indian birds a field of Indian science; his Handbook of the Birds of India and Pakistan, written with S. Dillon Ripley, remains a standard reference (Ali and Ripley 1968). Ali and his successors drew extensively on the knowledge of local hunters, trappers and villagers, often without acknowledgement in print (Rangarajan 2001).

docs.title: 17.4.2 Birds and Agriculture
docs.text: Farmers have always had an ambivalent relationship with birds. Parrots (śuka) are listed among the six traditional agricultural calamities (īti) — excessive rain, drought, locusts, rats, parrots and the incursions of neighbouring kings — and bird-scaring from crop platforms was, and is, the work of children and the poor. At the same time birds such as owls, egrets, drongos and mynas eat rodents and insects in the fields. In recent decades India has witnessed one of the most rapid declines of any bird group recorded: the collapse of the populations of Gyps vultures, which once disposed of the carcasses of cattle across the subcontinent, caused by residues of the veterinary drug diclofenac in carcasses (Oaks et al. 2004). The drug was banned for veterinary use in India in 2006. The vulture collapse illustrates how closely wild birds were bound to the agrarian economy of cattle described in Chapter 13.

docs.title: 17.4.3 Village Heronries and Bird Refuges
docs.text: Some of India’s best-known bird sites owe their survival to villagers. At Kokkare Bellur in Karnataka, painted storks and spot-billed pelicans nest every year in the trees of the village itself, and the villagers have long tolerated and protected them, valuing the droppings that accumulate under the nesting trees as manure; the village name itself refers to the storks (Kannada kokkare). At Vedanthangal in Tamil Nadu, a tank whose trees support a large colony of waterbirds, the local cultivators protected the birds by custom, and the colonial government recognised their protection in the nineteenth century; the site later became a bird sanctuary. Such places show a practical bargain between farmers and birds, in which the manure from heronries enriched the fields and tank water downstream. Elsewhere the relationship was one of royal sport: the wetlands of Keoladeo at Bharatpur in Rajasthan were developed by the rulers of Bharatpur as a duck-shooting preserve, at which enormous bags were recorded in the colonial period, before becoming a national park in 1982 and a World Heritage Site. The sarus crane, the tallest flying bird, still nests in the wet fields and village ponds of the Gangetic plain and Gujarat, where it is widely regarded as a symbol of marital fidelity and left unharmed.

docs.title: 17.5.1 Silk
docs.text: The Sanskrit word for silk, kauśeya, derives from kośa, “cocoon”. The Arthaśāstra distinguishes kauśeya from cīnapaṭṭa, “Chinese cloth”, showing that both local and imported silks were known (Kangle 1965). India is unusual in having several native silk-producing moths. Besides the mulberry silkworm (Bombyx mori), domesticated in China and introduced to India, wild or semi-domesticated species yield tasar silk (Antheraea mylitta and related species, on trees such as Terminalia), eri silk (Samia ricini, reared on castor) and the golden muga silk of Assam (Antheraea assamensis). Microscopic study of fibres from Harappa and Chanhu-daro has shown that silk from wild Antheraea moths was being used in the Indus civilisation in the third millennium BCE (Good et al. 2009). Rearing tasar and eri has long been the work of tribal and peasant communities in central and north-eastern India. Mulberry sericulture expanded in Bengal in the Sultanate and Mughal periods and was promoted in Mysore by Tipu Sultan in the late eighteenth century. The textile side of the story belongs to Volume 17.

docs.title: 17.5.2 Lac
docs.text: Lac (lākṣā; Hindi lākh, whence English “lac” and ultimately “lacquer”) is the resinous secretion of the scale insect Kerria lacca, which encrusts the twigs of host trees such as palāśa (Butea monosperma), kusum (Schleichera oleosa) and ber (Ziziphus mauritiana). It yields both a red dye (the source of alaktaka, the red colour with which women decorated their feet) and the resin used for varnish, sealing, ornaments, bangles and, in modern times, shellac. A hymn of the Atharvaveda (5.5) is addressed to lākṣā as a healing substance for wounds (Whitney 1905), and the Mahābhārata’s “house of lac” (lākṣāgṛha), built to burn the Pāṇḍavas, shows that its flammability was well understood. Lac cultivation — inoculating host trees with brood lac and harvesting the encrusted twigs — is an old practice of the forest communities of present-day Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and West Bengal, and India remains the world’s leading producer.

docs.title: 17.5.3 Bees and Honey
docs.text: Honey (madhu) is prominent in Vedic ritual and imagery, and the medical texts distinguish several kinds of honey according to the insects that produce them: Suśruta lists eight (Bhishagratna 1907). Three species of honeybee are native to the subcontinent: the giant rock bee (Apis dorsata), which builds huge open combs on cliffs and tall trees; the Asian hive bee (Apis cerana), which nests in cavities and has long been kept in log, pot and wall hives in Kerala, the Himalaya and the North-East; and the dwarf bee (Apis florea); there are also stingless bees. Honey-hunting from rock-bee colonies is a specialised and dangerous skill of forest communities such as the Jēnu Kuruba (“honey Kuruba”) of Karnataka and the Kurumba of the Nilgiris, who combine climbing technique, smoke and ritual with detailed knowledge of the bees’ seasonal movements. Modern apiculture with movable-frame hives was introduced in the twentieth century, and the European honeybee (Apis mellifera) later still.

docs.title: 17.5.4 Pollinators
docs.text: The greatest service insects render to agriculture is pollination. Many Indian crops — mustard and other oilseeds, pulses such as pigeon pea, cucurbits, many fruit trees, and cardamom and coffee in the hills — depend wholly or partly on bees and other insects to set seed and fruit. Wild bees, flies, wasps, beetles, butterflies and moths, as well as the honeybees, do this work, and the hedgerows, field margins, trees and fallows of mixed farming landscapes sustain them. Farmers and beekeepers have long observed the connection between flowering crops and honey; the rock-bee colonies of the Western Ghats and the cardamom and coffee plantations below them are linked in this way. The texts of the vṛkṣāyurveda tradition, concerned with making trees flower and fruit (Chapter 4), do not describe pollination by insects, which was first understood in Europe in the eighteenth century. In modern India, as elsewhere, the intensive use of insecticides, the loss of uncultivated land and the simplification of cropping systems are causes of concern for pollinator populations, and the deliberate placing of hives in orchards and oilseed fields to improve pollination has become part of agricultural extension.

docs.title: 17.6 Insects in Medicine, Lore and the Fields
docs.text:
The anthill (valmīka) has a special place in Indian lore. The poet Vālmīki is said to have been so absorbed in austerity that an anthill grew over him; in south India anthills (termite mounds) are worshipped as the dwelling of snakes; and Varāhamihira’s chapter on finding underground water (dakārgala) uses anthills near particular trees as signs of water below (Bhat 1981) (see Chapter 8). Termite-mound earth is used in some regions as a soil amendment and in building.

Locusts (śalabha) appear among the agricultural calamities mentioned above, and swarms periodically devastated crops in north-western India; the colonial and modern states organised locust warning services. The medical texts classify stinging and biting insects (kīṭa) among venomous creatures and describe the effects of their bites, including those of mosquitoes (maśaka) (Bhishagratna 1907). These classifications are of real historical interest, but they do not amount to a theory of insect-borne disease; that mosquitoes transmit malaria was established by Ronald Ross, working in India, in 1897–1898.

docs.title: 17.7.1 Serpents in Religion
docs.text: No group of animals has a larger place in Indian religion than the snakes. Serpent beings (nāga) appear in the Vedic texts, in the epics — the Mahābhārata opens its narrative frame with Janamejaya’s great snake sacrifice — and in Buddhist and Jain art and story: the serpent king Mucalinda shelters the meditating Buddha with his hoods, and the twenty-third Jain tīrthaṅkara, Pārśvanātha, is shown beneath a canopy of snake hoods. Viṣṇu reclines on the cosmic serpent Śeṣa, and Śiva wears snakes as ornaments. In village religion snakes are worshipped above all as guardians of fertility, of water and of the household: in the month of Śrāvaṇa, at the height of the monsoon when snakes are driven from their holes, women offer milk and flowers at anthills and serpent images on Nāgapañcamī; in south India stones carved with entwined serpents (nāgakal) are set up beneath sacred trees, often by women seeking children; and in Kerala the serpent groves (sarpakkāvu) attached to households and temples are among the best-known sacred groves (Chapter 11). The association of snakes with anthills and termite mounds, noted above, is part of the same complex of belief.

docs.title: 17.7.2 Snake Charmers and the Law
docs.text: Snake charming was the hereditary occupation of several itinerant communities, among them the Kalbeliyā (Sapera) of Rajasthan, who caught snakes, displayed them to the music of the gourd pipe (pūṅgī or bīn), and sold amulets and remedies against snakebite. The Wildlife (Protection) Act of 1972, which protected Indian snakes and forbade keeping them, made the occupation illegal, and many such families lost their livelihood without any alternative being provided. The Kalbeliyā songs and dances, which developed from their performances, were inscribed on UNESCO’s list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2010. Their case illustrates a recurring tension in Indian conservation between protecting animals and protecting the communities whose way of life depended on them (Chapter 16).

docs.title: 17.7.3 Snakes in the Medical Texts
docs.text:
The medical texts give snakes careful attention because of the danger they pose. The Kalpasthāna of the Suśruta-saṃhitā, devoted to poisons, classifies venomous snakes into groups that are recognisable to a modern reader: the hooded snakes (darvīkara), corresponding broadly to the cobras; the snakes marked with circular patches (maṇḍalin), broadly the vipers; and the striped or banded snakes (rājimant), among which the kraits are usually placed; together with non-venomous snakes and hybrids (Bhishagratna 1907). It describes the signs of bites by each group, distinguishes the effects of their venoms by the language of the doṣas, and lays down first aid and treatment: the binding of the limb above the bite, incision and suction, cautery, and a great range of antidotes and incantations. Caraka’s chapter on poisons covers similar ground (Sharma 1981). The classification by external appearance reflects long observation, and the recognition that the bites of hooded snakes and of vipers produce different effects is accurate; the treatments, as far as they have been examined, are not effective, and some, such as incision and tight tourniquets, are now known to do harm.

Snakebite

Snakebite is a medical emergency. The only effective treatment for envenoming is antivenom, given in a hospital by trained staff, together with supportive care. The victim should be kept still and taken to hospital at once. Cutting, sucking or burning the wound, tight tourniquets, herbal applications, incantations and visits to traditional healers are ineffective and can cause harm or fatal delay. Nothing in this chapter describes a usable remedy.

docs.title: 17.7.4 Snakebite and Agriculture
docs.text:
Snakebite is, above all, an occupational hazard of farming. Four species — the spectacled cobra (Naja naja), the common krait (Bungarus caeruleus), Russell’s viper (Daboia russelii) and the saw-scaled viper (Echis carinatus), often called the “big four” — cause most serious bites in India. Most victims are farmers and agricultural labourers bitten in the fields during the monsoon and harvest seasons, or people bitten at night while sleeping on the floor of their homes, where kraits come in search of rodents. A nationally representative mortality study estimated that snakebite killed about 58,000 people a year in India on average between 2000 and 2019, mostly in rural areas and among the poor (Suraweera et al. 2020), which makes it one of the gravest health burdens of agricultural work in the country. Delay in reaching hospital, often caused by first resorting to traditional healers, is a major factor in these deaths. Polyvalent antivenom against the big four is produced in India from venom collected in large part by the Irula snake-catchers’ cooperative of Tamil Nadu (Chapter 16).

Snakes are also farmers’ allies. The Indian rat snake (Ptyas mucosa), which is not venomous, and many other snakes feed largely on rats and mice in fields and granaries, and their killing on sight removes one of the main natural checks on rodents — themselves one of the traditional calamities of agriculture.

docs.title: 17.7.5 Monitor Lizards, Turtles and Tortoises
docs.text: The Manusmṛti (5.18) lists the five-nailed animals that may be eaten: the porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard (godhā), the rhinoceros, the tortoise and the hare (Olivelle 2005). The monitor lizard was hunted for meat and for its skin, which was used for drum-heads and leather, and is still hunted illegally; the Bengal monitor and other Indian monitors are now protected. Tortoises and freshwater turtles were eaten in many regions and protected in others: several temple tanks keep sacred turtles, and the tortoise appears in myth as the kūrma incarnation of Viṣṇu. On the coast of Odisha, at Gahirmatha and the mouth of the Rushikulya river, olive ridley sea turtles come ashore in their thousands to nest together in mass arrivals (arribadas) that are among the largest in the world; their protection from fishing trawlers, in whose nets many drown, has been a long-standing concern of conservationists and a point of conflict with fishing communities.

docs.title: 17.7.6 Frogs
docs.text: The Ṛgveda contains a famous hymn to the frogs (7.103), in which the croaking of the frogs at the coming of the rains, after lying silent through the dry season, is compared to the chanting of brahmins at a year-long rite (Jamison and Brereton 2014); whether its tone is reverent, humorous or both has been debated. In the twentieth century Indian frogs became an export commodity: large bullfrogs were caught in paddy fields for the trade in frogs’ legs to Europe and the United States, until India banned the export in 1987, in part because the depletion of frogs was thought to increase insect pests in the rice fields. The episode is a small but clear example of the connection between the wildlife of the fields and the health of the crops.

docs.title: 17.8.1 Fish in Texts and Edicts
docs.text: Fish were a major source of food in much of India, particularly in Bengal, Odisha, Assam, the coasts and the river valleys, as well as being the subject of religious restrictions in others (Achaya 1994). The Arthaśāstra expects fishermen to pay dues to the state for the use of boats and waters, under the superintendent of shipping (Kangle 1965). Aśoka’s fifth pillar edict forbids the catching and sale of fish on certain days of the month and protects some kinds of fish altogether (Singh 2008). The Mānasollāsa of Someśvara III (1131) includes fishing among the pleasures of a king and names many kinds of fish, with the baits and methods appropriate to each (Shrigondekar 1925). Among the freshwater fishes most valued in the east were the carps — rohita (rohu, Labeo rohita) above all — and the hilsa (ilīśa); the rearing of carp in village ponds, stocked with fry collected from rivers in the monsoon, is an old practice of Bengal and neighbouring regions.

docs.title: 17.8.2 Inland Fisheries and Fish Culture
docs.text: Inland fisheries — in rivers, floodplain lakes, tanks, ponds and estuaries — were as important as sea fishing for most Indians who ate fish. Village tanks were commonly leased for fishing, and the right to fish them was often a source of income for temples and village bodies as well as a matter of dispute between communities. In Bengal and Assam, floodplain wetlands (bil, bhēṛī) were managed for fish, and in the twentieth century the wetlands east of Calcutta developed a remarkable system in which the city’s sewage is led into shallow ponds where it is purified by sunlight and algae while supporting large fish harvests, with vegetables grown on the embankments and rice downstream; the East Kolkata Wetlands were designated a wetland of international importance under the Ramsar Convention in 2002. In the coastal backwaters of Kerala and the khazan lands of Goa, fish and prawns are trapped in tidal fields between rice crops (Chapter 10). Since the 1970s, scientific carp culture, using induced breeding of the major Indian carps (rohu, catla and mrigal) developed by Indian fisheries scientists, has transformed inland aquaculture.

docs.title: 17.8.3 Lagoons, Migratory Fish and Temple Fish
docs.text:
Some of India’s most productive fisheries lie in coastal lagoons. The largest, Chilika in Odisha, is a brackish lagoon whose fish, prawns and crabs have long supported the fishing villages around its shores, which held customary rights to particular fishing grounds. From the 1980s and 1990s the spread of commercial prawn culture in the lagoon, backed by outside investors and landholders, brought bitter conflict with the traditional fishing communities, while the silting of the lagoon’s mouth threatened its ecology until a new channel to the sea was cut in 2000. The lagoon is also home to a small population of Irrawaddy dolphins.

The hilsa (Tenualosa ilisha), the most prized fish of Bengal, lives in the sea and the estuaries and migrates far up the rivers to spawn during the monsoon. Its runs once reached well up the Ganga and its tributaries; barrages and dams, among them the Farakka barrage on the Ganga, have blocked or reduced these migrations, and river catches upstream have declined. The mahseer (species of Tor), the great game fish of Himalayan and peninsular rivers, has suffered from dams, dynamite fishing and pollution. In several places, however, fish have long been protected by religious custom: at riverside temples in the Western Ghats — the stretch of the Tuṅgā at Śṛṅgeri is a well-known example — and at shrines in the Himalayan foothills, the fish in the temple waters are fed by pilgrims and may not be caught. Such temple pools have served, in effect, as refuges for mahseer and other fish whose populations have collapsed elsewhere, and conservationists have drawn attention to them as examples of the protective effect of sacred sites, comparable to the sacred groves of Chapter 11.

docs.title: 17.8.4 The Fish in Myth
docs.text: The oldest version of the Indian flood story, in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (1.8.1), tells how Manu rescued a small fish that grew and in return warned him of the coming flood and towed his boat to safety; in the Purāṇas the fish becomes the first incarnation (avatāra) of Viṣṇu. Modern suggestions that the sequence of avatāras encodes biological evolution are a reading imposed on the myth, not a meaning found in the texts.

docs.title: 17.8.5 Pearls, Conch and Coral
docs.text:
Pearls (muktā) were among India’s most famous products. The pearl banks of the Gulf of Mannar, between south India and Sri Lanka, were fished from antiquity: the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (1st century CE) mentions the pearl fishery near Korkai in the Pāṇḍya kingdom, and the Arthaśāstra lists the sources of pearls, beginning with the Tāmraparṇī river (Kangle 1965). The pearl-divers of this coast were mainly Paravar fishermen, most of whom became Catholic Christians in the 1530s under Portuguese influence. Gemmological texts — the Bṛhatsaṃhitā’s chapter on pearls, the Ratnaparīkṣā ascribed to Buddhabhaṭṭa, edited with other Sanskrit lapidaries by Finot (1896) — grade pearls by size, shape, lustre and colour with much practical knowledge, but also list mythical “sources” of pearls such as elephants’ heads, serpents, clouds and bamboo, alongside the oyster.

The sacred conch (śaṅkha, the shell of Turbinella pyrum) has been fished in the Gulf of Mannar and worked into bangles, ladles and trumpets since Harappan times (Kenoyer 1998); the conch-cutters of Bengal (śāṅkhārī) were a well-known craft caste. Coral (pravāla, vidruma), by contrast, was largely red Mediterranean coral imported through the Red Sea trade, though the reefs of the Gulf of Mannar, Lakshadweep and the Andaman Islands were well known to local fishermen.

docs.title: 17.8.6 River Dolphins, Crocodiles and Turtles
docs.text: The Ganges river dolphin (Platanista gangetica), an almost blind dolphin of the Ganga–Brahmaputra system, is probably the creature called śiśumāra or śuśuka in some Sanskrit texts, though the identification is not certain (śiśumāra also names a crocodile-like constellation). It was declared India’s national aquatic animal in 2009 and is endangered by dams, pollution and fishing nets. The gharial and the mugger crocodile were common in the rivers; the makara, the composite water-monster that serves as the mount of the river goddess Gaṅgā and decorates temple doorways, draws on them and on fishes, though it is a creature of art rather than natural history. Freshwater turtles and tortoises were eaten, protected in some temple tanks, and given cosmic meaning in the tortoise (kūrma) incarnation of Viṣṇu.

docs.title: 17.9 Fishing Communities and Their Knowledge
docs.text:
The real repository of Indian knowledge about the sea and rivers is the practice of the fishing communities: the Koḷī of the Konkan and Gujarat coasts, the Mukkuvar of Kerala and Kanyakumari, the Paravar and Paṭṭiṉavar of the Tamil coast, the Kaivarta and Jalia castes of Bengal and Odisha, the Mallāh and Nishād of the Ganga, and many others. Their knowledge covers the seasons and movements of fish shoals, the relation of catches to winds, currents, tides and the moon, the location of fishing grounds and submerged rocks, the construction of boats, nets and traps, and the reading of the sea’s colour and of birds working over shoals. On the Kerala coast fishermen exploited the chākara, the calm, fish-rich mud banks that form near the shore during the monsoon. Customary institutions regulated access to fishing grounds and settled disputes in many coastal villages (Agrawal 2001).

Most of these communities occupied a low place in caste hierarchies, and their knowledge was seldom recorded by the literate. Since the mid-twentieth century mechanised trawling, the motorisation of boats, coastal pollution and the decline of river fisheries have transformed their livelihoods; seasonal bans on trawling during the monsoon breeding season, adopted by coastal states from the late 1980s, owed much to the campaigns of traditional fishworkers. Fisheries and the maritime world are treated more fully in Volume 19.

docs.title: Summary
