docs.text: Indian knowledge of birds, insects and aquatic animals is spread across poetry, law, medicine, divination and court memoirs, and lived above all in the practice of specialist communities. Snakes, central to Indian religion and classified with real care in the medical texts’ chapters on poison, remain a grave hazard of agricultural work, for which antivenom, not traditional remedy, is the only effective treatment; frogs, monitor lizards and turtles have their own histories of use and protection. Vedic and classical poetry used birds mainly as symbols and developed conventions, some grounded in observation and some fanciful; Aśoka and the Arthaśāstra protected lists of birds and animals; the omen literature, falconry treatises and Jahāngīr’s memoirs and paintings record real observation; the Mṛgapakṣiśāstra is too uncertain to be relied upon. India’s native silk moths, its lac insect and its honeybees supported old industries in which tribal and forest communities were the experts. Fishes, pearls, conch and coral were important in diet, trade and ritual, and the knowledge of fisherfolk, though rarely written, was the most detailed of all.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Dave (1985) on birds in Sanskrit literature; Ali and Ripley (1968) for Indian birds; Good et al. (2009) on early silk; Thackston (1999) for Jahāngīr’s observations; Rangarajan (2001) for the history of wildlife in India.

docs.title: Chapter 18: Agrarian Society and Change: Caste, Land Grants, the Indo-Islamic World and Colonial Rule
18.1 Texts and Agrarian Society
docs.text: The treatises discussed in the earlier chapters of this volume — the Kṛṣi-Parāśara, the Vṛkṣāyurveda texts, the elephant and horse books — describe how fields, gardens and animals should be managed. They say much less about who did the work, on whose land, for whose benefit, and under what compulsion. Yet agricultural knowledge in India, as everywhere, was embedded in a social order: in rules about who might plough and who might own land, in the obligations of tenants and labourers, in revenue systems that decided how much of the harvest the cultivator kept, and in political changes that brought new crops, new irrigation devices and new markets. This chapter sketches that history from the early centuries CE to the mid-twentieth century. It does not attempt a complete agrarian history of South Asia, for which readers should turn to Ludden (1999), the two volumes of the Cambridge Economic History of India (Raychaudhuri and Habib 1982; Kumar 1983) and, for the Mughal period, Habib (1999). Its aim is to place the knowledge traditions of this volume within the society that produced and used them.

docs.title: 18.2 Who Worked the Land: Varṇa, Caste and Agricultural Labour
18.2.1 Agriculture in the Normative Texts
docs.text:
In the normative literature agriculture belongs, together with cattle-keeping and trade, to vārttā, the livelihood assigned to the vaiśya. The Arthaśāstra defines vārttā in exactly these terms and treats it as one of the four branches of knowledge a king must master (Kangle 1965; Olivelle 2013). In practice, already in the Mauryan and post-Mauryan periods much of the actual cultivation was in the hands of śūdras. The Arthaśāstra, in its chapter on settling the countryside, recommends founding villages consisting mostly of śūdra cultivators, and its crown farms under the superintendent of agriculture (sītādhyakṣa) were worked by slaves, hired labourers and convicts as well as by sharecroppers (Kangle 1965). Sharma (1980) traced how the śūdra, originally a servile category, came over the first millennium CE to be identified above all with the peasantry.

The Pali canon gives a complementary picture. Its gahapati, the landed householder, appears as a substantial farmer who employs dāsas (slaves) and kammakaras (hired workers) on his fields (Chakravarti 1987). The well-known story of the brahmin Kasibhāradvāja, who was supervising a ploughing with hundreds of ploughs when the Buddha came for alms, shows a large landholder directing the labour of others; the Buddha’s reply turns ploughing into a metaphor for spiritual practice (Sutta Nipāta 1.4, vv. 76–82; Section 2.10).

The Manusmṛti’s advice that brahmins and kṣatriyas should avoid the plough (Section 2.9) had lasting effects. In much of India it became a taboo against brahmins personally handling the plough. It did not prevent brahmins from holding land; it meant that brahmin and other high-caste landholders had their land ploughed by tenants and labourers of lower status. The prestige of not ploughing, and the stigma attached to manual labour in the fields, were an enduring part of the agrarian order.

docs.title: 18.2.2 Peasants, Labourers and Agrestic Servitude
docs.text:
From the early medieval period onwards, caste and agrarian position were closely linked, though never identical. In most regions a set of locally dominant cultivating castes — for example the Veḷḷāḷar of the Tamil country, the Reḍḍi and Kamma of Andhra, the Kuṇbī of Maharashtra, the Jāṭ of the north-west — held or controlled land, often alongside brahmin and temple holdings. Beneath them were tenants and labourers, many of whom belonged to castes that were treated as untouchable. In the wet-rice regions of the far south, the agricultural labour of the paddy fields was performed largely by groups such as the Pallar and Paṟaiyar in Tamil Nadu and the Pulayar and Cherumar in Kerala, who were held in hereditary agrestic servitude: they were attached to land and to masters, could be transferred with the land, and in Malabar were bought and sold. Colonial legislation (the Indian Slavery Act of 1843) withdrew legal recognition from slavery, but forms of bonded and attached labour persisted long afterwards.

Detailed studies of particular regions show how such relationships worked and changed. Breman (1974) studied the hāli system of south Gujarat, in which Dubla farm servants were bound to Anāvil brahmin landowners, and showed how a relationship described by landowners in the language of patronage became, under commercial pressure, one of exploitation without protection. Prakash (1990) examined the kamiyā labourers of south Bihar and the way colonial officials came to define them as “bonded” labour. In the north Indian village of Karimpur, William Wiser described the jajmānī system, in which service castes (carpenters, blacksmiths, potters, barbers, washermen, leather-workers and others) received shares of the harvest from landholding patrons in return for customary services (Wiser 1936). Wiser presented these exchanges as a stable reciprocity; later scholarship has emphasised the inequality and coercion within them.

The handling of dead cattle, of hides and of leather — indispensable to an agrarian economy that ran on bullocks and leather buckets — was assigned to castes such as the Cāmār and Mādiga and was a central marker of their exclusion. B. R. Ambedkar argued that the stigma attached to beef-eating and to the handling of dead cattle was a key element in the origin of untouchability (Ambedkar 1948); the history of cattle and caste is discussed further in Chapter 13. In irrigated regions, rights to water were also structured by caste: Mosse (2003) shows how the management of south Indian tanks encoded caste hierarchy in the allocation of water, the duties of tank servants and the honours of temple festivals (see Chapter 8).

docs.title: 18.2.3 Women’s Work and Women’s Knowledge
docs.text:
The agricultural treatises were written by men and address the male householder. Yet women’s labour has been central to Indian agriculture: in transplanting and weeding rice, in harvesting and threshing, in seed selection and storage, in the kitchen garden, in dairying and the care of animals, and in processing grain. Many of the work songs of the paddy fields are women’s songs. Much of the practical knowledge of seeds and of food processing discussed in Chapters 9 and 14 was carried by women. Their rights over land, however, were limited: under most customary and textual regimes women inherited land rarely, and only in the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries did Indian law begin to give daughters equal rights in agricultural property (the Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act of 2005 made daughters coparceners). Agarwal (1994) has argued that independent land rights for women are among the most important determinants of their welfare and status in rural South Asia.

Scholarly Note: Reading the Agricultural Texts Socially

When the Kṛṣi-Parāśara advises the farmer to inspect his cattle shed or to supervise the sowing, it addresses a householder who commands the labour of others. Its knowledge is real, but it is managerial knowledge. The knowledge of the ploughman, the transplanter and the herder — much of which never reached writing — has to be recovered from ethnography, oral tradition and the observations of outsiders. Both kinds of knowledge belong in a history of Indian agriculture.

docs.title: 18.3 Land Grants and Agrarian Expansion, c. 300–1200 CE
docs.text:
The most abundant documents of Indian agrarian history for the first millennium and a half CE are inscriptions recording grants of land, mostly on copper plates. Kings and local rulers granted villages or plots to brahmins (brahmadeya, agrahāra), to temples (devadāna) and to Buddhist and Jain monasteries, often with rights to the revenue and sometimes with exemption from the entry of royal officials. The grants specify boundaries — trees, tanks, streams, anthills, fields of named cultivators — and so preserve a precise if fragmentary picture of the rural landscape (Singh 2008).

Historians have interpreted the spread of land grants in different ways. One influential view, associated with R. S. Sharma and with D. D. Kosambi’s earlier work, saw in them the fragmentation of royal authority and the subjection of the peasantry (“Indian feudalism”); others have stressed instead the integration of new regions and peoples into state society, the extension of cultivation into forest and frontier land, and the role of brahmin settlements and temples in agricultural colonisation (Kosambi 1956; Singh 2008). What is not in doubt is that this period saw a great expansion of settled, plough-based and especially rice-based agriculture — in Bengal and Odisha, in the Deccan, and in the river deltas of the south — often at the expense of forest and of forest peoples, many of whom were absorbed as peasant castes.

In the Tamil country, the inscriptions of the Pallava and Cōḻa periods show villages governed by assemblies: the ūr of non-brahmin landholders and the sabhā of brahmin settlements, grouped into localities (nāṭu). The famous inscriptions of Uttaramērūr (10th century) set out rules for the committees of a brahmin village assembly, including one for the tank. Temples were great landholders and creditors, financing irrigation and receiving produce (Singh 2008). In the Vijayanagara period (14th–16th centuries), as Morrison (1995) has shown for the region around the capital, the state, temples and local elites invested in reservoirs, canals and terraced fields, intensifying agriculture in a semi-arid landscape.

docs.title: 18.4 Agriculture under the Delhi Sultanate
docs.text:
The establishment of the Delhi Sultanate in the early thirteenth century brought northern India into close connection with the Persianate world of Central and West Asia. Its agrarian significance lay in three areas: revenue, irrigation and technology (Raychaudhuri and Habib 1982; Habib 2008).

The Sultanate assigned the revenue of territories (iqṭāʿ) to military commanders in return for service. ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn Khaljī (r. 1296–1316), according to the historian Baranī, demanded half of the produce as land revenue in the Doab around Delhi, assessed by measurement, and sought to reduce the share taken by village intermediaries. Muḥammad bin Tughluq (r. 1325–1351) raised the revenue demand in the Doab, with disastrous results in a period of drought, and later attempted to extend cultivation through a special department and state loans. Fīrūz Shāh Tughluq (r. 1351–1388) built canals from the Yamuna and the Sutlej and laid out gardens around Delhi (Section 8.11).

The period also saw the spread of new techniques and products, above all the geared “Persian wheel”, whose right-angled gearing let animals drive the older pot-wheel efficiently (Section 8.9; (Habib 2008)). Sericulture expanded, especially in Bengal; sugar refining and the distillation of spirits developed; and new fruits and garden plants arrived with the Persianate court culture.

docs.title: 18.5.1 Revenue, Measurement and the Crops of an Empire
docs.text:
The Mughal empire (1526–1857, effectively to the early eighteenth century as a major power) was above all an agrarian state. Its revenue system, as reformed under Akbar in 1580 by Rāja Ṭoḍar Mal and others, assessed the land revenue on the basis of measured land and of cash rates fixed for each crop, derived from averages of past yields and prices (the zabṭ or dahsāla system). The great administrative survey of the empire, the Āʾīn-i Akbarī of Abū’l-Faẓl (completed in the 1590s), records these crop rates for the provinces season by season, together with prices, wages and lists of fruits, vegetables and flowers (Abū’l-Faẓl 1873). Read as a source of agricultural history, it shows a diverse agriculture: many varieties of rice, wheat, barley and millets; pulses and oilseeds; cotton, sugarcane, indigo, opium poppy and hemp; vegetables and spices. It also shows what was not yet there: the crops of the Americas — maize, chillies, tobacco, groundnut — were absent or marginal at the end of the sixteenth century and spread in the seventeenth and later centuries (tobacco reached Akbar’s court only at the very end of his reign) (Habib 1999).

Irfan Habib’s study of the Mughal agrarian system remains the fundamental work (Habib 1999). It distinguishes the resident peasant (khud-kāsht) from the non-resident cultivator (pāhī-kāsht), describes the zamīndārs with hereditary rights over the land revenue of villages, and argues that the high revenue demand, levied largely in cash, pushed peasants towards cash crops and markets and, in bad years, into flight and revolt. The famine of 1630–1632 in Gujarat and the Deccan, described by Dutch and English observers and by Mughal chroniclers, showed how drought, war and the revenue demand could combine with terrible effect. Habib’s interpretation has been debated — some historians see more regional variation and more peasant prosperity — but the documentary picture of a commercialised agriculture embedded in a revenue state is generally accepted (Raychaudhuri and Habib 1982).

docs.title: 18.5.2 Cash Crops and Regional Specialisation
docs.text: By the seventeenth century several regions were known for specialised production for distant markets: indigo from Bayana near Agra and from Sarkhej near Ahmedabad; cotton and cotton textiles from Gujarat, the Coromandel coast and Bengal; raw silk from Bengal; sugar from Bengal and the Gangetic plain; pepper from Malabar. European trading companies bought these products in large quantities, and their records, together with those of Indian merchants, show how closely the peasant producer was tied to merchant credit (Raychaudhuri and Habib 1982). Trade and crafts are treated in Volumes 17 and 19.

docs.title: 18.5.3 The Village Order in the Deccan
docs.text: Records from the Deccan of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, under the Deccan sultanates and the Marathas, give an unusually clear picture of the internal organisation of the village. Hereditary rights and offices were called watan. The village headman (pāṭīl) and the accountant (kulkarṇī) held their offices and associated lands by inheritance, collected the revenue and represented the village to the state. Cultivators with permanent hereditary rights in their fields (mirāsdārs) were distinguished from tenants and outsiders who cultivated on temporary terms (upari). A group of village servants and artisans — traditionally reckoned as twelve, the bārā balutedār, including the carpenter, the blacksmith, the potter, the barber, the washerman, the leather-worker and the Mahār, who served as watchman, messenger and remover of dead cattle — received fixed shares of the harvest (balutā) from each cultivating household in return for their customary services. The balutā system is the Deccan counterpart of the north Indian jajmānī relations described above: it bound the village together in a web of reciprocal obligations, but on profoundly unequal terms, and it fixed the Mahār and other Dalit servants in the most degraded tasks. B. R. Ambedkar, himself born into a Mahār family, made the abolition of the Mahār’s hereditary watan service one of his early political causes in the 1920s and 1930s.

docs.title: 18.6 Gardens and Horticulture in the Indo-Islamic World
docs.text: Gardens were not new to India. Sanskrit literature knows the royal pleasure garden (udyāna, upavana) and its pavilions, ponds and flowering trees, and the arbori-horticultural chapters of the Bṛhatsaṃhitā, Surapāla and the Upavanavinoda were written for such gardens (Chapter 4). Someśvara’s Mānasollāsa (1131) includes garden pleasures among the enjoyments of a king (Shrigondekar 1925). But the Persianate garden brought by the Sultans and Mughals had a distinctive form and ideology, and it transformed the landscape of northern India (Moynihan 1979; Wescoat and Wolschke-Bulmahn 1996).

docs.title: 18.6.1 The Chahār Bāgh
docs.text:
The classic Persianate garden is the chahār bāgh, the “fourfold garden”: a walled rectangle divided into four by raised walkways and water channels meeting at a central pool or pavilion, often further subdivided. Running water, fountains and cascades were essential; so were shade trees, fruit trees and flowers planted in the sunken beds. The form carried associations with the gardens of paradise in Islamic tradition, whose four rivers it was sometimes understood to evoke, as well as with royal power over land and water (Moynihan 1979).

Bābur (r. 1526–1530), the founder of the Mughal dynasty, was a passionate maker of gardens. His memoirs, the Bāburnāma, complain that Hindustan lacked running water and walled gardens, and describe how he laid out gardens at Agra soon after his conquest, using water-wheels to raise water from the Yamuna (Thackston 1996). The same memoirs contain careful descriptions of the animals, birds, trees and fruits of India — the mango, the banana, the jackfruit, the rhinoceros, the parrots — written with a naturalist’s eye and a newcomer’s frankness. They are among the most important pre-modern descriptions of Indian natural history.

docs.title: 18.6.2 Mughal Gardens and the Science of Water
docs.text:
Under Bābur’s successors the garden became one of the chief arts of the empire. In Kashmir, the gardens of the Dal lake — the Shālīmār Bāgh begun under Jahāngīr and the Nishāt Bāgh built by his brother-in-law Āṣaf Khān — exploited the mountain slope to create terraces with cascades and channels fed by springs. In Lahore, Shāh Jahān’s Shālīmār garden (1640s) was supplied by a canal. The tomb gardens of Humāyūn in Delhi and of Mumtāz Maḥal (the Taj Mahal) in Agra applied the chahār bāgh plan on a monumental scale. Behind these works lay real hydraulic skill: the lifting of water by wheels, the regulation of channels, the construction of tanks and the management of gradients (Wescoat and Wolschke-Bulmahn 1996). Garden-making also stimulated horticulture — the cultivation and grafting of fruit trees, the introduction of Central Asian melons and grapes, and the planting of avenues and orchards. The pineapple, brought by the Portuguese from the Americas, was known at the Mughal court by Jahāngīr’s time.

Jahāngīr’s observations of plants and animals, and the natural-history painting of his court, are discussed in Chapters 16 and 17.

Two Garden Traditions

The Sanskrit Vṛkṣāyurveda tradition and the Persianate garden tradition met in India. The first emphasised the care, nourishment and treatment of individual trees and plants; the second, the geometry of the garden as a whole and the control of running water. Gardeners (mālī) and water engineers working for Mughal, Rajput and Deccani patrons drew on both, and the gardens of Rajput palaces such as Amber and Udaipur combine the two.

docs.title: 18.7 Persian Writing on Fields, Crops and Gardens
docs.text: From the thirteenth to the nineteenth century Persian was the language of government over much of India, and a large body of Persian writing bears on agriculture: revenue manuals and village accounts, the great survey of the Āʾīn-i Akbarī, memoirs and chronicles, regional histories and topographies, and a few manuals of agriculture and gardening. Little of it is agricultural instruction in the manner of the Kṛṣi-Parāśara or the Vṛkṣāyurveda texts. Its value lies mostly elsewhere: in administrative records that measured, counted and priced, and so preserved a picture of what was grown, where, and with what yield, more detailed than anything in the Sanskrit sources. Its limits are those of the revenue office. Like the Sanskrit treatises, it sees agriculture from above, and the knowledge of the cultivator appears in it only indirectly.

docs.title: 18.7.1 The Āʾīn-i Akbarī as an agricultural record
docs.text:
Akbar’s revenue reforms required uniform measures, and Abū’l-Faẓl’s account of them in the Āʾīn-i Akbarī is in effect a description of how land and harvests were to be known (Abū’l-Faẓl 1873; Habib 1999). Length was measured in the imperial yard (gaz-i Ilāhī); fields were measured with the surveyor’s jarīb, which, the Āʾīn records, was changed in the 1570s from a hempen rope, which shrank and stretched with the damp, to lengths of bamboo joined by iron rings; and the unit of area, the bīgha, was fixed at sixty by sixty gaz.

The Āʾīn classifies land not by soil but by the regularity of its cultivation. Polaj is land cultivated for every harvest and never left fallow; parautī is land left out of cultivation for a time so that it may recover its strength; chachar has lain fallow for three or four years; and banjar has been uncultivated for five years or more. Polaj, and parautī when it was cropped, paid the full revenue; chachar and banjar were assessed at reduced rates that rose year by year to the full rate, an arrangement meant to encourage the reclamation of waste. The scheme is a revenue classification, but it rests on the cultivator’s own distinction between land in continuous use and land resting under fallow (Chapter 10), and the word banjar is still the ordinary term for uncultivated land in the revenue records of northern India.

For land of the polaj class the Āʾīn gives, crop by crop, the yield per bīgha of good, middling and bad land. The average of the three was taken as the standard yield, and one-third of it as the state’s share. Converted into money at local prices, these shares produced the cash rates (dastūr) per bīgha for each crop in each assessment circle, and the ten-year averages of 1580 became the dahsāla rates (Section 18.5; the fiscal system is discussed in Volume 19). The crops covered run from wheat, barley, gram and other pulses, rice, sorghum and the millets, oilseeds and cotton to the high-value crops — sugarcane, indigo, opium poppy, betel leaf, melons and vegetables — each with its own rate. As a by-product of taxation, the Āʾīn thus preserves the most detailed crop and yield statistics of any pre-modern Indian state.

Modern historians have used these figures in different ways. Shireen Moosvi built from them a statistical reconstruction of the output, revenue and income of the empire around 1595 (Moosvi 1987), and Irfan Habib mapped the distribution of crops, manufactures and resources in his Atlas of the Mughal Empire (Habib 1982). Both Moosvi and Habib (1999) concluded, with due caution about the figures, that yields per unit of land in the late sixteenth century were not very different from those recorded around 1900, while the area under cultivation was considerably smaller. The Āʾīn’s accounts of the twelve provinces note the characteristic produce of each, from the rice of Bengal to the saffron fields of Kashmir (Section 10.6). Its chapters on the imperial household describe the fruit-house, with the melons, grapes and other fruits brought from Kabul, Badakhshan and Samarqand and those now grown in India by gardeners from Iran and Central Asia; they list the fruits of India and their prices; the flowers of India, with their colours and seasons; and the perfumery, whose rose and other scents are discussed in Chapter 5. Other chapters regulate the imperial stables of elephants, horses, camels, oxen and mules, with the daily rations of each class of animal (Chapter 15). Taken together they are a record of the plants and animals of a sixteenth-century court as precise, in its way, as Bābur’s memoirs.

docs.title: 18.7.2 Manuals of agriculture and gardening
docs.text:
Persian writing on agriculture belongs to the wider Islamicate tradition of books on filāḥa (Persian falāḥat), “husbandry”. In Arabic that tradition goes back to the tenth-century Nabataean Agriculture of Ibn Waḥshiyya and includes the agronomists of al-Andalus, among them Ibn al-ʿAwwām of Seville (late twelfth century). In Persian, the Ilkhanid vizier Rashīd al-Dīn (d. 1318) wrote a work on agriculture and arboriculture, the Āthār wa aḥyāʾ, that took account of plants from India and China. Closest to India in time and milieu is the Irshād al-zirāʿa (“Guide to agriculture”), written in Herat in 1515 by Qāsim b. Yūsuf Abū Naṣrī Haravī. It describes the cultivation of grains, vegetables, flowers and fruit trees around Herat, the seasons of the agricultural year, grafting and the layout of the walled garden, and it shows how closely the Timurid chahār bāgh was tied to practical horticulture (Subtelny 1997). This was the world in which Bābur grew up, and his successors brought gardeners from Iran and Central Asia to India.

Manuals were also written in India. The best known is a short Persian treatise on cultivation, the Nuskha dar fann-i falāḥat (“Treatise on the art of agriculture”), which deals with fruit trees, flowers and vegetables and is ascribed to Dārā Shukoh (1615–1659), the eldest son of Shāh Jahān. An English translation by Razia Akbar was published by the Asian Agri-History Foundation (Akbar 2000), which also published Surapāla and the Kṛṣi-Parāśara (Section 1.7); the text’s sources, date and authorship still await critical study. Persian versions of Indian works on animals — the Sālotar books on horses derived from the Śālihotra tradition (Chapter 15) and works on hawks and hunting — show the same movement of knowledge between Sanskrit and Persian that is better known in medicine and astronomy. Earlier still, al-Bīrūnī’s Arabic account of India (c. 1030) had drawn extensively on Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā, the source of so much Indian rain lore (Chapter 3).

docs.title: 18.7.3 Revenue papers and the language of the fields
docs.text:
Below the level of the empire, revenue was assessed and recorded in village and district papers kept in Persian and in the regional languages. The best-studied series come from the Kachhwāhā state of Amber (later Jaipur) in eastern Rajasthan, whose arhsaṭṭā records, in Rajasthani, give for many villages the area under each crop and the revenue due from it from the later seventeenth century. S. P. Gupta and others have used them to reconstruct cropping patterns, the stratification of the peasantry, and the spread of new crops, among them tobacco and maize, in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries (Gupta 1986). Comparable records survive from the Deccan in Marathi, written in the Modi script and full of Persian terms (Section 18.5).

The administrative vocabulary of these records has outlived the states that created it. Kharīf and rabī for the two cropping seasons (Section 9.12), zamīndār and kāshtkār for landholder and cultivator, khasra for the field register, jamabandī for the record of rights and rents, girdāwarī for the seasonal inspection of crops and jarīb for the measuring chain are all Persian or Arabic words that remain in everyday use in the land records of northern India, alongside Indic terms that the Āʾīn itself used, such as banjar for waste. Colonial land administration inherited this apparatus and the village accountants (paṭwārī) who kept it, and built its own agricultural statistics upon it (Section 19.8).

docs.title: 18.7.4 Observers and chroniclers
docs.text: Persian poets and historians also wrote about Indian agriculture as observers. Amīr Khusrau (1253–1325), in his long poem Nuh Sipihr (1318), praised India’s flowers and fruits above those of Persia and Central Asia. The Moroccan traveller Ibn Baṭṭūṭa, who served the Delhi Sultan Muḥammad bin Tughluq in the 1330s and 1340s, wrote in Arabic of the fertility of the land, which gave two harvests a year. Bābur’s memoirs survey the plants and animals of Hindustan with a newcomer’s frankness (Section 18.6), and Jahāngīr’s record his own observations as a naturalist (Chapters 16 and 17). Later topographical histories, such as Sujān Rāy Bhaṇḍārī’s Khulāṣat al-tawārīkh (1695), describe the provinces of the empire and their produce. These works are uneven as evidence, but together with the revenue records they make the Persian archive the richest single source for the agriculture of India between the fourteenth and the eighteenth centuries (Habib 1999).

docs.title: 18.8.1 New Revenue Settlements
docs.text:
British rule, beginning with the East India Company’s acquisition of the revenue administration (dīwānī) of Bengal in 1765, reorganised the relationship between the state, landholders and cultivators (Ludden 1999; Kumar 1983). Three main systems emerged:

  • The Permanent Settlement of Bengal, Bihar and Odisha (1793) fixed the revenue in perpetuity and recognised the zamīndārs as proprietors of the land, leaving cultivators as their tenants; tenant protection came only gradually through later tenancy legislation.

  • The Ryotwari settlements of Madras and Bombay (from the early nineteenth century, associated with Thomas Munro) assessed revenue directly on individual cultivators (ryots), at rates that were for long very high.

  • The Mahalwari settlements of the North-Western Provinces and the Punjab (from 1822) assessed revenue on village or estate communities.

All three turned land into a saleable commodity, and debt and sale of land to moneylenders became a recurring source of rural conflict, as in the Deccan riots of 1875.

docs.title: 18.8.2 Commercial Crops and Their Costs
docs.text: Colonial rule intensified the production of crops for export. Indigo was grown in Bengal and Bihar under a system that compelled peasants to cultivate it on terms dictated by European planters; the Indigo Revolt of 1859–1860 in Bengal, and Gandhi’s Champaran campaign of 1917 in Bihar, were responses to it. Opium was grown under a government monopoly in Bihar and around Benares for export to China. The American Civil War (1861–1865) created a cotton boom in the Deccan, followed by collapse. Jute in eastern Bengal, tea in Assam and the hills (worked by indentured labourers recruited from central and eastern India), coffee in the south and wheat for export from the newly irrigated Punjab were further examples (Kumar 1983; Ludden 1999).

docs.title: 18.8.3 Famine
docs.text: The late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries were punctuated by catastrophic famines: Bengal in 1770, the Great Famine of 1876–1878 in the south and west, and the famines of 1896–1897 and 1899–1900. Davis (2001) has argued that the late-Victorian famines resulted from the interaction of El Niño droughts with colonial policies that prioritised revenue, exports and market principles over relief; Roy (2011) gives more weight to the droughts themselves and to the weakness of transport and credit. After the Famine Commission of 1880, the government adopted Famine Codes that organised relief works and food distribution, and famine mortality declined — until the Bengal famine of 1943, in which between two and three million people died in most estimates. Amartya Sen’s analysis of that famine, which showed that it occurred without a catastrophic decline in food availability and was driven by the collapse of the purchasing power (“entitlements”) of rural labourers, artisans and fishermen, has become a classic of economic thought (Sen 1981). In every famine the landless — agricultural labourers, many of them Dalits, and village artisans — died in disproportionate numbers.

docs.title: 18.8.4 Colonial Agricultural Science and Indian Practice
docs.text: The colonial state at first regarded Indian agriculture as backward and in need of improvement. Its more perceptive observers, above all Voelcker (Section 7.5.2), found Indian cultivators skilled and placed the obstacles in shortages of manure, water, credit and fuel. The departments, research institutes and colleges that grew out of this concern, from the Famine Commission of 1880 to the high-yielding varieties of the 1960s, are the subject of Chapter 19; colonial botany, veterinary science and forestry are treated in Chapters 6, 13 and 11 (Arnold 2000).

docs.title: 18.8.5 Plantations and Indentured Labour
docs.text: A different agrarian world grew up on the plantations. Tea was planted in Assam from the late 1830s and later in Darjeeling, the Dooars and the Nilgiris; coffee in Kodagu, Mysore and the Nilgiris; and indigo, before its decline, in Bengal and Bihar. Plantations needed large, disciplined labour forces in thinly populated regions, and planters recruited them from the Adivasi and low-caste populations of Chotanagpur, the Santal Parganas and the Central Provinces, often through contractors and under penal contracts that made leaving the estate a criminal offence. Mortality on the journey and in the early years on the estates was very high. The plantation economy thus brought into being a new class of wage labourers, uprooted from their own agrarian communities, whose descendants still form a large part of the population of the tea districts (Kumar 1983; Ludden 1999).

docs.title: 18.8.6 Peasant Movements
docs.text:
Colonial agrarian policy provoked resistance from cultivators, often in alliance with, and sometimes against, the nationalist movement (Ludden 1999). Among the best-known episodes are:

  • the Indigo Revolt in Bengal (1859–1860), in which cultivators refused to grow indigo for European planters;

  • the Deccan riots of 1875, directed against moneylenders who had acquired peasants’ land, which led to the Deccan Agriculturists’ Relief Act of 1879;

  • the Champaran (1917) and Kheda (1918) campaigns led by Gandhi, against compulsory indigo cultivation in Bihar and against revenue collection after crop failure in Gujarat;

  • the Eka and Kisan Sabha movements of tenants in Awadh in the early 1920s, and the rebellion of Muslim Mappila cultivators in Malabar in 1921, in which agrarian grievances against landlords were entangled with religious conflict;

  • the Bardoli satyagraha of 1928 in Gujarat against an increase in land revenue;

  • the founding of the All India Kisan Sabha in 1936, which gave peasant organisation a national form;

  • the Tebhāgā movement of sharecroppers in Bengal (1946–1947), who demanded two-thirds of the crop instead of half, and the armed peasant uprising in Telangana (1946–1951) against the landlords of the Nizam’s state.

The colonial state also legislated to protect cultivators from losing land to moneylenders — the Punjab Land Alienation Act of 1900, for instance, restricted the transfer of land from “agricultural tribes” to others — in ways that were shaped as much by political calculation as by concern for the peasantry. These struggles placed land reform at the centre of the agenda of independent India.

docs.title: 18.9 After Independence
docs.text: The independent Indian state inherited a stagnant agriculture, deep inequality in land and a recent memory of famine. In the early 1950s most states passed laws abolishing zamīndārī intermediaries; tenancy reform and ceilings on landholding followed, with very uneven implementation. Vinoba Bhave’s Bhūdān (“land gift”) movement, begun in 1951 in Telangana, sought voluntary donations of land for the landless. Large irrigation projects, community development programmes and agricultural universities were established. In the mid-1960s, after two severe droughts and dependence on food imports, India adopted the package of high-yielding varieties, fertiliser and irrigation known as the Green Revolution. Its scientific and institutional origins are described in Chapter 19, and its achievements and costs in Chapter 20.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: The knowledge traditions of Indian agriculture were embedded in a society in which the right to own land, the duty to labour on it and the stigma of particular kinds of work were distributed by caste and gender. Normative texts assigned agriculture to the vaiśya but discouraged high castes from ploughing; much of the actual cultivation was done by śūdra peasants and by labourers held in various forms of servitude, many from castes treated as untouchable, and by women whose work was rarely recorded. Land grants of the first millennium CE document the expansion of settled agriculture. The Sultanate and Mughal states brought new revenue systems, canals, water-wheels, gardens and fruits, and left a Persian archive of measured fields and crop rates richer than any earlier record. Colonial rule turned land into a commodity, promoted export crops and presided over devastating famines.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Ludden (1999) is the best single survey. For the Mughal period see Habib (1999), Raychaudhuri and Habib (1982), Moosvi (1987) and Habib (1982), and for the Persian agricultural manuals Subtelny (1997); for the colonial period Kumar (1983); for caste and labour Sharma (1980), Breman (1974) and Prakash (1990); for women and land Agarwal (1994); for gardens Moynihan (1979) and Wescoat and Wolschke-Bulmahn (1996).

docs.title: Chapter 19: Science, Famine and the State: Agricultural Research in India, 1870–1970
19.1 From Revenue to Improvement
docs.text:
For most of Indian history the state took an interest in agriculture chiefly as the source of its revenue. The Arthaśāstra’s superintendent of agriculture ran crown farms and recorded rainfall; Sultanate and Mughal officials measured fields and fixed cash rates for each crop; the early East India Company settled the land revenue with zamīndārs and ryots (Chapters 3 and 18). Rulers also built canals and tanks, laid out gardens, kept studs and promoted particular crops, as Tipu Sultan promoted mulberry silk in Mysore. But there was no permanent institution whose business was to study crops, soils, pests and animals and to change the way cultivators worked.

Between about 1870 and 1970 that changed. A colonial government that had seen itself mainly as a collector of revenue came, under the pressure of famine, of imperial demand for raw materials and later of Indian political opinion, to accept the improvement of agriculture as one of its duties. It created departments of agriculture, research institutes and colleges, crop-breeding stations, a statistical service and, in 1929, a central council for agricultural research. After independence these institutions were enlarged and redirected, and in the mid-1960s they carried out the programme of high-yielding varieties that came to be called the Green Revolution.

This history belongs in a volume on Indian knowledge of fields, plants and animals for two reasons. The new institutions studied Indian crops, soils and practices, sometimes with real respect for the knowledge of cultivators, as in the work of Voelcker and Howard (Chapters 7 and 10), and often without it. And the people who worked in them were increasingly Indian, so that by the middle of the twentieth century there was a body of Indian agricultural science — in sugarcane breeding, plant pathology, cotton technology and the statistics of crop surveys — whose results were used well beyond India. Historians disagree about how far colonial agricultural science served the cultivator rather than the treasury and the export trade (Kumar 1995; Arnold 2000); both motives are visible in what follows.

Several related subjects are treated elsewhere: revenue settlements, commercial crops, plantations, famines and peasant movements in Chapter 18; colonial irrigation in Section 8.12; the veterinary services and cattle breeding in Sections 13.6 and 13.12; colonial forestry in Chapter 11; monsoon forecasting in Chapter 3; and the economic history of the famines in Volume 19 (Vāṇijya and Samudra). The consequences of the Green Revolution for land, water and farmers are assessed in Chapter 20; this chapter tells how it came about.

docs.title: 19.2 Before the Departments: Gardens and the Transfer of Plants
docs.text:
Before there were departments of agriculture, the East India Company’s interest in plants was expressed through botanical gardens and learned societies, whose purpose was as much commercial as scientific. The Calcutta garden at Sibpur, founded in 1787 on the proposal of the army officer Robert Kyd, was intended to grow plants of commercial value, such as spices and timber trees, and to acclimatise useful plants from elsewhere; its botanical work under William Roxburgh and his successors is described in Section 6.9. In 1820 the Agricultural and Horticultural Society of India was founded in Calcutta on the initiative of the Baptist missionary William Carey. It distributed seed of vegetables, fruit trees, cottons and sugarcanes from other parts of the world, held shows and published transactions, and drew in Indian landholders as well as Europeans. Smaller gardens, such as the one at Saharanpur taken over by the Company in 1817, served as trial grounds for the north.

The most consequential of these early ventures was tea. The botanist John Forbes Royle, superintendent at Saharanpur, was among those who argued that tea could be grown in the Himalaya, and in 1834 the Governor-General, William Bentinck, appointed a Tea Committee to pursue the idea. Tea plants growing wild in upper Assam, whose leaves the Singpho and other hill peoples already used, were brought to the Company’s attention in the 1820s and 1830s; after initial doubts the Assam plant was accepted as a form of the tea plant, and the Assam Company began commercial planting in 1839. Between 1848 and 1851 Robert Fortune, working for the Company, collected tea plants and seed in China and brought Chinese tea makers to the north-western Himalaya. In the event the Assam plant and its hybrids came to dominate the plantations of the Brahmaputra valley, while Chinese types did best in the cooler hills of Darjeeling. The plantation system that followed, with its indentured labour, is described in Section 18.8.

Tea was one of many transfers. Cinchona was brought from the Andes to the Nilgiris and Darjeeling in the 1860s (Section 12.5), and seeds of the Pará rubber tree, collected in Brazil in 1876 and raised at Kew, were distributed to the gardens of Ceylon, Malaya and India; rubber plantations spread in Travancore and Malabar in the early twentieth century. Historians of empire have described the botanical gardens as the nodes of an imperial network for moving useful plants around the world (Drayton 2000; Grove 1995). In India that network rested on local knowledge at many points: the hill peoples who knew the wild tea, the gardeners (mālī) who propagated the plants, and the Indian artists and informants on whom the botanists depended.

docs.title: 19.3 Famine and the Making of Agricultural Departments
docs.text:
The immediate origin of the colonial agricultural services was famine. The Orissa famine of 1866, in which perhaps a million people died, was followed by official inquiries that blamed, among other things, the government’s ignorance of the state of the crops and of food stocks. In 1871 Lord Mayo’s government created a Department of Revenue, Agriculture and Commerce. Its first secretary, Allan Octavian Hume — known today as a founder of the Indian National Congress and as an ornithologist (Chapter 17) — wanted it to collect reliable agricultural statistics, run experimental farms and prepare for famine. The department was cut back for reasons of economy and Hume was removed from it in 1879, the year he published his argument for a reformed agricultural administration (Hume 1879).

The decisive document was the report of the Famine Commission of 1880, presided over by Richard Strachey, which followed the great famine of 1876–1878 (Indian Famine Commission 1880). Its best-known recommendations concerned relief: that the state should accept a duty to save life; that the able-bodied should be employed on public works at a subsistence wage and the infirm relieved without work; and that each province should have a Famine Code setting out in advance how scarcity was to be recognised and relief organised. Provincial codes followed from 1883. But the commission also recommended that each province should have a department of agriculture, whose first task would be to collect accurate information about crops, prices and the condition of the people, and whose second would be to improve agriculture. A reconstituted Department of Revenue and Agriculture was set up in the Government of India in 1881, and provincial departments were organised in the following years.

For two decades these departments did little research. Their energy went into land records and statistics; a few experimental farms, such as those near Madras and at Kanpur, tested imported implements and crops, often with poor results (Section 7.15). The famines of 1896–1897 and 1899–1900 produced two further commissions, in 1898 under James Lyall and in 1901 under Antony MacDonnell, and an Irrigation Commission (1901–1903). The 1901 commission argued that relief should begin early, before people had sold their cattle and implements, and pressed for agricultural improvement, irrigation and rural credit. The Co-operative Credit Societies Act of 1904, which provided for village credit societies, was one response. In this way famine policy and agricultural policy grew up together: the same reports that organised relief works also called for research into crops and soils.

docs.title: 19.4 Voelcker, Pusa and the Imperial Scientists
docs.text:
Voelcker’s report of 1893, whose findings on Indian practice are described in Section 7.5.2, also recommended that the government employ trained scientists, and in 1892 an agricultural chemist was appointed to the Government of India.

Research on a larger scale came under Lord Curzon (Viceroy 1899–1905). An Inspector-General of Agriculture was appointed in 1901. A gift of £30,000 from the American philanthropist Henry Phipps, placed at Curzon’s disposal, was used to found an Agricultural Research Institute and College on a government estate at Pusa in north Bihar, which had earlier served as a stud farm (Chapter 15); the institute opened in 1905. The name comes from the village. The story, still sometimes repeated, that “Pusa” is an acronym of “Phipps of USA” is a later invention. The institute was renamed Imperial in 1919, was damaged in the Bihar earthquake of 1934 and moved to New Delhi in 1936, where it became, after independence, the Indian Agricultural Research Institute.

Pusa was organised around a small number of imperial specialists, each responsible for a discipline across the whole of India. Some of their work became standard. E. J. Butler, the Imperial Mycologist, surveyed the fungal diseases of Indian crops and summarised them in Fungi and Disease in Plants (1918), the first systematic account of plant diseases in India (Butler 1918). H. Maxwell-Lefroy, the Imperial Entomologist, published Indian Insect Life (1909), a manual of the insects of the plains, many of them crop pests (Maxwell-Lefroy and Howlett 1909). Albert Howard and Gabrielle Howard, the imperial economic botanists, surveyed the wheats of India and began the breeding work described below. In the provinces, colleges of agriculture were founded or reorganised in the years around 1905–1910 at Poona, Kanpur, Lyallpur, Nagpur, Coimbatore and Sabour, and an Indian Agricultural Service was created for the senior staff.

The senior posts were held almost entirely by Europeans until the 1920s, and research priorities reflected imperial interests: export crops such as cotton, jute, wheat and indigo received more attention than millets and pulses, and very little was done for the rain-fed farming of the poorest regions. The fate of indigo shows the limits of science in the service of a declining trade. After synthetic indigo came on the market in 1897, the Bihar planters and the government financed research at Pusa and on the plantations into better varieties and processing, in the hope of making natural indigo competitive; the effort brought a brief revival during the First World War, when German dyes were cut off, but could not save the industry (Kumar 2012). Yet the institutions also trained Indian scientists, built up collections and field stations, and produced knowledge that later Indian governments used. Kumar (1995) has argued that colonial science was shaped above all by the needs of empire; even on that view its Indian heirs inherited working institutions.

The colleges founded in the first decade of the century had a difficult start. Their students came mostly from literate, landholding and often high-caste families, and most sought posts in the agricultural and revenue departments rather than returning to farm; the Royal Commission of 1928 was among those who observed that agricultural education had become a route to government service. The cultivators themselves were reached, if at all, through demonstration plots, agricultural shows, leaflets in the regional languages and the advice of the department’s field staff. The distance between the college-trained officer and the cultivator whose knowledge Voelcker had praised was a recurring weakness of the colonial system, and the extension services of the 1950s and the agricultural universities of the 1960s (Section 19.12) were in part attempts to close it.

docs.title: 19.5 Breeding Better Crops
docs.text: Indian cultivators had always selected their seed (Section 9.14). What the research stations added was deliberate crossing between chosen parents, the testing of progeny in replicated field trials, and the multiplication and distribution of named varieties. Four crops illustrate the work and its results.

docs.title: 19.5.1 Wheat and its rusts
docs.text:
Albert and Gabrielle Howard began by classifying the wheats actually grown in India, which turned out to be mixtures of many types. From them they selected pure lines and made crosses, and their varieties Pusa 4 and Pusa 12, valued for yield and for grain quality, were widely grown in the United Provinces and the Punjab in the 1910s and 1920s. In the Punjab canal colonies the breeders at Lyallpur produced their own varieties, among which C 591, released in the 1930s, remained in cultivation for decades and was used as a parent in later breeding.

The great enemy of wheat was rust. Three rust fungi — black (stem), brown (leaf) and yellow (stripe) rust — caused heavy losses in some years. K. C. Mehta of Agra College showed, in studies carried out from the 1920s to the 1940s, that the rusts could not survive the hot summer of the plains, and that infection was renewed each season from spores that persisted on wheat and grasses in the hills — the Himalaya in the north and the Nilgiri and Palni hills in the south — and were carried down by the wind. His work explained the pattern of rust epidemics and pointed to remedies, among them breeding for resistance. At the Imperial (later Indian) Agricultural Research Institute, B. P. Pal bred rust-resistant wheats of the NP (“New Pusa”) series in the 1940s and 1950s.

docs.title: 19.5.2 Sugarcane at Coimbatore
docs.text:
The canes long grown in northern India were thin, hardy and low in sugar; the thick “noble” canes of the tropics (Saccharum officinarum) were rich in sugar but did poorly in the cold winters and dry summers of the north (Section 9.8). In 1912 the Government of India appointed the botanist C. A. Barber as sugarcane expert at Coimbatore, chosen because there, unlike in the north, sugarcane flowers and sets seed, so that crosses can be made. The north Indian canes he studied were later named Saccharum barberi in his honour. Barber and his successor T. S. Venkatraman crossed noble canes with the wild S. spontaneum and with Indian canes, and in 1918 released Co 205, the first commercially grown variety derived from a cross between the noble cane and S. spontaneum. It combined much of the sugar content of the one with the vigour and hardiness of the other.

The Coimbatore (“Co”) canes spread across northern India in the 1920s and 1930s and raised yields of cane and sugar substantially. Together with the tariff protection given to the industry by the Sugar Industry (Protection) Act of 1932, they made possible the rapid growth of modern sugar factories in the United Provinces and Bihar, which within a decade made India largely self-sufficient in factory-made sugar. Coimbatore varieties and their descendants were also taken up by breeders in other cane-growing countries. The station became the Sugarcane Breeding Institute. Its work is perhaps the clearest case of an Indian research institution of the colonial period whose results changed agriculture far beyond India.

Coimbatore was also where one of the first Indian women in plant science made her name. E. K. Janaki Ammal (1897–1984), who had taken a doctorate in botany at the University of Michigan, worked as a geneticist at the sugarcane station in the later 1930s on crosses between sugarcane and related grasses, and on the chromosome numbers of the canes. She went on to write, with C. D. Darlington, the Chromosome Atlas of Cultivated Plants (1945), and after independence was invited back to reorganise the Botanical Survey of India.

docs.title: 19.5.3 Cotton for the mills
docs.text:
India’s indigenous cottons (Gossypium arboreum and G. herbaceum) produced short-staple fibre that suited hand-spinning and the Indian mills but not the machinery of Lancashire, which wanted the longer staple of American upland cotton (G. hirsutum). From the 1840s the East India Company and later the Cotton Supply Association tried to introduce American cotton, hiring American planters for the purpose. Most attempts failed, but “Dharwar-American” cotton took hold in the southern Maratha country, and in the early twentieth century American-type varieties bred at Lyallpur, such as 4F and 289F, spread through the Punjab canal colonies, while “Cambodia” cotton, another upland type, was established in parts of Madras.

An Indian Cotton Committee reported in 1919, and in 1921 the Indian Central Cotton Committee was set up, financed from 1923 by a cess on cotton. It funded breeding stations in the main cotton tracts, a technological laboratory at Matunga in Bombay for testing the spinning quality of new varieties, and the Institute of Plant Industry at Indore (1924), where Albert Howard developed the Indore method of composting (Section 10.7). Indian breeders improved the indigenous cottons as well as the American ones. After independence their work led to Hybrid-4, released in Gujarat in 1970 by C. T. Patel and often described as the first commercial cotton hybrid in the world.

docs.title: 19.5.4 Rice
docs.text: Rice was India’s largest crop, but systematic research on it came later and was dispersed among the provinces. From the 1910s and 1920s Madras, Bengal, Bihar, the Central Provinces and other provinces set up paddy-breeding stations which selected pure lines from the immense number of local varieties (Section 9.3). Some of these selections, such as GEB 24 from Madras, became parents of many later varieties. The Japanese occupation of Burma in 1942, which cut off India’s imports of Burmese rice, and the Bengal famine of 1943 made rice research a national concern, and the Central Rice Research Institute was founded at Cuttack in 1946. In the 1950s it was the centre of an international indica–japonica hybridisation project sponsored by the Food and Agriculture Organization, whose hybrid material was distributed to the participating countries; the variety Mahsuri, selected from it in Malaysia, was later widely grown in eastern India.

docs.title: 19.5.5 Other crops and the commodity committees
docs.text:
The plantation industries financed their own research: the Indian Tea Association set up an experimental station at Tocklai in Assam in 1911, and a coffee experiment station was established at Balehonnur in Mysore in the 1920s. An Indian Lac Research Institute was founded at Namkum near Ranchi in 1925 to study the lac insect and its host trees (Section 17.5). After the desert-locust plagues of the late 1920s and early 1930s a Locust Warning Organisation was created in 1939 to watch the breeding grounds of the Thar and give warning of swarms — the modern successor of a calamity that the Sanskrit lists of īti had always included (Chapter 10).

The Indian Central Cotton Committee became the model for a series of “commodity committees”, each financed by a cess on its crop and each running its own research stations: for jute (1936), sugarcane, coconut, tobacco, oilseeds, arecanut and other crops in the 1940s. The Indian Central Jute Committee, for example, financed the breeding of jute at its own laboratories and paid for Mahalanobis’s sample surveys of the jute area (Section 19.8). Boards for the plantation crops followed after independence, among them a Rubber Research Institute at Kottayam in 1955. The commodity committees gave the growers and processors of particular crops a direct stake in research, but they also divided it crop by crop, and in 1965–1966 most were abolished and their institutes transferred to the reorganised Indian Council of Agricultural Research.

docs.title: 19.6.1 Research for rain-fed farming
docs.text: Most of India’s cultivated land has always depended on rain alone, and the research stations’ early concentration on irrigated and commercial crops left this majority of farmers with little to gain. The famines of the Deccan, which struck above all the black-soil country of uncertain rainfall, eventually prompted research into “dry farming”. In the 1930s, with support from the Imperial Council of Agricultural Research, dry-farming stations were set up in the Bombay Presidency at Sholapur and Bijapur and in other provinces. From the Bombay experiments N. V. Kanitkar and his colleagues developed what became known as the Bombay dry-farming method: bunding of fields to hold rain where it fell, shallow cultivation to conserve moisture, lower seed rates and wider spacing so that plants did not exhaust the stored water, and modest applications of farmyard manure. Much of this codified what Deccan cultivators already did, and its main legacy was the programmes of contour bunding undertaken by the Bombay government from the 1940s. After independence a Central Arid Zone Research Institute was founded at Jodhpur in 1959 to study the Thar, and a co-ordinated research project on dryland agriculture followed in 1970. But rain-fed farming remained the poor relation of agricultural research through the Green Revolution, a neglect that later critics, and the millet-growing regions themselves, have often pointed out (Chapter 20).

docs.title: 19.6.2 Quarantine, weeds and pests
docs.text:
The movement of plants around the empire also moved pests and weeds. The Destructive Insects and Pests Act of 1914 gave the government powers to regulate the import of plants and to prevent the spread of pests, and so began plant quarantine in India. Some of the worst problems were plants introduced as ornamentals or curiosities. Water hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes), a South American floating plant brought to Bengal as an ornamental in the late nineteenth century, spread through the rivers, tanks and rice fields of the delta so rapidly that the Bengal Water Hyacinth Act of 1936 required occupiers to destroy it on their land. Lantana, a South American shrub planted in gardens and hedges, invaded forests and pastures across the country, and the North American Parthenium weed, widely believed to have arrived with imported grain in the 1950s, became a serious weed of fields and wasteland and a cause of allergic illness.

Biological control had an early Indian chapter. Prickly pears (Opuntia), introduced from the Americas, had spread over large areas of dry land in southern India by the mid-nineteenth century. A cochineal insect (Dactylopius ceylonicus) that feeds on one of these species was deliberately transferred from northern to southern India in the 1860s and destroyed the infestations there; the episode is often cited as one of the first deliberate uses of an insect to control a weed. After the Second World War synthetic insecticides — DDT, BHC and their successors — came into use against crop pests as well as malarial mosquitoes, and their heavy and often unsafe use later became one of the main charges against the Green Revolution (Chapter 20).

docs.title: 19.7 Fish and Fertiliser
docs.text: Two other fields of applied research show the same pattern of colonial beginnings and post-independence expansion, and the same mixture of borrowing from and replacing local practice. (The parallel history of the veterinary and dairy institutes is told in Sections 13.6 and 13.12.2.)

docs.title: 19.7.1 Fisheries
docs.text:
Fisheries were the last of the rural industries to receive official attention. In Madras, Frederick Nicholson, a civil servant already known for his advocacy of co-operative credit, organised a fisheries bureau from 1907 that studied the sardine and mackerel fisheries of the west coast, encouraged the curing of fish in yards supplied with salt, and experimented with fish oil and fish manure. Bengal held an inquiry into its inland fisheries in the same decade. Systematic research began only at independence: a Central Inland Fisheries Research Station was set up at Barrackpore near Calcutta and a Central Marine Fisheries Research Station, both in 1947; the marine station moved in 1949 to Mandapam on the Palk Bay. From 1952 the Indo-Norwegian Project in Kerala introduced mechanised boats, ice plants and new nets to the fishing villages around Quilon, beginning the motorisation of Indian sea fishing and, with the export boom in prawns that followed in the 1960s, the conflicts between trawler owners and traditional fishers described in Section 17.9.

The most important single advance concerned the Indian major carps — rohu, catla and mrigal — which breed only in flooded rivers during the monsoon and will not spawn in still ponds. For generations the stocking of village ponds had depended on specialist spawn collectors, especially in Bengal, Bihar and Odisha, who knew the rivers, stretches and days on which the fish spawned, gathered the fertilised eggs and fry in fine cloth nets and sold them to pond owners. Their knowledge sustained pond culture but could not guarantee supply. In 1957 Hiralal Chaudhuri and K. H. Alikunhi, working at the inland fisheries station’s centre at Cuttack, induced carps to spawn in captivity by injecting them with extracts of fish pituitary glands (“hypophysation”). The method made hatcheries possible; Chinese carps were introduced from 1959; and from the 1970s “composite” culture of several Indian and Chinese carps that feed at different levels of the same pond multiplied the yield of inland aquaculture (Section 17.8). Here a scientific technique took over a task that had depended on the field knowledge of a small occupational community.

docs.title: 19.7.2 Manures and fertilisers
docs.text:
Indian cultivators had always manured their fields with dung, ash, oilcake, tank silt, sheep and goat penning, and green manures (Section 7.5). Voelcker’s report of 1893 identified the shortage of manure as one of the chief limits on Indian agriculture, blamed the burning of dung as fuel for want of firewood, and regretted the export of bones and oilcake that might have enriched Indian soils (Voelcker 1893). For the next half-century official advice concentrated on conserving and improving these organic manures — better storage of dung, composting, green manuring with sunn hemp and dhaiñcā — an emphasis that culminated in Howard’s Indore method (Section 10.7). Chemical fertilisers, chiefly imported ammonium sulphate, were used mainly on plantations and on high-value crops such as sugarcane.

Domestic production of nitrogen fertiliser began in the 1940s, at Alwaye in Travancore and, on a much larger scale, at Sindri in Bihar, which went into production in 1951. Consumption remained small until the high-yielding varieties, bred precisely to respond to heavy doses of nitrogen, made fertiliser the centre of the new package. Within two decades India had become one of the world’s largest users of chemical fertiliser, and the subsidies that kept it cheap became one of the most durable features of agricultural policy. The older advice on manures did not disappear; it re-emerged, with the problems of soil health discussed in Chapter 20, in the organic and natural-farming movements.

docs.title: 19.8 Counting Fields and Harvests
docs.text:
Every government that taxed land needed to know what was grown on it. The Mughal records of measured land and crop rates (Section 18.7) were succeeded by the colonial village papers: a register of fields maintained by the village accountant (paṭwārī), and seasonal crop inspections in which he recorded what was sown on each field. These gave reasonably good figures for the area under each crop. Yields were another matter. Officials estimated the condition of the standing crop in “annas” — sixteenths, as of the rupee — of a full or normal crop, according to provincial convention; these ānāvārī or “annewari” estimates were made by eye, were influenced by the wish of local officials to show (or to avoid showing) scarcity, and were widely recognised as unreliable. A modified form of the method has survived in some states’ procedures for declaring drought.

Indian statisticians made the crop survey into a science. P. C. Mahalanobis, who founded the Indian Statistical Institute in Calcutta in 1931, designed from 1937 a series of sample surveys of the area under jute in Bengal, in which the province was divided on the map into small cells, a random sample of cells was visited, and the share of jute in them was used to estimate the total. He extended the method to the yield of rice by “crop-cutting”: harvesting and weighing the grain from small plots chosen at random within randomly chosen fields. His long paper of 1944 in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society set out the theory and practice of these surveys and made them known internationally (Mahalanobis 1944).

At the Imperial Council of Agricultural Research, P. V. Sukhatme, its statistical adviser from 1940, developed crop-cutting surveys for wheat and rice that were adopted across India in the 1940s and 1950s and became the basis of official yield estimates (Sukhatme 1954). The two men disagreed, sometimes sharply, about method, including the size of the plots to be harvested: Sukhatme’s experiments suggested that very small plots tended to overstate yields, and the official surveys used larger ones. The National Sample Survey, begun in 1950, carried the method into social and economic statistics generally. The randomised and replicated field trial, following the methods of R. A. Fisher, became standard in Indian agricultural experiments in the same years. Out of the administrative need to know the size of the harvest came one of India’s most widely adopted contributions to modern statistics.

docs.title: 19.9 Indian Critics and Rural Reconstruction
docs.text:
From the late nineteenth century Indian writers offered their own diagnosis of agrarian poverty, and it differed from the official one. Where officials stressed the cultivator’s methods, his debts and the pressure of population, the early nationalist economists pointed to the state’s demands. Dadabhai Naoroji’s argument that India suffered a “drain” of wealth to Britain, set out in Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901), and Romesh Chunder Dutt’s Economic History of India (1902–1904) laid much of the blame for poverty and famine on high and inflexible land revenue and on the decline of Indian manufactures, which drove more people onto the land. Dutt pressed the case in open letters to Lord Curzon in 1900, and Curzon’s government replied in its Land Revenue Resolution of 1902, denying that the revenue assessment caused famine. The controversy set the terms of a long debate in which, as Chapter 18 shows, the distribution of land and the burden on the cultivator were never separable from questions of technique.

Others turned to practical work in the villages. At Sriniketan, near Santiniketan in Bengal, Rabindranath Tagore founded an Institute of Rural Reconstruction in 1922, with the English agronomist Leonard Elmhirst as its first director; it combined agricultural demonstration, co-operatives, crafts, health work and education, in the belief that villagers should be helped to help themselves rather than be improved from above. Gandhi’s constructive programme placed village industries, cattle care and the production of compost and manure within a vision of self-reliant villages, and the All India Village Industries Association (1934) took up oil pressing, paddy husking by hand and other rural crafts that machines were displacing (Chapter 14). In the princely state of Baroda and elsewhere, rulers and their ministers sponsored agricultural departments and co-operative societies. Indian manufacturers, such as Laxmanrao Kirloskar with his iron ploughs (Section 7.15), sought to supply improved implements that cultivators could afford. These efforts were small beside the scale of rural India, but they kept alive an alternative idea of improvement — one that began from the village and its own resources — which reappeared in the community development programme of the 1950s and, later, in the movements for low-input farming discussed in Chapter 20.

docs.title: 19.10 The Royal Commission on Agriculture and Rural Uplift
docs.text:
By the 1920s rural indebtedness and the low productivity of Indian agriculture had become public questions. Malcolm Darling’s The Punjab Peasant in Prosperity and Debt (1925) showed that even in the prosperous canal colonies most cultivators were in debt to moneylenders, and traced the debt to the insecurity of agriculture, the growth of land values as security and the costs of social obligations (Darling 1925). F. L. Brayne’s “rural uplift” campaign in Gurgaon district in the 1920s tried, with much publicity and limited lasting effect, to change village practice by exhortation: better seed, manure pits, ploughs, sanitation and thrift. Under the constitutional reforms of 1919 agriculture became a provincial subject administered by Indian ministers, so that agricultural policy was now partly in Indian hands.

The Royal Commission on Agriculture in India was appointed in 1926 under the chairmanship of the Marquess of Linlithgow, later Viceroy, and reported in 1928 (Royal Commission on Agriculture in India 1928). Its terms of reference expressly excluded the ownership of land, the rights of landlords and tenants and the assessment of land revenue. Within those limits it surveyed nearly everything else: research and education, demonstration, cattle and fodder (Section 13.12.2), irrigation, forests, marketing, credit, co-operation and rural health. Its most important institutional recommendation was a central body to promote and co-ordinate research. The Imperial Council of Agricultural Research was established in 1929 (it became the Indian Council of Agricultural Research after independence), funding schemes in the provinces and drawing together work that had been scattered. Following the commission’s emphasis on marketing, an Agricultural Marketing Adviser was appointed in 1935, and the Agricultural Produce (Grading and Marking) Act of 1937 introduced the “Agmark” grades that are still in use.

The exclusion of land questions from the commission’s remit was criticised then and since. Indian nationalists and later historians argued that the distribution of land, rent and the burden of revenue and debt were the main obstacles to agricultural improvement, and that a commission forbidden to discuss them could treat only symptoms (Ludden 1999). Within a year of its report the world depression of 1929–1933 roughly halved the prices of many crops and deepened the indebtedness Darling had described.

docs.title: 19.11 War, Famine and “Grow More Food”
docs.text: The Second World War brought food to the centre of policy. With Burmese rice cut off and the army’s demands rising, the government launched a “Grow More Food” campaign in 1942–1943 to persuade cultivators to shift land from cash crops to food grains and to supply seed, manure and help with minor irrigation. It came too late and was too small to prevent the Bengal famine of 1943, whose causes are discussed in Section 18.8 and in Volume 19. Wartime controls — procurement of grain, rationing in the cities and restrictions on movement between provinces — outlasted the war and shaped the food administration of independent India. Partition in 1947 then gave most of the canal-irrigated wheat and cotton land of the Punjab and Sind, and much of the jute land of eastern Bengal, to Pakistan, while India kept most of the population. The new state began life with a food deficit.

docs.title: 19.12 Planning for Food, 1947–1965
docs.text:
The first answer of independent India was extension rather than new technology. Benjamin Siegel has shown how food became a central question of Indian nationalism and planning in these years, as leaders argued over self-sufficiency, rationing, austerity and the dignity of a nation that depended on imported grain (Siegel 2018). A pilot project in Etawah district (from 1948), led by the American planner Albert Mayer, used village-level workers to bring improved seed, manure, implements and sanitation to cultivators. Its approach was generalised in the Community Development Programme, launched on 2 October 1952, and in the National Extension Service that followed in 1953, which sought to reach every village through block development officers and multi-purpose village-level workers. A Grow More Food Enquiry Committee (1952) had concluded that the wartime campaign failed because it treated food production as a narrow departmental matter rather than as part of the development of village life as a whole. Large dams and canals were built in the same years (Section 8.12), and the abolition of zamīndārī and tenancy reform were pursued with uneven success (Section 18.9).

Food production rose in the 1950s, mainly because more land was cultivated and irrigated, but not fast enough. From 1956 India imported large quantities of American wheat under the PL-480 programme (Chapter 20). In 1959 a team sponsored by the Ford Foundation, in its report India’s Food Crisis and Steps to Meet It, predicted a serious food gap by the mid-1960s and recommended concentrating fertiliser, credit, improved seed and extension in districts with assured water. The resulting Intensive Agricultural District Programme began in 1960–1961 in seven districts and was later extended.

The research system was rebuilt at the same time. Agricultural universities on the model of the American land-grant colleges, combining teaching, research and extension in one institution, were founded with help from American universities: the first at Pantnagar in Uttar Pradesh in 1960, followed by the Punjab Agricultural University at Ludhiana in 1962 and others in most states. “All-India co-ordinated” projects, in which stations across the country tested the same material under a common plan, began with maize in 1957; the first Indian maize hybrids were released in 1961, a hybrid sorghum (CSH-1) in 1964 and a hybrid pearl millet (HB-1) in 1965. The millet hybrids, built on a narrow genetic base, later suffered serious epidemics of downy mildew, an early warning of the risks of uniformity. A National Seeds Corporation was set up in 1963 to multiply and distribute certified seed, and the Indian Council of Agricultural Research was reorganised in 1965–1966 under B. P. Pal to take charge of the central research institutes.

docs.title: 19.13 The High-Yielding Varieties
docs.text:
The semi-dwarf wheats that transformed Indian agriculture had a long international pedigree. Dwarfing genes from the Japanese variety Norin 10 were brought to the United States after the Second World War, and crossed into the spring wheats of the programme led by Norman Borlaug in Mexico, supported by the Rockefeller Foundation and the Mexican government. The Mexican semi-dwarfs had short, stiff straw that did not fall over under heavy fertiliser, responded strongly to nitrogen and water, and were insensitive to day length, so that they could be grown far from Mexico.

At the Indian Agricultural Research Institute, M. S. Swaminathan sought out this material, and Borlaug visited India in March 1963. Small quantities of seed were tested in the winter of 1963–1964 and in national demonstrations on farmers’ fields in the following seasons. After the drought of 1965, the government, with C. Subramaniam as minister for food and agriculture, decided on a large-scale programme: about 250 tonnes of Mexican seed were imported in 1965 and some 18,000 tonnes of the varieties Lerma Rojo 64A and Sonora 64 in 1966. Indian breeders selected from the Mexican material amber-grained wheats closer to the taste of Indian consumers, released in 1967 as Kalyan Sona and Sonalika, which soon covered much of the irrigated wheat land of the north-west. India’s wheat harvest more than doubled between 1964–1965 and 1971–1972.

Rice followed more slowly. The semi-dwarf Taichung Native 1 from Taiwan and IR8, released by the International Rice Research Institute in the Philippines in 1966, gave high yields under irrigation and fertiliser, but were susceptible to pests and diseases in Indian conditions and their grain was not liked. An All-India Co-ordinated Rice Improvement Project, begun in 1965, produced Indian semi-dwarf varieties, beginning with Jaya in 1968, and the spread of high-yielding rice to the eastern and rain-fed rice regions took two more decades. The term “Green Revolution” itself was coined in 1968 by William Gaud of the United States Agency for International Development.

The new seeds were promoted as part of a package — fertiliser, pesticides, irrigation, credit, guaranteed prices through the Agricultural Prices Commission and procurement by the Food Corporation of India (both created in 1965) — whose long-term consequences are discussed in Chapter 20. Table 19.1 lists the principal institutional landmarks of the century described in this chapter.
